Uniform Title: Mantrakoṣa Author: Āśāditya Tripāṭhī Manuscript: NGMCP 5-470 Reel Number: A 169/8

Description: The *Mantrakoṣa*—“A Treasury of Mantras”—is, as its title suggests, a compendium of mantras along with matters concerning their recitation within the context of ritual practice. This late work was composed by a certain Āśāditya Tripāṭhī. He derives his material from various sources, such as the *Prapañcasāratantra*, which he occasionally cites by name. The text consists of sixteen chapters (*paricchedas*). At the beginning of each chapter, he announces the subject matter he intends to explain; this is first listed, followed by the titles of the chapters, which are as follows:
1) The Exposition of the Fruit of Worship.
2) Now, the definition of the materials for worship; 3) the description of the fruits of worship;
4) now, the modes of worship (*pūjopacāra*); the chapter on flowers;
now, incenses; the description of the materials for worship.
5) Now, initiation (*dīkṣā*). A concise exposition of initiation.

6) Now, the examination of the fitness of the teacher and the disciple. The union of mantras (*mantramelana*). 7) Now, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*). An exposition of the purification of the elements.
8) Now, the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
9) Now, the Sārasvata-mantras; the exposition of the Sārasvata-mantras.
10) Now, the Śrī-mantras; the exposition of the Āditya-mantra.
11) Now, the mantras of Gaṇapati; the exposition of the Gaṇapati mantras.
12) Now, the Śaiva mantras; the exposition of the Nṛsiṃha mantra.
13) Following the exposition of the mantras of the five shrines (pañcāyatana), various other mantras are now being stated.

Therein, first, the procedure for the Gāyatrī is written. (14) Now, the description of various mantras; the description of the Agneya weapon and other mantras. (15) Now, since the yantra is to be discussed, the technical definitions of the substances for the fire-oblation (homa) are written first. The description of the yantra.
16) Now, the mudrās employed at the beginning of the worship of the deities and other rites are written down.
Notes: Revision 0: December 17, 2013.
Country of Publication: India.
1a) Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Having prostrated before the Sun, Vighneśa, Śiva, Durgā, and Hari in succession,
I shall reveal the excellent mantras, along with their ancillaries, which have been well-guarded in secrecy.
The ritual applications have been learned by me from the scriptures through the grace of my teacher;
nevertheless, only the worship is here written down out of respect for the weight of the text.
Those mantras which were corrupted by the *Maṃtrakoṣa* in the twentieth section are now being written down here, preceded by their worship and other rituals along with their fruits.
In the first chapter, however, the fruit of worship is presented in sequence,
along with the specific details of liṅga-worship and an analysis of the substrates for the deity.
The fruit of the Śāligrāma and its examination and so forth [are treated] in the first;
in the second, however, are the materials for worship, the terminology, and the sequence of the ritual procedure.

The description of garments and other items, the definition of those authorized to speak on the ritual form, the characteristics of the vessel, the *arghya* offering, and likewise the bathing vessel and so forth.
If a worship is performed devoid of the requisite materials, one shares in what is undesirable;
however, by giving to a distinguished recipient, one shares in a distinguished fruit.
The merit arising from bathing with ghee and other substances, especially for the Sun and other deities,
as well as the materials for worship, are here described in brief.
In the third [chapter], the application of unguents is declared, as well as which flowers are acceptable and which are not,
along with the common flowers for all [deities] beginning with the Sun.
In the fourth [day], incense, lamps, and so forth, as well as garments and ornaments;
in the fifth, the initiation into the mantra; and in the sixth, [the rites] of both the teacher and the disciple.
1b) Furthermore,
the examination and unification of mantras according to the direct path;
and in the seventh [chapter], the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), both in detail and in brief.
In the eighth [chapter], the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa) according to the divisions beginning with Keśava;
in the ninth, the mantras of Sarasvatī; and in the tenth, the sequence of Śrī.
In the eleventh [chapter] are the mantras of the Sun; in the twelfth, those of the King of Physicians (Vaidyarājika);
in the thirteenth, those of Śiva; and in the fourteenth, those of Durgā.
The Vaiṣṇava mantras are in the fifteenth [chapter], while the Nārasiṃha mantras are in the sixteenth;
various other mantras are in the seventeenth, and certain others are in the eighteenth.
The nineteenth [chapter] concerns the yantras, and the twentieth concerns the mudrās and the rosary;
thus, in this sequential narration, there shall be salutation and the seeking of the hidden.
There is no means more accessible than the Treasury for crossing the ocean of mantras;
there is no means more accessible than mantra for crossing the ocean of existence.
Without one who knows the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), without a sacred site (*tīrtha*), without a gift (*dāna*), and without austerity (*tapas*, there can be no attainment);
for in the worship of the gods beginning with those of heaven, water, recitation (*japa*), and meditation (*dhyāna*) are more essential than flowers.
Heaven is to be achieved by great people through manifold exertions and wealth;
yet that very same heaven is achieved by people through worship using merely a mantra.
Therefore, in this terrible Kali age, men who are devoid of wealth and learning should perform the worship of the gods with faith.
Likewise, if one is unable to perform the worship of the deity even with flowers and other offerings,
then one accomplishes heaven and so forth through the recitation of mantras alone.
And so it has been said by Manu:
"A Brāhmaṇa is perfected by recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter."
One should act without pride and act with friendliness; such a person is called a Brāhmaṇa.
The mention of a "Brāhmaṇa" is merely illustrative; rather, wherever one has the authority [to perform a rite], one should mutter the mantra pertaining to that [rite]. It is said in the *Bharata*:
"Longevity, wealth, sons, cattle, knowledge, and great fame."
Indeed, a person reciting [this] attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

If laziness arises during the recitation, then the deity will certainly not grant a boon through meditation. Likewise, it is said that all sages attained supreme perfection through meditation. That meditation is of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and without attributes (nirguṇa). Those seeking liberation should practice the attribute-less; the one with attributes is as declared in the scriptures and purified by mantra.

This is to be performed by householders; these mantras are written here. In response to the doubt—how can the attainment of heaven and so forth be accomplished through mere worship with wild flowers and the like?—authoritative statements are recorded. This is because of the maxim: "No one, however dull-witted, acts without first having a purpose. And thus it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
But he who, with restrained senses and endowed with a spirit of devotion, constantly worships the deity— he too shall attain non-attachment.
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "One who does not worship Śiva, Bhāskara, Agni, Keśava, and Kauśikī even in their mind, goes from the world of the gods to a downward state."

2b) Not honoring with the mind and with faith; or alternatively, "not honoring even with the mind" is stated because of the necessity of performing worship, as [the text] continues from that point. Kauśikī-Durgā.

In this context, the sequence of worship should not be inferred from the order of the textual recitation; for it is observed as the practice of the learned that the worship of the deity follows immediately after the conclusion of the worship of the Sun.

In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "The merit of one who gives a hundred thousand milch cows to those who have mastered the Vedas is less than that of one who worships the Sun for a single day; the latter's merit is greater."
Even in the case of general worship of the gods, the fruit of gifting a cow is obtained, or perhaps even more;
and thus says Yājñavalkya:
"Massaging those who are weary, service to guests, and the worship of the gods."
Wiping oneself with the water remaining after washing a Brahmin’s feet is equal to the gift of a cow.
In the *Harināthabandha* and other works, the reading is found in this way:
"He who might give a hundred thousand cows to those who have mastered the Vedas,
and he who would worship the Sun, or Śiva, or Keśava for even a single day [are equal]."
O best of men, the merit of that person shall be even greater than that;
it is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices.
These [merits] are not worth even a sixteenth part of the worship and veneration of the Sun.
"Arcā" means an image.
Likewise, those who always sacrifice with sacrifice and give gifts are always [rewarded].
Those who always subsist on air and likewise worship the suns [the twelve Ādityas], [attain this].
Those men who always worship the Great-Souled Lord of Obstacles (Vighnarāja),
for them all prosperity and all spiritual perfections arise.
The food of that man who worships an image of the Goddess that is devoid of the proper characteristics is not welcomed; therefore, one should avoid such an image.
Thus, one should worship [the goddess] who possesses the [auspicious] marks upon hearing [of] this undesirable [result].
However, the description of those marks has not been written here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "A thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of the worship of Maheśa."
As long as death has not arrived, as long as one's vital energy has not failed,
and as long as there is no impairment of the senses, for that long alone should one worship the Lord.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Those kings who do not worship Śiva, the Lord of the three worlds, in this world are not fit vessels for heaven, liberation, or even sovereignty."
It is better to give up one's life or even to have one's head cut off than to eat without having first worshipped the three-eyed Lord.
He whose worship of Śiva is clearly carried out throughout his entire life, covered as he may be with human skin, is Rudra himself; of this there is no doubt.
They say that space is the *liṅga* and the earth is its pedestal;
it is called the *liṅga* because it is the abode of all beings and because of their dissolution (*layana*) therein.
He who worships me in an image has worshipped Viṣṇu;
he who worships all my forms has worshipped the Liṅga.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"When the Liṅga is worshipped, everything mobile and immobile becomes worshipped;
therefore, the worship of the Liṅga should be performed by those of great soul."
Wandering through thousands of various births for many thousands of lifetimes,
how indeed can one attain liberation without the worship of the Śiva-liṅga?
3b) Even one who is attached to all the senses, or even one joined with all sins—
he too goes to Śiva, O Goddess, who worships a liṅga here in this world.
The man who worships me in an image for a full one hundred and eight times is equal to one who worships me in a linga for a single day; of this there is no doubt.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "He who, having fashioned an earthen liṅga, worships it upon an auspicious altar, becomes wealthy and glorious in this very world; indeed, he is born as Rudra."
"Śubhavedikaṃ" means endowed with a beautiful altar. In the Brahmapurāṇa:
"Hara, Maheśvara, Śūlapāṇi, and Pinākadhṛk."
"Paśupati, Śiva," and "forgive me"—this is the dismissal.
Bringing the clay, kneading it, consecrating it,
and invoking [the deity], as well as bathing, worshiping, saying "forgive me," and dismissal.

Oṃ, salutation to Hara; I fetch the clay. || 1 || Oṃ, salutation to Maheśvara; I knead the clay. || 2 || Oṃ, salutation to the Trident-bearer; I establish the clay. || 3 || Oṃ, salutation to the Wielder of the Pināka bow; I invoke Śiva into the clay. || 4 || Oṃ, salutation to Paśupati. || 5 ||
One should perform the bathing with water for the feet and other offerings. (5) "Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva"—with these words, one should worship.
(6) This is the sequence of worship. And it is stated in the Āgama: "The earthen [liṅga] bestows success.
Having fashioned the earthen liṅga with the *viṃva* [mantra], one should worship it at the three junctions of the day.
Listen to the fruit of his merit, up to ten times elevenfold.
With this very body, Rudra is born upon the earth,
destroying the sins of all mortals through both sight and touch.
Likewise, having fashioned a linga the size of an *āmalaka* fruit and worshipped it—
whether it be made of gold or precious gems— one is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having fashioned a linga out of clay, ashes, a ball of cow dung, or made of copper or bell-metal,
and having worshipped it even once, one shall dwell in heaven for ten thousand kalpas.

In the Devīpurāṇa: "A wooden liṅga bestows wealth, a crystal liṅga grants all desires; likewise, a liṅga made from the Narmadā mountain or even any other excellent material is indeed like [the aforementioned] liṅgas."

O best of Brahmins, having fashioned it and worshipped it, you shall obtain your desired fruit. It may be made of wood from an auspicious tree, or otherwise, even from stone; in all such cases, the *liṅga* may be rough, small, large, or flat in shape, and its pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) may be of uneven color.
A defective [liṅga] or one with a defective base is [unacceptable]. One lacking the correct proportions (mānonmāna) is not to be worshipped, as is a base lacking the correct proportions.
A tawny (kapila) bāṇaliṅga is prohibited; however, one that has the luster of a ripe jambu fruit is not prohibited. Regarding the bath (sāna):
the width at the top of the liṅga should be equal to the height of the liṅga, or twice that.
The circumference of the pedestal (piṇḍī) should be established in that same manner.
The upper portion, the lower portion, the height, and the channel (praṇālikā) of the pedestal should all be equal to those of the liṅga. Thus it is stated in the Brahma Purāṇa.
Whoever should draw it even with a finger, using white or red pigments,
and having drawn it, should worship it, he too shall become a Lord of the Gaṇas.
Even while playing with dust, if a man fashions a linga,
he obtains through that merit a kingdom complete with its subjects and its thorns (enemies).
Now, regarding the fruit of the worship of the Goddess,
as stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa (4b):
Rites such as the Agnihotra, the Vedas, and sacrifices accompanied by priestly fees— even all these—
are not equal to even a hundred-thousandth part of the worship of Caṇḍikā.

Likewise, O Bhārata, another who would always worship or even bow down to Durgā is a yogi, a sage, and a wise man; liberation stands within his grasp. Likewise, he is a donor, a sage, a sacrificer, an ascetic, and one who has visited all sacred fords.
"Whoever should always worship Durgā with flowers, perfumes, and ointments," and so forth.
Now, the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu. It is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:

"When Viṣṇu is propitiated, one obtains whatever one desires in the mind—whether earthly ambitions, heaven, or even that abode which is praised by the gods. Thus ends the description of the fruit of propitiation.

But it does not refer merely to worship. "Worldly" refers to sons and so forth; "praiseworthy in heaven" refers to the state of Indra. Even though the worldly fruit of worshipping Viṣṇu is not seen [in this life], it should nevertheless be understood as an incidental result.
As stated in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
I shall now fully describe the worship of the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus,
by performing which all the sages have attained supreme perfection.
And in the Narasiṃha-pūjā:
"He who constantly worships Narasiṃha, the best of gods, shall partake in heaven and liberation; there is no need for deliberation on this matter."
Therefore, having become single-minded and by means of a lifelong vow,
one obtains one's heart's desire through the worship of Narasiṃha.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa,
Yama addressed one being cooked in hell:
"Why was the Lord Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions, not worshipped by you?"
If the prescribed substances are unavailable, one should worship even with water alone.
Yogayājñavalkya also says:
"Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra; Viṣṇu, the god Divākara (the Sun);..."

"Therefore, I consider none other than Janārdana to be most worthy of worship," and from such statements, the worship of Viṣṇu is established as obligatory and must necessarily be performed; furthermore, the procedure for daily bathing is recorded in the Viṣṇu-smṛti.

Then, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and being pure in conduct, one should worship the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, who is without beginning or end, either before an image of the deity or on a consecrated spot; it is stated that at the conclusion of this, the Vaiśvadeva rite is to be performed according to the prescribed rule.
After the worship of the Sun, the Narasiṃha Purāṇa also states:
"Then, having bowed to the Lord from the water, the master of the house [should proceed] again."
Then, according to the prescribed rite for the Brahmasūkta, one should worship Viṣṇu;
thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva offering and the bali-rite according to the rules.
By reflecting on such statements as these, one understands that the Vaiśvadeva rite follows the worship of Viṣṇu;
thus, the worship of Viṣṇu is obligatory.

Now, regarding the supports for the deity: "The wise have declared that the complete worship of Hari is performed in these six [supports]: in a horse, in fire, in the heart, in the sun, on a sacrificial altar, and in images. Thus, these six locations are the most excellent. Furthermore, the fruit and greatness of worship in other places, such as the Śālagrāma stone and so forth, has been described. And likewise, the Blessed Lord said:
Whether it be a certain heart, a single cloth, or a painting,
or whatever human being might worship me in a circle produced from a portion of my splendor.

In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa: "For those who perform ritual acts, the God is in the fire; for the wise, the God is in heaven; for those of small intellect, Hari is in images; and for yogis, He is in the heart."
The wise constantly worship Hari with oblations in the fire, with flowers in the water, with knowledge in the heart,
and with meditation in the solar orb.
And so it has been said: "Nārāyaṇa, seated upon a lotus throne in the midst of the solar disc, should always be meditated upon—
wearing armlets, golden earrings, a crown, and a necklace, possessing a golden body, and holding the conch and the discus."
5b) Although the worship of water-vessels and so forth has been prescribed for Hari, it should nevertheless be understood to apply to others as well; and thus says Śātātapa:
The deities are eternally present in the earth, in water, in fire, and in the sun in heaven; likewise, they reside in food, in gold, in brahmins, and in cows.
"The deities of water are for humans; the celestial deities are for the wise; for the foolish, they are in wood and clods of earth;

but for one seeking liberation, the deity is in the Self. The phrase "the celestial deities exist" is to be understood as the ellipsis. In these substrates, the deities are to be worshipped. However, water-worship is forbidden for Śiva. For Viṣṇu, however, the fruit of worshipping the Śālagrāma stone is superior.
One should worship Hari in a discus produced from a Śālagrāma stone according to the *Brahmapurāṇa-uttarakhaṇḍa*;
by doing so every day, one has effectively performed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Just as fire, though latent within wood, becomes manifest at the end of the friction, so too does the Lord reveal Himself through this worship.

"In whatever manner Hari is all-pervading, one should worship him in the Śālagrāma. There is no ritual consecration (saṃskāra), such as the installation of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), for the Śālagrāma, because He is eternally present there. "Hari does not delight in Lakṣmī in the same way that He delights in His own city."
Just as [the deity] always moves within the wheel of the Śālagrāma stone.
The Agnihotra has been performed by him, and the earth along with its oceans has been given as a gift,
by whom Hari was worshipped in the form of the Śālagrāma stone.
Furthermore, he who worships with devotion a hundred Śālagrāma stones shall dwell in the world of Hari and be born here as a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Even that lowest of men who is pervaded by lust, anger,
and greed goes to the world of Hari by worshipping the Śālagrāma stone.
The man who always worships Govinda at Śālagrāma shall not fall from heaven until the dissolution of all beings.
Now begins the examination of the Śālagrāma.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa* and the *Varāha Purāṇa*, it is stated:
"When two wheels are seen at the level of the doorway, he is to be known as Vāsudeva; he has white garments and is exceedingly beautiful."
When two wheels are joined together at the eastern part, that is to be known as Puṣkara; it is Saṃkarṣaṇa, red in appearance and exceedingly beautiful. (2)
Pradyumna is characterized by a subtle wheel, a reddish-yellow luster, and likewise a long body that remains stable; it is pleasant, yet possesses many fissures. (3)
Aniruddha, however, is blue-hued, circular, and exceedingly beautiful;
he is the god endowed with three lines and marked by a lotus.
The deity Nārāyaṇa is dark-complexioned, neither too short nor too tall; he is endowed with a broad chest like a stone slab and has a wide, pleasant right side.
Parameṣṭhin is red in luster; he holds a discus as well as a lotus, and on his back he has a very beautiful and abundant mark in the shape of a bimba fruit.
Kapila is situated within the Narasiṃha [form], adorned with a broad face;
worship does not take place otherwise than through the observance of celibacy (brahmacarya). || 7 ||
Likewise, Viṣṇu is black in color and adorned with a large disc;
furthermore, a line in the shape of a mace is observed on the region of his back. (8)
The Vārāha [liṅga] has a spear-shaped mark; it possesses two unevenly placed discs, resembles sapphire in color, is thick, and is further marked with three lines.
Likewise, his back is elevated like a tortoise, filled with circular whirlpools;
he possesses a greenish hue and is marked by the Kaustubha gem.
He should be known as Hayagrīva when there is a line approaching the discus,
joined with many dots and having a blue form at the back.
Vaikuṇṭha, possessing the luster of jewels and gems, bore a single discus and likewise a lotus upon its gate; the lines there were as beautiful as sacrificial posts (yūpa).
This deity is in the form of a fish, adorned with long lines, joined by two dots, of a dark (kārśya) complexion, and most beautiful. || 13 ||
Likewise, the god Trivikrama, dark-hued and of great splendor,
has a mace and a discus on his left side, while there are lines on his right shoulder.
One who is round-shaped and short is proclaimed to be Vāmana;
he resembles the flax flower (atasī-puṣpa) and is marked above with a dot (bindu). 15.
Likewise, the god Sudarśana is dark-complexioned and possesses great luster;
on his left side are a mace and a discus, while there is a line on his right.
And Śrīdhara is to be recognized by his being marked with a forest garland; he has the appearance of a kadamba flower and is endowed with five lines. || 17 ||
It may be of various colors and infinite, marked by the coils of a serpent;
it is filled with infinite forms and bestows the fruits of all desires. || 18 ||
He whose face is seen above in all the intermediate and cardinal directions—he is to be known as Puruṣottama, the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation. (19)
On the peak arising from Śālagrāma, a horn-like protrusion is seen;
by its power, one named Yogeśvara destroys even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Likewise, Dāmodara is established in the middle with a thick disc;
it is crowded with sprouts of dūrvā grass and endowed with yellow lines. || 21 ||
The glossy [color] is said to bring success; the thin [color], moreover, brings fame;
the pale [color] burns away sins; and the yellow [color] bestows sons and fruits.
A dark blue complexion is seen as auspicious, while a red one bestows disease;
a parched complexion constantly brings affliction, and a pale one grants poverty.
The Kapilā cow, when honored through the practice of celibacy, removes sin;
indeed, Hari is eternally present within the Śālagrāma stone.
There, bathing and giving gifts yield results superior to those of all other holy fords;
though difficult to attain, they bestow their fruit upon the practitioner after a long time.
Those that are uneven should be discarded everywhere, as they yield contrary results.
The deity originating from Śālagrāma is one [form], while the deity originating from Dvārakā is another.
7a) Where there is a union of both, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt. Wherever there is a Śālagrāma stone, there is always Vārāṇasī.
Always endowed with the origin of Dvārakā and consisting of all sacred fords (tīrthas),
the Śilā of Dvārakā should be worshipped only when it is white in color, and not when it is any other color.
And so it has been said:
"She of white complexion bestows sons, grandsons, wealth and the like, as well as happiness, liberation, and prosperity; therefore, one should always worship her by name."
One that has holes, a mouth [opening], or is defiled by defects should be abandoned as it bestows poverty;
for it is said: "A [line] that is triangular, uneven, perforated, or likewise broken [is inauspicious]."
A half-moon-shaped [mark] should be abandoned; those that are devoid of worship, gaping-mouthed, upward-facing, uneven, or crooked circles [are likewise to be avoided].
A Śālagrāma with a terrible form, an unadorable mouth, and likewise deep-set cavities [is inauspicious].
Now follows the examination of the discus in the case of both the door-slab and the Śālagrāma.
With one discus he is Sudarśana; with two, Nārāyaṇa, endowed with Śrī;
with three, he is indeed Acyuta; and with four, Janārdana.
He is called Vāsudeva by five [syllables], Pradyumna by six;
Baladeva by seven, and Puruṣottama by eight.
Navavyūha consists of nine, Daśajanmaka of ten,
Aniruddha of eleven, and Mādhava is twelvefold.
Beyond this is Ananta, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The fruit differs according to the different forms. In the worship of many forms, there is great fruit.
The worship of the twelve stones must certainly be performed.
By whoever [this] is seen, saluted, bathed, worshipped, or praised,
there is merit equal to ten million sacrifices, bestowing the fruit of ten million sacred fords.
"One should diligently worship whichever form one desires;
when that is worshipped, one obtains the fruit both in this world and in the next," so it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.
One should worship [the deity] in all the forms during the day, and in the fires at night;
facing east, west, or north during the morning, evening, and night respectively.

The mantra is used according to the respective times: by this it is meant that in the morning one faces east, in the evening one faces west, and at night one faces north. Furthermore, the worship of an image is recommended because of the ease of meditating upon the Sun and other deities therein, as well as due to the greater fruitfulness of the worship; however, in the case of Śiva, the worship of the *liṅga* [is prescribed].
Praise.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: It may be made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise of clay;
or it may be made of brass, or of other metals, or likewise of copper and bell-metal.
An image of the deity made even of pure wood is praised;
indeed, O Lord, it may range from the size of a thumb-joint up to a span.
In domestic settings, the wise do not recommend making images that exceed the prescribed dimensions;
"arcā" means an image. Regarding the subject of divine images, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"Beginning from one finger-breadth up to twelve finger-breadths."
Worship in the home is fully described; worship in a temple is even more auspicious.

Likewise, that [image] with matted hair (jaṭā) is not auspicious for the home; similarly, the Śailajā (stone-born) [image] is not to be worshipped in the home. "Stone-born" means made of stone. A four-armed [image] may be used in the home; a multi-armed image-deity may be used in the home. However, one that is cruel or fierce (aghorā) must not be used in the home, as it brings about the fruit of fear. Thus concludes the description of the fruits of the Pañcāyatana worship.
8a) In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "One should seek health from the Sun, and one should seek wealth from Agni."
One should desire knowledge from Śaṅkara, and one should desire liberation from Janārdana.
In such statements, it is said that the sun and other planets bestow their swift results (*śīghraphala*), but not that there is a cessation of other results.
Even the worship of Brahmā yields great fruit. Thus it is said in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"He who worships Viriñci, the lotus-seated one, with devotion, quickly becomes a recipient of kingdoms, including that of the gods, and of liberation."
Better is the abandonment of the body, better is the descent into hell,
than that one should eat before having worshipped the Lord who is born from the lotus.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Fruits of Worship," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhin.
Now follows the definition of the materials for worship.

In this regard, Viṣṇu states: "One should not perform worship of the gods at night while holding water in one's hand"—this is the specific rule. Baudhāyana says: [The cloth] worn, scented, torn, or used as an upper garment, provided it is not displaced;
when joined with humans, it is not for the gods, nor is it [suitable] when it has been loudly proclaimed, or when it is used for wrapping, lying down, or sitting.

The meaning is that one should offer to the deity what has been used by humans, wiped with the hand, and washed. One should give to whichever deity whatever kind [of garment] has been prescribed for him. Alternatively, white is suitable for all; however, blue or dyed cloth is not [suitable], whereas un-dyed cloth is dear to Sūrya.
There is also a figurative application [of the term] to one another.
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"Furthermore, whoever should give an ornament to a Brahmin or to a deity..."
He shall go to the world of Varuṇa, adorned with various ornaments;
born on earth in due time, he shall become a king, a lord of islands.
Likewise: By the gift of a sacred thread to the gods or to a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa learned in the four Vedas with a purified intellect; of this there is no doubt.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O tiger among the Bharatas, that Brāhmaṇa who worships the gods out of greed for wealth certainly goes to hell after death."
Whoever, out of greed for wealth, should perform fire-rituals in all temples everywhere, shall attain a downward rebirth.
The phrase "devapūjādikam" (worship of the gods, etc. is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. In the Devīpurāṇa:
"Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, if he knows the Mātṛmaṇḍala and is conversant with the Tantras, [he may perform it] after having consecrated [the site]."
In the ritual of worship, one who is excellent is best; neither a beast nor an actor, nor one who has not reached the final stage of life, nor a hypocrite, is declared to be an auspicious worshipper.
In this context, "animal" (*paśu*) refers to one who is ignorant of the scriptures of worship. A "kuśīlava" is a wandering actor. In the *Devīpurāṇa*:
"Pure, wearing fine garments, wise, observing silence, devoted to meditation, free from desire, venerable, and devoid of attachment to worldly traditions (*āgama*)."
Having worshipped oneself with fragrant white unguents and the like,
one should worship the deities at an auspicious moment while they are seated upon their respective thrones.
One should cause the invocation, as well as the water for the guest-offering and the water for the feet, to be given using a golden vessel.
Now, the general *arghya*:
With red bilva, unbroken rice, flowers, curd, dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and sesame seeds—
this is prescribed as the general *arghya* for all the gods.
9a) In the absence [of actual substances], one should mentally imagine curd, *dūrvā* grass, and so forth,

at an auspicious moment (*sumuhūrta*) and time of merit (*puṇyakāla*), such as the forenoon and so on. In the phrase "argha, pādya, and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes bathing and other rites.

One who is devoted to the five-fold offerings (paṃcopacāra) should, in this context, place the vessels according to their utility. "Red" refers to red sandalwood and other fragrant substances; Lakṣmīdhara states that "red" means saffron. Some do not desire red [substances] for the Liṅga. The worship of the deity should be performed without contradicting one's own respective dharma. And so it is said:
Having abandoned their respective duties, the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas perform worship alone; the deities do not accept that [worship].
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "A heap of merit is proclaimed even without a mantra;
if this [act] is joined with a mantra, the merit is a hundred times greater."
Because even by means of the name of a deity, it bestows the fruit of worship.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Wherever there is an image of the gods that can endure an anointing with ghee,
twenty-five palas [of ghee] should be offered to it with faith."
One hundred and eight *pala* should always be given for the bath;
and by way of number, two thousand *pala* constitute a great bath (*mahāsnāna*).
That conduct by which one proceeds in all directions should be given;
indeed, that which is attached to the limbs of Brahmā and that which belongs to Viṣṇu are bestowed upon the Brahmins.
Whatever has come into contact with the body of Rudra, one should burn it all in the fire instantly;
however, that which belongs to other gods, one should cast away among the lowly.
Then that which was offered to the Mothers— namely, the remainder of the food offerings (naivedya) and so forth— should be given to the Brahmins.
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"One should show respect toward worthy recipients (pātras), for they alone are the most excellent;
indeed, without a worthy recipient, the performance of offerings and sacrifices is not accomplished."
Therefore, O Great Sage, they say that the vessel is the foremost limb of the sacrifice;
whatever weapon is prescribed for whom, that shall be his insignia.
A bowl of thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed as the best;
the medium is three parts less than that, and the smallest is twelve finger-breadths.
One should never hold an alms-bowl that is less than eight finger-breadths in size;
it may be of various wonderful forms and shaped like a lotus.
One should provide conch shells and bowls with the luster of blue lotuses;
for whoever should perform the consecration or sacrificial rite without a bowl [is at fault].
All efforts such as invocations and the like become fruitless, and there is the loss of wealth.
If the offering of oblations (bali) is omitted, there will be famine; if it lacks fragrance, there will be misfortune;
likewise, if it lacks incense, there will be agitation; and if it lacks cloth, there will be loss of wealth.
If [the chariot] lacks jewels, one will lose one's beloved wife; if it lacks a banner, one will be leaderless;
if it lacks a parasol, the parasol is destroyed; and if it lacks a canopy, one shall become a denizen of hell.
If the Vedyā is missing, there will be destruction of either the self or the city;
if the Dīpa is missing, the performer shall always encounter misfortune.
If the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is lacking, all of that becomes useless; there is no doubt about this.
But if it is devoid of mantras and vidyās, even though complete, it perishes.
When accompanied by the vessel-mantra, it becomes the destroyer of all defects;
however, in the absence of these, all that should be offered mentally at the beginning of the worship and other rites.
Likewise, O Sage, by offering with a golden vessel, one obtains all desired things;
but by offering the *argha* with a silver vessel, one obtains long life, sovereignty, and sons.
One obtains good fortune with a copper vessel, and merit with those made of clay.

In this manner, for the purposes of offering water (argha), bathing, food offerings (naivedya), sacrificial oblations (bali), incense, and so forth, wooden bowls, earthenware bowls, lotus bowls, bowls made of palāśa leaves, copper bowls, gold bowls, and silver bowls are each progressively more highly recommended than the preceding ones.
Broken vessels made of any material are forbidden;
however, even those broken by copper, gold, silver, conch, or mother-of-pearl may be accepted.
Brahmā said:
The person who bathes Keśava with water contained within a conch shell obtains the fruit of [giving] a thousand Kapila cows.

Whoever places holy water from a sacred ford into a conch shell and bathes Keśava with it on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī), even with a mere drop, shall deliver a hundred generations of their lineage.
Having taken the milk of a tawny cow and placed it in a conch shell,
one who bathes Janārdana with it shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand sacrifices.
Whatever water clings to the conch and is whirled over Keśava, he constantly honors it with his head; what need has he then for bathing in the Gaṅgā?
The offering of water for honor (*argha*) using a conch vessel should be performed for all [deities] except Śiva;
however, it is more extensive for Viṣṇu.
Indeed, he who performs a circumambulation with a conch after having offered the *argha* [attains great merit].
By him, the seven continents together with the oceans were circumambulated.
The number of circumambulations is as follows:
one should offer seven circumambulations to Caṇḍī, three to Gaṇeśvara,
four to Keśava, and half a circumambulation to Śiva.
Now follows the removal of the divine garlands and so forth.
Removing the garlands from the deity, collecting the remains of the divine offerings,
and bathing all the deities are recorded as having the same fruit as the gift of a cow.
Now, regarding the Sun:
in that regard, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states:
"Beholding and avoiding living beings with a soft and fine broom..."
By performing the sweeping slowly and carefully, one obtains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
For as many particles of dust as are cast into the abode of the Sun,
for that many days does a man remain in heaven, free from all impurity.
As many times as one performs the worship of the Sun according to the prescribed rites with royal unguents,
for that many thousands of yugas one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
10b) The waving of the lustration lamp (nīrājana) and the ritual lamp (ārātrika) above [the deity].
Whatever merit has been accumulated over thousands of millions of years by that dust is all consumed by a bath of ghee, just as fire consumes fuel.
Having performed a bath with ghee on the seventh lunar day while the sun is present, that man,
having uplifted seven generations of his lineage, is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Likewise on the eighth day of the bright fortnight,
as on the seventh or the eighth,
O best of kings, bathing the tree with cow’s milk is the destroyer of great sins.
Having bathed the Sun with curd, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
he who bathes the Sun with cold water for the sake of his ancestors [attains the same].
The ancestors, being satisfied, lead him from even hell to heaven;
likewise, having bathed the Sun with cool water, he offered it with milk.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one is glorified in the world of Agni;
having performed these three baths and having worshipped Bhāskara.
A person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices;
by performing an ablution with mercury, one gains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
Likewise: "Just as no one should ever transgress the ritual bathing of the Sun, so should one perform it with great effort; for its transgression brings about inauspiciousness."
The doer who transgresses [this] shall go to the Tāmisra hell, and he shall go to the Raurava hell.
Now, the arghya offering.
Having offered the *arghya* with flowers mixed with sandalwood water to the Sun,
one is honored in the world of the Sun, endowed with the prosperity of sons and grandsons.
11a) Whoever, having filled the eightfold vessel, offers it upon the head of the Sun,
shall sport for ten thousand years within the solar orb.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, clarified butter, curd, as well as honey,
red karavīra flowers, and likewise red sandalwood.
This eightfold massage was indeed devised by Brahmā;
the fruit that one obtains by offering the arghya with a wooden arghya-vessel [is as follows].
Therefore, O lord of men, Mṛtyuñjaya has declared that the merit from the gift of a copper vessel is ten times greater than that.
A copper vessel is equal in merit to two leaves of the *palāśa* or *padma*;
however, a silver vessel should be known to be worth half a *lakṣa*—of this there is no doubt.
Everything placed in a golden vessel becomes ten million times more effective for the Sun;
likewise, this applies in sequence to the bath, the food offering, the sacrificial oblation, the incense, and so forth.
The fruit of that [gift] increases progressively according to the specific excellence of the vessel;
just as the fruit of offering the arghya with a vessel made of gold and the like is understood, so too should it be seen in the case of bathing and other rites.
The merit that is obtained by one who has mastered the Vedas through the gift of a silver vessel is said to be a hundredfold greater from the gift of a clay vessel dedicated to the Sun.
The fruit is declared to be exactly the same for both the wealthy and the poor; however, he who, despite possessing wealth, fails through delusion to perform the ritual in full detail, [is at fault].
One whose mind is overcome by greed does not obtain that fruit;
the same should be understood regarding Śiva as well.
The specific detail regarding Śiva is found in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "A person who bathes the liṅga even once with cow's milk... (11b).
He does not shine by means of this [wealth], nor is he honored in the heavenly world.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over a thousand crores of kalpas,
that sin is undoubtedly burnt away by anointing the Liṅga with ghee.
Having performed a bath with ghee on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, a man who does so even once at the Liṅga,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
He who bathes me with honey is glorified in the world of the ancestors;
he who performs my bathing with highly fragrant oil [attains the same].
To him who performs singing and instrumental music at the time of bathing or during the three junctions of the day, I grant the fruit of an Atirātra sacrifice and good fortune.
Listen to the fruit of merit for that person who performs dance, facial music,
or instrumental music such as singing and dancing, for as many steps as they take.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are [performances], one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
although the fruit of dancing and so forth has been described specifically for the worship of Śiva, it should be understood that by the worship of others as well, one attains their respective worlds.
Now, regarding Viṣṇu, the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa* states:

"Having offered worship, as well as the *arghya*, the water for washing the feet (*pādya*), and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) to the God of gods according to the prescribed rite, one is liberated from all sins."
O King, he who bathes Narasiṃha with devotion using milk is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having bathed Viṣṇu once with curd, one becomes stainless and pleasing to behold;
being served by the most excellent beings, he attains the world of Viṣṇu.
The man who performs the bathing of an image of Hari with honey,
having ascended to the world of Agni, shall dwell thereafter in the city of Viṣṇu.
He who performs a ceremonial bath with ghee is especially honored throughout all the worlds;
mounting a divine celestial chariot, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having rubbed [the image] with powders made from barley and wheat and having washed the Lord of the Gods with warm water, he shall attain the three worlds.
Now, [the ritual] for Durgā.
O lord of men, it is declared that bathing with the five products of a tawny cow (pañcagavya), as well as with curd, milk, and ghee, yields a hundredfold more merit than other methods.
Whatever sin has been accumulated over thousands of millions of years,
all of that goes to destruction like salt in water.
From the others, [he takes] the other [portion] from the five products of the cow.
Likewise, O King, by the auspicious and ritual application of ghee to the Goddess according to the rules,
one whose soul is purified of all sins is glorified in the world of Durgā.
O Hero, he who, endowed with faith and devotion, bathes Candrikā according to the prescribed rite with milk, is glorified in the world of the Moon.
He who bathes Durgā according to the prescribed rite with curd is glorified;
he shines in a celestial chariot and is honored in the world of Durgā.
The man who bathes Caṇḍikā with sugarcane juice is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu by means of a golden celestial chariot.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight, one should worship Caṇḍikā according to the prescribed rites.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who bathes [the image] with ghee:
specifically, ten ancestors, ten descendants, and oneself.
Having been rescued from the ocean of existence, one is glorified in the world of Durgā.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Worship," in the illustrious *Maṃtrakośa*.
Now, the ritual offerings for worship.
And likewise, in the *Prapañcasāra*:
"The seat, welcome, the water for the feet along with the arghya,
the water for sipping, the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), as well as the bath, garments, and ornaments."
One should employ fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood in the worship; these are the sixteen services (upacāras).

The ten services (upacāras) in their proper order are: arghya, pādya, ācamana, madhuparka, ācamana again, and then the offerings beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya).
The five-fold worship consists of offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with the food offering (naivedya).
Worship is said to be of three kinds; one should resort to one of these.
Now, regarding fragrances: their characteristics are as follows. Furthermore, in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"One who has anointed themselves with devotion using sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and lotuses, bestows that which is most desired."

With lotuses and lotus-wood; this applies to all [the deities]. Now, for the Sun: he who obtains sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron, mixed with camphor and likewise combined with musk, [should offer it] to the Sun.
Having spent that equal and slender year in the abode of the three heavens, he is born again on earth as a king of kings; of this there is no doubt.
Fanned with a palm-leaf fan and anointed with auspicious fragrances,
he shall dwell in Vīramitrapura for ten thousand years.
The same should be understood regarding Śiva as well.
Now, regarding Viṣṇu, the Narasiṃha Purāṇa states:
"With saffron, agallochum, śrīkhaṇḍa, and sandalwood, [one should prepare] the image of Acyuta."
O Indra among kings, by anointing [the deity] with devotion, one shall dwell in heaven for ten million kalpas.
Now, regarding Durgā: In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, it is said:
"He who anoints Durgā with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor is honored in the divine world of Śakra for one hundred and one equal years."
Having applied fragrant unguents, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
having anointed the Āryā with sandalwood paste, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
By anointing [the body] with black agallochum, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
by anointing the limbs of the Noble One with saffron, one obtains the fruit of a thousand [such sacrifices].
One should offer to the God a mace adorned with a jeweled handle, or else one with a handle of gold, silver, and so forth; hear now the fruit of that merit.
With the tips of his hands occupied by chowries and surrounded by celestial women,
he shall dwell for a long time in the city of the gods, situated in a celestial chariot of great splendor.
Thus, the fruit is equal for all the gods.
Now, the flowers.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
With flowers grown in the forest or leaves produced on the mountain—
fresh, without holes, sprinkled with water, and free from insects— [one should worship].
Or, out of devotion arising from self-delight, one should worship the gods with water from a pond;
however, [one should avoid] flowers infested by worms or insects, those that are withered, and those that have been stale.
One should discard flowers that have fallen on their own as well as those that are damaged;
one should not worship the deity with buds, nor should one offer anything that is unripe.
13b) One should carefully avoid fruit that has been pierced by a bird,
as well as flowers that are neither prohibited nor specifically prescribed; "mukula" refers to a bud.
If flowers are not obtained, one should offer even leaves;
if leaves are also unavailable, one should offer even fruits.
Even by the absence of fruits, [one honors] the grasses, shrubs, and herbs;
indeed, even when herbs are not obtained, one becomes worshipped through devotion.
O tiger among kings, for each individual flower offered, the fruit is ten gold pieces; for garlands, that same reward shall be doubled.
"A Brāhmaṇa should personally gather sacrificial fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth;
by performing rituals with items brought by a Śūdra or purchased, he falls low.
Thus, it is said that [the act] performed by oneself yields the fruit of the intention."
In the event of inability, one may accept even that which has been purchased or brought by a Śūdra, provided it has been consecrated with sprinkling (prokṣita),
because it has been accepted by the great multitude (mahājana).

Regarding the offering of flowers such as the *lakṣā*, even a flower purchased with wealth acquired through righteous means must certainly be offered; likewise, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He who performs the worship of Keśava with flowers purchased with wealth acquired through righteousness [attains the highest merit]."
Without doubt, he will uplift seven previous generations and others who are envious.
Nevertheless, they consider that sacrificial fuel, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and so forth, become pure through purification by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) as their final step.
O Lord, that which was worn on the upper body, that which was held in the left hand, the lower garment that was worn, and that which was washed within the water; [all these are offered].
"The deities do not accept that flower once it has reached the state of being *nirmālya* (used). Thus it is written in the *Haribhaktigrantha*.

14a) Even taking flowers that have not been given should be performed for the sake of constant worship, according to the statement: "And for the sake of the deity, a flower is not stolen," as Manu has declared. Hārīta says:
If any twice-born ones, having performed their ablutions, gather flowers, the deities do not accept them; they become like ashes, just as wood [is consumed].

One should not take [the offering] for one's own sake without having performed the worship of the deity; however, one may take it for the sake of others. Furthermore, after the daily worship, it may be taken for the purpose of worship on another day.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
One should avoid flowers that are scentless or have a pungent odor; however, even those devoid of fragrance, such as sacred kuśa grass and the like, should be accepted if they are pure.
"O Tejaḥkānti Karavīra, you remain for a watch (three hours) day and night;
the meaning is that you then become *nirmālya* (an offering discarded after worship) upon that [deity]."
In the case of tulasī, bilva leaves, and all kinds of lotuses,
as well as those from the houses of garland-makers, there is no fault of being stale.
Mudgara-kadaṃba flowers should be offered at night to Nibhānava;
golden kadaṃba flowers should be offered at night to Śaṅkara.
Flowers that remain from the day [are acceptable], as are *mallikā* flowers by day and night;
*mudgarāṇi*—known as *mugarāvelī*—should be given and accepted. Furthermore, even the leaves of prohibited flowers, when woven into garlands of prescribed flowers, do not cause any fault.
The fruit is greater when one offers flowers that one has personally cultivated than when one offers flowers cultivated by another;
likewise, there is a greater fruit from offering specific flowers than from offering flowers offered in a general manner.

14b) Furthermore, in the absence of prescribed flowers and leaves, the offering of what is both prescribed and prohibited does not entail fault. However, when specific prescribed flowers are unavailable, that which is both prohibited and prescribed must not be accepted. This is the general rule regarding what is acceptable and what is unacceptable.
Now, the general flowers for all [the planets], beginning with the Sun, are:
jasmine, *śamī*, *kuśa* grass, *kubja*, *mallikā*, and *karavīraka*.
Nāgapuṣpa, punnāga, āśoka, and red flowers, as well as blue lotuses,
vaṃcaka, iṣikā, kuṭaja, padma, bilva, and pavitraka.
All these are prescribed here as equal for all the gods;
the *kubjaka* is well known as *kaṅku-āṭi*, and the *mallikā* is well known as *velī*.

*Nāga* refers to *nāgakesara*; *punnāga* is well known as *punnāga*. Now, regarding what is prescribed and prohibited for all [deities]: the *pāṭalā* and the leaf of the *śamī* tree are beneficial and harmful respectively for Durgā;
while the *kunda*, the *palāśa* flower, and *dūrvā* grass are [beneficial] for the worship of Śiva.
Kumuda, kuṅkuma, reṇu, and tagara are for the worship of the Sun.
Acchovaka, karṇikāra, and kiṃkirāta belong to Hari;
furthermore, kiṃkirāta is also known as pītāmrātaka.
Tilaka, mālatī, vāṇa, tulasī, and bhṛṅgarājaka [belong to Viṣṇu].
Whatever is prohibited or enjoined for the sake of Śiva’s fortress (Śivadurga) shall be [binding].
*Tilaka* is known as *tilakā*;
*mālatī* is known as *goduma*, or else as *kākamācī*, because it is mentioned separately from the *jāti*. *Vāṇa* is well-known in the world as *kṛṣṇageṃṭhī*.
15a) Others say that the *āmrātaka* is well-known in the world as the *prabheda*. The *vāṇa* is the *kaṭasarayā*.
The *jaya* is the *kāśa*, the white lotus, and likewise the white *mandāraka*.
For both Durgā and Viṣṇu, there shall be both that which is prohibited and that which is prescribed.
It is known as Jaya and Jayantī.
Agasti, rati, muktā, tirīṭa, hare, and harau;
likewise apāmārga, asyapatra, sūrya, durgā, hita, and ahita.
*Atimuktaka* is the vine known as *ośadhī*; *trīṭa* is the *lodhra* flower.
Dhattūra, Śiṃśapā, Mandāra, and Aparājitā are not beneficial for Sūrya or Viṣṇu; likewise, Damana is not beneficial for Śiva or Sūrya.

"Śiṃśayāti urā" (The Śiṃśapā tree is the breast). The worship of Śiva on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra is prescribed [for this], but is prohibited at other times. Now, the prohibited [times]:
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: the kṛṣṇalona, unmattaka, kāñcī, as well as girimallikā,
kaṇṭakārī, and any other flower devoid of fragrance [are not to be offered].
The Sun should not be worshipped with flowers produced from the *āmrātaka* tree;
if the reading is *āmrātakajaiḥ*, it should then be explained as "with *kuṭaja* flowers."
*Kṛṣṇalā* is known as *karañjī* or *ghoṃghacī*;
or it may be *kāñcī* or *vāhī*. *Girikarṇikā* is *aparājitā*. In the absence of *kaṇṭakī*, *javā* and *reṇukā* are to be used;
however, some say they are not even prohibited. Likewise, those [plants] which have no prohibition and are endowed with fragrance and color [are also acceptable].
Those flowers should be offered to the Sun, the light of the world;
all these are prescribed as offerings for his feet.
15b) He who, out of a desire for flowers, should climb the divine tree at that very moment—
the worshipper [should take] fragrant flowers and others as well.
Whether it be the killing of a Brahmin or the consumption of liquor, one is cooked here for eternal years.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who offers even a mere fragment of a *kṛtapañjaka* made of fire-stones upon the head of the Sun.
One shall remain upon half of Indra’s throne for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
in this way, the fruit should be understood in brief according to one's wealth.
This result should be understood to apply to others as well. Now, that which is forbidden for Śiva:
In that regard, the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa states: "One should avoid the flowers of the ketakī, atimukta, kunda, yūthī, madantikā, śirīṣa, sarja, and bandhūka."
*Madaṃtikā* is known as *madayantī* in the Gauḍa region; others say it is the *puṣpa* that resembles the *yūthī*. *Sarja* is the *śāla* tree. *Indrataru* is the *siṃdhuvāra*.
*Kundapuṣpa* is prescribed for the annual worship in the month of Māgha, but is forbidden at other times. Likewise:
One should avoid flowers that are scentless or have a pungent odor; however, even those devoid of fragrance, such as kuśa grass and the like, are to be accepted if they are pure.
Now, regarding Durgā: there is no specific prohibition at all. That has been stated again: "For the goddesses, one should avoid the *arka* and *mandāra*;

likewise for Sūrya, the *tagara*; for Śiva, one should avoid the *kunda*; and likewise for Hari, the *unmatta*. These prohibitions apply to other goddesses, but not to the form of Durgā. [She may be worshipped] with *karavīra* and *arka* flowers.
And with *śiṃśapā* and *aparājita* [trees].
Even a single *droṇa* flower for Lakṣmī is forbidden in the *Sāhasrī*.
Even for Viṣṇu, there is no prohibition regarding specific types of flowers.

And it has been said by Viṣṇu: "One should offer flowers that are not foul-smelling, nor those with a pungent odor, nor those produced from thorns—even if they are white and fragrant. One should not offer red flowers;
however, one may offer even red flowers if they are made of saffron or are water-born. In this regard, the water-born [lotus], saffron, pāṭalā, trisaṃdhyā, and karavīra [are recommended]."
Flowers from the pāribhadra, śamī, palāśa, aśoka, kuśa, and varja, as well as red flowers, are prohibited.
In the Viṣṇudharma: "The *kauṭaja*, the *śālmalī* flower, and the *śairīṣa* offered to Janārdana undoubtedly bestow fear and disease."
The flowers of the *krakara*, as well as those of the *dhattūra*,
the black *kuṭaja*, and the *arka*— these must never be offered to Janārdana.
[Krakara and karīraka. In the *Viṣṇurahasya*:

"One should not worship Viṣṇu with flowers that have already been used, nor with those fallen to the ground, nor with those that are withered, nor with those from which the petals have fallen, nor with those that have not yet blossomed."
In the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa*,
these words of Nārada were addressed to King Śantanu regarding the conquest of his splendor: "By means of those [powers] which are swiftly manifested and forcibly displayed..."
From this point forward, O lord of the earth, do not worship the remains of offerings (nirmālya) belonging to the divine Narasiṃha, nor those of other deities, O lord of the earth.
Thus end the prohibited flowers.
Now, the prescribed flowers and leaves are being described.
Regarding that, concerning the Sun,
it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* (16b):
Mālatī, Mallikā, Dūrvā, Kāśī, and Muktakā; Pāṭalā, Karavīra, Jayā, Jayantī, and likewise Aparājitā.
Caṃpaka, urrottaka, kunda, vāṇa, varvara, mallikā, aśoka, kubjaka, lodhra, and likewise vāṭarūṣaka.
Other hundred-petaled lotuses, as well as those called *vaka* and *anka*,
and likewise *agasti* and *kiṃśuka*, are for the purpose of worshipping the Sun.
*Mallikā* is well known as *velī*. *Pāṭalā* is well known as *pāḍarī*. *Atimuktaka* is the *mādhavī* creeper.
*Kubjaka* is *kūā*. *Rotaka* is *roharī*. *Vāṇa* is well known as *kṛṣṇageṃṭhī*. *Varvaramallikā* is well known as *vavarī*. *Āṭarūṣaka* is *vāsaka*. *Vṛkāhva* is well known as *kula*. Now...
Leaves: the bilva leaf, the śamī leaf, the leaf of bhṛṅgarāja,
and the tamāla leaf— these are always dear to Hari, O Tapana.
Tulasī, Kālatulasī, as well as red sandalwood,
and the leaf and flower of the Ketakī, bring immediate satisfaction to the Sun.
Now, regarding the specific flowers and specific fruits of the sun, it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
One obtains the same fruit from giving ten *niṣkas* of gold as one does from offering a single *karavīra* flower upon an *arka* tree.
Having partaken [of the meal], he who worships the Sun with *arka* flowers with a concentrated mind becomes like the Sun in splendor and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Japā, karavīra, bilva leaves,
padmaka, vakapuṣpa, darbha flowers, śamī flowers, and likewise utpala.
17a) He who worships Ravi with a thousand red lotuses, a hundred blue lotuses,
or with red *karavīra* flowers;
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
the glorious one, possessing prowess equal to the sun, shall dwell in the city of Arka.
Śamī flower and the blossom of bṛhatī are indeed equal; karavīra, jātī, vakula, and pāṭalā are likewise to be known as such.
The white mandāra flower and the white lotus are considered equal to that;
the nāgacaṃpaka, punnāga, and mudgara are likewise recorded as being equal.
Vṛhatī is Kaṇṭakārikā; Nāga is Nāgakesara; Mudgara is Vicakila; and Bahupatra is Mallikā. Now, regarding the flowers prescribed for Śiva, according to the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:

Having given a hundred pieces of gold to a worthy recipient endowed with the virtues of austerity and moral conduct who has mastered the Vedas, one obtains the same fruit as that of [giving] a flower.
Karavīra, uśīra, arka, unmatta,
pāṭalā, bṛhatī, and likewise girikarṇikā.
Likewise, the flowers of the kāsa, mandāra, aparājitā,
other śamī flowers, as well as kubjaka and śikhinī;
Apāmārga, lotus, the flower of *samī*, and *uṣaṇa*; likewise *campaka*, *uśīra*, *tagara*, and indeed *nāgakesara*.
The *puṃnāga*, the *kiṃkirāta*, and the auspicious *droṇapuṣpa*; likewise the *śiṃśapā*, the *udumbara*, as well as the *jayā* and the *mallikā*.
O auspicious one, the flowers of the *yajña* tree, as well as the beloved *vilva*,
the flowers of the *kusuma* tree, and likewise those of the *kaṅkata* tree [are offered].
Blue lotuses and water lilies, as well as red lotuses, and all fragrant flowers, both those growing on land and aquatic lotuses.
I take [her] upon my head; may she, through devotion, make me known to the Goddess. She is known as Śikhinī, Curikā, Kaṅkatī, Vyāghrapadī, and Ṭaṇṭārī.
Now, the specific fruits resulting from flowers offered to Śiva.

In that regard, the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa states: "By giving a *pala* of gold to one who is endowed with austerity, virtue, and good qualities, and who has mastered the Vedas, one obtains the fruit of [offering] flowers."
Likewise, by offering even a single arka flower to Śiva,
one obtains the same fruit as that gained by giving ten measures of gold.
Arka, karavīra, bilva, and the flower of the droṇa tree;
likewise apāmārga, kuśa flowers, and śamī flowers.
A single *dhattūraka* flower and even a single blue lotus (*utpala*) would be superior to thousands of [other flowers], each succeeding one being more excellent than the last.
Listen to the meritorious fruit of him who, with devotion and according to the prescribed rites, offers a garland of a thousand blue lotuses to Śiva.
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
the glorious one, possessing prowess equal to Śiva, shall dwell in the city of Śiva.
Whatever fruit has been proclaimed for the remaining varieties of flowers,
one is honored in the world of Śiva in accordance with that fruit.
Karavīra is to be known as equal to jātī, vakula, and pāṭala;
the white mandāra flower is also equal to that karavīra.
It is taught that [the leaves] are equal to the *nāgacaṃpaka*, *puṃnāga*, and *dhattūra*;
one should worship the *liṅga* with unbroken *bilva* leaves.
Completely liberated from all sins, that man who worships a liṅga even once with dhattūra flowers is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having obtained the fruit of a hundred thousand cows, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
one should worship a liṅga even once with devotion using vṛhatī flowers.
Having obtained the fruit of the gift of ten thousand cows, one shall go to Śiva.
Now, the flowers prescribed for Durgā.
In the Devīpurāṇa, Brahmā said:
Listen, Śakra, I shall explain in brief the meditation on flowers:
with flowers produced in their proper season, such as mallikā, jāti, and kubjaka;
With white and red flowers, as well as pale lotuses,
and with *kiṃśuka*, *tagara*, *kiṃkirāta*, and *campaka* blossoms.
And likewise with *vakula*, *mandāra*, *kunda* flowers,
*tirīṭaka*, *karavīra*, *arka* flowers, *śiṃśapā*, and *aparājita*.
With flowers of four kinds— white, red, yellow, and black—
and those produced from the *dhattūra*, *atimukta*, *bandhūka*, and *agasti* plants.
With *damanaka* flowers, *siṃduvāra*, fragrant *maruvaka*,
as well as with creepers of the *brahmavṛkṣa* and very tender stalks of *dūrvā* grass.
18b) With clusters of *kuśa* grass, very beautiful *bilva* leaves,
and red flowers, both aquatic and terrestrial;
One should worship with whatever leaves and flowers are available, auspiciously consisting of all medicinal herbs,
as well as with grains, all types of leaves, and flowers.
Now, the principal fruits of that very [practice] are as follows; in this regard, the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa states:

Whatever fruit is obtained when hundreds of thousands of gold pieces are given to a brahmin who is devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice and has mastered the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences; [that same fruit is obtained by honoring such a person].
O King, by worshipping Caṇḍikā with a garland of bilva leaves and with guggulu incense, one obtains that very fruit.
O lord of men, by worshipping Goddess Durgā with a garland of bilva leaves,
one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
He who worships Caṇḍikā with Karavīra flowers,
having obtained the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, is glorified in the world of Durgā.
Having worshipped Caṇḍikā with a garland of lotuses and then partaken [of the offering],
one attains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Durgā.
The man who worships Caṇḍikā with Vakapuṣpa flowers and fragrant powders obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Whoever worships Caṇḍikā with garlands of Droṇa flowers,
having obtained the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, is glorified in the world of Śakra.
He who worships Caṇḍikā with kuśa grass, flowers, and garlands,
having obtained the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, is glorified in the world of the ancestors.
Having worshipped the Noble One with faith using garlands of *śamī* flowers,
one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
He who worships Caṇḍikā with garlands of blue lotuses,
having obtained the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Among all flowers, the blue lotus is indeed preeminent;
he who offers a garland made of a thousand blue lotuses [attains great merit].
Listen to the meritorious fruit for one who worships Durgā according to the prescribed rites:
for thousands of crores of years and hundreds of crores of years.
Having become an attendant of Rudra, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
so too is he who worships Caṇḍikā with devotion using fragrant flowers.
Whether it be a *mālatī* or a *mallikā*, one shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Now, the rites prescribed for Viṣṇu are set forth in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa.
With *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jñānī*, *ketaka*, *aśoka*, and *campaka*; with *munnāga*, *nāgavakula*, *padmaka*, *utpala*, and other such [flowers].
The worship of Hari with these other flowers is also highly praised; whoever worships Him in this manner shall obtain the fruit of one gold coin for each flower.
In the Vāmana Purāṇa: "The jasmine, the śatāhvā, the sumanā, the kunda, the beautiful puṭa, as well as the vāṇa, the campaka, the aśoka, the karavīra, and the yūthikā."
Pāribhadra, Pāṭalā, Vakula, Giriśālinī, Tilaka, Jāsuvanaja, Pītaka, and also Tagara.
For these fragrant flowers, as well as others, are praised for the worship of Acyuta,
with the exception of the ketaki.
19b) *Ghattūraka* and *ketakī* are the flowers prescribed for the Narasiṃha form.
Regarding the phrase "elsewhere," some say these [plants] are prohibited. *Śatāhvā* is well known as *sauṃphu*; some call it *śatāvarī*.
*Sumanāḥ* is the golden jasmine (*suvarṇajātī*). *Cārupuṭa* is, according to some, the *vicakila*. *Pāribhadra* is the *phalahada*.
*Jāsuvanajña* is the *japā* flower. *Pītaka* is the *piyarī*. *Śaṃśayā* is also the *kuṣmāṇḍa*, according to the scriptures.
It is prescribed: "The breast is auspicious. It is written in the *Haribhakti* that there should be a design of Bandhūka flowers on the breast.
Even the leaf of the *jayantī* is prohibited in that very context. Now, regarding the leaves, the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa* states:
"First [the leaf] of the *apāmārga*, then the *bhṛṅgarāja*;
after that, the *khadira* is excellent, and following that, the *śamī* leaf."
The blade of dūrvā grass is superior to that; even more so is the blade of kuśa grass.
Damana is superior to that, and the leaf of the bilva tree is superior to that.
Even compared to the bilva leaf, the lasī leaf is superior for Hari;
and among these, he who worships Hari with leaves that have been stepped over [by others] is likewise [distinguished].
Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"A single Tulasī leaf is equal in value to a pala of gold."
O Indra among kings, it becomes equal [in merit] to what is given upon the head of Keśava.
There is no recipient equal to a Brahmin, no gift equal to fragrant incense,
no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, and no leaf equal to the Tulasī.
One should worship Hari with a hundred thousand Tulasī leaves during the month of Kārttika;
for every leaf offered, O best of sages, one obtains the fruit of a pearl.
Now, the flowers and fruits belong to Viṣṇu alone.
20a) In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa: "Austerity, virtuous conduct, and these qualities [are found] in a worthy recipient who has reached the further shore of the Veda."
Whatever fruit one may obtain by giving ten pieces of gold;
A mortal obtains that same fruit by offering a flower to Hari,
just as when a single *droṇa* flower is presented to Mādhava.
By giving ten pieces of gold, a man obtains that fruit;
O King, by means of a particular flower, one obtains a fruit even greater than that.
In this manner, listen to how the Puṣpottara [rite] should be performed,
with the *droṇapuṣpa*, the *khādira*, the *śamī*, the *bilva*, and likewise the *vaka*.
The *naṃdyāvarta*, *karavīra*, as well as the white *kiṃśuka*,
*śukapuṣpa*, *tamāla*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, and *ketakī*.
At the three junctions of the day, one should offer *mālatī* flowers, as well as white [flowers] at the three junctions,
and *kunda*, *śatapuṣpa*, *mallikā*, and *jāti* flowers.
Each subsequent one is superior to thousands of preceding ones;
among all varieties of flowers, the jasmine flower is the most excellent here.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who, with devotion and according to the prescribed rite, offers a most beautiful garland made of a thousand jasmine flowers to Viṣṇu.
For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas,
that glorious one, possessing prowess equal to Viṣṇu, shall dwell in the city of Viṣṇu.
Even thousands of offenses and hundreds of transgressions,
the Lord of Gods, when worshipped with even a single leaf, forgives with ease.
By worshipping the Lord of Gods, the Consort of Kamalā, with a single lotus,
one effects the destruction of sin for ten thousand times ten thousand years.
If the Lord whose banner is Garuḍa is worshipped with even a single *ketakī* petal,
one becomes a destroyer of gods, dwelling among the gods for a thousand years.
Whoever offers a golden *ketakī* flower to Janārdana,
the Garuḍa-bannered Lord removes the sins accumulated over ten million lifetimes.
In the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"O twice-born ones, one should indeed offer the leaves of the bhr̥ṅgarāja, the bilva, the vakapuṣpa,
and also those of the bījapūra."
The offering of even a single leaf to any one of these destroys great sins;
for them, flowers are praised as offerings, and they are adorned with garlands of sons.
Even its sprouts may serve as leaves for the worship of Hari;
likewise, all the gods are to be worshipped with flowers, trees, leaves, and sprouts of edible plants as prescribed.

"One should not worship Viṣṇu with unhusked grains (akṣata), nor Śiva with water from a conch. Barley is recommended for Viṣṇu; water from a conch is for others except for Śiva. This concludes the convention regarding the specification of flowers. Thus, in the absence of the prescribed flowers and leaves, other flowers and fruits may also be used.

That which is not prohibited is to be accepted. As for the statement, "With flowers produced in the forest, or with leaves grown on the mountain," this means that worship should be performed even with prescribed flowers that are not prohibited. Here, the word *vā* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and not the sense of option (*vikalpa*). However, the conjunction of many flowers and leaves is for the sake of their respective specific results.
Contradictory.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Chapter on Flowers," in the *Mantra-koṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhī.
21a) Now, regarding incenses (*dhūpa*). Among them, for the Sun, the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa* states:
"Fragrances such as *śumbha* and incenses such as *vijaya* [are offered]."
Furthermore, those who know the Dharma should always report this to Divākara.
O King, by burning guggulu resin along with clarified butter and likewise kuḍuruka incense,
one attains birth in the house of a knower of the four Vedas and experiences constant happiness.
By burning devadāru, nameru, śrīvāsa, kunduru,
and śrīphala mixed with rājya, one shall obtain prosperity.
Nameru is guggulu; some say it is a particular species of superior tree. Śrīvāsa is well known as that which originates from the śara reed. Kunduru is the resin of the sallakī tree.
By means of incense—one that is pungent yet fragrant—one attains heaven;
by means of incense made of camphor and agallochum, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
With *tuṣka* and *sihlaka*. Now, regarding Śiva: In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*, it is said:
"If one offers black agallochum (*kṛṣṇāguru*) and camphor as incense to Maheśvara continuously for half a month, hear now the fruit of that merit."

For thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas, that illustrious lord of the earth shall dwell in the auspicious city of Śiva; at the end of that time, he [shall attain liberation].
Now, regarding Durgā, it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"Black agallochum, camphor, sandalwood, and likewise storax..."
O lord of men, a person should offer this incense to the Blessed Lady.
One obtains desires in this world and is glorified in the realm of Durgā;
O bull among the Bharatas, one should offer guggulu resin mixed with ghee to Durgā.
21b) By worshipping according to the rules with devotion for half a month, one obtains the fruit of giving a thousand cows.
Of all incenses, guggulu is dear to Durgā.
Especially when combined with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), it constantly increases delight.
Now, regarding Viṣṇu: therein, Viṣṇu [prescribes] that no product of a living being should be used for the purpose of incense. In the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:
"Ruhikākṣa, kaṇa, dāru, sihlaka, aguru, and white [fragrance]..."

Conch, nutmeg, and *ruhikākṣa* (which is *jaṭāmāṃsī*)—these are indeed the favorite incense materials for Viṣṇu (*śrīśa*). *Kuṇa* is *guggulu*; *dāru* is *devadāru*; *śitā* is camphor (though some say it is sugar); and *śaṅkha* is *nakhī*. Thus, for Viṣṇu (*śrīśe*). Likewise:
O Indra among kings, the devoted Narasiṃha then offers as incense guggulu known as mahiṣa, combined with sugar.
Perfumed and freed from all sins,
he shines resplendent in a celestial chariot accompanied by hosts of apsarases.
Having reached the world of Vāyu, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. Now, regarding initiations (*dīkṣā*): therein, concerning the Sun, it is said in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"Furthermore, having lit a lamp with ghee or with sesame oil..."
He goes to the world of the Sun, surrounded by hundreds of millions of lamps.
He is glorified in the world of heroes, which consists of all the worlds.
Now, regarding Śiva, [it is said] in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
By the offering of a ghee lamp to Śiva,
one obtains a divine celestial chariot extending for a hundred yojanas, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
22a) The offering of an oil lamp to Śiva is forbidden.
Now, [the ritual] for Durgā.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
If a person lights a lamp with either ghee or oil,
he obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Durga.
He who worships Caṇḍikā by offering a lamp of oil,
having obtained the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, rejoices together with men.
Now, [the ritual] for Viṣṇu.
Nothing at all should be used for the purpose of a lamp except ghee or sesame oil.
In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
If a person should light a lamp with ghee or oil for Viṣṇu according to the rules and with devotion, hear now the fruit of his merit.
Having abandoned all evil, possessing a radiance equal to a thousand suns,
he attains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Vishnu.
Now, regarding the procedure for the offering of lamps, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"Having given those [lamps], one should not harm them, nor should they be devoid of oil;
however, one who steals a lamp is reborn as a mouse in a lowly state."
Yama is common to all.
By the offering of flowers to the deities, one is born endowed with prosperity;
and that man who offers incense attains an exalted state.
He shines, illuminating the world, like a sighted man holding a lamp.
Now, regarding food offerings (*naivedya*). Among these, concerning the Sun, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*:
