One should prepare well-prepared food from one prastha of shali rice;
having offered the caru-oblation to Surya, especially on the seventh lunar day.
22b) A *prastha* consists of sixteen *palas*.
Samyāva, kṛśara, apūpa, and pāyasa, as well as samyāvaka;
curd-rice, rasāla, modakas, pūḍikās, and aṅgulas.
For as many grains of rice as there are in that food offering by count,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the world of the Sun.
Rasālā is a milk-based preparation containing sugar, spices, and fruit.
In the offering of water, rice-pudding, ghee,
and various foods, the merit is ten times greater when they are sprinkled with ghee and offered as fried cakes.
For in whatever measure the objects of sense are sweet, fragrant, and consist of foods, drinks, meats, and their fruits, to that same extent [is the result].
He who offers to the Sun a vessel made of Arka leaves, filled and accompanied by the Madhuparka offering,
shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Having placed a pure and auspicious mirror before the Sun,
he should adorn its perimeter with white garlands and sandalwood paste.
One is honored in the world of the Sun for thousands of kalpas;
by the gift of a mirror to another, an equal fruit shall arise.
Now, for Śiva.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
One should prepare a prastha of śāli rice and make well-prepared food;
one should especially offer this caru-oblation to Śiva on the fourteenth day.
For as many grains of rice as there are in that food offering by count,
for that many thousands of years one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
23a) One should offer molasses, sugar-candy, ghee,
and various foods; one should also present well-ripened fruits such as the mātuluṅga.
Now, [the ritual] for Durgā.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
One should give food unmixed with jaggery, sugar-candy, and the like;
having attained the fruit of being a Vaiṣṇava, such a person who honors human guests is glorified in the world of the Sun.
O King, by the gift of jaggery, sugar-candy, ghee, and likewise of sugar,
as well as of foods cooked with ghee, one attains the state of Brahmā.
He who offers rice cooked with milk, sweetened curd-milk, as well as drinks and jujube fruits to Durgā, goes to the abode of Śiva.
O Indra among kings, he who offers water, a ketaki flower, or white sandalwood paste dedicated to Durgā shall become a leader of the Gaṇas.
Śaśikarpūra;
and he who offers mangoes, coconuts, dates, and citrons to Durgā shall go to the supreme state.
Now, [the ritual] for Viṣṇu.
Therein, Viṣṇu [is the deity].
One should not consume buffalo milk for the purpose of an offering; however, one may consume cow's milk, curd, and ghee.
A goat is praised as fit for a boatman; likewise, the buffalo, the sheep, and the goat are declared unfit for sacrifice. So too are the meat of five-nailed animals, the boar, and fish.
In the Varāha Purāṇa.
Everything made of rice should be taken, all of it auspicious and endowed with flavor;
this should be offered with the mantra, and no one at all should touch it.
23b) *iṅgudī* fruits, *vilva*s, *badara*s, and *āmalaka*s; as well as *kharjūrī*, *panasa*, and indeed the fruit of the *punnāga*.
By [offering] a sprout of betel vines, one shall attain the heavenly realm,
as well as supreme good fortune in this world and unsurpassed beauty.
The word "kiśalaya" (sprout) is to be understood as the remainder [of the category].

Many such fruits, roots, vegetables, and so forth have been mentioned for the purpose of the *naivedya* (food offering). They have not been written here due to the bulk of the text. With the exception of Śiva, the meat of all [animals] may be offered.
And the water from the feet (pādodaka) should be drunk. This is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"It bestows immediate fruit, it is meritorious, it destroys all sins;
it is the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the destroyer of all suffering."
The auspicious water from Viṣṇu’s feet is meritorious and destroys evil dreams;
he in whose stomach resides the water from Viṣṇu’s feet and the food offered to him (naivedya).
One does not incur misfortune through sin; rather, it perishes by itself.
Likewise, he who drinks even as much as a drop of water from the Śālagrāma stone [is purified].
Furthermore, a man who possesses liberation need not drink his mother’s milk again;
what purpose is served by consuming thousands of millions of sacred bathing places?
If one drinks even a drop of water originating from a Śālagrāma stone, [it is as if one has performed] the five-fold service (pañcopacāra). Thus ends the section on the five-fold service.
The sixteen modes of service, however, are as follows:

Invocation, welcome, offering of a seat, water for the feet, water for sipping, water for bathing, garments, sacred thread, scents, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, joining of palms in reverence, circumambulation, and dismissal.
Now, the gifts to be given to the Sun.
In this regard, [it is stated] in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
One should worship the Sun with garments that are dear to oneself, as well as with other auspicious articles; likewise, one should honor the Lord of Auspicious Light.
The garments were most variegated, substantial, and soft;
they were new, substantial, and possessed a fresh luster, yet were devoid of hair.
For as many thousands of years as the number of threads in that garment is said to be, for so long one is honored in the world of the Sun.
A sacred thread (*upavīta*) made of three strands, white or bright yellow, fashioned from silk thread or similar material,
should be offered with curd to the Sun by those who have mastered two Vedic branches and the Vedāṅgas.
Having fashioned a divine white great banner, or one with seven colors,
resounding with a network of small bells and adorned with a peacock-feather parasol.
But that man who, endowed with supreme faith, gives this Arka-plant,
rejoices in heaven like a god for a hundred divine Manvantaras.
One who gives an umbrella made of a jeweled handle, or one made of silver, gold, and so forth,
rejoices in the worlds of the Sun, seated upon an excellent celestial chariot.
Whoever should fasten a great bell with a loud sound, joined with a chain and made of bronze or iron, in a temple of the gods;
The glorious follower of the Son of the Sun (Yama), who is exceedingly dear to Vradhna,
[plays] the bherī, mṛdaṅga, paṭaha, ḍamaru, muraja, and other drums.
He who offers musical instruments made of bamboo, bell-metal,
and other materials to Vradhna is honored in the world of Vradhna for ten thousand divine ages.
Having given even a small or a large amount of materials for the Sun’s sacrifice according to one's own wealth and disposition,
one is glorified in the world of the Sun.
From that, the solar region is equal in extent to the practice of the Bhāskara [mantra];
for embodied beings who die here, it brings about union with the Sun.
O King, this measurement of the solar field established by men is traditionally recorded;
one should designate it as half a krośa, or even half of that, or half again.
Therefore, one should construct dwellings provided with solar courtyards; near the vicinity of the temple of Manu, whatever water stands before it [should be utilized].
She is called Sūryagā; one who bathes there shall go to heaven.
Whoever constructs a long pond, a step-well, or a tank at the abode of the Sun [attains the same].
By giving cows, or even buffaloes, elephants, or horses from his vessel, one rescues a hundred generations of his lineage and is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who makes a gift to the Sun:
it is inexhaustible for the fulfillment of all desires, and he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
Listen to the fruit of merit for that lord of the earth who gives to the Sun the earth endowed with water and capable of causing all crops to sprout.
O best of beings, for as many thousands of yugas as there are particles of dust found upon the surface of the earth, he is honored in the world of the Sun.
One should fashion a grove for Rāma, adorned with *rāma*, *vilva*, and other trees, as well as *jātī*, *jaṃbīra*, *nāraṅga*, *karavīra*, and *kubjaka* shrubs.
As many leaves, flowers, creepers, and fruits as there are,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the world of the Sun.
Thus, many causes of merit have been indicated; they are not written out here for fear of excessive length. The mention of the sun is merely an illustration.
In this same manner, everything regarding Śiva, Durgā, and Viṣṇu should also be understood for the purpose of attaining their respective worlds.

Since describing each of these individually would result in excessive prolixity, the procedure for the ritual substances of worship is given in brief. All these materials for worship, purified by the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), should be offered to the deities.
As for mantras, for those of the three twice-born castes (*traivarṇika*), the Vedic ones alone are primary; for others, they are secondary.

Mantras are those employed in the Āgamas and similar scriptures. In their absence, however, for the three higher castes as well as for women and Śūdras, only those mantras declared in the Pañcarātra are primary, not the Vedic ones, because they lack authority over the latter. Therefore, even for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, the mantras mentioned in the Āgamas are admissible provided they are not in contradiction with the Vedas. And it has been said:

In the *Vārāha Purāṇa* it is said: "In the absence of Vedic mantras, the procedure prescribed in the *Pañcarātra* is [to be followed]. Furthermore, it is stated that the mantras taught in the *Āgamas* possess potency (*savīrya*). Likewise, in the *Prapañca*:
"In the Kṛta age, [the path] is according to the way taught in the Śrutis; in the Tretā age, through the state of praise (*stutibhāva*)."
In the Dvāpara age, [the teachings] were spoken as Purāṇas; in the Kali age, they arise from the Āgamas.
For Brahmins born in the Kali age are like Śūdras;
their accomplishment shall come through the path of traditional scripture (Āgama), not by the Vedic way.
If some best of the twice-born has performed his duties and conquered his senses, the Sāvitrī and other mantras will certainly bear fruit for him; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, these [mantras], when received from the mouth of a guru preceded by initiation (dīkṣā), lead to the attainment of results; they do not do so otherwise.
And likewise, because it is heard that for one who is uninitiated there is what is undesirable:
"For the uninitiated, all that is done through the left [hand] is fruitless."
A man who is always devoid of initiation always attains birth in the womb of a beast.
A mantra performed by chance, one that is concealed, or one whose fruit is merely logical;
or where the meaning is seen to be contrary to the Gāthās—that [mantra] is useless.
Furthermore, for one who has correctly mastered even a single mantra, there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished;
what then to say of a man possessing many mantras—he is indeed Vyāsa himself.
Therefore, even a single mantra should be received through initiation and mastered from the mouth of the Guru; for this reason, these mantras are explained here in detail.
It is not the case that mantras which have not been received preceded by initiation from the mouth of the Guru are capable of yielding fruit, nor otherwise.
For it is said:
"If a disciple, out of affection, greed, or partiality toward his own kin, should initiate one who is unworthy, then the offense against the deity falls upon that guru."
Thus, out of fear of displeasing the deities, a mantra must be imparted only after initiation; that initiation is now briefly explained.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Ritual Substances," in the *Śrīmantrakośa*.
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall explain initiation (dīkṣā),
without which the entire fruit of mantra cannot be obtained.
Because it bestows divine knowledge and thereby effects the destruction of sins,
it is for that reason called "dīkṣā" by the teachers who are knowers of the Tantras.

Although initiation is of four kinds, nevertheless, for the sake of convenience regarding place, time, and other factors, the procedure for initiation for one who performs ritual action is here stated in brief.
26a) Therein, first is the examination of the teacher and the disciple.
Of pure lineage and stainless, devoted to purified conduct,
belonging to a stage of life (āśramin), free from anger, and a knower of the true meaning of all scriptures.
One whose intellect is fixed upon the worship of the Saguna forms, who is grateful, affectionate toward disciples,
skillful in bestowing grace through the physical form, and devoted to the Great Mantra.
One who knows the measure of the *ahāyo* [the breath], whose tradition is pure, and who is an abode of compassion—
one endowed with such characteristics as these would be a Guru, a treasure-house of majesty.
The disciple should be of pure lineage, illustrious, humble, and pleasing in appearance;
truthful in speech, devoted to merit, possessed of vast intellect, and free from hypocrisy.
A disciple who possesses such characteristics as being youthful, self-controlled, having all his faculties intact, and being an abode of compassion is entitled to initiation.
Now, the months for initiation during the pure period.
Initiation in Caitra would be painful; in Vaiśākha, it bestows all accomplishments;
in Jyeṣṭha, it would bring about death; and in Āṣāḍha, it destroys one's kinsmen.
In Śrāvaṇa, it bestows prosperity upon men; in Bhādra, it is not so, as it brings about suffering.
In Āśvina, there shall be success in all things; in Kārttika, it bestows an increase in knowledge.
In Mārgaśīrṣa she is Śubhakṛt, and in Pauṣa she is Jñānavināśinī;
in Māgha she is Medhāvṛddhidā, and in Phālguna she is Vijayapradā.
The bright fortnight is more auspicious than the dark fortnight; among the lunar days, those excluding the Riktās and the Kuhū are preferred.

26b) The constellations are Uttara, Trayarohiṇī, Citrā, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, Revatī, Puṣyā, Aśvinī, Hasta, and Nakṣatra. The days of the week are all except Maṅgala (Tuesday). The fixed signs (sthiralagna) are those known as Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius.
Now follows the ritual application.

Therein, first of all, having performed the recitation for well-being (*svasti*) and the auspicious day of success (*ṛddhipuṇyāha*), one should choose a preceptor (*ācārya*). Having given a three-dimensional image (*tri-paṭi*) along with ornaments and other offerings according to one's capacity, [one should say]: "Today, etc., from you, I wish to receive such-and-such a mantra."

In order to perform the rites such as the *homa* which constitute the limbs (*aṅga*) of that [ceremony], I choose you, [Name] of such-and-such lineage, [Name] of such-and-such *śarma*, student of such-and-such Veda, for the office of *guru*, with these sandalwood paste, betel leaves, unbroken rice, betel nut, ornaments, and garments;
"I am chosen," is the reply. Then—
The Guru, having entered into a state of intoxication (*mada*), prepares four *argha* vessels;

having placed white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, tips of *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, flowers, water, and fruits therein, he takes up the *argha* and says: "For the liberation from bonds of the bound souls (*paśus*) submerged in the ocean of worldly existence, I salute You alone as my refuge; You who are ever-fond of devotion."

"O God of gods, grant me permission; by your grace, I shall release these bound souls (paśus) who are fettered by the bonds of material nature (prakṛti). Having thus offered the arghya, [he recites]: "Salutation to Anantāsana; salutation to Vimalāsana; salutation to Yogāsana; salutation to Padmāsana."
Having offered *kuśa* grass consecrated with these mantras and having worshipped the seat, one should sit there facing the east and say: "Oṃ, salutation to the Gurus; oṃ, salutation to Gaṇapati.
Having thus worshipped the Guru and Gaṇapati on the left and right sides respectively,

and having placed the articles of worship on the right side and the food offerings (naivedya) and so forth on the left side, one should light lamps with ghee using wicks containing camphor. Immediately thereafter, [one should light others] with five-colored [wicks].
Having constructed one of the mandalas, such as the Sarvatobhadra,

having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and the placement of the letters of the alphabet (mātṛkānyāsa), and having performed the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and the placement of syllables upon his own body for the mantra to be given;
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra*, one should worship up to the *ādhāra-śakti* and so forth, ending at Meru and extending as far as the heart.
Above that, one should worship Dharma and the other [qualities] upon the two shoulders, the two thighs, and the corners of the pedestal.
One should worship Adharma and the others upon the face, the sides, the navel, the flanks, and the limbs of the pedestal, within the heart-lotus.

One should contemplate [the deity] from the *satva* principle up to the ultimate reality (*paratattva*). Having worshipped there with mental offerings (upacāras) from the *pīṭha* up to the end of the worship, one should mentally resolve that the deity resides within one's own heart. Then, one should begin the installation of the arrow (*śara*) in front.

There, for the fire: having worshipped the ground for the *argha* offering with "Oṃ, salutation to the fire-maṇḍala, whose self consists of the ten dharma-kalās," [one worships] "Oṃ, to the sun-maṇḍala...

Having worshipped the vessel placed there with the mantra "Obeisance to the one whose self consists of the twelve meanings and digits," and having washed the conch upon it with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ" and performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*),
and having poured water into it with the root mantra, [he worships] the water with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the lunar mandala whose self consists of the sixteen nectar-digits."

Having worshipped [them], one should offer sandalwood with the mantra "svāhā," unbroken rice grains (akṣata) with the mantra "vaṣaṭ," perform the veiling (avaguṇṭhana) with the mantra "hum," and protect them with the mantra "astrāya phaṭ. Then, at that place, one should say: "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, please be present in this water!"
Having invoked the *tīrtha* waters, displayed the *gāminī* and *dhenu* mudrās, and protected them with his own mudrā,

he should cover the conch with both hands, recite the root mantra ten times, and pour that water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel situated on the right side; with that water, he should sprinkle himself and the sacrificial ground.

Then, having worshipped the deity conceived as one's own body upon the *dhāra-pīṭha* with the concluding mantra, and having invoked the Lord there into the heart-lotus, one should worship Him with five handfuls of flowers on one's own head, heart, *mūlādhāra*, feet, and all limbs—excluding the food offering (*naivedya*). Then, one should invoke the Lord into the conch. Then...
One should then add the eight fragrant substances (gandhāṣṭaka) there. They are as follows:
sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, chora, saffron, gorocana, jaṭāmāṃsī, and kapi—these they know as the eight fragrances of Śakti.
Caurakacūru; Kapiḥsī.
28a) Sandalwood, agallochum, hrīvera, kuṣṭha, saffron, sevyaka,
jaṭāmāṃsī, and murā— these are considered the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu.
*Hrīvera* is camphor-water; *sevyaka* is *sīra*; and *mura*.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, tamāla, water (jal), saffron, kuśīta, and kuṣṭha— these constitute the eightfold Śaiva fragrance.
Thus, having stirred the eightfold perfumes according to the respective deities within the conch, one should invoke all the *kalās* therein and worship them.
Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to Amṛtā (1); Oṃ āṃ, to Mānadā (2); Oṃ iṃ, to Pūṣā (3); Oṃ īṃ, to Tuṣṭi (4); Oṃ uṃ, to Puṣṭi (5); Oṃ ūṃ, to Rati (6); Oṃ ṛṃ, to Dhṛti (7); Oṃ ṝṃ, to Śaṅkhinī (8);
Oṃ ḷṃ, to Caṇḍikā (9); Oṃ ḹṃ, to Kānti (10); Oṃ eṃ, to Jyotsnā (11); Oṃ aiṃ, to Śrī (12).

12 Oṃ Oṃ, obeisance to Mr̥ti; 13 Oṃ Ūṃ, obeisance to Aṅgadā; 14 Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Pūrṇā; 15 Oṃ Aḥ, obeisance to Pūrṇāmṛtā. Having worshipped thus, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths): "The vital breaths of Amr̥tā and the other lunar digits (*somakalā*) are here; the life-force (*jīva*) of Amr̥tā and the others is established here. Amr̥tādīnāṃ... [etc.]

May all the sense organs—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and breath—of Amṛta and the others come here and remain for a long time in happiness; Svāhā! Again, I invoke the twelve digits (kalās) beginning with Tapanī. Having thus invoked them: Kaṃ Bhaṃ, obeisance to Tapanī. 1 Khaṃ Vaṃ, obeisance to Tāpinī. 2 Gaṃ Phaṃ... 3

One should worship as follows: *dhūmrāyai* 3 *ghaṃ yaṃ*; *marīcyai* 4 *ṅaṃ maṃ*; *jvālinyāi* 5 *caṃ dhaṃ*; *rucyai* 6 *chaṃ daṃ*; *suṣumṇāyai* 7 *jaṃ thaṃ*; *bhogadāyai* 8 *jhaṃ taṃ*; *viśvāyai* 9 *ñaṃ ṇaṃ*;
*rodhinyai* 10 *ṭaṃ ḍhaṃ*; *dhāriṇyai* 11 *ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ*; *kṣamāyai*. Thus one should worship.

In the same manner, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the rite of installing the vital breaths), [reciting] "The vital breaths of the solar digits (*kalā*) beginning with *tapanī* are here the vital breaths," and so forth. Again, one should invoke [the deities], saying, "I invoke the ten digits of fire beginning with *dhūmrārcis*."

One should worship the digits of Fire (agnikalā) as follows: "Obeisance to Dhūmrārciṣī" (1), "to Uṣmā" (2), "to Jvalinī" (3), "to Jvālinī" (4), "to Visphuliṅgī" (5), "to Suśrī" (6), "to Svarūpā" (7), "to Kapilā" (8), "to Havyavāhanā" (9), and "obeisance to Kavyavāhanā" (10). Thus one should worship. Of the digits of Fire...

"Prāṇā iha prāṇā," and so forth. Then, the kalās of the Praṇava: one should invoke the ten kalās of Brahmā, who consists of the kalās of the letter *a*, beginning with Sṛṣṭi, with the mantra "I invoke [the kalās]," and worship them with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). *kaṃ* to Sṛṣṭi, obeisance; 1. *khaṃ* to Ṛddhi; 2. *gaṃ* to Smṛti; 3. *ghaṃ* to Medhā; 4. *ṅaṃ* to Kānti; 5. *caṃ*...

Having worshipped with: "Oṃ Lakṣmyai ṣaṃ namaḥ" (6), "Oṃ Dūtyai chaṃ namaḥ" (7), "Oṃ Sthirāyai jaṃ namaḥ" (8), "Oṃ Sthityai jhaṃ namaḥ" (9), and "Oṃ Siddhyai ñaṃ namaḥ" (10); [one performs] the installation of the vital breaths for the principles beginning with *sṛṣṭi* (creation) with the mantra: "The vital breaths of these are here, the vital breaths... and so forth; and [recites]: "Haṃsaḥ śuciṣad vasur antarikṣasad hotā vediṣad atithir duroṇasat..."

Having invoked with the *Ṛgveda* verse, "nṛṣad varasad vṛttasad vyomasad abjā gojā ṛtajā adrijāritaṃ vṛhat," one should worship. Then, having invoked with the words, "I invoke the ten kalās of Viṣṇu, whose essence is the syllable *ukāra*, beginning with Jarā," [one worships] with: *ṭaṃ janāyai namaḥ* (1), *ṭhaṃ pālinyai* (2), *ḍaṃ śāntyai* (3).
Ḍhaṃ to Aiśvaryā 4; ṇaṃ to Ratyai 5; taṃ to Vāmikāyai 6; thaṃ to Varadāyai 7; daṃ to Hlādinyai 8; dhaṃ to [Name] 9; naṃ to Dīrghāyai, obeisance! 10.

Thus one should worship. [One should perform the invocation of] the vital breaths of old age and so forth with the mantra "The vital breaths of old age are here, the vital breaths... and so on. Then, having invoked with the *ṛc*: "This Viṣṇu is praised for his heroic power; like a terrifying wild beast, he dwells in the mountains; in whose three wide strides all worlds abide," one should worship. Then [one worships] the form of Rudra consisting of the letter *M*.

Having invoked them with the words, "I invoke the ten digits beginning with Tīkṣṇā," [one offers salutation] as follows: *Paṃ* to Tīkṣṇā, *Namaḥ*; *Phaṃ* to Rodrī, *Namaḥ*; *Vaṃ* to Tayā, *Namaḥ*; *Bhaṃ* to Nidrā, *Namaḥ*; *Maṃ* to Taṃdrā, *Namaḥ*; *Yaṃ* to Kṣudhā, *Namaḥ*; *Raṃ* to Krodhinī, *Namaḥ*;
*Laṃ* to Kriyā, *Namaḥ*; *Vaṃ* to Utkārī, *Namaḥ*; *Śaṃ* to Mṛtyurūpā, *Namaḥ*. Thus [is the invocation] for Tīkṣṇā and the others.

"The vital breaths of the ten digits are here the vital breaths," and so forth. Then, having invoked with the mantra: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may he release us from death as the cucumber from its stem, for the sake of immortality," one should perform worship. Then, having invoked the four digits beginning with Pītā with the words "I invoke," [one offers] "Obeisance to Pītā" (1).

One should worship with: "Oṃ Saṃ to Saṃkhyetā, Haṃ to Aruṇā, Kṣaṃ to Asitā, [and] Namaḥ. Then, having invoked the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of the yellow and other colors, and so forth, one should worship after invoking with: "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our intellects. Then, having invoked the sixteen digits (*kalās*) beginning with Nivṛtti with the words "I invoke," [one worships] Aṃ...
Salutation to Nivṛtti 1; Āṃ, to Pratiṣṭhā 2; Iṃ, to Vidyā 3; Īṃ, to Śānti 4; Uṃ, to Indhikā 5; Ūṃ, to Dīpikā 6; Ṛṃ, to Recikā 7; Ṝṃ, to Mocikā 8; Ḷṃ, to Sūkṣmā 9; Ḹṃ... 29b) ...ḹṃ.

One should worship with: "Oṃ Sūkṣmāmṛtāyai namaḥ" (10), "Eṃ Jñānāyai namaḥ" (11), "Aiṃ Jñānāmṛtāyai namaḥ" (12), "Uṃ Āpyāyinyai namaḥ" (13), "Ūṃ Vyāpinyai namaḥ" (14), "Aṃ Vyomarūpāyai namaḥ" (15), and "Aḥ Anantāyai namaḥ" (16).
Then, for the sixteen kalās beginning with Nivṛtti, one should perform: "The vital breaths of Nivṛttyādi-kalās are here, the vital breaths are here," and so forth. Immediately thereafter—

Having invoked the verse, "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ shape the forms; may Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you," one should worship. Thus, having performed the worship of the Kalās in the conch, one should worship with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) the lotus situated in the center of the *Sarvatobhadra* or other mandalas, specifically in its pericarp (*karṇikā*).
Having placed rice grains upon that, rice husks upon those, *kuśa* grass upon those,
and a bundle of *kuśa* grass upon that, one should worship the pedestal (*pīṭha*) there, together with its foundational powers (*ādhāra-śakti*) and so forth;
upon that, one should place a pitcher made of gold, silver, or copper, or in its absence, one that is free from cracks.

Having placed the jar—which has a beautiful form, is free from defects such as discoloration, is wound all around with triple-stranded threads, is fumigated with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and whose interior has been washed with the *astra* mantra—one should install it while reciting the *praṇava*.
Then, having cast the five jewels into the middle of the jar, [one should recite]: *kṣaṃ laṃ haṃ saṃ ṣaṃ śaṃ vaṃ*.
laṃ raṃ yaṃ maṃ bhaṃ vaṃ phaṃ paṃ naṃ dhaṃ daṃ thaṃ taṃ ṇaṃ ḍhaṃ ḍaṃ ṭhaṃ ṭaṃ ñaṃ jhaṃ jaṃ chaṃ caṃ ṅaṃ ghaṃ gaṃ khaṃ kaṃ aṃḥ aṃ 30a)

Reciting the *viloma-mātṛkā*— namely *ūṃ uṃ aiṃ eṃ ḹṃ ḷṃ ṝṃ ṛṃ ūṃ uṃ īṃ iṃ āṃ aṃ*— as well as the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), one should fill [the vessel] with flowers, camphor, and other white, meritorious waters. Then, taking a small amount of water from the conch, one should contemplate the thirty-eight *kalās*.

The fifty *kalās*, the five *vyomans*, and the root mantra—these four constitute the essence of the deity; having taken them three times each, one should pour them into the pitcher. Then, having covered the mouth of the pitcher with the bedding of a horse and tender mango sprouts entwined with *indravallī*, one should regard it as the celestial tree (*suradruma*). Therein...

One should place a cup made of bell-metal or consisting of fruit. Then, one should wrap the pitcher with a pair of stainless linen cloths—*indravallī* being well-known as *idāruṇa*. In the absence of linen, having wrapped it even with two pieces of cloth and having meditated upon the form of the deity within the pitcher while reciting the root mantra.

One should display the six mudrās, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana). Then, having worshipped the deity there according to the previously mentioned procedure with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra), and having recited the mantra as many times as possible, one should offer the remaining services, present the offerings, and give the parasol, fly-whisk, and so forth, as well as betel leaf (tāmbūla). Having thus performed the worship, [one should attend to] the fire.

Having established [the fire] there according to the ritual of one's own *gṛhya* tradition, one should offer a single oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) for each of the principal deity, the pedestal deities (*pīṭhadevatā*), and so forth, in their respective order, using their individual names followed by *svāhā*. Then,
having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the deity with her specific *śakti*-root mantra, [one should proceed with] the limbs of the self (*svāṅga*) and so on.

30b) Having offered one oblation for each of the obstacles (varaṇas) by their respective names, he should again complete the fire sacrifice (homa), ending with the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). Then the disciple, together with his wife, should give a golden ring to the preceptor (guru).

Immediately thereafter, the Guru, having led the disciple near the fire, should bind the disciple’s eyes with a cloth while reciting the Netra-mantra. Then, taking the disciple by the hand while his eyes remain bound, he should lead him to the vicinity of the water-pot (kalaśa) and cause him to enter. Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā-letters upon the disciple’s body and having filled the disciple’s joined palms with flowers, [he should proceed].

In accordance with the prescribed rite, one should cast [the offerings] while reciting the root mantra for the pleasure of the deities of the jar (*kalaśadevatā*). Then, having removed the blindfold from the body of the disciple, one should dissolve the *mātṛkā* letters from *kṣa* down to *a* in reverse order according to the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and subsequently generate them through emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) in the forward order starting from *a*.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the Goddess’s mantra, one should worship the chosen deity residing within the water-pot (*kumbha*) with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). Then, having seated the disciple upon another mandala and accompanied by all musical instruments and the blessings of Brahmins,
one should lift up the pot while mentally reciting the *Mātṛkā* [syllabary] over the celestial trees situated at its opening.

One should sprinkle the heads of the disciples with waters consecrated by the root-mantra. Immediately after the consecration, having performed the *nīrājana* rite for the disciple using a cup filled with the water from the mouth of the ritual jar, and having dressed him in two pure garments, one should seat him near oneself.
Then, once he has sipped water and is seated facing the east,
the Guru, facing north, should slowly whisper the mantra into his right ear.

One should first offer water to the Brāhmaṇa. Having received the mere instruction from others, the disciple should recite [the mantra] eight times. Thereafter, the oneness of the Guru, the mantra, the deity, and the name of the disciple must be realized by both; then, having grasped the two feet of the Guru and placed them upon one's head.

One should offer one’s body, wealth, and life—all of it—to the guru. The guru, in turn, should say to the disciple who has completed his training: "Arise, dear child; you are gentle and possessed of perfect conduct. With a joyful mind, the disciple should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru. And it is said: "One should give the entire sacrificial fee to the guru."
With a joyful mind, he should afterwards gratify the Brahmins with various kinds of food and edibles, along with sacrificial fees.

In the *Prapañcasāra* as well: "Having bowed again to the Supreme Self who has assumed a body, one should give half of one's own wealth to the Guru, or a fourth part, or even a tenth; or else, setting aside what can be accomplished with material wealth, one should offer one's own body with a mind that is not subject to it. And it is said in the *Tantrarāja*: "From a teacher who is not [qualified]..."

A mantra that has been obtained, and repeatedly obtained, yet for which no sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is given— even if it is constantly recited— does not attain success. A practitioner who maintains constant devotion toward three things— the mantra, the preceptor of the mantra, and the deity of the mantra— attains his desired goal both in this world and after death.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Brief Exposition of Initiation," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhī.
31b) Now follows the examination of the suitability of the teacher and the disciple.
A Brahmin who is pure by descent from both mother and father, belonging to a lineage of purity through successive generations,
and who has completed the preparatory rites (puraścaraṇa) for mantras and the pure paths, is a Guru.
A Brāhmaṇa becomes fit after eight years and one month, a Kṣatriya king after two years and eight months,
a Vaiśya after three years, and a Śūdra after four years from the teacher.
One who is desirous of hearing [the teachings] should be accepted for the initiatory rites, sacrifices, vows, and so forth.
Now, the blending of mantras.
For it is said: "There is no friend equal to a mantra, nor is there an enemy equal to a mantra. Therefore, one should examine [the mantra] in many ways.
It is stated in the Āgama:
"Through secret instruction, the mantra protects, or rather, the practitioner (manu) is protected by it."
For one who recites [the mantra], it shall thoroughly purify the manifold afflictions born of the fear of cyclic existence.

According to the distinctions of the accomplished, the to-be-accomplished, and so forth; by one's own family or another family; by the divisions of child, adult, and old; and likewise by female, male, and neuter.
It is characterized by divisions of zodiac signs and lunar mansions, as well as by states such as sleeping or waking,
and further distinguished by portions of debt and wealth.
For instance, having divided [the diagram] into sixteen squares:

Indra (1), Agni (3), Rudra (11), Nava (9), Netra (3), Yuga (12), Dik (10), and Rtu (6)—by these [numbers], the Siddhas are established in the eight directions. [The sequence is: Siddha, Ari (Enemy), then Siddha, Ari-stha (Stationed with Enemy), Siddha, Sādhya, and then again Siddha. Siddha.
Susiddha-siddha; Siddha-ari; Sādhya-siddha; Sādhya-sādhya; Sādhya-susiddha; Sādhya-ari; Susiddha-siddha; Susiddha-sādhya; Susiddha-susiddha; Susiddha-ari. 32a)

The wise one should sequentially inscribe the letters born of the *lipi* (script) in the squares: sixteen (16), fourteen (14), five (5), seven (7), fifteen (15), three (3), and thirteen (13). One should write in the four corners in a clockwise direction as follows: *a-katha-ha* (1), *u-ṅa-pa* (2), *ḷ-jha-ma* (6), and *ū-ḍa-va* (5). Then, *ā-kha-da-la* (2), *ṛ-ca-pha* (4), and so forth.

*Ḷ ña ya 8 oṃ ṭa śa 7*—thus in the southern group of four. *I ga dha kṣa 21 ṛ ccha va 12 e ṭa ra 16 aṃ ṇa ṣa 15*—thus in the western group of four. *Ī gha na 1 ṛ ja bha 10 ai ṭha la 14 aḥ ta sa 1*—thus in the northern group of four. In this manner, the first letter of the practitioner’s name occurs in that square.
Starting from that [mantra] and proceeding clockwise, one should count them in the sequence of *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, and *ari*. Now, as for the result:
the *siddha* [mantra] is accomplished in time; the *sādhya* [is accomplished] through recitation (*japa*) and fire-oblation (*homa*);
the *susiddha* [grants results] even from the planets and gods; and the *ari* [mantra] cuts off one's very roots.
Thus is the sequence for each group of four.
Now, if the first syllable of the mantra occurs within a single group of four, then the sequence is as follows:
starting from the square containing the first syllable of the practitioner's name, it proceeds up to the group of four squares containing the syllables of the mantra.

The calculation of the *siddha* and other classes must then be performed: starting from that very square in which the first letter of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the letters of the mantra reside within a group of four squares, the calculation of the *siddha* and other classes is to be carried out again; this is the result. Thus, *siddha-siddha* is as previously stated, while *siddha-sādhaka* is double that.
A *siddha-susiddha* destroys enemies through recitation performed while facing upward; a *siddha-ari* (enemy of the *siddha*) harms one's kinsmen.
A *sādhya-siddha* [is achieved] through threefold recitation; a *sādhya-sādhya* is useless.
A *susiddha-ari* destroys one's own kin through ten thousand recitations; a *siddha-susiddha* [destroys] through five thousand recitations;
a *sādhyasusiddha* [destroys] those who are superior by a factor of three; and a *susiddha-ari* becomes a destroyer of one's relatives merely by its planetary influence.
A *siddha-ari* kills one's son, while a *sādhyāri* kills one's daughter.
If that [planet] is well-aspected, it destroys the wife; if it is an enemy, it brings harm to the practitioner.
One should not purify the mantras of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, and Varāha, nor the temple-mantra (prāsāda), nor the Praṇava, nor the piṇḍa-akṣara mantras, for they are already perfected.
In the case of a mantra obtained in a dream, one received from a woman, or likewise a garland-mantra,
as well as in all Vedic mantras, one should never purify the accomplished enemy.
One should accept the *siddha* and *susiddha* [mantras], but the wise person should avoid the *sādhya* and the *śatru*. One should abandon that mantra which has a *śatru* at its beginning or its end.
Now follows the division of one's own family from other families.
U, ṛ, r, va, ga, ja, ṅa, da, va, and la belong to the Earth (Pārthiva). Ṛ, ṝ, a, gha, jha, ḍha, dha, bha, va, and śa belong to Varuṇa (Vāruṇa).
I, ī, ai, kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pha, ra, and kṣa belong to Agni (Āgneya).
A, ā, e, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and ṣa belong to the air;
ḷ, ḹ, aṃ, aḥ, ṅa, ña, ṇa, na, ma, and sa belong to the ether.
The Varuṇa-mitra belongs to the Pārthiva, while the Āgneya belongs to the Māruta;
and among the syllables of the Pārthiva and Āpya, the Māruta stands as the enemy.
The watery [element] is the enemy of the fiery, and likewise the fiery is the enemy of the watery;
however, among all these, the ethereal is not in conflict with any of them.
A wise person should not effect a conjunction of mutually contradictory elements;
the first syllable of the practitioner's name must be the same as that syllable of the mantra.
If one should know that one's own family has a single deity presiding over the elements, then that indeed is one's lineage.
Alternatively, there is the distinction of hair and so forth.
Beginning from single-syllable mantras up to six-syllable mantras, they are called "children" by Bhairava; mantras consisting of twenty syllables [are likewise so designated].
Therefore, these other mantras are known as mature (prauḍha) and are situated in a state of rest.
Now follows the classification beginning with women.
Those mantras which end with *namas* and begin with the name of the wife of Agni (Svāhā) in the feminine form are to be known as neuter;
those ending with *huṃ phaṭ* are masculine.
The fruit of these corresponds to their names.
Now, the conjunction of zodiac signs (rāśimelana).
A, ā, i, and ī are in Aries; u, ū, and the triad of ṛ are in Taurus; ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are in Gemini; and likewise, the two vowels e and ai are in Cancer.
The two vowels *u* and *ū* are to be known as belonging to the Leo zodiac sign; these are the deities in their respective order.
*Aṃ*, *aḥ*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa*—these eight belong to Virgo.
In Libra, however, there is the *ka*-group; in Scorpio, the *ca*-group;
in Sagittarius, the *ṭa*-group; and in Capricorn, the *ta*-group.
In the sign of Aquarius (Kumbha), the group of gutturals (ka-varga) is proclaimed; in Pisces (Mīna), the letters ca, ya, ra, la, and va are proclaimed.
The method of calculation proceeds from the first letter of the practitioner's name up to the end of the zodiac sign.
One, five, and nine are known as the kinsmen; two, six, and ten are the servants;
three, seven, and eleven are the nourishers; and twelve, eight, and four are the slayers.
One should recite "the servant of kinsmen, the nourisher, the slayer" three times.
He who is a kinsman is a protector and a benefactor who expands all goals;
he who is a servant is nourishment, prosperity, power, and fame; he who is a fosterer is life and wealth; and he who is a slayer destroys these very things.
Now, regarding the conjunction of lunar mansions and the conjunction of planetary groups.
A belongs to the Āśvina group of deities; this [group] ending with O belongs to humans.
Ī is said to be the Kṛttikā nakṣatra; Ṛ, Ṝ, Ḷ, and Ḹ belong to the Brahma group of humans.
E belongs to the host of gods; Mṛgaśīrṣā likewise belongs to humans; Ārdrā belongs to the gods;
Uṃ belongs to the Aśvins (Punarvasū); Ka belongs to the host of deities; and Puṣya belongs to the host of deities.
The group beginning with *kha* and *ga* (kha-ga) belongs to the *khagauśleṣā* (the *śleṣā* star of the birds); *gha* and *ṅa* belong to the *maghārākṣasa* (the *maghā* star of the Rākṣasas).
*Ca* belongs to the *pūrvā mānuṣa* (the *pūrvaphalgunī* star of humans), while *cha* and *ja* belong to the two *uttaramanuṣya* (the *uttaraphalgunī* and *hasta* stars of humans).
Jha and Ña are Hasta, a host of gods; Ṭa and Ṭha are Citrā, then a Rākṣasa;
Ḍa is Svātī, a host of gods; Ḍha and Ṇa are Viśākhā, then a Rākṣasa.
Likewise, Anurādhā and Jyeṣṭhā constitute the Rākṣasa group;
Pa, Pha, and Mūla are like Rakṣasas; and Pūrvāṣāḍhā is human.
Bhottarā belongs to the class of humans (mānuṣagaṇa), and Viṣṇu is remembered as its presiding deity (devatā).
Yaraudhaniṣṭhā belongs to the class of Rākṣasas, and Lava-Āruṇa is the Rākṣasa deity.
The first syllable is *vaśau*, the second is *pūrvāmānuṣatuṣa*, the third is *sahā*, and the fourth is *uttarānṛjaḥ*.
The fifth is *aṃ*, the sixth is *akṣo*, the seventh is *revatī*, and the eighth is *daivogaṇayet*; these should be counted from the syllables of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
34a) The perfection of birth, the destruction of the opposing afflictions,
supreme friendliness and supreme benevolence, and [the attainment of] births and so forth again and again.
Thus, having counted nine times, the fruit is according to the name.
Then follow the asterisms of the Gaṇas:
Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Puṣya, Punarvasu, Kṛttikā, Mṛgaśiras,
Svātī, Śravaṇa, and Revatī are known as the nine Devagaṇas.
Ārdrā, Abhijit, Rohiṇī, and the three Pūrvas as well as the three Uttarās—these constellations are known as the hosts of gods;
the remaining ones are remembered as the hosts of Rākṣasas.
In this regard, there is this distinction:

there may be friendship between gods and humans, and between groups of gods and groups of humans, but not between groups of gods or humans and a group of Rākṣasas. A wise person should not effect a union with another who is hostile.

Because it has been stated thus: "Now [the calculation] for the two groups of Rākṣasas; now the clearing of debts and assets. The Sādhyas are multiplied by Indra (14), Nakṣatra (21), Netra (2), Havis (12), Pañcadaśa (15), Ṛtu (6), Veda (4), Vahni (3), Āyudha (5), Aṣṭa (8), and Nava (9).
The Viśvedevas are multiplied by Diś (10), Bhū (1), Giri (8), Śruti (4), Gaja (8), Agni (3), Muni (7), and Ṛṣi (5).
Then, multiply the digits of the practitioner's name by the Vedas (4), the seasons (6),
and the fires (3).
Having known the remainder from both [the result and the number of syllables] after subtracting the [number of] syllables of the deity's name, the debt is the sum of the greater remainder.
It may be so. This is its meaning: one should separate the consonants and vowels of the mantra.
Having separated the vowels and consonants of the practitioner’s name as well, one should set them aside.
Then, one should form the four groups of the Mātṛkā, beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ṭha*, and *va*: namely, *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*.

*ḷ*, *e*, *e*, *u*, *ū*, *aṃ*, *aḥ*—this is the first [group]. *Ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ña*, *ṭa*—this is the second. *Ṭha*, *ḍa*, *ḍha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*—this is the third. *Ba*, *bha*, *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, *ha*—this is the fourth. Thus, having taken each individual syllable from the four groups of consonants (*varga*), one by one...
Each group consists of four syllables. "A ka ṭha va" is the first; "i kha ḍa ta" is the second. In this manner, eleven groups are formed.
One should multiply each syllable of these eleven groups by these eleven numbers respectively. For example:

If the syllables of the *vargas* fall upon the mantra, one should multiply them by Indra and the others according to their respective numbers. If they fall upon the name of the practitioner, one should multiply them by the numbers beginning with 'A' (1) and so forth according to their respective numbers.
When both of these results are reduced by eight and eight respectively, if the remainder is a higher number [than the divisor], it shall be a debt (*ṛṇa*). If it is higher... [text ends]
One who possesses wealth is the debtor, while one who lacks wealth is the creditor; for one who does not accomplish that [debt], the status of being a creditor is required.
35a) Now,

the manner of those who have awakened from sleep: since all [the vowels] always grant their fruit to those who invoke them when they are awakened, for example, the sixteen gentle vowels (*saumya-svara*).
The consonants beginning with *va* and ending with *ma* belong to the Sun (*saura*). Those beginning with *ya* belong to Fire (*āgneya*). Among the vowels, *a, i, u, e, o,* and *aṃ* are short;
*ā, ī, ṛ, ai, au,* and *aḥ* are long; and *ṛ, ṝ, ḷ,* and *ḹ* are neuter.
Mantras are pervaded by these [vowels]. When the wind flows through the southern path, then [the vowel] is short.

The primary mantras become awakened. When the breath flows through the left channel (vāmamārga), then those whose primary element is fire (āgneya), those whose primary element is Śauri (Śaurapradhāna), those whose primary element is the Moon (saumya), and the neuters (napuṃsaka) of both [channels] become awakened. Thus it is stated in the *Śāradā*: "The letter *ra*, the *praṇava* (OM), and the final..."

In the southern prāṇa, those mantras abundant in the letter *ha* are awakened and belong to the fire element (*āgneya*). In the left [prāṇa], those abundant in the letters *sa* and *va* are awakened as they flow; these belong to the moon (*saumya*). In both [channels], all [mantras] are awakened, whereas elsewhere they are dormant. By means of the sound of both [channels], they are primarily neuter (*puṃsaka*). By this, mantras become bestowers of fruit at the time of giving and at the time of recitation (*japa*).

Now, those mantras beginning with *icchinnā* have not been written here due to the bulk of the text; they are omitted because they serve no purpose, for those mantras do not exist at all in this context. All such methods of mantra-combination as described above do indeed combine with the mantra;
however, mantras that possess many virtues and few defects should be adopted. As for that which by this—
Because it is difficult to understand in this manner, a more accessible version is written here for those who are approaching it.
If the first syllable of the name is also that same syllable of the mantra, then they coincide. As it has been said:
"The syllable of the practitioner which is also the syllable of the mantra..."
If one should know it to have a single elemental deity, that indeed belongs to one's own family.
This is the diagram written according to the method of combining the zodiacal signs with the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
For names beginning with 'a', the mantras *a*, *ā*, *ka*, *ga*, *ha*, *kha*, *da*, and *la* are combined.
For names beginning with 'ka', the mantras *a*, *ā*, *kha*, *ya*, *dga*, and so forth are combined.

For names beginning with *tha* and so forth, *ha*, *ha*, *jha*, *ma*, *kha*, *da*, *ga*, *dha*, *cha*, and *dyā* are joined; for names beginning with *ha* and so forth, *a*, *ā*, *ka*, *kha*, *dha*, *kṣā*, and so forth are joined.
The letters beginning with *u* in a name, as well as *e*, *o*, *pha*, *ṛ*, and those beginning with *ṣa*, are inauspicious.

For names beginning with the letter *ṣa*, the letters *pha*, *dhā*, *dyā*, *e*, or *vā* follow; for names beginning with the letter *ru*, the letters *ya*, *ra*, *e*, *dha*, *chā*, and so forth, join together.
For names beginning with the letter *ma*, the letters *ka*, *pa*, *kha*, *e*, *ṭa*, *ra*, *i*, *gā*, and so forth, join together.
The vowels beginning with *a*, as well as *u*, *ū*, *ja*, *ṭha*, *śa*, *tu*, *pa*, *ṇa*, and those beginning with *kha*, are joined with *mila*.
For names beginning with the letter *u*, the first letters are *u*, *va*, *i*, *ga*, *dha*, *cha*, and so forth;
for names of proponents (*vādin*), they are *ḍa*, *u*, *ḍa*, *ka*, *ṣa*, and so forth.

For names beginning with 'ā', mantras beginning with *kha*, *da*, *la*, *gha*, *lā*, and *ghā* are joined; for names beginning with *kh*, mantras beginning with *ā*, *i*, *ga*, *gha*, *ḍā*, and so forth are joined.
36a) For names beginning with the letter *da*, mantras beginning with *kha* and *la* are joined;
for names beginning with the letter *ca*, mantras beginning with *ṛ*, *ṭa*, *śa*, and *ja* are joined.
For names beginning with *a* and so forth, the mantras beginning with *pha*, *śa*, *ja*, *bha*, *na*, and *śa* are joined.

For names beginning with *pha* and so forth, those beginning with *ai* and so forth are joined. For names beginning with *ya* and so forth, those beginning with *ā*, *ai*, *ṭha*, *la*, *ī*, and *nā* are joined.

For names beginning with *ḍa* and so forth, those beginning with *oṃ*, *śa*, *u*, *pha*, *ṇa*, *ṣa*, *na*, *śa*, and *bha* are joined. For names beginning with *śa* and so forth, those beginning with *ṛ*, *pha*, *ṣa*, *kṣa*, and *ta* are joined.

For names beginning with *ja*, [the seed-syllables] begin with *ī*, *ga*, *dha*, *cha*, *ṭa*, *gha*, *na*, and *ṭha*. For names beginning with *gā*, [they] begin with *kṣa*, *ī*, *gha*, *ṭha*, *e*, and *a*. For names beginning with *dhā*, [they] begin with *ga*, *kṣa*, *e*, *gha*, *na*, *ka*, *tha*, and *ha*.
For names beginning with *chā*, [they] begin with *e*, *ra*, *ka*, and *ha*. For names beginning with *ṛ*, [they] begin with *cha*, *ta*, *aṃ*, *u*, *aḥ*, *va*, and *bha*.
For names beginning with *cha*, *ja*, *ta*, *sa*, *u*, and so forth; for names beginning with *va*, *ṇa*, *ja*, *bha*, *pa*, *nu*, *pā*, and so forth;

for names beginning with *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *i*, *na*, *ma*, *a*, *ka*, and so forth; for names beginning with *ra*, *e*, *ca*, *ai*, *la*, *i*, *na*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *a*, *ka*, *tha*, *ha*, and so forth; for names beginning with *ṇa*, *ṣa*, *na*, *sa*, *bha*, *tu*, *da*, *upa*, and so forth; [and] for names beginning with *ī*.

For those beginning with *gha*, [the substitutes] are *la, a, ka, tha, ha, ma, ā, da*, and so forth. For those beginning with *ghā*, [the substitutes] are *la, a, ka, ha, ma, ā, kha*, and so forth. For those beginning with *nā*, [the substitutes] are *la, bha, ja*, and so forth. For those beginning with *jā*, [the substitutes] are *ta, i, sa, ṛ, ca, jha*, and so forth. For those beginning with *bhā*, [the substitutes] are *pa, va, ca, pha*, and so forth. For those beginning with *ḍā*, [the substitutes] are *la, gha, na, ma, a, ka, tha, ha, ā, da*, and so forth. For those beginning with *tā*...
May he protect you from the sky; may he protect you from the sky for one named Sādin.

36b) Even if other types [of combinations] do not coincide, nevertheless this conjunction of the asterism with the heap in the house-cells must certainly be required; for, [it is] favorable to the house-cells of one's own asterism and zodiacal sign.

One should worship the *manus* because they are eternally established. Furthermore, even the *sādhya-mantras*, through their association with the *siddha* and *susiddha* [categories], are to be understood as being auspicious despite being otherwise contradictory.
Next is the sprinkling with water,
followed by beating, awakening, consecration, purification, and nourishment.
Satisfying, kindling, and concealment—these are the ten purificatory rites for mantras.

1. Extraction of the mantra from the *mātṛkā* is "Birth" (*janana*). 2. Reciting each individual syllable of the mantra interspersed with the *praṇava* (oṃ) is "Life" (*jīvana*). 3. Having written the letters of the mantra, striking each syllable with sandalwood water empowered by the wind-seed (*yaṃ*) is "Striking" (*tāḍana*). 4. [Striking] the written syllables of the mantra with *karavīra* flowers for each syllable...
4. The striking (*hanana*) and awakening (*bodhana*) [of the mantra] with as many repetitions of the fire-seed (*vahni-bīja*) as there are syllables in the mantra; 5.

the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) by sprinkling with fresh mango leaves as many times as there are syllables in the mantra; 6. the burning (*dahana*) and purification (*vimalīkaraṇa*) by means of *oṃ hrauṃ*; 7. the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) by sprinkling with water using this same [seed-syllable].
The libation with the root mantra, the libation [repeated] eight times (9); the kindling of the victory preceded by the seeds *oṃ* *hrīṃ* *śrīṃ* (10);

the non-disclosure and concealment of the mantra (11). Thus, even mantras that are defective become purified through these ten consecrations (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, [they are purified] by means of the vowels beginning with *a*, together with their nasalization (*anusvāra*) and their final visarga-sounds.
The Meru [arrangement] is encapsulated by each of the *mātṛkā* letters beginning with *ka*, both in direct and reverse order.
This is the method of recitation using a rosary (*akṣamālājapa*). Recitation of mantras performed according to this method bestows swift success and yields the fruit of the letter *ka*.
They come into being.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Melting of Mantras," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhī.
Now, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).

Having sat down upon a soft seat in the bound lotus posture (padmāsana), [one should say]: "May the spirits, piśācas, pretas, and guhyakas depart! Whatever deities dwell here, established upon this earth—may those beings who are established upon the earth withdraw! May those beings who create obstacles perish by means of the rākṣasa!"

"By the command of Śiva"—with these words, one should expel the obstructors who have been seized with a fierce gaze. Having prayed to the Earth: "O Goddess, the worlds are supported by you; you, O Goddess, are supported by Viṣṇu; and you, O Goddess, support me—make this seat pure," one should perform the binding of the directions with three claps of the hands, saying: "To the Aghora-weapon, Phaṭ!"

Having performed the *choṭikā* (finger-snap) with the mantra "To the Śārṅga bow, together with the arrow, the iron shaft, and the weapon Sudarśana, Phaṭ," one should discharge the weapon in the northeast corner. With the mantra "O Fire-Wall, stay, stay," one should form three fire-walls using the index finger. The seer (*ṛṣi*) is the Inner Controller within the body, the primordial Puruṣa.
The Moon is the true deity; the application is for the sake of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. This is the seat-mantra of Meru (37b).

The seer (ṛṣi) is Pṛṣṭha, the meter (chaṃdaḥ) is Sutala, the deity (devatā) is Śrī Kūrma, and the application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of a seat upon the peak of Mount Meru. With these mantras—“Oṃ, salutation to the Infinite Seat (Anantāsana), 1; to the Pure Seat (Vimalāsana), 2; to the Yoga Seat (Yogāsana), 3; salutation to the Lotus Seat (Padmāsana), 4”—one should place consecrated kuśa grass upon one’s own seat. Oṃ, [to] Earth and the rest...

Having formed the resolve, "Having withdrawn the great elements into myself, I shall dissolve them along with my own self into the supreme ether," one should contemplate the locations of earth and the other elements.
From the feet up to the knees is said to be the station of Earth;
from the knees up to the anus is proclaimed to be the station of Water.
That which is proclaimed as the locus of fire extends from the anus to the heart; that of wind is described as extending from the middle of the heart up to the middle of the eyebrows.
In this context, "space" is said to extend from the midpoint between the eyebrows up to the crown of the head.
Therein, at the location of earth, resides the function of the feet and the sense of locomotion.

O you who arise from the earth, the sense of smell, and the feet; O Brahman, having recollected the *nivṛtti-kalā*, the *samāna-vāyu*, and the *kuṇḍalinī* residing at the *mūlādhāra* which pervades from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head and is swallowing [the elements], [one should recite]: *oṃ hrīṃ brahmaṇe pṛthivy-adhipataye*.

Having recited this mantra, "Nivṛtti-kalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should withdraw [the breath] into the self through the door of Kuṇḍalinī. Then, again, in the place of the tongue (ayām-sthāne), having remembered the act of giving while established in the water of the sense of taste (rasanā-jala) which is to be taken from the hand (hastādāna) for the sake of Viṣṇu, one should perform the offering.

38a) Having recited this mantra: "Oṃ, to Viṣṇu, the lord of waters, the essence of the *pratiṣṭhā*-kalā, huṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should withdraw all of these into oneself through the gateway of Kuṇḍalinī. || 2 ||

Furthermore, having recollected the anus in the place of fire as the *visarjanīya* (the letter *m*) in the form of emission, and having recollected the eyes, fire, Rudra, Vidyā, and Vyāna, one should recite this mantra: "Oṃ hrūṃ! To Rudra, the lord of fire, whose self is the Vidyā-kalā, huṃ phaṭ svāhā! and then withdraw [these elements] into the Self through the door of Kuṇḍalinī.

Furthermore, at the station of Vāyu, one should attend to its object by recollecting the tangible, the Lord of Speech, Śānti, and Apāna; having uttered this mantra: *oṃ hye īśānāya vāyvadhipataye śāntikalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, [one should worship] Kuṇḍalinī.

One should dissolve all these gatekeepers into the Supreme Self. Then, in the place of space, having recollected speech, the face, the objects of speech, the sense of hearing, space, Sadāśiva, and Śāntyatīta, as well as the vital breaths, [one should recite]:
*oṃ hauṃ sadāśivāya ākāśādhipataye śāntyatītakalātmane huṃ phaṭ svāhā*.

Having recited this mantra, one should dissolve all these [elements] into the Supreme Self through the door of Kuṇḍalinī. One should dissolve that Kuṇḍalinī, which has reached the tip of the forehead, into the Nāda-śakti of the size of a thumb; the Nāda into the Bindu-śakti; and that [Bindu] into the Mūla-śakti by means of the Praṇava. Having dissolved that as well, one should [dissolve it] into the attributeless Supreme Self.
One should withdraw [the elements] with the mantra *hṛm hūm phaṭ*. Having thus withdrawn them, one should perform the drying and other [purificatory] rites of one's own body.

Drawing the breath in through the *iḍā* [left nostril], while meditating on the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, which is smoke-colored and possesses great radiance, located below the navel, one should recite [the mantra] thirty-two times during the retention (*kuṃbhaka*).

38b) By means of that [wind], one should cause the body of the "sin-man" (*pāpapuruṣa*), which is situated in the left side of the abdomen, facing downwards, the size of a thumb, and fashioned from the storehouse of rebirth (*upapātaka-kośa*), to wither away. One should exhale that wind through the *piṅgalā* [nāḍī]. || 1 ||

Again, having drawn the air through the *iḍā* and joined it at the *mūlādhāra*, one should contemplate there the seed-syllable *ram*, which is the color of vermilion (*piṅgala*). While performing the *kuṃbhaka* (retention), burning one's own body and the personification of sin (*pāpapuruṣa*) with that syllable while reciting the seed-mantra *ram* sixty-four times, one should expel the personification of sin as ash-colored smoke through the *piṅgalā*. Again, through the *iḍā*...

Having drawn in the breath and led it to the *brahmarandhra*, one should contemplate there, within the thousand-petaled lotus, the seed-syllable of eternal nectar (*nityāmṛtabīja*) which is white in color; then, sprinkling one's own body with the stream of nectar flowing from that [lotus], one should mutter the seed-syllable *kūṃbhake laṃ* sixty-four times. || 3 ||

Again, having drawn in the breath through the *iḍā* and joined it with the *mūlādhāra*, one should meditate there upon the seed-syllable of earth (*laṃ*), which is dark green in color; while turning one's own body into ashes, one should mutter that syllable sixty-four times during the *kumbhaka* retention. Again, having drawn in the breath through the *iḍā*.
Having meditated on the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* of Bhuvaneśvarī at the *mūlādhāra*,

while forming the limbs beginning with the head and feet, one should recite [the mantra] sixty-four times during the *kumbhaka* breath-retention. (5) Having thus produced the gross body, one should create the subtle body by uttering the *praṇava* three times for oneself.
Having emanated from his presence the power of the root (mūla-śakti), the power of sound (nāda-śakti), and the power of the bindu (bindu-śakti) by means of the mantra "hrīṃ namaḥ,"...

"Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to Sadāśiva, the lord of space, whose essence is the *kalā* beyond tranquility (*śāntyatīta-kalātman*). By means of this mantra, [one should worship] the breath of the self in the form of the *bindu*, which is beyond tranquility.

Having generated Sadāśiva as space, along with the ear, sound, speech, the mouth, and that which is to be spoken, one should place them in the location of space. || 1 || "Oṃ hyeṃ, salutation to Īśvara, the lord of speech, whose nature is peace and the kalā; salutation to the Lord of Peace. [One should place] the wind, the sense of touch, the tangible, the organ of generation, and their respective objects in the location of air.

One should place [them] in the station of Vāyu. "Oṃ hrūṃ, salutation to Rudra, the lord of splendor, whose self is the Vidya-kalā"—with this, one should place Vyāna, Vidya, Rudra, Agni, the eye, form, Vāyu, emission (visarga), and its objects in the station of Agni.

3. "Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of water, the self of the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā. Having thus created the *udāna*, *pratiṣṭhā*, Viṣṇu, the sense of taste (*rasanā*), the essence (*rasa*), the hands, and the act of taking (*ādāna*), one should establish them in the place of the waters. 4. "Oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the earth, the self of the *nivṛtti* kalā. Thus [one establishes] the *samāna* and *nivṛtti*.

Having created the Brahma-earth, the fragrant foot, and the path and destination through emanation, one should establish the earth in its proper place. Thus, having produced the subtle body and performed the pervasion of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and root-energies within one's own body with the *praṇava*, [one should act] with vessels filled with nectar-water.

"May I consecrate myself with jars fashioned of gold, held in the hands of the goddesses of the directions"—having thus consecrated himself, he should invoke the Supreme Self into his heart with the *praṇava* (Om).
Then, he should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the ritual installation of the vital breaths). It is as follows: [of] the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra...
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the seers; the Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan are the meters; Prāṇa is the deity;
the application is for the purpose of the installation of Prāṇa.
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hoṃ saṃ haṃ saḥ. May my vital breaths (prāṇas) remain here;

may my life remain established here. May all my senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and breath—having come right here, remain happily for a long time. Svāhā haṃsaḥ saṃ. Thus is the consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
With the mantra, one should establish the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and the senses in their respective locations.

Then, having performed the *mātṛkā-nyāsa* according to the method to be described hereafter, one becomes purified and fit for recitation, worship, and other rites. Furthermore, if one is capable of performing it in such detail, then even a concise purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) may be done.

The procedure is as follows: having performed the binding of the directions and so forth, one should withdraw the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) along with the individual self (*ātman*) and the mind into the Supreme Self by means of the *praṇava* (OM).

Then, while reciting the seed-syllable *yam* thirty-two times, one should dry up the entire body together with the personified sin (*pāpapuruṣa*). During the retention (*kuṃbhaka*), one should recite the seed-syllable *ram* sixty-four times.

One should reduce one's own body to ashes. Then, drawing in the breath through the *iḍā* [left nostril] and performing *kumbhaka*, while reciting the seed-syllable *vam* sixty-four times, one should sprinkle the ashes of one's own body. Likewise, with a stream of nectar flowing from that [seed-syllable], while performing *kumbhaka* and reciting the seed-syllable *lam* sixty-four times—

One should form a lump of the body's ashes. Again, in the same manner, while reciting the *bhuvaneśvarī* seed-syllable *hrīṃ* sixty-four times during the *kuṃbhaka* breath-retention, one should fashion the limbs beginning with the hands, head, and feet.

One should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (installation of life-force) as before. Thus ends the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) according to the three mandalas. Now, the procedure for the purification of the elements according to the five mandalas is written below: *Hrāṃ* salutation to the *nivṛtti-kalā*;
1. *Hrīṃ* to the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*; 2. *Hrūṃ* to the *vidyā-kalā*; 3. *Hyaiṃ* to the *śānti-kalā*; 4. *Hauṃ*... [5]

"Obeisance to the Kalā Śāntyatītā. With these mantras, following the sequence of *prāṇāyāma*, one should purify the five maṇḍalas at the feet, below the navel, in the heart, at the throat, and in the head.
Now, their forms: the Earth maṇḍala is quadrangular, yellow in color, and marked with eight thunderbolts (*vajra*).

1. The water-mandala, marked [with the syllable *laṃ*], accompanied by the seed-syllable *laṃ*, having Brahmā as its presiding deity, is white in color, shaped like a bow, situated within two lotuses, and consists of the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, with Viṣṇu as its deity. 2.
The fire-mandala is triangular, endowed with a svastika, and at its center consists of the seed-syllable *raṃ*.

Contemplating with five mantras: (3) the wind-maṇḍala, whose essence is the deity Rudra, marked with six dots, having the seed-syllable *yaṃ* at its center, smoke-colored, and having Īśvara as its presiding deity; (4) the space-maṇḍala, circular, situated within the letter *ha*, blue-colored, and having Sadāśiva as its presiding deity.
One should purify the defects produced by the five sense organs. Thus concludes this purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) through the five maṇḍalas.
This is the seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Bhūtaśuddhi," in the *Mantrakosa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhī.
Now follows the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
Furthermore, that pure *binduka*, as well as those beginning with the remnants of the *kalās* and so forth, joined with Śrīkaṇṭha and the others,
and likewise with Śakti, Kamalā, and Māra— one by one— these ten individual installations (*nyāsas*) have been declared separately.

All these [mantras] ending with the sacrifice to Brahmā are intent upon accomplishing the success (*siddhi*) of the practitioner; they are wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*) for one’s intentions. Other [mantras] may also be mentioned. For the Mātṛkā-mantra: Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the divine Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), Sarasvatī in the form of the letters is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is as a constituent part of all mantras. Oṃ aṃ kaṃ khaṃ...

Gaṃ ghaṃ ṅaṃ āṃ, salutation to the Heart, whose essence is knowledge (jñānātmane). 1 Iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ, svāhā to the Head, for the sake of Power (śaktyai). 2 Uṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ oṃ, vaṣaṭ to the Crest-lock (śikhā), for the sake of Strength (balāyai). 3 Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ, huṃ to the Armor (kavacāya), for the sake of Sovereignty (aiśvaryāya). 4

Having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with: *ūṃ paṃ phaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ oṃ tejasenetra-trayāya vauṣaṭ* (5) and *aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaḥ aḥ vīryāyāstrāya phaṭ* (6), one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*). [The deity] whose face and arms are fashioned from the distinctions of the fifty letters...
I meditate upon her whose body possesses feet, hips, and breasts,

who is radiant and adorned with matted locks bearing a digit of the moon, who is as white as the moon or a jasmine flower, whose hands hold a rosary, a water-pot, a lotus, and display the gesture of granting boons, and who rests upon a lotus.

I bow to that Goddess Bhāratī, who is as pure as a digit of the moon and whose breasts and hips bear no small weight. In her upper right hand is a rosary (*akṣasraj*), and in her upper left hand is a water-pot (*kumbha*);
this is the sequence of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) beginning with the letter *u* and ending with the letter *kṣa*. These are the locations for the ritual placement.

One should assign the syllables to the locations starting from the heart: first on the two eyes, the two ears, the two cheeks, the two lips, the roots of the two teeth, and the face; then on the two arms, the joints, the tips of the fingers, the two sides, the back, the navel, and the abdomen; then on the heart, the roots of the two arms, the other [parts], the throat, and the armpits; and finally on the pair of hands and feet, and the various limbs starting from the abdomen, assigning them according to their names ending with "pāpaka."
In due order: now follows the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (Antarmātṛkānyāsa).
One should place the sixteen vowels upon the sixteen-petalled lotus at the throat;
one should place the twelve consonants beginning with 'ka' upon the twelve-petalled heart-lotus.
41a) One should place the ten vowels beginning with *au* upon a ten-petalled lotus;
and one should place the six [consonants] beginning with *va* within a six-petalled lotus situated in the center of the *liṅga*.
One should place the four vowels on the base and the four consonants beginning with 'va' on the four petals;
'ha' and 'kṣa' are placed on the lotus situated between the eyebrows—this is declared to be the *lipinyāsa*.
One should perform one or the other of these two.
Now, the worship.

Having performed *prāṇāyāma* with the root mantra and having established the vessel for the *argha* offering according to the prescribed rite, one should place [the following mantras] in another vessel: "Oṃ, salutation to Ādhāraśakti" (1); "to Mūlaprakṛti" (2); "to Maṇḍūka" (3); "to Kālāgnirudra" (4); "to Kūrma" (5); "to Ananta" (6); "to Mahāvarāha" (7).

One should worship in successive layers, saying: "Obeisance to the Earth (8), to Mahāmeru (9), to the Kalpavṛkṣa tree (10), to the Golden Pavilion (11), and to the Jewel Lion-throne (12). Having conceived a square pedestal above that, beginning from the southeast corner, one worships: "To Dharma (1), to Jñāna (2), and to Vairāgya (3)."

One should worship with "Oṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ" (4) in the corners of the pedestal (*pīṭha*). Then, on the sides of the pedestal: "Oṃ adharmāya namaḥ" (1), "ajñānāya" (2), "avairāgyāya" (3), and "anaiśvaryāya namaḥ" (4). Then: "taṃ tamase namaḥ" (1), "raṃ rajase" (2), "saṃ sattvāya" (3), "māṃ māyāyai" (4), "viṃ vidyāyai" (5), "āṃ ātmane" (6), and "paṃ" (7).

One should worship in successive layers with the mantras: "Obeisance to the Supreme Self" (7), "Obeisance to the Self of Knowledge" (8), and "Obeisance to the Self of the Fire-mandala" (9). Above that, having visualized an eight-petaled lotus, one should write the seed-syllable *hmau* in its pericarp (*karṇikā*). On the filaments (*keśara*), one should write the pairs beginning with *aṃ āṃ*, and [the groups] *ka ca ṭa ta pa ya śa*.
One [version] consists of seven groups of one hundred thousand; in this manner, one should write eight groups on the eight lotus petals.
Having drawn a circle of fire outside of that, one should write the syllable *ṭha* in its corners and the syllable *va* in the cardinal directions.
Having invoked the previously mentioned Goddess Sarasvatī into the pericarp of the lotus, one should worship her with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*).

41b) One should worship the limbs (aṅgas) in the directions of Agni, Īśāna, Asura, and Vāyu, as well as in front and behind. Everywhere, the worship of the limb-deities (aṅgadevatās), beginning with the crest-lock (śikhā), ends with "namaḥ. Having worshipped in the locations of the filaments with "aṃ āṃ namaḥ," [one should worship] on the petals.

One should worship the eight inscribed divisions: *oṃ medhāyai namaḥ* (1), *prajñāyai* (2), *prabhāyai* (3), *vidyāyai* (4), *dhiye* (5), *dhṛtyai* (6), *smṛtyai* (7), *budhyai namaḥ* (8). Thus one should worship on the petals starting from the east. With *vidyaiśvaryai namaḥ*, one should worship in front, upon the pericarp of the lotus. *Brāhmyai* (1)...

One should worship in one's own directions with the mantra: "Salutation to Māheśvarī 2, Kaumārī 3, Vaiṣṇavī 4, Vārāhī 5, Māhendrī 6, Cāmuṇḍā 7, and Mahālakṣmī. One should worship in one's own directions with the mantra: "Salutation to Indra 1, Agni 2, Yama 3, Nirṛti 4, Varuṇa 5, Vāyu 6, Kuvera 7, and Īśāna."

Then, having recited [the mantra] according to one's ability, one should dismiss the Goddess. One hundred thousand recitations constitute the *puraścaraṇa*; one million recitations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

A fire sacrifice (*homa*) consisting of ten parts of pure sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*) should be performed. For three months, the wise practitioner should drink water consecrated by that [mantra] at the beginning of each day, using the *vidyā*. By this means, even a mute person becomes proud of his poetic talent.
And one attains supreme accomplishment within twelve months.

The Indian devotee worships through ritual placements, recitations, fire-offerings, worship, and meditations; endowed with splendor, he soon becomes a poet and triumphs over Vyāsa and others by being free from old age, death, and disease.
The three metals—silver, gold, and copper—are likewise the forms of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni;
silver is known as the Moon, gold as the Sun, and copper as the Fire.
The proportions of the metals are specified by the number of the vowels and consonants;
with those metals, one should fashion a mudrā that is unalloyed and well-proportioned.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand times plus one, the practitioner should then touch it and offer oblations;
the mantrin should pour the remnants of the oblation into that [liquid] along with clarified butter, according to the previously mentioned number.
Having placed those two mudrās into the jar according to the procedure prescribed for consecration,
one should, with a concentrated mind, invoke the Goddess and worship her with the ritual offerings.
Having consecrated him, the Guru should give that ring to the disciplined disciple:
"This is a protection that destroys minor ailments, poisons, fevers, and the like."
One should provide special protection against tigers, thieves, wild beasts, and the like;
by wearing this, O Lord of Anuja, one attains victory in battle.

"By the number of vowels and so forth" means by the numbers sixteen, twenty-five, and ten. And thus it is stated in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The portions beginning with the consonant-classes and the vowels shall, in order, be gold, silver, and copper.
This *rucaka* [necklace] thus fashioned shall constantly grant the goals of the practitioner. As for the sequence of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), it is pure.

First: The Sṛṣṭinyāsa accompanied by the Visarga. The seer (ṛṣi) and other details are as previously stated. The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) end with the Visarga. The meditation (dhyāna): [He who] possesses the luster of vermilion, is adorned with immeasurable ornaments, has three eyes, and holds a book, a rosary, a deer, and a goad; [with] one standing at his side...
One should also meditate upon the Blessed Lady, who has a golden luster and holds a book and a rosary in her lotus-like hands.
In his upper left and right hands, he holds a book and a rosary;
below that, the Lord holds a young deer and a water-vessel. The Goddess holds a book in her left hand and a rosary in her right.
The worship and other rites are as before. As for the sequence of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): *aḥ* namaḥ, *āḥ* namaḥ, *iḥ* namaḥ, and so forth.

The placement of stability (*sthitinyāsa*) consists of the letters ending with the *visarga* and the *bindu*. Everything is as before. The sequence of placement (*nyāsakrama*), however, is as follows: *aṃḥ namaḥ*, *āṃḥ namaḥ*, *iṃḥ namaḥ*, and so forth. The placement of withdrawal (*saṃhāranyāsa*) consists of the same letters joined with the *bindu* in reverse order.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as before. The visualization (*dhyāna*) is: [holding] a rosary, a deer, and a raised trident.

Bow down to Varṇeśvarī, who holds a sun and a moon, possesses three eyes, has the crescent moon upon her head, is crimson in hue, dwells within a lotus, and is bent by the weight of her breasts. [The rites of] nyāsa, worship, and so forth are as before.

Beginning from the lower right hand, one places the rosary and other implements. As for the sequence of placement (*nyāsa*): *kṣaṃ namaḥ*, *laṃ namaḥ*, and so forth. Now, for the purpose of Sarasvatī, [the mantra] begins with the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*). The seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), and deity (*devatā*) are as in the case of the Mother-goddesses (*mātṛkā*).
As for the sequence of placement: *aṃ aiṃ namaḥ*, *āṃ aiṃ namaḥ*, and so forth. Now...

The Gāṇapatya Nyāsa for the purpose of pacifying obstacles: Gaṇaka is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Sarasvatī in the form of Gaṇapati is the deity (devatā); the application (viniyoga) is for the pacification of obstacles. The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) begins with *gāṃ gīm* and so forth.
The meditation (dhyāna): [He holds] a citron fruit, a mace, a sugarcane bow, a goad, a lotus, a noose, and an elephant goad.
