whose splendor consists of the gestures of protection and boon-granting; who is adorned with immeasurable ornaments; and whose two upper hands hold lotuses, while those below them display the gestures of protection and boon-granting.
Having thus meditated and invoked the deity upon the pedestal described in the Saura-mantra, [perform] as previously stated...

One should worship according to the prescribed ritual. The first enclosure (āvaraṇa) consists of the limbs (aṅgas). The second [enclosure] consists of the planets beginning with Soma and ending with Ketu. One should worship in the directions starting from the east with "Salutation to Soma," "to Budha," "to Bṛhaspati," and "to Śukra. One should worship in the corners with "to Aṅgāraka," "to Mandā," "to Rāhu," and "to Ketu. [Then perform] the recitation (japa).
Having offered [the oblation], one should conclude the rite. The materials for the *argha* offering are those previously mentioned; in their absence, whatever is available may be used.

The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of twelve hundred thousand recitations. Thereafter, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) of food mixed with ghee, numbering one thousand times that amount. Now, the seed-mantra of Mārtaṇḍa is *hyauṃ*. There is no [separate] seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth. The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) begins with *hrāṃ hrīṃ*, and so on.

Or by means of *dhraṃ dhriṃ* and so forth, [one performs] meditation: [One should meditate on the Lord] who possesses a natural luster resembling a golden lotus and coral, who holds with his lotus-hands a beautiful six-winged [bee], two lotuses, a discus, a spear, a noose,
a very beautiful conch, a rosary, and a skull-cup, and who has three eyes.

We worship Him who delights in the faces of the playful goddesses, who is beloved by Mārtaṇḍa (the Sun), who wears a crown of jewels, and who is radiant with necklaces. In His right and left hands, He holds a *khaṭvāṅga* and a lotus; beneath those, a discus and a spear (*śakti*); and beneath those, a noose and a goad (*aṅkuśa*).

Holding a rosary and a skull-bowl beneath that [left hand], having thus meditated, one should invoke and worship the deity upon the Saura-pīṭha. The enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas), the planets, and the world-protectors (lokapālas). The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of three hundred thousand [recitations].
The oblation is performed with lotuses in the tenth part.
Enclosed by the seed-syllable *viṃ* (dhṛ), which bestows the fruits of all desires—
this being the seed-syllable *viṃ* as in "dhṛ"—
the mortal who recites this mantra [attains] fame, sons, strength, and splendor.
One shall accomplish incomparable perfection of speech, prosperity, and even good fortune.

Now, the Ghṛṇimantra: Oṃ Ghṛṇi Sūrya Āditya. Devabhāga is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), Sūrya is the deity (devatā), Ghaṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Riṃ is the power (śakti), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of one's desired goal.

*Satyatejojvalajvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*—homage to the heart. 1. *Oṃ brahmatejojvalajvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*—the head. 2. *Viṣṇutejojvalajvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*—the crest-lock. 3. *Oṃ rudratejojvalajvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*—the armor. 4. *Oṃ*... [the eye]. 5.

*Agnitejo-jvalajvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*—the Eye (5). *Sarvatejo-jvalajvālāmaṇi huṃ phaṭ svāhā*—the Weapon (6). One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: *Aṃ* to Āditya, on the head (1); *Iṃ* to Ravi, on the face (2); *Oṃ* to Mānava, on the heart (3); *Ṛṃ* to Bhāskara, on the private parts (4); *Ḷṃ* to Sūrya, on both feet (5). *Oṃ.*

One should place [the syllables] *śi* on the head (1), *ra* on the face (2), *ṇi* on the neck (3), *sū* on the heart (4), *rya* on the abdomen (5), *ā* at the navel (6), *di* on the secret place (7), and *tyaḥ* on the two feet (8). The visualization (*dhyāna*): Seated upon a lotus as red as the dawn, holding a lotus and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons in his hands, he possesses three eyes and, by his own radiance, [illuminates] the circle of the moon.

May the Sun-god, adorned with hundreds of ornaments, protect you! Having meditated thus—[the deity] holding two lotuses in his upper pair of hands, and the gestures of boon (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) in his lower right and left hands—one should invoke the Lord upon the solar pedestal (*saura-pīṭha*) and worship him.
The first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) consists of the limbs (*aṅga*): *Oṃ ādityāya namaḥ*, 1; *ravaye namaḥ*, 2; *bhānave namaḥ*, 3; *bhāskarāya namaḥ*, 4.
Thus for the cardinal directions. For Uṣā (1), Prajñā (2), Prabhā (3), and Saṃdhyā (4)—*namaḥ*—thus for the intermediate directions. Then [the offerings] to Brāhmī and the others.

In the presence of Lakṣmī, one should worship with the mantra "Obeisance to Aruṇa. Then [one worships] Agni, then Mahān, then the Lokapālas. Having offered the recitation (japa) to the retinue of Sūrya with the mantra "Obeisance to the retinue of Sūrya" in the intermediate directions, one should dismiss them. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of eight hundred thousand [recitations]. The fire-oblation for Ravi is performed by offering fuel-sticks from milk-exuding trees smeared with the three sweets (madhuratraya).

One should recite the *Śāradā* mantra eight thousand times. Then, one should perform sevenfold libations with water consecrated by that mantra; this brings supreme auspiciousness and destroys poverty, sin, and the causes of mental affliction. Having worshipped the Lord along with his retinue upon a sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*) prepared with an eight-petaled lotus and well-filled with water from the *kuṃbha* vessel and other sacred waters, one should likewise worship the fire upon the sacrificial ground.

Having composed himself, one who has fasted on every seventh day (saptamī) should prepare a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) of *kapilā* cow’s milk, mix it with clarified butter (*ājya*), and offer it into the fire one thousand times. Then, having consecrated holy water for bathing with mantras, he should sprinkle her with it; thereafter, having bowed and worshipped her again, the husband may engage in sexual union. Now, another mantra: *oṃ kholkāya svāhā*.

*Khaṃ khaṃ kholkāya svāhā*—this is one method. For this mantra, Sūkṣmarṣi is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and Sūrya is the deity (*devatā*). It is for the purpose of attaining desired objects. *Sūkṣmakāya svāhā* is the heart (*hṛdaya*) 1; *Sūkṣmaṃ tejase svāhā* is the head (*śiras*) 2; *Sūkṣmakāya svāhā* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*) 3.

*Sūkṣmavastrāya svāhā*—the armor (*kavaca*). 4. *Sūkṣmakāya hūṃ phaṭ*—the weapon (*astra*). 5. Meditation and so forth are as before. "May we know the seven-horsed one; may we meditate upon the thousand-rayed one; may that Sun inspire us. With this Gāyatrī, one should display the Sky-mudrā (*vyomamudrā*). The preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
An oblation of one thousand and eight offerings each should be performed with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *vilva*, *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, and *udumbara*, smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter.
From that, the accomplishment of the mantra occurs; as before, the offering of water (argha) results in the destruction of all sins. Now, regarding the Ṛgveda:

"Udyantā" is the *ṛc* mantra dedicated to Āditya. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Praskaṇva, its meter (*chandaḥ*) is Anuṣṭubh, and its deity (*devatā*) is Sūrya. Worship and other rites are performed as before. In the *Taittirīyaka*, the five rays beginning with "Yo'sāvādityaḥ" are well known. Having performed worship and other rites as before, and having recited [the mantra], one should dismiss [the deity]; thus all success (*sarvasiddhi*) is attained.

Now follows the Ajapa Haṃsa mantra: *Haṃsaḥ*. Its seer (ṛṣi) is Brahmā, its meter (chandaḥ) is Gāyatrī, its deity (devatā) is the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of one's desired goal. The six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) are: *hlāṃ hlīṃ hlūṃ hlaiṃ hlauṃ hlaḥ*, and so forth; or alternatively, *hsrāṃ hsrīṃ*, and so forth. The meditation (dhyāna): [One should meditate upon the Self] as radiant as the rising sun...

May that body of Tripura—the root of the universe, which is both solar and fiery—protect you; it has the form of lightning, half-mooned hair, and holds a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a boon-granting hand, and an axe in its lotus-like hands. Adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh jewels, it is moon-crested and three-eyed, with its right and left arms encircling [the consort].

Having meditated on [the deity] holding a noose and an axe, with the lower two hands displaying the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, one should invoke and worship the Lord upon the Saura-pīṭha.

The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*). In the cardinal directions: "Salutation to the Self of Truth (Ṛtātman) 1, to the Universal Self (Viśvātman) 2, to the Supreme Self (Paramātman) 3, to the Human Self (Narātman) 4. In the intermediate corners: "Salutation to the one born of Truth (Ṛtajā) 1, to the one born of the waters (Abjajā) 2, to the one born of the cow (Gojā) 3, to the one born of the mountain (Adrijā) 4."
And [one should worship] the world-protectors in their respective directions, as well as their weapons. The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one million two hundred thousand recitations.
The fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed with milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, consisting of one-tenth of that number.
One should mutter the mantra one hundred and eight times over water that is composed of nectar.
Whoever should consecrate [another] by recollecting this would become free from all affliction.
By this very procedure, a person obtains longevity, health, wealth, and desired objects; one afflicted by poison becomes free from poison.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Āditya Mantras," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhī.
Now, the mantras of Gaṇapati.

Therein, the single-syllable [mantra] is *gaṃ*. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Gaṇapati, its meter (*chandaḥ*) is Triṣṭubh, its deity (*devatā*) is Gaṇapati, and its seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*) are *gaṇa* and *maṃ* respectively. The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of prosperity preceded by the pacification of all obstacles.
One should perform the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) with the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*)—this applies everywhere. *Gāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ* (1); *gīṃ*...
*Śirase svāhā* (2); *Gūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (3); *Gaiṃ kavacāya huṃ* (4); *Gauṃ netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* (5); *Gaḥ astrāya phaṭ* (6). Then, the meditation (*dhyāna*):
[One should meditate upon the Lord] who is red, endowed with red unguents, garments, and flowers, pot-bellied, moon-crested, and possessed of three eyes.

May the Lord Vighnarāja—the King of Obstacles—be for the prosperity of the gods who bow before him; he whose hands and feet are dwarfed by three [units], whose nose is curved like a citron, who holds at the tips of his hands a noose, a goad, and a fruit, who displays the boon-granting gesture, who has the face of an elephant, who is adorned with ornaments, and who sits upon a lotus throne. In his right upper and lower hands are the noose and the boon-granting gesture; in his left upper and lower [hands]...
Having meditated thus— [the deity] with goads and nooses in both hands— and having performed the mental worship upon the *mātṛkā-pīṭha* starting from the *ādhāra*, [one proceeds].

One should worship on the lotus petals starting from the east with: "Obeisance to Tīvrā," "to Jvālinī," "to Nandā," "to Bhogadā," "to Kāmarūpiṇī," "to Ugrā," "to Tejovatī," and "to Satyā. One should worship in the center with: "Obeisance to Vighnanāśinī. Having worshipped the pedestal with: "Obeisance to the Lotus-Throne of All Powers (Sarvaśakti-kamalāsana)," [one should worship] upon its pericarp.

Having invoked the deity, one should worship Him with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya). One should worship in the four directions with the following: "Salutation to Gaṇādhipa" (1), "to Gaṇeśa" (2), "to Gaṇanāyaka" (3), and "salutation to Gaṇakrīḍa" (4).
Then follows the limb-enclosure (aṅgāvaraṇa): "to Vakratuṇḍa" (1), "to Ekadanta" (2), "to Mahodara" (3), and "to Gajānana" (4).
"Lambodarāya 5, Vikaṭāya 6, Vighnarājāya 7, Dhūmravarṇāya 8, Namaḥ" [are to be placed] on the petals.

In those very [deities] are the Brahmā-group and others, as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions and their weapons. Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana). The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of four hundred thousand recitations; the fire-oblation (homa) is one-tenth of that, amounting to eighty thousand.
With sweetmeats, flattened rice, parched grain, barley meal,
pieces of sugarcane, coconuts, pure sesame seeds, and well-ripened plantains.
The wise have declared that the obstacle consists of eight substances;
one who has mastered the mantra should perform the applications as set forth in the ritual manuals.
One should daily satisfy Gaṇanāyaka with pure water,
diligently offering four hundred and forty-four [libations] at the beginning.
A person shall obtain their desired goal, even more than that, within a single *maṇḍala*.
A *homa* performed with coconuts on the fourth lunar day bestows prosperity.

Starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, the wise man should, day by day until the fourth, [offer oblations] with flattened rice, parched grain flour, fried grain, and sesame seeds respectively.
One should offer four hundred oblations, and all living beings will become submissive;
an oblation of rice mixed with sesame seeds bestows great fortune (Mahālakṣmī).
By offering oblations of parched grain mixed with the three sweets, one bestows a maiden.

Ga-gaṃ | Gau-ge | This is the sequence of worship for these [mantras]. Glauṃ | This is another mantra. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth are as before. Gaṃ is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), Aṃ is the power (*śakti*), Laṃ is the peg (*kīlaka*). Glāṃ, glīm, and so forth constitute the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth are as before. Goṃ is Amara. Meditation and so forth are as before.

Now, the mantra for swift propitiation: *Gaṃ* to Gaṇapati, the Swift Propitiator, obeisance. For this [mantra], Gaṇapati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Virāṭ is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Gaṇapati is the deity (*devatā*), and *gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and power (*śakti*). It is for the attainment of desired objects. *Gaṃ gīṃ gūṃ gaiṃ gauṃ gaḥ* are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgāni*). The visualization (*dhyāna*): [He] holds a noose and a goad...
One should meditate upon him who fulfills the desires of the sages like a wish-fulfilling creeper,
whose head is adorned with a crescent moon, who has three eyes, whose cheeks are ruddy, and who has the face of an elephant;
who is radiant with brilliant ornaments, possesses a large belly, is gracefully seated upon a lotus throne, and has four faces and eight arms.

For the attainment of prosperity, men should always meditate upon the lotus-feet [of the deity]. Above the right and left hands, the noose and the goad are to be visualized; below those, the wish-fulfilling creeper and the tusk; and on the trunk, the citron fruit. Having thus meditated and performed the mental worship, one should perform the external worship together with the powers (śaktis) such as Tīvrā and the rest.
Having invoked the deity upon the seat of Gaṇeśa, one should worship him with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya). [The names are:
1. Vighna, 2. Vighnanāyaka, 3. Śūra, 4. Vīra, 5. Varada, 6. Bhavatrā.

One should worship [the deity] in the directions starting from the east with the mantra: "Obeisance to Ekarada (7) and Lambodara (8). Then one should worship the [deities] beginning with Brāhmī and the world-protectors (lokapālas). Having offered the food offering (naivedya) and performed the recitation (japa), one should perform the dismissal (visarjana). The preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand [recitations].
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets (trimadhura) or with the eight substances, ten thousand times each.

One should offer oblations daily with clarified butter and cooked rice; within a year, one shall become possessed of abundant food. By offering milk-rice (*pāyasa*), a person attains great prosperity. Now follows the four-syllabled mantra of Heramba: *Oṃ Gūṃ Namaḥ*.
For this mantra, there is no seer (*ṛṣi*) and so forth. Heramba is the deity. The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) consists of *Gāṃ*, *Gīṃ*, and so on. The visualization (*dhyāna*):

[He beholds] the bull-vehicle, which possesses the luster of pearls, gold, blue lotus stalks, and saffron, and is endowed with three eyes; [he beholds] the moon-bearing Heramba, radiant as the sun, who bestows pride, rut, fearlessness, joy, and a small axe; and [he beholds] the garland consisting of his own head-lotuses, along with a mallet and a goad.

I worship him who holds [these] with his three pairs of arms: in the lower right and left hands, the gestures of boon-granting (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*); above those, a sweetmeat ball (*laḍḍuka*) and a tusk; above those, an axe (*paraśu*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*); above those, a lotus garland and a mallet (*mudgara*);
and above those, a goad (*aṅkuśa*) and a trident (*triśūla*). Having invoked Gaṇapati upon a golden pedestal endowed with intensity (*tīvra*) and other qualities, one should worship him as described.
The description of the colors of the five faces beginning with the one at the top is the *pīṭhamantra*: Oṃ huṃ huṃ mahāsiṃhāya. (64b)

Having worshipped the seat with "Oṃ, obeisance to Gāṅgeravāsana," one should invoke the deity and worship Him with offerings such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas); the second of Vighna, Vināyaka, and others; the third of Brāhmī and the other goddesses; and the fourth of the world-protectors (lokapālas). [One should recite the mantra] three hundred thousand times.

The *puraścaraṇa* consists of a fire sacrifice (*homa*) performed with lotuses or sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*), ten parts of which are offered for every hundred. Now follows the four-syllabled mantra of Gaṇapati: *Oṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ*. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Śukra, its meter (*chandas*) is Gāyatrī, its deity (*devatā*) is Gaṇapati, its seed-syllable (*bīja*) is *Grīṃ*, its power (*śakti*) is *Hrīṃ*, and it is for the attainment of desired objects. *Grāṃ* is the heart (1); *Grīṃ* is the head (2).
GRŪṂ—the crest-lock (śikhā) 3; GRAIṂ—the armor (kavaca) 4; GRAUṂ—the eyes (netra) 5; GRAḤ—the weapon (astra) 6. Meditation (dhyāna):
Golden-hued, clad in golden garments, with a large belly and body, beautiful arms, and three eyes;
holding in his hands a noose, a rosary, his own tusk, and a mallet, while bearing a lotus in his [fourth] hand; adorned with golden ornaments.

One should meditate upon that Gaṇeśa, who resembles the rising sun, who is endowed with power, who is the end of obstacles, who dwells within all obstacles, and who is bowed to by the three worlds; he holds a noose and a goad in his upper right and left hands respectively,
and below those, he bears a rosary and a tusk.
Having meditated thus—"A sweetmeat [offered] with the trunk of the trunk"—one should invoke and worship the Deity upon the previously mentioned pedestal.

First, the limb-enclosure (*aṅgāvaraṇa*): "Salutation to Vakratuṇḍa," "to Ekadaṃṣṭra," "to Mahodara," "to Gajānana," "to Laṃbodara," "to Vikaṭa," "to Vighnarāja," and "to Dhūmravarṇa"—thus [on the petals]. On the petals.
Within those very [mandalas] are the Brahma-deities and others, as well as the world-protectors (lokapālas). Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should dismiss [them].
The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) consists of three hundred thousand recitations; the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds is one-tenth of that number.
One who offers oblations daily with ghee and cooked rice shall become possessed of food within a year;
by offering milk-rice, a person attains great prosperity.

Now follows the twelve-syllable mantra of Śaktigaṇapati: *hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ mahāgaṇapataye svāhā*. The seer (ṛṣi) of this is Gaṇaka, the meter (chandaḥ) is Trivṛt-Anuṣṭubh, the deity (devatā) is Śaktigaṇapati, and the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and powers (*śakti*) are *gaṃ* and *svāhā*. For the attainment of desired objects: *hrāṃ gāṃ* is the heart mantra (1).
*Hrīṃ gīṃ* for the head (2); *hrūṃ guṃ* for the crest-lock (3); *hraim gaiṃ* for the armor (4); *hrauṃ grauṃ* for the eyes (5);

*hraḥ graḥ* for the weapon (6). The visualization (*dhyāna*): [I meditate upon] the Moon-crested Lord, who has three eyes, whose face is washed by the waters of worldly existence, and who holds in his own hands a lotus, a goad, and a jewel-pitcher; [and upon] her who rests upon his lap...
We worship you, whose splendor is like that of a lotus, who placed his hand with its curved claws upon the womb of the Goddess, and who wears a jeweled crown.

In the upper right and left hands are a lotus and a goad; the trunk holds two jeweled jars used to cover their source. Alternatively, starting from the lower right hand, there is a quartet beginning with a lotus. Thus, he stands in the midst of an ocean of nectar, resembling a red lotus.
Resembling ten million suns, he held a noose, a goad,
and a sugarcane staff, and was drinking from a goblet the juice extracted from sugarcane.

Having meditated upon the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśa) as being accompanied by Śakti, who holds a lotus and rests upon his left lap, one should worship him while holding a cup with the trunk of his hand.

One should meditate on the noose and goad in the right and left upper hands; below those, a cup of molasses and sugarcane juice, from which [the deity] is drinking the sugarcane juice from the edge of the cup with a stalk of sugarcane. Thus, on the previously mentioned seat—

Having invoked [the deity] together with the Śakti, one should worship. One should worship on the petals and in the center with the mantra: "Obeisance to Vāmā (1), Jyeṣṭhā (2), Raudrī (3), Kalavikarṇī (4), Balavikariṇī (5), Balapramathinī (6), Sarvabhūtadamanī (7), and Manonmanī (8). [Then worship] Pramoda (1) and Sumukha (2).

One should worship with "Salutation to Durmukha" (3) and "Salutation to Vighnanāśaka" (4) in the cardinal directions. One should worship with "Āṃ, salutation to Brāhmī" (1), "Īṃ, salutation to Māheśvarī" (2), "Ṛṃ, salutation to Kaumārī" (3), "Ṝṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇavī" (4), "Ḷṃ, salutation to Karāhī" (5), "Aiṃ, salutation to Māhendrī" (6), "Aṃ, salutation to Cāmuṇḍā" (7), and "Aḥ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī" (8). One should also worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions.

Having performed the recitation (*japa*), one should dismiss the deity. The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is as previously described. Now follows the mantra of Viri-Gaṇapati: *hrīṃ virivirigaṇapati varavarada sarvalokaṃ me vaśam ānaya svāhā*. For this mantra, Gaṇapati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Viri-Vighneśvara is the deity (*devatā*). It is for the purpose of attaining subjugation (*vaśya*) and other such powers.
The Application (viniyoga): *Hrīṃ*, the heart of Viri-viri; 1 *Hrīṃ*, the head of Gaṇapati; 2 *Hrīṃ*, the crest-lock of the bestower of boons (*varavarada*);
3 *Hrīṃ*, the eye that looks upon all the worlds; 4 *Hrīṃ*, bring [them] under control, the armor (*kavaca*); 5 *Hrīṃ* svāhā, the weapon (*astra*). 6 The Meditation (dhyāna):
[One should meditate on the Lord] who has the luster of vermilion, an elephantine face, and three eyes, holding a noose and a goad in his hands.
I worship the one whose head is adorned with the crescent moon and who holds a honey-filled skull-cup.

66a) [He whose] body is embraced by Puṣpā, who holds the tip of a banner in her hand; [he whose] lotus-like hand shines as she places it upon his lap; [he] who has taken hold of the Earth, with a shining lotus in his hand—[this is] the upper right [hand].

In his two left hands he holds a noose and a goad; in the two lower hands, a skull-cup containing honey and the source of nourishment (the yoni) are to be meditated upon. Having thus meditated, one should invoke the deity onto the pedestal (pīṭha) endowed with intensity and other qualities, and worship him.
The first circuit of worship is performed with Vāmā and the others; the second with Āmoda and the others; the third with the limbs (aṅgas).

The fourth [consecration] is with the Mothers; the fifth with the World-Protectors (Lokapālas); the sixth with Vava and the others. The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of four hundred thousand recitations. The fire sacrifice (*homa*) is performed with ten parts of the eight substances smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). Now follows the mantra of Sundarīvallabha: *Oṃ hrīṃ gūṃ viri virivi Vināyaka, bestower of boons, heart of all the worlds...*

*mevaśaṃ kurukuru svāhā*. The *ṛṣi* and other [limbs] are as before. *Oṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* (1); *hrīṃ śiraḥ* (2); *gūṃ śikhā* (3); *virivirivināyaka* for the armor (*kavaca*) (4); *varavarada sarvaloka hṛdayaṃ netraṃ* (5); *mevaśaṃ kurukuru svāhā* for the weapon (*astra*) (6). Meditation and so forth are as before. Now, the *trailokya*...

The Deluding Mantra (*mohanamantra*). It consists of thirty-four syllables: *oṃ namo bhagavate ekadaṃṣṭrāya hastimukha lambodarāya ucchiṣṭa mahātmane āṃ kroṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gaṃ svāhā*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as before. The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is performed with the final seed-syllables. The meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*pūjā*), and so forth [are to be performed].
As previously stated, there is another mantra for deluding the three worlds,
consisting of thirty-three syllables: *vakratuṇḍaikadaṃṣṭrāya klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ*.
*Gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details are as previously stated. *Vakratuṇḍaikadaṃṣṭrāya klīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ gaṃ*—*namaḥ* to the heart (1).
*Gaṇapati varavarada*—to the crest-lock (*śikhā*) (2). *Sarvajanaṃ*—the armor (*kavaca*) (3). *Mevaśamānaya*—to the two eyes (*netra*) (4).

*Svāhā* to the weapon (*astra*), five times. The meditation (*dhyāna*): [He is] five-faced and ten-armed, accompanied by Śakti, O Great Gaṇapati, together with the weapons mentioned in the mantra. Everything else is as previously stated. Now, another mantra for Śakti-Gaṇapati, consisting of eleven syllables: *Oṃ hrīṃ gaṃ hrīṃ vaśamānaya svāhā*.

The *ṛṣi* and other [constituent parts] are as previously stated. Oṃ hṛdayam (Heart) 1; Hrīṃ Gaṃ Hrīṃ śiraḥ (Head) 2; Vaśaṃ śikhā (Crest) 3; Ānaya kavacam (Armor) 4; Svāhā netratrayam (Three Eyes) 5; with the entire mantra, the weapon (*astra*). Meditation (*dhyāna*):
Holding in his hands the crescent moon, the boon-granting gesture (*varada*), the noose (*pāśa*), and the goad (*aṅkuśa*), and touching the lotus... [his own face].

I constantly meditate upon the Lord, who is exceedingly fond of enjoyment, whose elephantine face is as red as the *japā* flower, who has three eyes and the crescent moon as his crest-jewel; he is untouched by the hand of any excellent woman, yet he touches the tip of the banner with the hand of a dark-limbed maiden holding a lotus. With his lower right and left hands, he holds two excellent stalks of sugarcane.

In her upper two hands, she holds a noose and a goad; with her right hand she holds Lakṣmī, and with her left she holds his (Viṣṇu’s) emblem. The worship and other rites are as previously described. The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of three hundred thousand recitations.
The fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed with ten parts of fresh rice-cakes smeared with clarified butter.
Having offered cakes smeared with the three sweets, one shall subjugate kings on earth;
by offering a coconut on the fourth lunar day, one shall obtain great prosperity.
One shall bring women under one's control by means of salt combined with sweet substances.
Now follows the fifty-five-syllable garland mantra: Hrīṃ Krauṃ Oṃ Gaṃ Namaḥ Sarvavighnādhipāya Sarvārthasiddhidāya Sarvaduḥkhapraśamanāya Ehyehi.
O Bhagavān, paralyze all hearts! Staṃbhaya staṃ bhaya hrīṃ gaṃ gīṃ namaḥ svāhā kroṃ hrīṃ. The ṛṣi and other [limbs] are as stated for the Mahāgaṇapati mantra. Now follows the Mahāgaṇapati mantra.

It consists of twenty-eight syllables: *oṃ śrīṃ hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ gaṃ gaṇapataye varavarada sarvajanaṃ me vaśamānaya svāhā*. For this [mantra], Mahāgaṇapati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Trivṛt-Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Mahāgaṇapati is the deity (*devatā*), *gaṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *svāhā* is the power (*śaktiḥ*), and *glauṃ* is the bolt (*kīlaka*).
The application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of Mahālakṣmī: Oṃ Gaṃ, salutation to the heart. 1 Śrīṃ Gīṃ, svāhā to the head.

2 Hrīṃ Gūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). 3 Klīṃ Glauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes. 4 Glauṃ Glaiṃ, huṃ to the armor (*kavaca*). 5 Gaṃ Gaḥ, phaṭ to the weapon (*astra*). 6 Meditation (*dhyāna*): [She resides] in the ocean of sugarcane juice...

One should meditate upon Him seated upon a jeweled throne beneath a Pārijāta tree on the island of Navaratna, situated within the pericarp of the Mother’s lotus, in the center of a hexagon. His uplifted lotus-hands hold a citron, a mace, a sugarcane bow, a discus, a lotus, a noose, a goad, a grain of rice, a tusk, and a jeweled jar filled with nectar.
He is to be meditated upon as embraced by his beloved, who holds a lotus in her hand and is adorned with blazing ornaments,
[the Lord] who is the origin, destruction, and maintenance of the universe.

The hand that creates obstacles bestows distinguished goals. Beginning from the lower right hand, the citron fruit, mace, sugarcane bow, axe, and discus are to be meditated upon. Beginning from the upper left hand, the lotus, noose, goad, vase, spear, and one’s own tusk are to be meditated upon.

One should meditate on him raining a continuous stream of jewels, pearls, and gold from the jars held in his lotus-like hands, showering all around the practitioner for the sake of complete prosperity. According to the opinion of some, he should be visualized starting from the upper right hand, joined with the *bījāpūra* [creeper] and so forth, proceeding in a clockwise direction. However, in the *Śāradātilaka*, in place of the word *ruj* (sickness), [it says... (Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete at the end.)

The trident is in the place of the goad, and the lotus likewise. And the visualization is as follows: [One should meditate on] the Lord with the face of a lordly elephant, crowned by the moon, possessing a ruddy luster and three eyes, who is constantly embraced out of passion by his beloved, whose hands hold a lotus and who rests upon his own lap.

I worship Him who holds in His hands a citron, a mace, a bow, a trident, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, a tusk, and a jewel-filled pitcher. One should meditate on Him gladdening the practitioner—who is overwhelmed with joy—with jeweled goblets flowing from the mouths of the ruby-pitchers held at the tips of His hands. Having thus meditated...

Having worshipped with mental offerings, one should worship Mahāgaṇapati— of the same form as previously described— in the center of the six-cornered figure within the pericarp of the lotus on the aforementioned Gaṇapati-pīṭha, using services such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth. Then, one should [worship] Lakṣmī, who is seated upon a lotus beneath the bilva tree standing in front, and [the deity] holding a discus and a conch in his hands.
One should meditate upon Vāsudeva. Having meditated thus, one should worship with the mantra: "Obeisance to Lakṣmī and Vāsudeva."

In the south, having meditated upon Gaurī beneath a banyan tree holding a noose and a goad, and Hara holding an axe and a trident, one should worship them with the mantra: "Obeisance to Gaurī and the Lord of Gaurī. In the west, beneath a peepal tree, [one should meditate upon] Rati holding a blue lotus, and [her consort] holding a bow and arrows.

68a) Having meditated upon Ratipati, one should worship with the mantra: "Homage to Rati and Rati. To the north, beneath a *priyaṅgu* tree, having meditated upon the Earth—who holds a *suvrīhi* creeper and stands upon ground, and who is the Boar holding a mace and a disc—one should [worship] Bhūmi.
One should worship with "Obeisance to the two Boars. Then, in the six corners starting from the east:
"Gaṃ, obeisance to Siddhi and Āmoda" (1); "Gaṃ, obeisance to Samṛddhi and Pramoda" (2); "Gaṃ, obeisance to Kānti and Sumukha" (3); "Gaṃ, obeisance to Madanāvatī and Durmukha" (4); "Gaṃ..."

One should worship with: "Obeisance to Madadrava and Avighna" (5), and "Obeisance to Madadrāvinī and Vighnakartṛ" (6). Then, on the two sides of the hexagon, one should worship with: "Obeisance to Śaṅkha and Vasudhārā," and "Obeisance to Padma and Vasumatī. According to the *Prapañcasāra*, this is for the front side.

On both sides of that, in the rear corners, the Siddhas and Maudyas are to be worshipped. On both sides, the Śaṅkha and Padma Nidhis are to be worshipped. Then follows the worship of the limbs (aṅga-pūjā). One should worship the previously mentioned limbs with "Oṃ Aṅga-hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth. Then [worship] Brāhmī and the others. In front, one says "Kumbhodarāya namaḥ."

Then [one should worship] the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their respective weapons. Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana). Now follows the procedure for the libation (tarpaṇavidhi).

In the morning, having worshipped Mahāgaṇapati and having placed the syllable *va*, the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*), into the water, one should mutter the seed-syllable *vaṃ* eleven times while touching that water. Contemplating that water as consisting of nectar, and reciting "I satisfy Mahāgaṇapati upon the head of the deity," one should [sprinkle it] with the root mantra eleven times.

One should satisfy [the deities] four times; or forty-four times; or more than that, four hundred times; or more than that, four thousand times. The sequence is as follows: having recited the root mantra...

Having uttered "I satisfy Mahāgaṇapati," one should perform the libation for his satisfaction. Then, with the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*, one should satisfy Gaurī together with Viṣṇu. Then, with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, one should satisfy Śrī together with Viṣṇu by performing the libation four times, saying, "I satisfy [Śrī] together with Viṣṇu. Again, with the seed-syllable of Gajapati, one should satisfy Mahāgaṇapati.
One should perform the libation four times with the mantra "I satisfy" (*tarpayāmi*). Then, one should satisfy Gaurī together with Śiva using the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*.
Again, one should satisfy Mahāgaṇapati with the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati; Rati together with Manobhava (Kāmadeva) with the seed-syllable of Kāma;
again, Mahāgaṇapati with the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati; and Bhūmi together with Varāha with the seed-syllable *glauṃ* of Bhū.

Again, [worship] Gaṇapati with the seed-syllable *gaṃ*; Gaṇapati together with Śakti and Vighna with the seed-syllable *gaṃ*; again Gaṇapati; [and] the creator of obstacles (Vighnakartṛ) together with Śakti with the seed-syllable *gaṃ*; again Gaṇapati. In this manner: *gaṃ* accompanied by Siddhi is Āmoda (1); *gaṃ* accompanied by Samṛddhi is Pramoda (2); *gaṃ* [accompanied by] Kānti...
With *gaṃ* [I propitiate] Sahisumukha together with Madanāvatī; with *gaṃ* [I propitiate] Durmukha together with Madadravā;
with *gaṃ* [I propitiate] Vighna together with Madadrāviṇī; with *gaṃ* [I propitiate] Vighnakartṛ together with Vasudhārā;
and with *gaṃ* [I propitiate] Śaṅkhanidhi together with Vasumatī. Thus [I propitiate] Mahāgaṇapati.

One should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) four times for each [deity], either individually or collectively. This is the procedure for libation. According to the opinion of some, those who lack the capacity for the libation including *Āmoda* and the others should perform the libation to them alone. Performing libation in this manner, one accomplishes whatever one desires. [The number of repetitions is] four hundred and forty-eight thousand.
Puraścaraṇa:
As previously stated, the homa is performed with ten parts of the eight substances, such as modaka and the rest.
One should daily satisfy the Leader of the Gaṇas with pure waters,
diligently offering forty-four oblations four hundred times.

A person who has attained perfection through recitation and other practices may obtain his desired goal, whether it be within the mandala or even more than that, by means of ritual application according to his excellent intention.
One should accomplish [the rite] with eight substances or others as prescribed by the ritual manual;
by offering lotuses one gains kings, and by auspicious blue lotuses (utpala), their wives.
He [honored] the ministers with full-blown white water lilies, the Brahmins with sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from the Pippala tree,
and the kings with excellent fuel-sticks arising from the Udumbara tree.

By means of *plakṣa* leaves, one brings Vaiśyas under control; by those produced from the *vaṭa* tree, a practitioner of mantras brings Śūdras under control. With honey, there shall be the acquisition of gold; with cow's milk, one obtains cattle.
By an oblation of clarified butter, a person attains great prosperity;
by curd, there shall be complete abundance; and by grains, one becomes a lord of food.
One desiring rain should offer oblations with the best fuel-sticks of reeds;
by offering oblations with *vakula* flowers, one obtains garments before long.

*namaḥ*. *Oṃ yaṃ namaḥ* to the two little fingers; *namaḥ*. *Oṃ huṃ namaḥ* to the palms and backs of the hands; *namaḥ*. Thus is the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*).
In this manner, one should perform the placement of the six limbs, beginning with the heart, using the syllables: *oṃ vaṃ namaḥ* at the center of the eyebrows;
likewise, one should place the syllables at the throat, the heart, the navel, the *liṅga*, and the *ādhāra*.
One should meditate here upon Gaṇanātha, who is all-pervading in his totality; who holds a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā;
whose beautiful luster resembles a blooming red gem; who is seated within the hollow of a lotus;
who is serene; and who, for the sake of Indirā, bestows a reddish-brown boon upon her to the right.

Beginning with the hand, the noose (*pāśa*) and other implements are to be meditated upon. Following the mental worship (*mānasika-pūjā*), one should invoke the aforementioned deity onto the *gaṇapati*-pedestal and worship Him with the ritual services (*upacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*):
1. Vidyā, 2. Vidhātrī, 3. Bhogadā, 4. Vighnaghātinī, 5. Nidhipradīpā.

One should worship with the words: "Obeisance to Pāpaghnī (6), Puṇyā (7), and Śaśiprabhā (8). On the petals, one should worship with the words: "Obeisance to Vakratuṇḍa (1), Ekadaṃṣṭra (2), Mahodara (3), Gajānana (4), Laṃbodara (5), Vikaṭa (6), Vighnarāja (7), and Dhūmraka (8). Then, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) as well.
Having offered handfuls of pure flowers, food offerings (naivedya), and so forth, one should dismiss the deity into one's own heart.

The libations (tarpaṇa) and other rites are as previously described. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations of the syllables. The fire sacrifice (homa) is performed with eight substances in ten parts of the total number. Endowed with celibacy and other virtues, one should perform twelve thousand recitations.

In both fortnights, having recited [the mantra] ten thousand times in sequence up to the fourth lunar day, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times. Poverty is destroyed within six months. [One should offer] food smeared with clarified butter every month.

Through thirty thousand oblations performed in sequence, there is a great increase of wealth. By the daily performance of a thousand oblations with young coconuts, betel nuts, and black pepper, there is an abundance of great wealth within just one month.
Likewise, by performing a thousand oblations every day with eight substances consisting of black pepper, cumin, and rock salt, [the same result is attained].

The accomplishment of many purposes occurs in merely a fortnight; there are many such applications, but they have not been written here for fear of making the book too voluminous. Now, another mantra: "O you who are the beloved of wealth and prosperity, the possessor of treasures and jewels, the destroyer of the hosts of Rākṣasas and of secret spells—this six-syllabled king of mantras."

The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details for this mantra are the same as those for Vakratuṇḍa. Now, another [mantra]: "O beloved of wealth and nourishment, O giver of treasures, O slayer of the hosts of Rākṣasas and of *valagas*, [homage] to Vakratuṇḍa, *huṃ*! The seer and other details for this one are also as before.
"Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa; may that Daṃṣṭrin inspire us. Thus [ends the section].
The Gāyatrī [meter]. Now, another six-syllable [mantra]: "To Megholkā, svāhā! The ṛṣi and other details are as before.

Now follows the Ucchiṣṭa Gaṇapati mantra: *Hastipiśācilikhe svāhā*. The seer (ṛṣi) of this is Kaṅkola by name; the meter (chandaḥ) is Virāṭ; the deity (devatā) is Ucchiṣṭa Gaṇapati; the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals. *Hasti* is the heart (1); *Piśāci* is the head (2); *Likhe* is the crest-lock (śikhā) (3); *Svāhā* is the armor (kavaca) (4); the whole [mantra] is the weapon (astra) (5).

The meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*pūjā*), and so forth are as previously described. During the *ucchiṣṭa* (remnant) period, while performing the application (*viniyoga*), recitation (*japa*), and other rites, he does whatever pleases him. Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gaṇapati Mantra," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhin.
70b) Now, the Śaiva mantras.

First, the Prāsāda [mantra]: *Hauṃ*. For the Prāsāda mantra, Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Paṅkti is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Sadāśiva is the deity (*devatā*), *Haṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Oṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the desired purpose. *Hāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ* (1); *Hīṃ* to the head, *svāhā* (2); *Hūṃ* to the crest-lock, *vaṣaṭ* (3); *Haiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ* (4); *Hauṃ*...

*Netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* (5); *Haḥ astrāya phaṭ* (6). Then, one should place the five mantras upon the fingers starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger: *Oṃ hauṃ īśānāya namaḥ* (1); *Oṃ haiṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ* (2); *Oṃ hūṃ aghorāya namaḥ* (3); *Hīṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ* (4); *Haṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ* (5). Thus, [the mantras are assigned] to the fingers beginning with the thumb and ending with the little finger.

Having performed the placement with those same fingers upon the head, heart, secret place, and feet, one should again place those five mantras on the eastern, southern, northern, and western faces. Then follows the meditation: [one should visualize the deity] holding a trident, a snake, a hammer, a bell, a sword, a horn, a thunderbolt, a noose, fire, and the gesture of fearlessness.

I bow to the Lord of Pārvatī, who rests upon a lotus, who resembles a crystal gem, who has five faces, and three eyes; whose head bears a mass of matted locks fashioned from fragments of the moon; whose body is beautiful with various graceful gestures; who bestows desired objects, and who is most gracious. (From the right lower [hand]...)

Beginning from the right hand and proceeding clockwise, the weapons beginning with the trident (śūla) up to the left lower hand should be visualized in sequence. On the right and left shoulders are the trident and the serpent; below those, the axe (ṭaṅka) and the bell (ghaṇṭā); below those, the goad (aṅkuśa) and the noose (pāśa); below those, the thunderbolt (kuliśa) and the hook (pāśa); and below those, according to some, the fire (agni) and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya). Thus it is said.
Having meditated, one should perform the external worship after the mental worship. Having established the *argha* water according to the previous procedure in the vessel for the deity’s mouth (71a).

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kālāgnirudra; to Ādhāraśakti (1); to Mūlaprakṛti (2); to Kūrma (the Tortoise) (3); to Mahāvarāha (the Great Boar) (4); to Ananta (the Infinite) (5); to Bhūmi (the Earth) (6); to Kailāsa (7); to the Kalpavṛkṣa (Wish-fulfilling Tree) (8); to the Ratnamaṇḍapa (Jeweled Pavilion) (9); to the Ratnasiṃhāsana (Jeweled Lion Throne) (10); and to the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) accompanied by Skanda and others (11).

Thus one should worship in successive layers above. Above that, having envisioned a square pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should worship in the corners of the pedestal with: "Obeisance to Dharma," "Obeisance to Jñāna," "Obeisance to Vairāgya," and "Obeisance to Aiśvarya. One should worship on the sides of the pedestal with: "Obeisance to Adharma," "Obeisance to Ajñāna," "Obeisance to Avairāgya," and "Obeisance to Anaiśvarya."

In the center, one should worship with: "Oṃ *taṃ* to Tamas, 1; *raṃ* to Rajas, 2; *saṃ* to Sattva, 3; *māṃ* to Māyā, 4; *viṃ* to Vidyā, 5; to the Ātman, 6; to the Antarātman, 7; to the Paramātman, 8; to the Jñānātman, 9; to the Fire-maṇḍala, 10; to the Sun-maṇḍala, 11;
to the Moon-maṇḍala, 12; *namaḥ*. Above that is an eight-petaled [lotus].

Having visualized a lotus, one should worship on the petals starting from the east and so forth with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmā," 1. "to Jyeṣṭhā," 2. "to Raudrī," 3. "to Kālī," 4. "to Kalavikariṇī," 5. "to Balapramathinī," 6. "to Sarvabhūtamadanī," 7. [and] "obeisance" (namaḥ), 8. Then, in the center: "Oṃ, obeisance to Manonmanī. Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One.

Having worshipped the seat with a handful of flowers, saying: "Salutation to the Infinite One, who is endowed with the power of the self of all attributes, and whose nature is the Yoga-pīṭha," one should invoke the Lord from the heart and worship Him there with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya).
There, in the western quarter, [one should meditate on] the four-faced one, white as a kunda flower, holding a deer, a rosary, and making the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.

Having meditated [upon him], one should worship Sadyojāta with the mantra: *oṃ haṃsadyojātāya namaḥ*. || 1 || On the left side, having meditated upon Vāmadeva—who has the luster of saffron and holds the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, as well as a battle-axe and a rosary—one should worship Vāmadeva with the mantra: *oṃ hiṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*. || 2 ||

71b) On the right side, one should visualize [the deity] with the luster of collyrium, four-faced, holding in his right and left hands, respectively, a rosary, the Vedas, a noose, a goad, a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, and a skull-cup.

One should worship with "Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghora. (3) Having meditated upon [the deity] in the western quarter as golden-colored, four-faced, and holding the Vedas, the rosary, the gesture of granting fearlessness, and the gesture of boons, as well as an axe, one should worship Tatpuruṣa with "Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa. (4) In the center [one should meditate upon the deity] who has the luster of a pearl, five faces, and is exceedingly gracious.
Having meditated upon [Īśāna] as holding a rosary, a Veda, a noose, a goad, a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a trident, and a skull-cup, one should worship Īśāna with:
*oṃ hauṃ īśānāya namaḥ*. In the corners starting from the southeast, one should worship Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and Śānti; and in the center, with: "Salutation to Śāntyatītā. || 5 ||

One should worship [thus]. This is the first round (*vṛtti*). The second [round] is with the limbs (*aṅga*). One should worship with: "Salutation to Ananta 1, Sūkṣma 2, Śaivottama 3, Ekanetra 4, Ekarudra 5, Trimūrti 6, Śrīkhaṇḍa 7, and Śikhaṇḍin. These, beginning with Ananta, are the tridents and thunderbolts... [text ends].
They should be meditated upon as having outstretched hands and possessing the colors of pale red, yellow, white, crimson, white, red, white, and smoky; they are seated upon lotuses.
Beginning from the northern petal: [one offers] to Umā (1), Caṇḍeśvara (2), Nandin (3), and Mahākāla (4).
One should worship with: "Salutation to Gaṇeśvara," "5. To Vṛṣa," "6. To Bhṛṅgiriṭi," "7. To Skanda," and "8. Salutation.
Umā and the others are to be meditated upon as having the luster of gold, sapphire, coral, emerald, pearl, white crystal, and ruby respectively.

One should worship Indra and the others in their respective directions, as well as their weapons. Having worshipped thus and offered the recitation (*japa*), having dissolved the retinue of the deity’s body, having dismissed the deity into one's own heart, and having performed the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should worship below the deity with "Obeisance to Caṇḍeśvara. This is the summary of the worship. However, some [say]:
They describe the seed-syllable (*bīja*) encased within the *hṛllekhā* mantra for recitation and other rites. The preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of eleven hundred thousand recitations.

The fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed with ten parts of *karavīra* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*). The placement of the five Brahmans (*pañcabrahmannyāsa*) has not been written here due to its length.
Thus, the best of practitioners should worship the deity every day;
having obtained prosperity along with sons, friends, and others, he rejoices.
Now follows the five-syllable [mantra].
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva. Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandaḥ), Śiva is the deity (devatā).

"Iṣṭārtha" is the seed-syllable (bīja), "Āya" is the power (śakti), "Naṃ" is the pin (kīlaka); its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of knowledge. Some say that at the time of recitation, one should use "Oṃ" as the seed-syllable and "Namaḥ" as the power. There is also the tradition that one should recite it preceded by the Praṇava and the Prāsāda mantra. Not so.

For the five syllables beginning with *kā*, the seers (*ṛṣi*) are Gotama, Atri, Viśvāmitra, Aṅgiras, and Bharadvāja; the meters (*chandas*) are Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Virāṭ; the deities (*devatā*) are Indra, Rudra, Hari, Brahmā, and Skanda; and their colors are yellow, black, smoky, white, and [the fifth].

72b) Having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the root mantra, [one assigns]: *oṃ* to the heart (1), *naṃ* to the head (2), *maṃ* to the crest-lock (3), *śiṃ* to the armor (4), *vāṃ* to the three eyes (5), and *yaṃ* to the weapon (6). Or else:
Oṃ, to the abode of the omniscient one, the heart; 1. Naṃ, to the abode of the three-fold [abodes], the head; 2. Maṃ, to the abode of beginningless awakening, the crest-lock;
3. Śiṃ, to the abode of self-sovereignty, the armor; 4. Vāṃ, to the abode of light, the three eyes; 5.
Yaṃ, to the abode of infinite power, obeisance, the weapon; 6. And the ritual placement (*nyāsa*): Naṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa; 1. Maṃ...
One should place [the mantras] on the index, middle, ring, little, and thumb fingers respectively: *aghorāya* twice (*śiṃ*), *sadyojātāya* (*vāṃ*), *vāmadevāya* (*yaṃ*), and *īśānāya namaḥ*.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the mouth, heart, secret place, navel, and head;
and one should also perform it on the faces directed east, south, west, north, and upward. Then follows the meditation (*dhyāna*):
The Great Lord (*Maheśa*), exceedingly gracious, blazing with all ornaments, holds in his arms an axe, a deer, and the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.

Dwelling in a lotus, clad in a tiger skin, he is to be meditated upon as having the luster of a mountain imbued with the nectar-like radiance of pearls and gems; five-faced, three-eyed, his lofty crown adorned with the brilliance of millions of crescent moons;
holding an axe and a deer in his right and left hands respectively.

Having meditated thus—[the deity] holding the gestures of fearlessness and boon-bestowal below that—one should perform the external worship. Having invoked the God upon the previously mentioned Śiva-pīṭha, one should worship Him with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya). The first enclosure consists of Īśāna and the others;
the second, of the limbs (aṅgas); the third, of Ananta and the others; the fourth, of Umā and the others; and [the fifth], of Indra and the others.

The fifth [offering] with those same weapons; thus, having worshipped, one should perform the dismissal (udvāsana) after the recitation. One hundred thousand repetitions of the syllables constitutes the *puraścaraṇa*. The fire-oblation (*homa*) should consist of ten parts of pure sesame seeds, or a sacrifice with milk-rice or milk-fuel-sticks (*samidh*).

73a) Now, the eight-syllable [mantra], or the five-syllable Śakti: *oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ śivāya hrīṃ*. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes are as before. *hrīṃ oṃ hrāṃ* is the heart (1); *hrīṃ naṃ hrīṃ* is the head (2); *hrīṃ*...
Maṃ hrūṃ—for the crest (śikhā), thrice; hrīṃ śiṃ hraiṃ—for the armor (kavaca), four times; hrīṃ vāṃ hrauṃ—for the eyes (netra), five times;

hrīṃ yaṃ hraḥ astrāya phaṭ—six times. Meditation (dhyāna): I bow to Hara, who holds a boon-granting gesture, a trident, and a skull-cup in his hands; who possesses a splendor like that of fire due to his love for me, the daughter of the mountain; and whose left hand rests upon the lap of the goddess seated on his left thigh.

Having meditated upon [the deity] whose body is encircled by a pair of red lotuses placed upon his thighs, one should visualize the [four] hands— beginning from the lower right hand— as bestowing boons (*varada*), holding a trident (*śūla*), a skull-cup (*kapāla*), and granting fearlessness (*abhaya*). Having thus meditated and performed mental worship (*mānasī pūjā*),
one should invoke the God onto the pedestal (*pīṭha*) prescribed in the Prāsāda mantra and worship Him with the ritual services (*upacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*).
Then follows the limb-enclosure (*aṅgāvaraṇa*). [The first enclosure] is in the center, east, south, west, and north.
The second is with Hṛllekhā and the others; the fourth with Brāhmī and the others; the fifth with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*).

After the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of ten hundred thousand [recitations], performed with [offerings] smeared with honey.

The oblation is performed with fourteen parts using fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of the *rājavṛkṣa* tree. Now follows the eight-syllabled *Urdhvanārīśvara*: *Oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ namaḥ śivāya*. Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chaṃdas*), Umāmaheśvara is the deity (*devatā*), *praṇava* (Oṃ) is the seed-syllable (*vīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *naṃ* is the pin (*kīlaka*), for the sake of one's desired object. As before, the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is performed.

And he is in a state of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). He should be visualized as golden-hued, with his left hand resting on the left shoulder of his beloved, while her left arm rests upon his chest; she holds a red lotus in her [left] hand, and her radiant left arm is extended across his body. He is adorned with all the beautiful ornaments, and his other hands hold an axe, a deer, and a wish-granting gem (*iṣṭaka*). He should be meditated upon thus.

Seated in the lotus posture, his body graced with the charm of the God of Love, he is the Lord of Pārvatī. With his lower left hand he touches his two breasts; with the right, he grants boons; and with the two upper hands, he holds an axe and a deer.
The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of eight hundred thousand recitations. A fire sacrifice (*homa*) with ghee should be performed for as many thousands [of times].
Worship and other rites are performed with the five-syllabled mantra (*pañcākṣarīmantra*). Now, the Mṛtyuñjaya [mantra]: Oṃ juṃ saḥ.

73b) For this [mantra], the seer is Kaholaka, the meter is Gāyatrī of the gods, the deity is Rudra Mṛtyuñjaya, the seed-syllable is *juṃ*, and the power is *saḥ* for the sake of one's desired goal. *Sāṃ* is the heart; *sīṃ* is the [head]; *sūṃ* is the tuft (*śikhā*).

*Saum* for the three eyes (4); *Saḥ* for the weapon (5). The visualization (*dhyāna*): Seated upon a lotus with joined petals, his head adorned with a crescent moon from which streams of nectar flow, wetting him;
he is endowed with the [three] eyes of the moon, fire, and sun, and holds the gestures (*mudrās*) along with a noose, a lotus, and a rosary of *vedākṣa* seeds.

I bow to the Lord, white as crystal, silver, or pearl. He should be meditated upon as holding the *jñānamudrā* and a noose in his right and left hands respectively, and bearing a rosary and the Vedas.
Following the mental worship (*mānasikapūjā*), one should invoke the Deity onto the pedestal (*pīṭha*) described in the *Prāsāda-mantra*.

One should worship with the ritual services (*upacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). The first enclosure (*āvṛtti*) is with [the deities] beginning with Aṭha; the second with those beginning with Ananta; the third with those beginning with Umā; and the fourth with those beginning with Indra. At the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of three hundred thousand repetitions, and the fire-oblation (*homa*) is one-tenth of that, performed with pieces of *guḍūcī* boiled in milk.
A person should daily offer eleven oblations with *dūrvā* grass;

this conquers untimely death and increases longevity and health. An oblation performed with three thousand excellent fuel-sticks (*samidh*) from the *sudhā-vallī*, *kāśmarī*, and *vakula* trees removes all forms of death and disease.
The *homa* performed with *siddhārtha* seeds destroys great [obstacles].
A *homa* performed with *apāmārga* is the destroyer of all diseases. Now, regarding *Nīlakaṇṭha*: *Proṃ trīṃṭhaḥ*.
Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes are as before. "Hara-hara svāhā" is the heart mantra (1).
74a) *Kapardine svāhā*, [offering to] the head (2); *Nīlakaṇṭhāya svāhā* (3); *Kālakūṭaviṣabhakṣaṇaya hūṃ phaṭ*, [offering to] the armor (4);
*Nīlakaṇṭhine svāhā*, [offering to] the weapon (5). Meditation: [He possesses] the splendor of ten thousand rising suns.

I bow to the illustrious Nīlakaṇṭha, who wears a matted lock of hair bound with the crescent moon, who is adorned with blazing lordly serpents as ornaments, and who holds in his hands a rosary, a trident, a skull-cup, and a khaṭvāṅga staff; he who possesses three eyes, shines with five faces, is beautiful, is clothed in a tiger skin, and wears a rosary of rudrākṣa beads.

I worship [Him]. Visualizing Him as holding a rosary and a trident with the two hands above the lower right hand, and a skull-cup and a *khaṭvāṅga* with the other two hands—one should perform mental worship (*mānasika-pūjā*) and, having invoked the Deity upon the pedestal described in the *Prāsāda*, worship Him according to the previously stated procedure. [Recite] three hundred thousand [times].

The *puraścaraṇa* consists of a fire-oblation (*homa*) of clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) and sacrificial food (*havis*) performed ten times the number of recitations. When the mantra has been thus perfected through worship and other rites, the practitioner—like a second Śiva (Nīlakaṇṭha)—will quickly destroy the two kinds of poison. One should sprinkle the person afflicted by poison with auspicious waters contained in a pitcher, over which this mantra has been recited.
One shall be instantly freed from poison; by touching and reciting [the mantra] over one overcome by poison, that person shall become free of poison in an instant.

Now, Caṇḍeśvara: *Rū gha jha gha phaṭ*. For this [mantra], the seer is Trika, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Caṇḍeśvara for the sake of one's desired object. *Dīpta phaṭ* is the heart (1); *Jvala phaṭ* is the head (2);
*Jvālini phaṭ* is the crest-lock (3); *Kaṭ phaṭ* is the armor (4); *Hana phaṭ* is the three eyes (5); *Sarvaṃ jvālini phaṭ*.
The weapon is meditation (dhyāna). May [it] protect [me], its rays reaching to the crescent moon held by Kapardin.

Lord Īśa holds a trident, a rosary, a water-pot, and an axe; his complexion and garments are red, he rests upon a crimson lotus, and his lotus-like face shines with three eyes. With his upper right and lower left hands he holds a trident and a rosary, and with his lower left and upper right hands he holds a water-pot and an axe.

The *jñeya* [is as follows]: "We know Caṇḍacaṇḍa; we meditate upon Mahādeva; may that Caṇḍa inspire us. This is the *Caṇḍagāyatrī*, which brings about the presence of Śiva. Having invoked the Lord into the Śaiva seat (*pīṭha*), one should worship Him. The first enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) is with the limbs (*aṅga*s); the second with the Mothers; the third with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*s).
"Caṇḍeśvarāya namaḥ" is the mantra for worship. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of three hundred thousand recitations.

The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with sesamum seeds and rice grains smeared with the three sweets (madhuratraya), numbering one-tenth of the recitations. Now follows the Cintāmaṇi mantra.

*Kṣmyrauṃ*. Kaśyapa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Cintāmaṇi-Īśvara is the deity (*devatā*), *Raṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Ṣaṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and *Maṃ* is the heart-lock (*kīlaka*). The application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of all knowledge and sovereignty.
*Raṃ* is the heart (1); *Kaṃ* is the head (2); *Ṣaṃ* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*) (3); *Maṃ* is the armor (*kavaca*) (4); *Raṃ* is the three eyes (5).
This is the Astra-mantra (6): Meditation.

He whose lofty crown is adorned with a serpent, the moon, and the Gaṅgā; whose feet are bowed to by the hosts of gods; who possesses three eyes and the grace of a woman; [holding] a serpent, an axe, a trident, a sword, fire, a skull, and an arrow.
May the Lord bearing the bow protect you for a long time— He who holds a serpent and an axe with His upper right and left hands,
a trident and a sword with the two below them, a fire and a skull-cup with the two beneath those,
and an arrow and a bow with the two lowest of all.

For the sake of prosperity, during the ritual of recitation, one should worship Maheśvara, who is half-female and half-male, charming with graceful gestures and expressions yet terrifying; he holds a noose, a blue lotus, a skull-cup, and a trident.

Alternatively: The Blessed Lady should be meditated upon as having sixteen arms occupied with spears, three eyes, six limbs, and possessing the color and ornaments of vermilion garments and unguents. Having invoked the deity upon the seat described for the Prāsāda [temple], 75a) Or else: The Blessed Lady should be meditated upon as having sixteen arms occupied with spears, three eyes, six limbs, and possessing the color and ornaments of vermilion garments and unguents. Having invoked the deity upon the seat described for the Prāsāda [temple], [one should worship].

One should worship with the services [of honor] such as water for the feet (pādya) and so forth. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas). The second [enclosure] consists of the previously mentioned bull and others. [The mantras are]: vṛṃ to Vṛṣa 1; kṣaṃ to Kṣetrapāla 2; caṃḍeśvarāya 3; duṃ to Durgā 4; guṃ to Guhā 5; naṃ to Nandī 6; gaṃ to Gaṇeśvara 7; saiṃ...
One should worship with "Salutation to Sainyapāla" (8 times) on the petals starting from the east. The third [circle] is with the Mothers;

the fourth is with the World-Guardians (Lokapālas). The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations. The fire-oblation (homa) is performed with sesame and rice grains smeared with the three sweets (trimadhura), consisting of one-tenth of that number.
Thus one should worship the supreme deity Ardhanārīśvara;
[the worshipper] becomes beloved of splendor, luster, fame, fortune, and speech.
This seed-mantra, as well as its corresponding visualization, destroys those respective afflictions: the poison of a scorpion sting, fever, burning sensations, delusion, headaches, and vertigo.
Now, as for the *tumburu* seed-syllable: *kṣmrūṃ*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] are as before.

The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are *kṣmrāṃ*, *kṣmrīṃ*, and so forth. The meditation (*dhyāna*): [I meditate upon] the four-faced one, who delights in the crescent moon as his ornament, who has three eyes, and who holds a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a noose, a goad, a trident, a skull-cup, and the Vedas.
I praise the Lord who is red, whose ornaments are priceless due to the destruction of Cipiṭa, and who wears a reddish garment.

One should meditate on him holding a noose and an axe with his upper left and right hands; a trident and a sword with the two below those; two fire-filled skull-cups with the two below those; and a bow and arrow with the two below those—so say some.
Alternatively, someone [may hold] the weapons beginning with the *khaṭvāṅga*, starting from the lower right hand;
[namely], the *khaṭvāṅga*, noose, and goad, beginning from the lower right hand.
Likewise, in the left [hands], he likewise holds a trident, a skull-cup, and a Veda.

Having invoked the deity upon the previously mentioned pedestal, one should worship him. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*). The second [enclosure] consists of recitation (*japa*) and so forth. One should worship [the goddesses] with "Salutation to Durgā," "1," "To Subhagā," "2," "To Karālī," "3," and "To Mohinī," "4," in the corners starting from the northeast (*īśāna*). One should also worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in their respective directions and their weapons. Having performed the recitation, one should dismiss the deity.
One hundred thousand recitations constitute the *puraścaraṇa*; ten thousand oblations with clarified butter and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) are performed. Now follows the Tryambaka mantra:
"We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity;
may he release us from death as one releases a cucumber from its stem, [but not] from immortality. Of this Tryambaka mantra...

Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chaṃdas), Tryambaka Rudra is the deity (devatā); the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of Mṛtyuñjaya and other goals. "Tryambakam" is the heart; "yajāmahe" is the head; "sugandhim puṣṭivardhanam" is the tuft (śikhā); "urvārukamiva bandhanāt" is the armor (kavaca); [the remainder] "mṛtyormukṣīya" is the eye.
One should place the three eyes (netratraya) on the two shoulders; the weapon-mantra (astra) on the two feet; and the ten syllables on the joints of the two feet and the shoulders.
One should place the five syllables on the secret place, the base, the belly, the heart, and the neck.
One should place ten syllables on the joints of the two arms and the shoulders; two on the nostrils; one on the mouth; and one on the eyes.

One on the two ears; one on the head—this is the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*). *Tryambakam* on the head (1); *yajāmahe* on the eyebrows (2); *sugandhim* on the eyes (3); *puṣṭivardhanam* on the mouth (4); *urvārukam* on the throat (5);
*iva* on the heart (6); *bandhanāt* on the belly (7); *mṛtyoḥ* on the private parts (8); *mukṣīya* on the feet (9).
One should place [the syllables] on the two thighs with "mā" (10), and on the two feet with "amṛtāt" (11). Thus is the placement of the feet (*padanyāsa*).
76a) [The deity] stands upon a very clear lotus; with two hands, he holds a full water-pot (*pūrṇakumbha*) resting within them.

May the Lord, who holds a Veda and a rosary in his two lotus-like hands, and who, with the other two hands, bears two jars eternally full and overflowing at their mouths to drench his body—which is graced by the crescent moon—upon his head; may he, the God whose mass of rays is pure, grant you what is dear. (The jars are held in the upper left and right hands.)

One should meditate on [the deity] sprinkling his own head with nectar from two jars, holding two jars filled with nectar in the hands below those, and holding a Veda and a rosary in the hands below those. In the *Śāradā-tilaka*, a deer is mentioned in place of the Veda. Thus, at the conclusion of the mental worship, upon the previously mentioned pedestal (*pīṭha*):

Having invoked the deity, one should worship him with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya). The first enclosure is performed with the limbs (aṅgas). One should worship on the petals starting from the east with the formula: "Obeisance to Arka (1), Indu (2), Dharaṇī (3), Toya (4), Anala (5), Vāyu (6), Ākāśa (7), and Ātman (8). [Then] to Ramā (1), Raktā (2), Prabhā (3), Jyotsnā (4), and Pūrṇā (5).

One should worship with: "Salutation to Uṣā (6), Pūraṇī (7), Svadhā (8). One should worship with: "Salutation to Viśvā (1), Vidyā (2), Sitā (3), Pracchī (4), Sārā (5), Saṃdhyā (6), Śivā (7), Ārdrā (8), Prajñā (9), Prabhā (10), Medhā (11), Kānti (12), Śānti (13), Dhṛti (14), and Mati (15)."

One should worship with: "Salutation to Dharā (1), Umā (2), Pāvanī (3), Padmā (4), Śāntā (5), Amoghā (6), Jayā (7), and Amalā (8). Then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions and their weapons. Having thus worshipped and performed the recitation (japa), one should dismiss the deity. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations.
An oblation (homa) consisting of ten parts each of bilva, palāśa, vaṭa, pippala, siddhārtha, milk-porridge (pāyasa), milk, and dūrvā grass [should be performed].

76b) Now, the mantra of Dakṣiṇāmūrti consists of twenty-six syllables: Oṃ hrīṃ, salutations to you, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who dwells at the foot of the banyan tree, whose limbs are solely intent on meditation, the Rudra.

To Śambhu: Oṃ Hrīṃ. For this [mantra], Śuka is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Dakṣiṇāmūrti Rudra is the deity (devatā), Oṃ is the seed-syllable (vīja), Hrīṃ is the power (śakti), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of one's desired object. Oṃ Hrīṃ Dakṣiṇāmūrtaye Hrāṃ Hṛdayāya Namaḥ 1. Oṃ Hrīṃ Tubhyaṃ Hrīṃ Śirase Svāhā 2. Oṃ Hrīṃ... [and so forth].
To the one dwelling at the root of the banyan tree: *hruṃ*, *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). (3) Oṃ *hrīṃ*, to the one whose limbs are solely intent on meditation:
*hraim*, *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*). (4) Oṃ *hrīṃ*, salutations to Rudra: *hrauṃ*, *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes (*netratraya*).
(5) Oṃ *hrīṃ*, to Śambhu: *hraḥ*, *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*). (6) Now, the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*): One [syllable] on the head, one on the forehead.

Two on the ears, one on each cheek, two on the nostrils, one on the mouth, eight on the joints of the arms, one on the throat, two on the breasts, one each on the heart and the navel, two each on the two parts of the hips, one on the private parts, and two on the joints of the feet; with these two [remaining fingers], the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) is performed. [This is according to] the *Śārada-tilaka*.

After the placement of the eyes (*nayananyāsa*), follows the placement of the ears (*karṇanyāsa*). In the *Prapañca* [Tantra], however, the placement of the ears comes first. Now, the meditation (*dhyāna*):

Seated upon the crescent moon, he holds with his arms the *mudrā* that bestows auspicious wealth, as well as an axe and a deer; one arm is placed upon his knee, while his matted locks are bound at the waist by an excellent serpent.

May Bhava, whose matted locks are bound together, who is white as milk, and who possesses three eyes—surrounded by sages such as Śuka and others—grant you purity of being. One should meditate upon him holding a mudrā and an axe with his two right hands (the upper and lower), and with his left hand holding a deer that is tucked beneath his knee. Having thus meditated:
After the mental worship, one should invoke the deity upon the pedestal described in the *Prāsāda* [Tantra] and worship him with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*).

The first enclosure consists of the limbs; the second, of the forms and powers (mūrti-śaktis); the third, of the bull and other [emblems]; the fourth, of the world-protectors (lokapālas); and the fifth, of their weapons. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of thirty-two hundred thousand recitations.
The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with sesamum seeds soaked in milk, or with oblation (havis) mixed with clarified butter, in a quantity equal to one-tenth of the recitations.
The best of practitioners, constantly meditating upon Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
attains the capacity for the exposition of the Astra-mantra within one year.

Ghee cooked with the pastes of *brāhmī*, rock salt (*saindhava*), white mustard (*siddhārtha*), *vacā*, *uṣṭrakarṇa*, and blue lotus (*utpala*), combined with fragrant substances, along with the juice of *brāhmī*.
Ten million recitations were performed by that Manu, well-accomplished;
it was drunk by Kavi, bestowing beauty, protection, longevity, prosperity, and fortitude.

Now follows the mantra consisting of twenty-four syllables: *Oṃ namo bhagavate dakṣiṇāmūrtaye mahyaṃ siddhiṃ medhāṃ prayaccha svāhā*. However, in the *Śāradātilaka*, it consists of twenty-two syllables, as the syllable "siddhim" is omitted. Furthermore, in the *Mantramuktāvalī*, the word "prajñām" (wisdom) is used instead of "medhām" at the end; therefore—

It consists of twenty-four syllables. According to some, the word "medhām" (wisdom) is preceded by "prajñām" (insight) for the sake of accomplishment. One should recite this mantra after placing the seed-syllable *vāgbhava* (*aiṃ*) there as a "stake" (*kīla*). Its seer (*ṛṣi*) is Brahmā; its meter (*chandas*) is the divine Gāyatrī; its deity (*devatā*) is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining all human goals. Oṃ.

The seed-syllable is *svāhā*, the power (*śakti*). *Ā hrāṃ* to the heart, *namaḥ* (1); *īṃ hrīṃ* to the head, *svāhā* (2); *oṃ hrūṃ* to the tuft of hair, *vaṣaṭ* (3); *aiṃ hraiṃ* to the armor, *huṃ* (4); *aṃ hrauṃ* to the three eyes, *vauṣaṭ* (5); *aḥ hraḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ* (6). Then follows the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*).
On the crown of the head, behind it, on the forehead, the two eyes, the two ears,
the two nostrils, and then on the two teeth and the two cheeks.
On the tip of the tongue, on the tip of the nose, on the pair of eyes, and on the throat;
likewise on the two arms, on the heart, on the navel, on the belly, and on the anus.
One should indeed place the syllables of the mantra upon the thighs, the knees, the shanks, the sides, the pair of feet, and likewise upon all the limbs and joints.
Having thus arranged the twenty-four syllables of the mantra, one should perform the meditation:
[He is] crystal-white and silver-hued,
holding a rosary of pearls, a jar of nectar, and the gestures of knowledge and wisdom in the tips of his hands, while having serpents for his lower garment.

I praise Dakṣiṇāmūrti, who has the moon as his crest-jewel, three eyes, and wears various ornaments; who holds a pearl rosary and a jar of nectar in his right and left hands respectively, and beneath them, the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā) and the gesture of wisdom (vidyā). Having thus meditated, one should invoke the Lord upon the Śiva-pīṭha and worship him with the ancillary mantras (aṅgas).

The first enclosure; the second with the eight pairs of vowels; the third with the eight groups beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa, la, kṣa*; the fourth with Ananta and the others; and the fifth with Sarasvatī, Brahmā, Āsana, Sanandana, Sanātana, Sanatkumāra, Śuka, and Vedavyāsa.

Pārvatī, Subhagā, Bhadrā, Krīḍāśakti, as well as Raudrī, Kālī, and Vijṛmbhā—these are the Śaktis of Dakṣiṇāmūrti. They are described as being clear, holding rosaries and books, and adorned with the colors [of their respective deities]. With these Śaktis, the sixth [day] is completed; the seventh is presided over by Indra and the others.

The eighth [offering] is with their weapons. Having thus worshipped and recited the mantra according to one's capacity, one should dismiss the deity. In this manner, one should recite the mantra at the western door of the Śiva temple. Four hundred thousand recitations constitute the *puraścaraṇa*.
The fire-oblation (*homa*) consists of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in a tenth part of that number. Now follows the application (*viniyoga*): water or food.
If one drinks [the water] consecrated twenty-five times with each of the twenty-five mantras, then the perfection of speech (*vāksiddhi*) will be attained and all diseases will be pacified.
On the thirteenth day, at the onset of night, having become silent and bringing offerings to the temple of Śiva, one should worship the God who increases learning and intelligence.
One desiring food should offer oblations of milk-rice with clarified butter. One desiring prosperity should offer a hundred oblations of lotuses or bilva fruits.

One desiring long life should offer oblations of dūrvā grass smeared with clarified butter and milk. To his preceptor he should give a cow or land; for him, whence could there be fear of death? And he obtains a son.
Facing the sun, one should perform twelve sprinklings with joined palms;
such a person attains all sovereignty and splendor, and is not afflicted by defects.
By satisfying the deity with water conceived as milk— seven times in the morning and evening, and twenty-one times at midday— one shall become happy.
From ten thousand oblations (*homa*) with *palāśa* flowers, one becomes preeminent in knowledge;
before even a full year has passed, one will become a leader among poets through direct perception.
One desiring prosperity should meditate upon the All-pervading Lord together with Gaurī standing at His side;
by performing ten thousand oblations, the practitioner of mantra shall attain abundant fortune.
The practitioner of mantras, being pure, should eat boiled rice cooked with cow’s urine;
or the practitioner may subsist on alms-food, or likewise, the ascetic may consume only barley-gruel.
Without having heard the Vedic scriptures, one certainly becomes a fool.
Now, that which is called "liberation" (yantra-mukti) is as follows:
One should fashion a ten-petaled lotus.

Having written the Praṇava joined with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), one should write two syllables of the mantra at the base of each petal; on the final petal, the remaining syllable.
