Outside of that, one should encircle it with the Mātṛkās.

78b) When this yantra is empowered through recitation (*japa*) and other means, and water or other substances [consecrated by it] are consumed, it shall result in great eloquence (*mahāsārasvata*). Now, another mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate dakṣiṇāmūrtaye mahyaṃ medhāṃ prayaccha*.

Svāhā. The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Brahmā, the meter (chandaḥ) is Gāyatrī, the deity (devatā) is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of Sarasvatī. The placement of mantras on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) beginning with the thumbs is performed with the limb-mantras: *Oṃ namo bhagavate* is the heart (1); *dakṣiṇāmūrtaye* is the head (2); *mahyam* is the crest-lock (śikhā) (3); *medhām* is the armor (kavaca) (4); *prayaccha*.
The three eyes: *svāhā* (5); the weapon: (6). Now, the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*):
on the crown of the head, behind it, on the forehead, on the two eyes, on the two ears, on the two nostrils, then on the two cheeks, and on the two rows of teeth.
On the tip of the tongue, on the tip of the nose, on the pair of lips,
in the throat, in the two arms, in the heart, in the navel, in the private parts, and likewise in the anus.
Furthermore, one who is not bound by other tantras should place the supreme [mantra] upon the thighs, the knees, the shanks, as well as the heels and the feet, and in all the joints of the limbs.
Meditation:
Having meditated upon the Lord of the World, the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
who is as white as a kunda flower, the moon, or a conch shell, and who is clad in a tiger skin.
Seated upon the explanatory seat (vyākhyā-pīṭha), she always tramples upon Apasmṛti;
in the palm of her left hand, she holds a manuscript illuminated by the fire of knowledge (jātavedas).
The god, whose two hands are resplendent with the gesture of exposition and a rosary,
is served by sages and bestows the fruit of all goals.

Alternatively: "Or else, having meditated thus: 'I visualize the one with matted hair, adorned with the crescent moon, possessing three eyes, resembling the moon, radiant, four-armed, bestowing knowledge, holding a rosary and a book in his hands, and [the other hand] at his heart. Having meditated in this way...

Having invoked the deity into the previously mentioned Śiva-pīṭha, one should worship Him with the services beginning with water for the feet (pādya). The first enclosure consists of the [deities of the] limbs: 1. Brāhmaṇa, 2. Śakra, 3. Sananda, 4.
Sanatkumāra, 5. Śuka, 6. Vyāsa, 7. Gaṇeśa, 8. Siddha, 9. Gandharva, and 10. Yogīndra.
One should worship with "Obeisance to Vidyādhara" (11 times). These [deities] should be visualized as Sarasvatī reading from a book.

The world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons should be placed in their respective directions. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations. The fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with ten thousand lotuses along with their stalks. When this mantra has been perfected through recitation and other means, the excellent practitioner—

With pure water consecrated by this mantra, the wise man should sprinkle his own head; he shall obtain prosperity and health. Standing in water reaching up to the neck and reciting the mantra one thousand times every day for a period of one month, he shall become the foremost among poets.

Now follows the Aghora mantra, consisting of fifty-one syllables: *hrīṃ sphura sphura prasphura prasphura ghoraghorataratanurūpa vama caṭacaṭa pracaṭa pracaṭa kaha kaha vama vama bandha bandha ghātaya ghātaya hūṃ phaṭ*. Of this mantra, [the deity is] Aghora.

The seer is Anuṣṭubh; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; the deity is Rudra of non-terrible form; the application is for the purpose of destroying all enemies and attaining all prosperity. Oṃ hrīṃ sphura sphura, salutation to the heart.

*Prasphura 2*, to the head *svāhā* 2; *ghoraghorataratanurūpa-śikhā* 3; *caṭa 2 pracaṭa 2*, the armor (*kavaca*) 4; *kaha 2 vama 2*, to the three eyes *vauṣaṭ* 5; *bandha 2 ghātaya 2*, to the armor *huṃ* 6;
*huṃ phaṭ*, to the weapon (*astra*) *phaṭ* 7. Thus is the six-limbed rite (*ṣaḍaṅga*). *Hrīṃ sphura 2*, at the crown of the head 1; *prasphura 2*.

*Netrayoḥ* (2), *ghora* on the face (3), *ghorataratanurūpa* on the throat (4), *caṭa caṭa* on the heart (5), *pracaṭa pracaṭa* on the navel (6), *kaha kaha* on the private parts (7), *vama vama* on the thighs (8), *bandha bandha* on the knees (9), *ghātaya ghātaya* on the shanks (10), and *huṃ phaṭ* on the feet (11). Then follows the visualization: [He is] like a water-laden cloud, with terrifying fangs.
The Lord should have three eyes, wear a serpent as an ornament, and be non-terrible (Aghora); he is clothed in red garments and has red unguents.
He holds an axe, a hand-drum, a sword, a shield, and an arrow. For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*), he resembles saffron in color; for liberation (*mukti*), he is like the moon.

Below that are the arrow and the bow; below that, one should visualize the trident and the skull-cup. Having thus meditated, one should invoke the Lord upon the previously mentioned Śiva-pīṭha and worship Him with the services beginning with water for the feet (pādya), according to the prescribed rule. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas): 1. to the axe (paraśu), 2. to the hand-drum (ḍamaruka), 3. to the sword (khaḍga), 4. to the shield (kheṭa), and 5. to the arrow (vāṇa).
One should worship on the lotus petals with the mantras: "Obeisance to the bow (kārmuka)," "to the trident (śūla)," and "to the skull-cup (kapāla).

Then one should worship Brāhmī and the others, as well as the guardians of the directions. Thus, at the conclusion of the worship, having offered the recitation (japa), one should perform the dismissal (visarjana). The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand [recitations]. The fire-oblation (homa) is performed with sesame seeds smeared with ghee, numbering one-tenth of that amount. This is the sequence.
A wise person should offer a thousand oblations each night with clarified butter, raw rice, sesame, mustard, and milk-rice; by this sacrifice, one shall destroy all [obstacles].

[It wards off] calamities such as *bhūtakṛtyā* and others. Now, the *Pāśupata-mantra*: *oṃ ślīṃ paśu huṃ phaṭ*. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] are as before. The deity is Paśupati. *Oṃ* is the heart (1); *ślīṃ* is the head (2); *ya* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*) (3); *śuka* is the armor (*kavaca*) (4); *huṃ* is the three eyes (5); *phaṭ* is the weapon (*astra*) (6). In the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), [the seed-syllables are] *huṃ* and *phaṭ*.

Some say that the syllables of the mantra are the ends [of the visualization]. Then follows the meditation: [He who is] radiant like the midday sun, bearing the moon, blazing with a glorious loud laugh, adorned with a multitude of serpents, with hair on his head quivering with drops of sweat, holding a trident in his lotus-hand—

One should meditate upon the Lord Paśupati, who holds a mallet and a sword along with a spear, who is all-pervading, whose four faces are formidable with fangs, and who is the embodiment of divine weapons. With his upper right and left hands he holds a trident and a mallet; with the hands below those, he holds a sword and a spear. According to some, this order is reversed.

Having meditated thus, one should invoke the deity upon the Śiva-pīṭha and worship Him. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas); the second, of Brahmā and the others; the third, of the world-protectors (lokapālas); and the fourth, of their weapons. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of six hundred thousand recitations. The oblation (homa) is performed with cow's milk-rice (pāyasa) in a tenth part of that number. Water consecrated by this [mantra]—

One should cast [the mantra] into the mouth of the one who has seized [the victim]; by the power of this mantra, the seizing spirit (graha) releases him immediately upon being invoked. A king should scatter arrows consecrated with this mantra in battle; in an instant, he shall conquer all enemies like a second Pārtha. Now follows the Kṣetrapāla mantra: *Oṃ kṣauṃ kṣetrapālāya namaḥ* (Oṃ kṣauṃ, salutation to Kṣetrapāla). *Kṣāṃ*.
*Kṣīṃ kṣūṃ kṣaiṃ kṣauṃ kṣaḥ*—thus is the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*). The visualization (*dhyāna*):
[He] resembles a mountain of blue collyrium, with tawny hair rising upward.

"I bow to the God, the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa), who has fierce eyes, who wears a mass of matted hair, who is clothed in the directions, who is adorned with serpents, who has formidable fangs, and whose body is wondrous. Having thus meditated and having invoked the God upon the Śiva-pīṭha, one should worship Him. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas), starting from the east.
One should worship on the petals with: "Salutation to Analāya (1), Ardhvakeśāya (2), Karālāya (3), Ghaṇṭāravāya (4), Mahākopāya (5), Piśitāśanāya (6), Piṅgalākṣāya (7), and Ardhvakeśāya (8).
One should also worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions and their weapons. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations.

An oblation consisting of one-tenth [of the total] is performed with sacrificial porridge (caru) smeared with clarified butter. "Come, come, O wise one, O Purupurubhuñjaya! Dance, dance! Ward off obstacles, ward off obstacles! O Mahābhairava-bhairava, accept the offering (bali) for the Kṣetrapāla, svāhā!
This is the mantra for the bali-offering. With this, one should present the bali to the Kṣetrapāla. By the giving of the bali, he becomes well-pleased.
The Guardian of the Field bestows luster, intelligence, strength, health, splendor, nourishment, fame, and prosperity.
Now follows the twenty-one-syllable Vaṭuka mantra: *hrīṃ vaṭukāya āpaduddharaṇāya kuru kuru vaṭukāya hrīṃ*. *Hrāṃ vāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ* 1; *hrīṃ vīṃ śirase svāhā* 2;
*hrūṃ vūṃ śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* 3; *hraiṃ vaiṃ kavacāya huṃ* 4; *hrauṃ vauṃ* [netrābhyāṃ vauṣaṭ] 5; *hraḥ vaḥ astrāya phaṭ* 6.

*vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes; *hraḥ vaḥ phaṭ* to the weapon. His meditation is declared to be threefold, according to the method of the *sāttvika* and other [qualities]. One should worship him who is like a crystal, whose face has hair and a smiling countenance, adorned with divine ornaments made of fresh gems such as small bells and anklets, possessing a radiant form and pure garments.
One should constantly meditate upon Vaṭuka, who has two eyes, is exceedingly serene, and holds a trident and a staff in his two hands.
Resembling the rising sun, three-eyed, with red unguents and garlands, smiling-faced, and holding in his hands the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a skull-cup and a trident.

I shall always meditate upon the God who removes all fear, whose neck is blue, who is adorned with hundreds of magnificent ornaments, who blazes with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, and who is clothed in garments as red as the bandhūka flower. One should meditate on him who is as beautiful as a dark mountain, holding a trident and a skull-cup in his upper right and left hands, and bestowing the gestures of boons and fearlessness in the two hands below them.
I bow to Maheśa, who bears the crescent moon, wears a garland of skulls, is clothed in the directions, and has tawny hair;

who holds the *ḍamaru* drum, the axe, the sword, the trident, the gesture of fearlessness, the serpent, the bell, and the skull-cup in his lotus-like hands; who has terrifying fangs, is adorned with serpents, and possesses three eyes.

Beginning from the lower right hand— which is adorned with tinkling jeweled bells, anklets, and so forth— one should meditate, proceeding clockwise, upon the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), the goad (*śṛṅgi*), the sword, the trident, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the serpent, the bell, and the skull-cup (*kapāla*).
This sattvic meditation is declared to ward off untimely death,
to produce longevity and health, and to bestow all sovereignty and happiness.
The *rājasa* meditation has been described as bestowing the attainment of dharma, desire, and wealth;
the *tāmasa* meditation subdues enemies and destroys sorcery, spirits, and disease.

Having meditated thus according to one's preference, one should invoke the Lord upon the lotus within the hexagon on the Śiva-pīṭha and worship Him according to the previously described procedure. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas) within the hexagon: to Asitāṅga, Ruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmattabhairava, Kapālātman, and Bhīṣaṇāsya.
7. *Saṃhārā* namaḥ. 8. Thus one should worship upon the petals.
81b) Outside of that, [one worships] the son of Ḍākinī, the son of Rākinī, the son of Lākinī, and the son of Kākinī. 1. 2. 3. 4.

One should worship with "Obeisance" (namaḥ) to: 4. Śākinī-putraka, 5. Hākinī-putraka, 6. Mālinī-putraka, 7. Devī-putraka, and 8. [Devī-putraka]. In the ten directions: 1. Umā-putraka, 2. Rudra-putraka, 3. Mātṛ-putraka—[one should worship] with "Obeisance" (namaḥ) to the south; to Ūrdhvamukhī-putraka above; and to Adhomukhī-putraka below with "Obeisance" (namaḥ).

Thus below. Outside of that, on the lotus petals: Brāhmī, to the son, in the east; Māheśvarī, to the son, in the northeast; Vaiṣṇavī, to the son, in the north; Kaumārī, to the son, in the northwest; Indrāṇī, to the son, in the west; Mahālakṣmī, to the son, in the southwest; Vārāhī, to the son, in the south.

"Cāmuṇḍā to the little son"—thus [it is said] in the southeast. Again, on the outer petals: "Salutation to Dhenuka (1), Tripurāntaka (2), Vetāla (3), Vahnivījākhya (4), Kālāntaka (5), Karāla (6), Ekapāda (7), Bhīmarūpa (8), Acala (9), and Hāṭakeśvara (10)"—with these words, one should worship them in the ten directions. Then...

One should worship Śrīkaṇṭha and the others. Having thus recited [the mantra], one should perform the dismissal (visarjana). The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand repetitions of the syllable.

The fire-oblation (homa) is performed with sesame seeds smeared with the three sweets (trimadhura), numbering one-tenth of that count. One should worship the deity Vaṭuka according to the prescribed method; such a person becomes the master of virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation. [He overcomes] obstacles...
Having propitiated Durgā and offered the oblation according to the prescribed rite, the practitioner of mantra shall accomplish his desired objects and obtain the prosperity as described. 82a)
Rice cooked with sesame, minced meat, ghee,
parched rice flour, sugar, jaggery, alms-food, meat broth, and cakes, all mixed together and anointed with honey.
Having formed a morsel and worshipped the deity to be propitiated according to the previously mentioned method, one should offer that very oblation with red sandalwood, flowers, and other offerings.
In that regard, the practitioner of mantras accomplishes his tasks through the offering of oblations;
the practitioner should perform homa with clarified butter and shall thereby attain the success as described.
One should offer oblations in the cardinal directions with dappled flowers for the sake of subjugation; by means of these, one shall bring people under control.
For the attainment of a son, the wise man should offer oblations with full-blown white water-lilies.
For the attainment of wealth and grain, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and rice;
by offering handfuls of bilva leaves, one obtains great prosperity.
One may bring women under one's influence with salt mixed with sweet substances;
for one desiring rain, one should offer oblations with the excellent fuel-sticks of the cane tree (*vetasa*).
Seated upon a tiger skin, one should offer ten thousand oblations of sesame seeds;
the spirits and other such beings flee away and, out of fear, do not look toward that direction.
One pala of powdered *vacā*, consecrated with mantra and stirred with cow’s clarified butter,
should be divided and consumed by a barren woman desiring sons.
A disciplined Brāhmaṇa, self-controlled and pure, should offer a Sāttvika oblation, thereby obtaining a son who is well-disciplined and endowed with intelligence, health, and strength.
One should prepare with this mantra the sacred ash that grants the accomplishment of all aims:
uśīra, sandalwood, kuṣṭha, camphor, and saffron.
Having dried the root of white Arka, Vārāhī, Lakṣmī, [the root] from a milk-tree,
and the root of the Sūlvatara tree, one should grind them into a fine powder.
The powder is mixed with cow dung taken from the sky.
Having formed the piṇḍas and dried them,
one should burn them with the root mantra in the consecrated sacrificial fire and place those ashes in a pure vessel.
One should perfume the ashes purified by fire with *ketakī* and *mālatī* flowers; then, having touched the well-honored ashes, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Whoever takes this and applies the *puṇḍra* every day at dawn,
his diseases, malevolent spells, injuries, and great planetary afflictions shall perish.
No danger from enemies, thieves, wild animals, or the like arises for his dwelling;
all his riches increase, and he is honored by all people.

The king, along with his ministers and retinue, shall become subject to him. *Ghanasāra* is camphor. One should catch [the smoke] in the sky with cow-dung held such that it does not fall to the ground. Now follows the *Khaḍgarāvaṇa* mantra, consisting of one hundred and seventy syllables: *Oṃ namaḥ paśupataye oṃ*.
Homage to the Lord of Beings! Oṃ, homage to Rudra! O Lala-khaḍgarāvaṇa, sport, sport! Move, move! Dance, dance!
O you whose body is smeared with ashes from the cremation ground, who wear a garland of bells and skulls, who are clothed in a tiger skin, and who have the moon as your crest-ornament!
To the one who wears a black serpent as a sacred thread: *vala 2 valā 2*, O protector of the non-returning! *Hana 2* (slay, slay)!
For the protection of the beings, in the center of the mandala: *kaṭṭakaṭṭa*! Subdue with the trident of Rudra!
Pacify! Penetrate! Caṇḍāsidhārādhipati, Rudra commands: *svāhā*! The seer and the meter are not [to be recited].

83a) *Khāṃ khīṃ khūṃ khaiṃ khauṃ khaḥ* are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅgāni*). The visualization (*dhyāna*): [He] holds a bell, a skull-cup, an ear, a severed head, a shield, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a trident, and a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and is free from fear.

I praise the Lord whose limbs are red, who is adorned with the crescent moon, who has three eyes, five faces, and a lotus, and who wears crimson garments. One should meditate upon his ten weapons, beginning from the lower right hand and ending with the lower left hand. However, some [meditate] on the lower right and left [hands].
Having meditated on the bell and skull-cup in the two hands; above those, the goad and the garland of severed heads; above those, the khaṭvāṅga and the trident;

and above those, the hand-drum (ḍamaru) and the gesture of fearlessness—having thus visualized and performed the mental worship, one should invoke the deity upon the pedestal described in the Prāsāda [Tantra] and worship Him with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya). The mantra for worship is: *Oṃ bhūtādhipataye*.

Svāhā! The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*). Then, upon the petals, one should worship with: "Salutation to Culu-kaṇḍā (1), Praskhalinī (2), Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā (3), Phalgunī (4), Ṭiriṭilī (5), Mattamālikā (6), Khiṅkhilī (7), and Cadrāṅkita-jaṭā (8). [Then]: "Aiṃ Hyai! Salutation to Kaumārikā (1) and Brāhmī (2). [And] to [Kārttikī] (3).
To Vārāhī 4, to Vaiṣṇavī 5, to Vināyaka 6, to Cāmuṇḍā 7, and to Māheśī 8, [I offer] obeisance—thus in the cardinal directions.
To Raudra and Piṅgala, obeisance 1; to Śmaśānaniṣaṇṇau 2;
to Dṛḍhakarṇa and Bhṛṅgiriṭi 3; to Āmardaka and Mahākāla 4.

One should worship in the directions starting from the east with the formula: "Obeisance to Kauṇapa and Āla," "to Kumbhakarṇa and Śoka," and "to Bhallaṭa and Horā. [Then one worships] Indra and the other world-protectors (lokapālas), whose splendor is inseparable from that of the Daityas.

May the Man-Lion (Nārasiṃha) protect you—he who is encircled by garlands of flames, whose three eyes are the sun, moon, and fire, whose tongue is blazing, whose fangs are fierce, and who bears a face with disheveled hair. At the time of meditation, for the pacification of anger, one should touch the right arm while praising Śiva, and the left arm while praising Brahmā; thus it is gentle (saumya).

Meditation. Having meditated thus, one should invoke the deity upon the *pīṭha* mentioned in the Nārāyaṇa mantra and worship Him with the ritual services (*upacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*). Then follows the worship of the limbs and the retinue (*aṅgāvaraṇa*). One should worship on the petals in the directions starting from the east as follows: "Obeisance to the Lord of Birds" (1), "to Śaṅkara" (2), "to Śeṣarāja" (3), and "obeisance to Brahmā" (4). [Then] "to Śrī" (1) [and so forth].

One should worship with "Salutation to Hrīḥ (Modesty)," "Salutation to Dhṛtiḥ (Fortitude)," and "Salutation to Puṣṭiḥ (Nourishment)" on the petals at the corners. One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions and their weapons outside of them. Having worshipped in this manner and having recited [the mantra] as much as possible, one should dismiss the deity. This mantra is to be recited encased by the Praṇava and the Bhuvaneśvarī mantra, thirty-two tens of thousands of times.

The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*): One becomes perfected through thirty-two hundred thousand recitations (*japa*). There should be a fire-oblation (*homa*) of that same number of thousands of lotuses smeared with clarified butter (*ājya*). When the mantra has been perfected through recitation and other means according to one's desire, one should accomplish the desired objects.
The visualization (*dhyāna*) therein is as follows: Narahari, possessing the splendor of ten million rising suns, resplendent with a crown and a necklace.

I worship Him whose mouths are terrifying with fangs and whose many long arms have nails that flash like fire; who possesses three eyes—the nature of fire, the moon, and the sun—piercing through asuras, nāgas, fire, the moon, and the sun; who bears a mass of matted hair as fearsome as a cluster of lightning, and vomits forth fire. Thus is the fierce meditation (*krūradhyāna*). Now, the gentle (*saumya*):
One should contemplate this [mantra] for gentle tasks and employ it for cruel ones; the practitioner of mantra should offer oblations with lotuses and bilva wood kindled in the fire.
One attains a thousandfold prosperity by means of bilva leaves, or likewise with its flowers or fruits; from an oblation of dūrvā grass, one gains freedom from disease.
One who recites mantras should daily consume white *vacā* at dawn;
such a practitioner of mantra attains perfection of speech, becoming like Vācaspati himself.
When a bad dream occurs at night, one should bathe and recite this mantra;
through the placement of the mantra, a good dream arises while remaining awake.
In a terrifying great forest, from tigers, thieves, wild beasts, and the like, this Manu-mantra,
when recited by the practitioner, shall protect one from all other dangers as well.
By the power of this mantra, the practitioner shall quickly destroy poisons, seizures, and great fears with ashes consecrated by it.
Having visualized oneself as a most terrifying lion, fearsome with claws and fangs,
one should thereafter meditate upon the enemy as a young deer.
Having grasped the edge of the petal, one should quickly cast it again in the various directions;
by this, the eradication of the enemy along with his sons, friends, wife, and others occurs.
Having first assumed the name Mṛtyupadeśādhyam, Hari himself,
while remembering his enemy being devoured by sharp claws and the tips of fangs, [acted].
One should constantly recite the mantra one hundred and eight times without sloth;
before long, the enemy, who is dear to Yama, shall perish from the mandala.

Now, the *nṛsiṃhabīja*: *kṣauṃ*. Its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent elements] are also as before. Now, the sixty-seven-syllable *jvālāmālā-mantra*: *oṃ kṣauṃ namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya jvālāmāle pradīptadaṃṣṭrāya agninetrāya sarvarakṣoghnāya*.

For the destruction of all malevolent beings, for the destruction of all fevers: *daha 2 paca 2 rakṣa 2 huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details for this [mantra] are as before. *Oṃ kṣauṃ namo bhagavate narasiṃhāya hṛdayāya namaḥ* (1). To the one garlanded with flames, whose fangs are blazing.
123b) *Śirase svāhā* (2). *Agninetrāya sarvarakṣoghnāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (3).
*Sarvabhūtavināśanāya sarvajvaravināśanāya kavacāya hūṃ* (4). *Daha 2 paca 2 rakṣa*.
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with: "To the two eyes, *vauṣaṭ* (5); *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*, *phaṭ* to the weapon (6)," one should perform the meditation (*dhyāna*):

"Blazing with the acquisition of great splendor, possessing two eyes that never cease [to see], radiant with the crests of fire, with a lotus-face of uplifted fangs, scattering [terror] and causing fear to the Rākṣasas..."
"I worship Nṛhari, who is terrifying with his mass of matted locks and who bears the conch, discus, sword, and shield.
Having meditated thus, one should invoke the deity upon the previously mentioned pedestal and worship Him with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya).

One should worship the deities of the enclosure and so forth, as well as the previously mentioned deities. After performing worship in this manner, one should recite the mantra according to one's capacity.

One should dismiss the deity. The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations. The *homa* sacrifice should be performed with the clarified butter of a tawny cow (*kapilājya*), consisting of one-tenth of that number.
The ritual applications (*prayoga*) and so forth are as stated for the King of Mantras (*mantrarāja*). Specifically, this is for the destruction of minor spirits (*kṣudrabhūta*) and the like.
Now, the six-syllable mantra (*ṣaḍakṣaramantra*): *Āṃ hrīṃ kṣrauṃ kroṃ huṃ phaṭ*. For this, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*).

The *paṅkti* meter, Narasiṃha Harihari as the deity, for the sake of desired objects: *kṣrāṃ kṣrīṃ kṣrūṃ kṣreṃ kṣrauṃ kṣraḥ astrāya phaṭ*. Meditation (*dhyāna*): With eyes rolling in fury, his own mouth wide open, possessing the three eyes of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, with a reddish luster from the feet up to the navel and white above.
He bears the discus that has split the body of the lord of the Daityas, as well as the conch,
noose, goad, thunderbolt, mace, and plow; he is the formidable Man-Lion with sharp and fierce fangs, adorned with various ornaments made of jewels.

Having meditated thus, one should worship the deity upon the previously mentioned seat. Then follows the worship of the limb-enclosures (*aṅgāvaraṇa*): to the discus (1), to the conch (2), to the noose (3), to the goad (4), to the discus (5), to the Kaumodakī mace (6), and to the sword (7).

One should worship with "Oṃ Kheṭāya 8 Namaḥ" on the petals in the directions starting from the east; likewise, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in their respective directions and their weapons. Then, one should dismiss the deity. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of six hundred thousand recitations, and the fire-oblation (homa) consists of six thousand oblations of clarified butter.
By offering pieces of *amṛtā* fruit four thousand times over four days according to this rite,
the oblation destroys the fever caused by planetary influences.
There are many such applications. What is the use of saying more here? Among all mantras uttered, there is no other mantra equal to these that bestows grace like a shadow.

Now, Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha: *Kṣauṃ*, obeisance to Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha. Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of one's desired object. *Ī haṃ*, obeisance to the heart, the blissful self, the fierce, heroic Mahāviṣṇu. *Ī haṃ*.

To the blazing one facing all directions, for the Self who is dear, svāhā to the head. 2. To this terrifying Nṛsiṃha, the light of the Self, vaṣaṭ to the tuft of hair (śikhā). 3. To this death of death, I bow, for the Self of Māyā, huṃ to the armor (kavaca). 4. To this entire [being], for the Self of ignorance, phaṭ to the weapon (astra). 5. O Krodha...
For the sake of pacifying [the influence of] Kṣamā and the other directions, one should touch the right arm and recite the Śalabha mantra. The mantra is:
*oṃ hauṃ namaḥ śivāya mahāśalabhāya svāhā*. (124b)

For the purpose of self-protection, there exist numerous seed-syllables (*bīja*) enclosed within the syllables of mantras; however, they have not been written here for fear of making the text too voluminous. When a great danger has arisen, one should recite the mantra ending with *bhīṣaṇaṃ stambhaya bhīṣaṇaṃ bhīḥ*. Alternatively—
At the end of the mantra, one should recite: "Protect me, protect me! Regarding protection during the ritual placement (nyāsa) of mantras and other rites, it is as follows:
"May Keśava protect my feet; may Nārāyaṇa protect my shanks;
may Mādhava protect my hips, and Govinda protect my private parts."
May Viṣṇu protect my navel; may Madhusūdana protect my belly;
may Trivikrama protect my chest; and may Vāmana protect my heart.
May Śrīdhara protect my throat, Hṛṣīkeśa my face,
Padmanābha my eyes, and Dāmodara my head.
O fair-eyed one, when one has thus performed the ritual placement upon the limbs, neither spirits, vetālas, nor rākṣasas can even transgress its shadow at the time of recitation.
Therefore, O Goddess, one should practice meditation with every effort.
May Keśava, who possesses the discus and has the luster of gold, protect me from the front.
Behind him is Nārāyaṇa, bearing a conch shell, resembling a dark blue cloud;
Mādhava, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, stands above, wielding a mace.
On the right side was the great archer Govinda, radiant as the moon;
on the left was Viṣṇu, the wielder of the plow, resembling the filaments of a lotus.
In the southeast is Madhusūdana, lotus-eyed and holding a mace;
in the southwest is Trivikrama, sword in hand and blazing with the luster of fire.
In the northwest is Mādhava, radiant like the rising sun;
in the northeast is Puṇḍarīkākṣa Śrīdhara, whose weapon is the paṭṭiśa.
Viṣṇuprabhu, Hṛṣīkeśa,
and Padmanābha— possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns— should place the mallet (mudgara) in the northern direction and the heart-mantra in the center.
Possessing all weapons, all powers, all-knowing, and facing in every direction;
resembling an indragopaka insect, with a noose in hand, he is unconquered.
Having pervaded the body both externally and internally, Dāmodara remains there;
thus is the "Twelve-Cage" (Dvādaśapañjara), which is entirely free from blemish.

"I have entered; there is no fear whatsoever for me"—with these words, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Having thus established protection, one should invoke the Deity upon the previously mentioned pedestal, display the six mudrās beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*), and recite: "Victory is yours, O Lotus-eyed One! Salutations to You!"
O Creator of the Universe! Salutations to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Puruṣa! Salutations! [The meditation on Śiva:

Surrounded by lotus-faced beings in the Ocean of Milk, bearing the boon-granting discus, the Pināka bow, and the gesture of fearlessness, possessing the luster of the moon, adorned with great and excellent ornaments, he is embraced by Ramā upon the thousand-hooded king of serpents.

"May this Nṛhari, who has the brilliance of the sun, whose throat is blue, and who sits upon the lotus of yoga, purify [me]. Thus, at the conclusion of the worship, one performs the worship of the Vyūha with the nine words beginning with 'I bow to the Fierce One' (ugraṃ namāmyaham), etc.: Oṃ to Bhīma 1, Ugra 2, Nayana 3, Nīla 4, Candra 5, Bhayaṅkara 6, Viśveśa."

One should worship with "Oṃ, salutation to Kamalā" (7) and "Oṃ, salutation" (8) on the petals starting from the east. On those very same [petals], one should worship with "Salutation to Śraddhā" (1), "to Ṛddhi" (2), "to Samṛddhi" (3), "to Maharddhi" (4), "to Kāmā" (5), "to Bhīmā" (6), "to Mahānanā" (7), and "to Dīpti" (8). Thus, these and many other enclosures (āvaraṇas) exist, though they have not been detailed here.

Having thus performed worship and recited [the mantra] according to one's ability, [one should say]: "O you who guard the most secret of secrets, accept the recitation performed by me; may accomplishment arise for me through the grace of you, the deity residing in my heart."

One should offer the recitation (japa). Having praised and bowed, one should dismiss [the deity]. There are many varieties of this [rite]. Now follows Vidāraṇanṛsiṃha: *Kṣauṃ jaya-jaya Nṛsiṃha*. For this mantra, Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Vidāraṇanṛsiṃha is the deity, *Jaṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), *Haṃ* is the power (śakti), and its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of desired goals.

*Kṣrāṃ kṣrīṃ*, etc., is the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*). The meditation (*dhyāna*): May He protect [us]—He whose form is naturally fierce, who is distorted with passion, shining with sharp fangs, and bearing the discus, conch, noose, goad, thunderbolt, mace, and the weapon called *dāraṇa*; red in appearance from the navel downwards and white above, adorned with divine ornaments.

May the Lord Viśeṣa—the best among all gods, the Nārasiṃha whose eyes are the sun, fire, and moon—protect you for a long time. Worship and other rites are to be performed as with the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*). Now, the Divine Nṛsiṃha:
O You whose hair-ends are like molten gold, whose flaming eyes are like glowing coals!
O divine lion, whose touch with claws surpasses that of a diamond, homage be to you!
The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Brahmā; the meter (chandaḥ) is Anuṣṭubh; the deity (devatā) is the Divine Nṛsiṃha; the seed-syllable (bīja) is the letter *ra*;

the power (śakti) is the letter *e*; it is for the sake of one's desired goal. The five-limbed ritual (*pañcāṅga*) is performed with the four quarters [of the mantra] and the whole [mantra]; the meditation, worship, and so forth are as previously described.

126a) Now follows the twelve-syllable Nṛsiṃha mantra: Oṃ kṣrauṃ mahānṛsiṃhāya namaḥ kṣrauṃ oṃ. For this, Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ), Śrīnṛsiṃha is the deity (devatā), and the syllable *kṣa* is the seed-syllable (bīja). Oṃ.
The Śakti is Raṃ, the Kīlaka is Rakṣas, and the Viniyoga is for the attainment of the desired object. The meditation on the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and so forth are as before.

Now, another thirteen-syllable mantra: *sahasrāra-jvāla-mṛtyu-nāśana svāhā*. The meditation (*dhyāna*) begins with "the sun, the moon, the seven-flamed one," and so forth; everything else is as before. Now, Vīranṛsiṃha: *oṃ namo bhagavate vīranṛsiṃhāya jvālāmālāpinaddhāṅgāya agninetrāya*.

For the destruction of all beings, for the destruction of all enemies: *hana 2 daha 2 paca 2 rakṣa 2 hrāṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā*. For this [mantra] also, everything is like the *vidāraṇa* [mantra]. Now, another mantra of Vīranṛsiṃha:
*oṃ namo bhagavate vīranṛsiṃhāya jvālāmāline dīptadaṃṣṭrāyāgninetrāya*.

To the destroyer of all rākṣasas, the annihilator of all bhūtas, the destroyer of all diseases, the destroyer of all defects, the destroyer of all fevers: *hana* 2, *daha* 2, *paca* 2, *bandha* 2, *rakṣa* 2, protect me!
*huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. For this [mantra] also, everything is as before. Again, within the Vīranṛsiṃha [section]: *oṃ*.

Homage to the Blessed One, the Heroic Man-Lion, who wears a garland of flames, whose fangs are blazing, whose eyes are fire, the destroyer of all rākṣasas, the annihilator of all bhūtas, the annihilator of all diseases,
and the annihilator of all obstacles.
126b) *sarvadoṣavināśanāya hana 2 daha 2 paca 2 bandha 2 rakṣa 2 māṃ māṃ māṃ huṃ huṃ huṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*. For this [mantra] as well, everything is as before. Now, the Aparājita [mantra]:

Nṛsiṃha: The Four Hundred. Om, salutation to the Blessed One, the Infinite, the thousand-headed, who reclines upon the ocean of milk, who rests upon the couch of the coils of Śeṣa; salutation to Him whose vehicle is Garuḍa, to Vāsudeva;
salutation to the yellow-robed one, to Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
O Śirorāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, bestower of boons, salutations to You! [Protect us from] the Asuras,

Daityas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Siddhas, Yoginīs, Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, Brahmarākṣasas, Vināyakas, Pūtanās, Grahas, Skandas, and other leading Grahas, as well as the Grahas of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).

Slay, slay! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Churn, churn! Intoxicate, intoxicate! Seize, seize! Destroy, destroy! Terrify, terrify! With the discus, the mace, and the thunderbolt, reduce to ashes the elemental spirits, the ghost-spirits, the vetāla-spirits, and the jambhaka-spirits, as well as the vetālas themselves! O Thousand-Armed One, conquer with your thousand weapons and arms! O Vijayā, Parājitā, and Pratihata, [conquer]!

O thousand-eyed one, blaze, blaze! Flare up, flare up! O you of universal form, Madhusūdana, Great Being, Nārasiṃha, Nārāyaṇa, Padmanābha, Dāmodara, Hṛṣīkeśa, subduer of all beings, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, crusher of all serpents!
O destroyer of all poisons, O delighter of all gods,
O Maheśvara among all deities, through the differentiation of all mantras, O destroyer of all fears, O destroyer of all fevers!
O pacifier of all suffering, O remover of all diseases, O Janārdana, O God of gods, bestower of boons, homage be to you!

For this [mantra], Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the meter (chandaḥ), and Aparājita Nṛsiṃha is the deity (devatā) for the attainment of desired objects. The six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) begins with *kṣrāṃ kṣrīṃ* and so forth; the meditation (dhyāna) and other rites are like those of the six-syllabled mantra (*ṣaḍakṣara*). Now follows Aparājita Nārāyaṇa Nṛsiṃha: *Oṃ namo bhagavate anantāya sahasraśīrṣāya kṣīrodārṇavaśāyine*.

Salutations to Vāsudeva, who reclines upon his remaining serpent-couch, whose vehicle is Garuḍa, who is clothed in yellow garments; O Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Hayagrīva, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, Trivikrama, Matsya, Kūrma, Kṛṣṇa, Kalki, Rāma, bestower of boons, Janārdana, God of gods, salutations be to you!

Asuras, Daityas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Bhūtas, Pretas, Piśācas, Apasmāras, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Siddhas, Yoginīs, Ḍākinīs, Śākinīs, Brahmarākṣasas, Pūtanās, Vetālas, and the planetary spirits (grahas)— the spirits of death, the spirits of the dead, the spirits of Piśācas, the spirits of wind, the spirits of fever, the spirits of the lunar mansions, and these others as well.
Slay the great grahas! Burn them! Grind them! Cook them! Release them! Crush them! Cause them to enter [the body]!

Destroy them! Terrify them! With the wheel of all weapons, with the mace, the conch, the Śārṅga bow, and the thunderbolt—with everything—reduce them to ashes! O thousand-armed one, to the one whose weapons and arms are a thousandfold!
Victory, victory! O Ananta, O Aparājita, O thousand-eyed one, blaze, blaze! O Pradīpta-viśvarūpa, Madhusūdana, Hṛṣīkeśa, Mahāpuruṣa, Vaikuṇṭha, Nārāyaṇa, Govinda!

O Padmanābha, O Dāmodara, O Subduer of all beings, O Wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, O You who are saluted by all beings, O Destroyer of all beings, O God, O Maheśvara, O You whose weapon-mantra destroys all planetary influences, O Destroyer of all mechanical devices!
It destroys all diseases, breaks all seals, annihilates all fevers,
attracts all spirits, liberates from all bonds, destroys all suffering, pacifies all portents of death,
destroys all enemies, and [destroys] all poisons...

Everything [for this] is like that of the eight-syllable [mantra]. Now, the eight-syllable [mantra] of Nṛsiṃha: *namo narasiṃhāya*. Everything for this is like that of the five-syllable [mantra]. Now, the six-syllable [mantra]: *oṃ kṣrauṃ namaḥ svāhā*. For this, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chaṃdaḥ*). The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) begin with *kṣrāṃ*, *kṣrīṃ*, and so forth.

The worship is as before. Now, Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha: *kṣrauṃ* to Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] are as before. Now, Kopana-Nṛsiṃha: *oṃ kṣrauṃ* to Kopana-Nṛsiṃha, *svāhā*. The seer and other [limbs] are as before. "Seated upon the glorious lotus throne"—this is the peaceful meditation (*śānta-dhyāna*).
Beholding him whose three eyes possess the radiance of a thousand suns and resemble thunderbolts, who is like a mass of flashing lightning,
whose body is ever ablaze with divine ornaments and terrifying fangs, and whose nails are sharp—

I bow to the Narasimha who stands with a body that is both massive and immense, shattered by the many staff-like arms of the split Daityas; the rest is as before. Now, the Splendorous Nṛsiṃha: Oṃ Kṣrauṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, to Nṛsiṃha; obeisance to you, the splendor of splendors.
Obeisance to the one who manifests and re-manifests, whose claws are vajras and whose fangs are vajras, who has awakened to the karmic tendencies and the vulnerabilities of others, the Seizer;
Oṃ Svāhā. The meter is Gāyatrī. The meditation:
[He is] two-armed, holding a discus and a conch, adorned with all ornaments.
One should meditate on [the deity] blazing with a radiance equal to ten million suns, with the flames of his fangs.

Now, another mantra of Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha: *Oṃ īṃ haṃ kṣrauṃ haṃ īṃ oṃ*. For this, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and "the self-abiding one seated on a lotus" is the visualization (*dhyāna*). Now, Puccha-Nṛsiṃha: *Haraye viṣatrāte kṣrauṃ namo bhagavate mahāpucchāya*.

To Narasiṃha. Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra], Gāyatrī is the meter (chanda), and the meditation (dhyāna) is like that of the six-syllable [mantra]. Now, Narasiṃha is established in his own state: *Oṃ namaḥ śrīnarasiṃhāya pratiguṇakeśarasaṭāyakhaḍgāntāyudhakara-āla-damṣṭrālocana gadra 2 marda 2*.

*Jāti* 2, *jālitaṃ* 2, *devaṃ* 2, *tvaṃ*, cause your own possession [to cease] 2, *svāhā*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details for this mantra, as well as the visualization (*dhyāna*), are as before. It paralyzes many *grahas*, *bhūtas*, and so forth. The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations. One should observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) while eating only one meal a day for eight days. From that, success (*siddhi*) is attained. Now, another mantra: *Oṃ*.
*Kṣrauṃ*, salutation to the Blessed One, Narasiṃha. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [limbs] are as before.
128b) Now, the *Vila* Narasiṃha: *Oṃ*, salutation to the Blessed One, Narasiṃha, the vanquisher of Daityas and Dānavas.
To him whose entire splendor is like a thousand times ten million blazing fires, who has adamantine claws and fangs as weapons,

whose thick mane and whiskers are scattered like vast, radiant crystal, whose roar is like the sound of drums amidst the waters of the agitated great ocean, and whose heart is within all mechanical devices— come, come!
O Blessed One, Narasiṃha, O Puruṣa of the moving and the unmoving! By the truth of Brahmā, quiver, yawn, and rend asunder!

Shatter all the netherworlds (pātālas) and terrify them with the mountain-shaking roar of the lion of gods! Overwhelm all forms of magical diagrams (yaṃtras)! Strike down, strike down all the lords of the species! Bind, contract, rend asunder, and shatter!

O you who possess infinite flames, cause an immersion through the continuous connection of garlands of fire; with the wheel of the thunderbolt-missile possessing infinite flames, destroy all the netherworlds on every side; with the net of arrows possessing infinite flames, bind all the netherworlds on every side;
with the cage of arrows possessing infinite flames, surround all the netherworlds for the sake of those dwelling in the world of the gods.
Draw out their hearts now quickly! Burn! Burn! Cook! Cook! Dry up! Cut them down until they have fallen into a state of total confusion! *Phaṭ* from the netherworlds!
*Phaṭ* from the forms of the yantras! *Phaṭ* from the classes of yantras! [Protect] me along with my companions!

Protect us, O Blessed One, Viṣṇu in the form of the Man-Lion (Nārasiṃha), from all sins, from all weapons, and from all fears and calamities! *Oṃ hrīṃ kṣrīṃ phaṭ iṃ kāstu te huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Because this mantra is already perfected (*siddha*), there is no need for [the preliminary rite of] *dṛṣyā* and so forth. The preparatory practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of ten thousand recitations. This very [mantra is it].
The cutter of the surrounding bonds. Now, the six-syllable mantra:
ĀṂ HRĪṂ KṢRAUṂ KROṂ HUṂ PHAṬ. The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is Vāmadeva.
The Paṅkti meter; Nṛsiṃha is the deity for the fulfillment of desired aims. Kṣrauṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja); Hrīṃ is the power (śakti).

Oṃ Āṃ, salutation to both thumbs (aṅguṣṭhābhyāṃ namaḥ) 1. Oṃ Īṃ Hrīṃ, salutation to both index fingers (tarjanībhyāṃ namaḥ) 2. Oṃ Ūṃ Kṣrauṃ, salutation to both middle fingers (madhyamābhyāṃ namaḥ) 3. Oṃ Ūṃ Ṛṃ Krauṃ, salutation to both ring fingers (anāmikābhyāṃ namaḥ) 4. Oṃ Aiṃ...
*Huṃ*, salutation to the two little fingers (5); *Oṃ aṃ phaṭ*, salutation to the palms and backs of the hands (6).

One should place these syllables upon the heart and other limbs. The meditation is as follows: "May [the deity] protect [me] without departing. The worship diagram (*pūjā-yantra*) is exactly as previously described; however, the remainder is that Bhuvaneśvarī is to be worshipped in the center of the hexagon. Then—
Having invoked the deity upon a Vaiṣṇava pedestal, one should worship him. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (of the deity).
One should worship the discus, conch, noose, goad, thunderbolt, mace, sword, and shield upon the petals.

One should also worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations of the syllable; [the daily offering] is one thousand.
One should offer oblations with apāmārga fuel-sticks soaked in ghee. Now follows the Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha.

*Sahasrārajvālāvartin kṣrauṃ hanahana huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. For this mantra, Jayaṃta is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Jagatī is the meter (*chaṃdaḥ*), and Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha is the deity (*devatā*) for the attainment of desired objects. *Kṣrauṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *huṃ* is the power (*śakti*). *Cakrarājāya svāhā*, obeisance to the heart; 1. *Jvālācakrāya svāhā*, [obeisance] to the head; 2.
*Mahaccakrāya svāhā*—the crest-lock (*śikhā*). 3. *Gajecakrāya svāhā*—the armor (*kavaca*). 4. *Asurāntaka-cakrāya svāhā*—the weapon (*astra*). 5. Meditation (*dhyāna*):
Seated upon the pericarp of the wheel’s hub, possessing a radiance like the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālāgni*).
And [he saw] Danuja with his mouth wide open, and Hari holding four discs.

One should meditate upon him who stands at the foot of an Ashoka tree, who possesses three eyes, whose form is fierce, who destroys all living beings, and whose limbs are prohibited from being depicted in yoga-paintings.
Having meditated thus, one should invoke the deity upon a Vaiṣṇava seat and worship Him.

Now follows the Thousand-Syllabled Narasimha Mantra: Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ kṣrauṃ! O you who are the embodiment of wrath, O Narasimha, O supreme person, O releaser from the shackles of dharma and adharma, O Kālapuruṣa, O one anointed by Time, O Lord of the Universe, O you who are established within the poison of the world as the essence of consciousness, the light of eternal awareness, and the one who transcends the path of time.
O Greatly Compassionate One, whose heart-lotus is like the sun that never rises nor sets; O You who are the singular essence of consciousness seated within the four petals;
O Fourfold Self, Twelvefold Self, Twenty-fourfold Self, Twenty-fivefold Self, You of hundreds of thousands of forms—come, come, O Blessed Lord Nṛsiṃha, Puruṣa, Krodheśvara, and Ramā!
O Mahādeva Vināyaka, whose feet are saluted by thousands, who possesses the fire at the end of time and waters like millions of suns;

O stainless one, pure through the power of knowledge of a thousand-fold wisdom; O tawny-eyed one, whose weapons are the bristling mane and gleaming tusks, and whose claws are weapons that bring about the end of the lords of the Dānavas; O you whose body is drenched in blood, come, O Bhūta, to the presence of Yama!
Arise, arise in an unobstructed form through the power of the Lord of the Sky-Wheel! Burn, burn the accumulation of ignorance!

Manifest, manifest the sovereignty of wisdom! Oṃ, you who are all-knowing and expanded by the blossoming of the remainder! Oṃ, you who are established in the supreme treasure-house of the abode of holy beings! Homage! [Destroy] the fear of bad dreams!
The fear of shackles, the fear of the wilderness, the fear of poison, fever, *ḍākinīs*, *kṛtyās*, sacrificial rites, and sorceresses, the fear of thunderbolts, and the fear of famine.

O Nṛsiṃha, Great Sāman-Person, O you who assume the form of the knowable, release me from the fear of burdens, the fear of death, the fear of the shadow-body (chāyā-skanda), the fear of thieves, the fear of water, pits, and fire, the fear of elephants, lions, and serpents, and from all fears such as birth, old age, and death; pacify them, pacify them!

O you who ward off all fears, the eight groups of eight, the sixty-four maidservants, the three sets of thirty-three crores of deities, and the one endowed with the lotus-feet of the King of Men— the thousand-faced, thousand-bellied, and thousand-eyed one!

O Vāsudeva, slayer of Madhu, who possesses a thousand feet, a thousand arms, a thousand tongues, and a thousand faces; who bears a thousand weapons; who is the beloved light that dispels darkness; who is the Lord of all mantras and the sovereign of the kings of mantras; who bestows the celestial state; who crushes the magical diagrams (yantras) of Pātāla; who utters a terrible, loud laugh; and who is the abode of sharp poison.

O Hṛṣīkeśa, who causes the manifestation of the Supreme Swan with the fierce horse-head; who is intent upon mocking the Lord of the Universe and the entire world; who grants boons at will; who is the devourer of all living beings without remainder; who bestows the great Siddhi of the Pisitāsṛg-laṃpaṭa Khecarī; O unconquerable, imperishable, and unmanifest one within the belly of the cosmic egg!

Obeisance to You who wear a garland of skulls and a necklace of ten million cosmic eggs; who possess the forms of Matsya, Kūrma, Varāha, Nṛsiṃha, Vāmana, and Viṣṇu—whose feet traverse the three worlds—and who, as Buddha, are endowed with the three strides of Rāma;
who are established upon the *praṇava* (Om), the support of the three principles (*ekatatva*), and whose crest is fixed there; Obeisance to Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭ, Vauṣaṭ, and Huṃ!
O Prāṇādhāra,
primordial deity, abiding in prāṇa and apāna, you who cause the birth and death of the twice-born as proclaimed in the Pañcarātra, O one of great body!
O crusher of the pride of the lord of Daityas, O mass of splendor! *oṃ klāṃ* [splendor], O bestower of boons, *puruṣa* phaṭ!

*oṃ saṃsaṃtya* [all-pervading] *puruṣa* phaṭ! *oṃ dhāṃ*, O Acyuta, phaṭ! *hūṃ*, O you of universal form, phaṭ! *oṃ hrauṃ*, O Haṃsa, phaṭ! *oṃ hrauṃ*, O Paramahaṃsa, phaṭ! *oṃ hraḥ*, O wearer of the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, phaṭ!
Oṃ hrauṃ, O bearer of incomparable form, phaṭ! Oṃ vāṃ, Vāsudeva, phaṭ! Oṃ hrīṃ, O embodied one, phaṭ!
Oṃ klīṃ, O formless one, phaṭ! Oṃ kṣrāṃ, O universal-formed one, phaṭ! Hrāṃ, O universal self, phaṭ! Oṃ sauṃ, O fourfold self, phaṭ! Oṃ kṣrauṃ, O bearer of the form of Nṛsiṃha, phaṭ! Oṃ klāṃ klaḥ!

O you who assume a form with the eight limbs arranged [in the mudrās], Phaṭ! Oṃ Hrauṃ, O you who possess the single form established by nature, Phaṭ! Oṃ Huṃ Huṃ Huṃ Ṣṭaṃ Kaṃ Khaṃ, devour [Amuka] and [Amuka], devour them both! Devour them! Klaṃ Klīṃ, bring the one being accomplished here, O Great-Souled One!
Manifest [your power]! Manifest! *kṣrāṃ kṣrīṃ kṣrūṃ kṣraiṃ kṣrauṃ kṣreṃ kṣra*!
Lift up, lift up the sins of those who have recited [this mantra]! *drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ klūṃ*! O Saṃnṛsiṃha, whose nature is flame, *svāhā*!
O Nṛsiṃha, whose nature is flame, *svāhā*! O Nṛsiṃha, whose nature is flame, *svāhā*! *Oṃ kṣrauṃ*.

Klīṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Oṃ. Of this Nṛsiṃha-sahasrākṣara mantra, the seer is the great sage Kapila, the meter is Jagatī, the deity is Śrī Nṛsiṃha, the seed-syllable is Kṣrauṃ, the power is Svāhā, the color is white, the accent is Udātta, and the application is for the propitiation of the Supreme Self, Nṛsiṃha. Oṃ Kṣraḥ.
"Obeisance to the thousand-armed one, the wielder of a thousand weapons, the Man-lion; Svāhā! To the Weapon, Phaṭ!
Having thus performed the purification of the hands, [one should assign the mantras] to the fingers and to the heart and other limbs: Oṃ Kṣrāṃ.

Svāhā to Nṛsiṃha, who has expanded with a thousand syllables; this is the heart (1). Oṃ Kṣrīṃ, svāhā to the Greatly Powerful and Fierce Nṛsiṃha; this is the head (2). Oṃ Kṣrūṃ, [to] Nṛsiṃha whose hair-ends are like molten gold, and so forth, [and] who has destroyed the fear of the world with his great roar; svāhā.

Having performed the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and the pervasive placement (vyāpaka): 1. *Sikhā*: Oṃ kṣraiṃ, svāhā to the blazing Nṛsiṃha, intoxicated by the pride of gold. 2. *Kavaca*: Oṃ kṣrauṃ, svāhā to the thousand-eyed one, whose form is the universe, the sustainer. 3. *Netra*: Oṃ kṣraḥ, svāhā to the thousand-armed one, who possesses a thousand weapons, the Nṛsiṃha. 4. *Astra*: Oṃ kṣraḥ, svāhā to the thousand-armed one, who possesses a thousand weapons, the Nṛsiṃha. Thus, having performed the placement of the six limbs and the pervasive placement.
Having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should meditate on Nṛsiṃha within the heart. Having meditated according to [the mantra] "udyadbhāsvat...", one should recite it.
There are other mantras as well, but they have not been written here for fear of increasing the bulk of the book.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Nṛsiṃha Mantra," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhī.
Following the explanation of the Pañcāyatana mantra, various other mantras are now stated.
First, the procedure for the Gāyatrī is written here:
for the Praṇava, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), the Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and the Supreme Self (Paramātman) is the deity;
for the three Vyāhṛtis, Prajāpati is the seer according to the Sāmavedic tradition.
Gautama, Bharadvāja, and Viśvāmitra are the ṛṣis for each [quarter] respectively;
the Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, and Anuṣṭubh are the meters; Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya are the deities. For the Gāyatrī [verse], Viśvāmitra is the ṛṣi and the Daivīgāyatrī is the meter.

131b) Regarding the mantra *savitā devatā vareṇyam*: here, *ra* is the Śakti; *va* is the Bīja; and the letter *ṇa* is the common Śakti, according to the scriptural authority that "the letter *ṇa* is strength (*vala*). Now follows the placement of the words (*padanyāsa*): *oṃ tat pādātmane namaḥ* (1). *Oṃ*.

Oṃ, salutation to the self that is the knee of Savitṛ. 2. Oṃ, salutation to the secret self, the most excellent (*vareṇya*). 3. Oṃ, salutation to the belly-self, the radiance (*bharga*). 4. Oṃ, salutation to the heart-self of the god. 5. Oṃ, salutation to the letter-self, "we meditate" (*dhīmahi*). 6. Oṃ, salutation to the eastern face, the intellects (*dhiyaḥ*). 7. Oṃ, salutation to the western face, "who" (*yaḥ*). 8. Oṃ, salutation to the head-self, "us" (*naḥ*). 9. Oṃ.

*pracodayāt astrāya phaṭ* (10). Again: *oṃ tat* to the self of the head (1); *oṃ savituḥ* to the self of the space between the eyebrows (2); *oṃ vareṇyam* to the self of the eyes (3); *oṃ bhargaḥ* to the self of the mouth (4); *oṃ devasya* to the self of the ears (5); *oṃ dhīmahi* to the self of the heart (6); *oṃ dhiyaḥ* to the self of the navel (7).

Oṃ yaḥ, to the secret self (guhyātman) 8; Oṃ naḥ, to the knee self (jānvātman) 9; Oṃ pracodayāt, to the foot self (pādātman) 10. Again: Oṃ tat, to the secret self (guhyātman) 1; Oṃ savituḥ, to the eye self (cakṣurātman) 2; Oṃ vareṇyaṃ, to the speech self (vāgātman) 3; Oṃ bhargaḥ, to the ear self (karṇātman) 4; Oṃ devasya, to the heart self (hṛdayātman) 5; Oṃ dhīmahi, to the knee self (jānvātman) 6; Oṃ...
To the one whose essence is the eye: *dhiyaḥ* (7); to the one whose essence is the forehead: *oṃ yaḥ* (8); to the one whose essence is the nose:

*oṃ naḥ* (9); to the head: *pracodayāt namaḥ* (10). Again: *Oṃ bhūḥ*, to that which is desirable of Savitṛ; *bhūr agnaye pṛthivyai brahmaṇe lokatrayātmane namaḥ* (1); *Oṃ bhuvaḥ*, we meditate upon the splendor of the divine.
Bhuvaḥ! Salutations to the intermediate space, to Vāyu, and to Viṣṇu, whose self is the three Vedas.
(2) 132a) Oṃ Svaḥ! May that which impels our intellects [be propitious]. Salutations to Svar, to Āditya, to the heavens, to Maheśvara, whose self is the three vital breaths (prāṇas).

*Namaḥ* (three times). The placement of the feet, heart, head, and beautiful feet is completed. Now follows the placement of the syllables together with their powers (*śakti*). *Oṃ tat prahlādinyai caṃpakanibhāyai namaḥ* 1 *Oṃ saprabhāyai śvetavarṇāyai* 2 *Oṃ vi nityāyai piṅgalavarṇāyai* 3 *Oṃ tuḥ viśvaprabhāyai indranīlanibhāyai* 4 *Oṃ r va*

To Vilāsinī, blazing with fire, 5; Oṃ Re, to Prabhāvatī, whose form is fire, 6; Oṃ Ṇi, to Jayā, who has the luster of lightning, 7; Oṃ Yaṃ, to Śāntā, who is red in color, 8; Oṃ Bha, to Kāntā, who has the color of a water-cloud, 9; Oṃ Rgo, to Durgā, who resembles red in color, 10; Oṃ De, to Sarasvatī.

Oṃ ma, salutation to Viśvarūpā, who resembles an emerald; 11. Oṃ va, salutation to Śuklarūpā; 12. Oṃ sya, salutation to Viśālā, who has the luster of gold; 13. Oṃ dhī, salutation to Īśā, who has the luster of a kunda flower; 14. Oṃ ma, salutation to Vyāpinī, who resembles a ruby; 15. Oṃ hi, salutation to Vimalā, who resembles a conch shell; 16. Oṃ dhi, salutation to Tamopahāriṇī.

17. Oṃ, salutation to Pāṇḍuraprabhā (She of Pale Radiance). 18. Oṃ, salutation to Sūkṣmā (The Subtle One), who resembles an indragopa insect. 19. Oṃ, salutation to Viśvayoni (The Source of the Universe), who resembles saffron. 20. Oṃ, salutation to Jayāvahā (The Bringer of Victory), who resembles the rising sun. 21. Oṃ, salutation to Pralayā (The Dissolution), who resembles a blue lotus. 22. Oṃ, salutation to Aparā (The Other), who resembles gorocana pigment. 23. Oṃ, salutation to Śobhā (Beauty).
Obeisance to her who is as white as a jasmine flower, the moon, and a conch shell (23). Obeisance to her whose form is auspicious and who resembles crystal (24).
Obeisance to that Agni, who resembles a *campaka* flower and is seated upon the lotus throne (132b).

Salutation to the one whose self is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. 1. Oṃ, salutation to that Prajāpati, who is dark-complexioned, seated upon a lotus throne, and whose self is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. 2. Oṃ, [salutation] to Viṣṇu, who resembles the color of tawny [light], seated upon a lotus throne, and so forth. 3. Oṃ tuḥ, salutation to Īśāna, who resembles sapphire (indranīla), seated upon a lotus throne, and so forth. 4. Oṃ rvaḥ.

To Āditya, blazing like fire, [Pañcākṣara-mantra] 5; Oṃ Re, to Bṛhaspati, who has the form of fire, 6; Oṃ Ṇi, to Indra, whose radiance is like lightning, 7; Oṃ Yaṃ, to Bhaga-deva, who is red in color, 8; Oṃ Bha, to Aryaman, who has the color of a water-cloud, 9; Oṃ Rgo, to Savitṛ, who resembles a red bull, 10; Oṃ De, to Tvaṣṭṛ, who resembles an emerald.

11 Oṃ vaṃ, salutation to Pūṣan, who is of white complexion. 12 Oṃ syaṃ, salutation to Indra and Agni, who possess a golden luster, are seated upon lotus-thrones, and whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. 13 Oṃ dhīṃ, salutation to Vāyu, who has the luster of a kunda flower. 14 Oṃ maṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva, who resembles a ruby. 15 Oṃ hiṃ...

To Mitra and Varuṇa, who resemble conch shells, [16] Oṃ, to the god Dhi-bhrātṛvya, who possesses a white radiance, [12] Oṃ, to those resembling Indra-gopa insects, who are seated upon lotus-thrones, whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and who belong to the Viśvedevas, [18] Oṃ, to Viṣṇu, who resembles saffron, [19] Oṃ, to us... [naḥ]
To the Vasus, who resemble the rising sun, svāhā. (20) To the Great-Grandfathers (*prapitṛ*), who resemble blue lotuses, svāhā.

(21) To Kuvera, who resembles yellow orpiment, svāhā. (22) To the Aśvins, who resemble kunda flowers, the moon, and conch shells, svāhā. (23) To Brahmā, who resembles crystal and is seated upon a lotus throne, svāhā.
Salutations to the one whose self is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. 24.
133a) Oṃ *ta*d agnaye pṛthivyātmane namaḥ 1. Oṃ *sa* prajāpataye avātmane 2. Oṃ *vi* somāya vahnyātmane 3. Oṃ *tuḥ* īśānāya vāṃ dyātmane 4. Oṃ *rva* ādityāya.

5. Oṃ, to the Self of Space (Ākāśātman), Bṛhaspati; 6. Oṃ Re, to the Self of the subtle element of smell (Gandhatanmātrātman), Bṛhaspati; 7. Oṃ Ṇi, to Indra, the Self of the subtle element of taste (Rasatanmātrātman); 8. Oṃ Yaṃ, to Bhagadeva, the Self of the subtle element of form (Rūpatanmātrātman); 9. Oṃ Bha, to Aryaman, the Self of the subtle element of touch (Sparśatanmātrātman);
10. Oṃ Rgo, to Savitṛ, the Self of the subtle element of sound (Śabdatanmātrātman); 11. Oṃ De, to Tvaṣṭṛ.

Oṃ hi, salutation to Mitra and Varuṇa, the selves of the nose; 16. Oṃ dhi.

Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Kṣaṇa, whose self is the touch. 45. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Past, whose self is the sight. 46. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Ignorance, whose self is the bondage. 55. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Desire, whose self is the attachment. 56. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Non-desire, whose self is the detachment. 57. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Mind, whose self is the intellect. 58. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Soul, whose self is the supreme self. 61. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Brahman, whose self is the absolute. 62. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Śiva, whose self is the auspicious. 63. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Viṣṇu, whose self is the pervasive. 64. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Indra, whose self is the sovereign. 65. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Agni, whose self is the fire. 66. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Varuṇa, whose self is the water. 67. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Yama, whose self is the restraint. 68. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Nirṛti, whose self is the destruction. 69. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Vāyu, whose self is the wind. 70. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Kubera, whose self is the wealth. 71. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Īśāna, whose self is the lord. 72. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Brahmā, whose self is the creator. 73. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Nārāyaṇa, whose self is the support. 74. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Kapila, whose self is the sage. 75. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Dakṣa, whose self is the skill. 76. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Manu, whose self is the progenitor. 77. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Soma, whose self is the moon. 78. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Agastya, whose self is the sage. 79. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Vasiṣṭha, whose self is the seer. 80. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Atri, whose self is the sage. 81. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Kaśyapa, whose self is the progenitor. 82. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Bhṛgu, whose self is the sage. 83. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Aṅgiras, whose self is the seer. 84. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Pulastya, whose self is the sage. 85. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Pulaha, whose self is the sage. 86. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Kratu, whose self is the sage. 87. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Marīci, whose self is the sage. 88. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Aṅgiras, whose self is the seer. 89. Oṃ, salutation to the one whose deity is the Bṛhaspati,
To Kuvera, whose self is intellect, 22. Oṃ da, to the two Aśvins, whose selves are ego, 23.
Oṃ yā, to Brahmā, whose self is the unmanifest, salutation, 24. Oṃ tat, salutation to the heart, 1.
Oṃ sa, svāhā to the head of Savitṛ, 2. Oṃ vareṇyam, vaṣaṭ to the tuft, 3. Oṃ bhargaḥ, huṃ to the armor, 4. Oṃ.
*Devasya astrāya phaṭ* (5); *oṃ dhīmahi netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* (6); *oṃ dhiyo yo naḥ pārśvābhyāṃ namaḥ* (7); *oṃ pracodayāt hastābhyām*.

*Namaḥ* (8 times). Again: *Tatsavitur* to Brahmā, the heart—*namaḥ*. *Oṃ vareṇyam* to Viṣṇu, the head—*svāhā* (2). *Oṃ bhargo devasya* to Rudra, the crest-lock—*vaṣaṭ* (3). *Oṃ dhiyaḥ* to Īśvara, the armor—*huṃ* (4). *Oṃ yo naḥ* to Sadāśivātman, the three eyes—*vauṣaṭ* (5). *Oṃ pracodayāt*.
*Astrāya Phaṭ* (six times). Then follows the Nyāsa of the Akṣara-Śaktis: Oṃ *tat-tat* to Tattvadhātrī 1; Oṃ *sa* to Samagrā 2;
Oṃ *vi* to Vimalā 3; Oṃ *tu* to Tuṣṭi 4; Oṃ *rva* to Vandhyā 5; Oṃ *re* to Revatī 6; Oṃ *ṇi* to Niravadyā 7; Oṃ *yaṃ* to Yajñavidyā 8; Oṃ *bha* to Bhargā 9; Oṃ *rgo* to Godā 10. Oṃ...

To Devinī, 11; Oṃ va, to Varadā, 12; Oṃ spa, to Spandanā, 13; Oṃ dhī, to Dhīrā, 14; Oṃ ma, to Madhurā, 15; Oṃ hi, to Himavatsutā, 16; Oṃ dhi, to Dhisnī, 17; Oṃ yo, to Yoginī, 18; Oṃ yo, to Yogadā, 19; Oṃ naḥ, to Narmadā, 20; Oṃ pra, to Pramathapriyā, 21; Oṃ co, to Coriṇī.
22. Oṃ da, to Dayitā; 23. yā, to Yājñī, obeisance. 24. The locations:

the joints of the feet, the four sections [of the arms], the navel, the heart, the two necks and arms, the joints of the shoulders, the mouth, the nose, the cheeks, the eyes, the ears, the eyebrows, and also the head—[these are] in the western, lunar, and southern [directions].

Having sequentially assigned the syllables to the faces and the upward-facing directions, the best of knowers of the Vedas [should perform] meditation upon the Gāyatrī; this meditation, following the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), is to be performed during the three junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*). At dawn, she has Brahmā as her deity, is red in color, wears red garments, is adorned with all ornaments, and possesses four arms.
One should meditate upon Gāyatrī as four-faced, mounted upon a swan, and holding a water-pot, a rosary, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

In the afternoon, one should meditate upon Sāvitrī, who has Viṣṇu as her presiding deity; she is dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, adorned with all ornaments, four-armed, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness, and mounted upon Garuḍa.
At midday, [one should meditate upon her] who has Rudra as her presiding deity; she is white-complexioned, dressed in white garments, and four-armed.

One should meditate upon Sarasvatī, adorned with all ornaments, mounted upon a bull, and holding a trident, a skull-bowl, the gesture of granting boons (*varada*), and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) in her hands. Alternatively, one may meditate upon Sāvitrī, whose faces possess the luster of pearls, the moon, gold, sapphire, and emerald; she holds a goad, a noose, a skull-bowl, and a rosary, and grants boons with two of her hands.

I worship her who bears in her hands the conch, the discus, and a pair of lotuses. Having meditated thus, one should invoke the Goddess into the center of the triangle upon the solar seat (saura-pīṭha) accompanied by the powers such as Tīvrā and others, and then display the mudrās.
They are as follows: Saṃmukha (1), Saṃpuṭa (2), Vivṛta (3), Ekamukha (4), and Dvimukha (5).
Three-faced (6), four-faced (7), five-faced (8), six-faced (9), having two lingas (10), narrow (11), with the tip pointing east (12), with the face of Yama (13), knotted (14), turned away (15),
facing downward (16), with a hanging fist (17), stepped upon by a fish (18), and stepped upon by a tortoise (19).
The boar-tread (varāhākrānta) 20, the lion-tread (siṃhākrānta) 21, the great-tread (mahākrānta) 22, the hanging (pralaṃba) 23, and the mallet (mudgara) 24—
these twenty-four mudrās are effective when used with the Gāyatrīs.
Mantras chanted in vain, as well as bathing and eating [without these], are likewise ineffective.
In the same way, a pilgrimage to sacred sites is indeed in vain if it is devoid of the ritual hand-gestures (mudrās).
For them, sacrifice, as well as fire-offerings and the worship of the gods, becomes fruitless;
therefore, the mudrās should always be understood by the learned who have applied themselves with diligence.

Having thus displayed the mudrās, one should worship Gāyatrī with the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya). One should worship [her] in the three corners [of the triangle] with: "Obeisance to Gāyatrī," "Obeisance to Sāvitrī," and "Obeisance to Sarasvatī.

To Brahmā 1, to Viṣṇu 2, and to Maheśvara 3—thus outside [the central deity]. To Ukha 1, Prajñā 2, Prabhā 3, and Sandhyā 4, salutations—thus in the four directions. Then follows the limb-enclosure (aṅgāvaraṇa): to Prahlādinī 1, Prabhā 2, Nityā 3, Viśvaṃbharā 4, Vilāsinī 5, Prabhāvatī 6, and Jayā 7.

Salutations to Śāntā (8), Durgā (9), Sarasvatī (10), Durgārūpā (11), Viśālā (12), Īśānā (13), Vimalā (14), Tamopahāriṇī (15), Sūkṣmā (16), Viśvayoni (17), Jayāvahā (18), Padmā (19), Parā (20), Śobhanā (21), and Bhadrarūpā (22). Thus ends the third enclosure.

One should worship upon eight lotus petals. Then [worship] Brāhmī and the others, and then the nine planets. [Recite] "Obeisance to the retinue of Āditya. Then the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped. Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight or twenty-eight times, one should dismiss [them] with the words, "On the northern peak. The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) consists of twenty-four lakhs [of recitations].

One should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with twenty-four thousand pure sesame seeds. One should offer milk-rice mixed with clarified butter, sesame, *dūrvā* grass, and fuel-sticks from milky trees, each separately, one thousand times. Thereupon, the *gāyatrī* becomes perfected (*siddhā*).
A knower of mantras should offer sesame seeds into the fire ten thousand times according to the number of the *tattvas*;
liberated from all sins, he attains a long life.
Then, for the sake of longevity,

the practitioner of mantras should offer three thousand oblations consisting solely of clarified butter as the sacrificial offering, along with *dūrvā* grass, the three [types of] *tila* seeds, and ghee.
If a person offers ten thousand oblations with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets, Mahālakṣmī shall belong to him within six months; there is no doubt in this matter.
The meaning is: "trimadhu" refers to honey, ghee, and sugar; one should offer oblations for the sake of Brahmanic glory with flowers produced from the Brahmavṛkṣa tree.

135a) Now, the method of accomplishment (*sādhanaprakāra*): Having first performed purification of the body and recited one hundred thousand [times] from the beginning of the *kṛt* mantra, multiplied threefold; [one should recite] that which includes the *tāraka*, the *avyāhṛti*, the head-mantra (*uttamāṅga*), the deity, and is employed with its meter (*chaṃdas*) and seer (*ṛṣi*).
And one should bathe properly at the three times of the day, with one's posture measured and the mind and senses fully restrained.

Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and intent upon the celestial realm, he should then commence the subsequent rite. Having observed the vow of milk for twelve days, and having offered a thousand oblations of cow’s ghee daily into a fire fueled by *khadira* wood,
he who has performed the consecration shall obtain a thousand gold coins (*niṣkas*) of gold.

By reciting it one thousand times during the three sessions at the three junctions of the day for one month, even he is liberated from great sins; furthermore, within six months, he is freed from the wheel of untimely death (*apamṛtyu*). If, while standing in water, one recites it one thousand times facing the solar disc, there is the attainment of gold; and if, when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu, one recites it one hundred thousand times over the leaves of the *mañjula* tree smeared with ghee in their midst, [the same result follows].
When oblations have been offered into the fire, the cloud then rains upon all the earth; the offering of ashes into the water wards off that rain.

Having fasted during a lunar eclipse and recited [the mantra] one thousand times over a tawny cow with a calf of the same color, along with ghee and white, potent fragrances, even a dull-witted person immediately attains intelligence upon drinking it. Thereafter, through its continued use, he shall live for a thousand years; by its sound he becomes a poet, and by its wisdom, he becomes like Bṛhaspati.
One who knows all the Vedas becomes like Garuḍa through vision; by offering oblations of Palāśa leaves, one obtains a treasure-trove.

One desiring splendor, strength, and nourishment [should offer] with clarified butter; likewise, longevity with Dūrvā grass, cattle with milk, a village with sesame seeds, and brilliance with rice grains.
135b) Through oblations of honey, milk, and ghee, even a king together with his retinue will certainly become submissive.
If hosts of enemies cause affliction— whether without cause or for some specific reason— then for them, this [rite]...
For the sorcery of causing enmity, eradication, or death among men and asuras:
taking wood from a solitary owl’s nest at night, which has been carried off and broken by an elephant,
and kindling it with fire held in the hand of a caṇḍāla, one who is full of blazing wrath at a crossroads— thus [one] does not [succeed].

Or, having prepared fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *aindrī* wood, mixed with mustard seeds and oil, one who recites the syllables of the enemy's name in reverse order while uttering the sound "hum," and offers eight thousand oblations, will cause that person to become unfortunate and disliked by all people. Furthermore, having taken earth from both banks of a river... [of] a man.
One should take an image of the Enemy of Māra (Śiva), its chest marked with the syllables of [the victim’s] name and its limbs smeared with mustard oil;
having entered it while it is visible, with one foot placed upon it mixed with oil,
one should bury it at a crossroads with sharp fires and the thorns of passion, once it has been beheld with the foot.

If [the breath] enters at the navel, one becomes afflicted with *tukhañja* (crippling); if at the belly, there is abdominal pain; if in the region of the throat, there is throat obstruction; if within the ears, there is severe earache; if in the region of the forehead, there is headache; if in the eyes, eye disease; and if in the heart, death. There are many applications of the *Gāyatrī*.
These have not been written here due to the excessive bulk of the text.
136a) Now, some disputants are addressed. Next is the *Durgā* mantra of Jātavedas:
"To Jātavedas we offer this Soma; may he burn away the wealth of the enemy. May he carry us across all difficulties, like two protectors."

"May Agni carry away our sins across the Sindhu. For this mantra, Marīciputra Kaśyapa is the seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Jātarūpiṇī Durgā is the deity (devatā), *duṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja), Agni is the power (śakti), and *raṃ* is the pin (kīlaka).
Its application (viniyoga) is for the subjugation of enemies and similar purposes. "To Jātavedas, the Sun, [I offer] salutation upon my heart. (1)

*Somam arātīyato śirase svāhā* (To the head of him who acts as an enemy, svāhā). 2. *Nidahāni vedaśikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (I burn them away; to the crest-lock of knowledge, vaṣaṭ). 3. *Sanaḥ parṣad ati kavacāya huṃ* (May he carry us across; to the armor, huṃ). 4. *Durgāṇi viśvā nāvāiva netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* (Across all difficulties, like with a boat; to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ). 5.

*Sindhur duritāny agniḥ astrāya phaṭ* (As Agni [crosses] the rivers and overcomes evils; to the weapon, phaṭ). 6. [The assignment of mantras to the body parts: Ankles, feet, shins, knees, thighs, hips, private parts, and navel.
The heart, the two sides, the two backs, the middle of the shoulders, the roots of the arms, the upper arms, the elbows, the forearms, the wrists, the palms,
the face, the nose, the eyes, the ears, the head, the brain, and the crown of the head— [all these] are well-examined.

The placement of the syllables is performed in a counter-clockwise direction. The placement of the words is upon the head, forehead, eyes, pair of ears, lips, tongue, throat, arms, heart, belly, hips, genitals, thighs, knees, shanks, and feet. Now, the visualization:
[one should meditate on her] possessing a radiance like a flash of lightning, seated upon the shoulders of the king of beasts, and terrifying, [surrounded] by maidens.

I meditate upon Durgā, who is of a ruddy nature, who bears the crescent moon, and possesses three eyes; she is attended by those whose hands sport with swords and shields, and she herself holds in her hands the discus, mace, sword, shield, arrow, bow, boon-granting gesture, and the threatening finger,
with the discus and mace positioned on her right and left sides respectively.

Below that, [visualize] a sword and a shield; below that, an arrow and a bow; and below that, a boon-granting gesture (varada) and a threatening gesture (tarjanī). Having thus meditated, [one should place] Jayā, Vijayā, Bhadrā, and Bhadrakālī, together with [their attendants], upon the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus on the Daurga pedestal.
Sumukhī and Vyāghramukhī—may these grant victory today! Therein, having invoked the Goddess within the hexagon, one should worship her.
The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅgas*). [Salutations] to Agni Jātavedas 1; to Agni Saptajihva 2;
to Agni Havyavāhana 3; to Agni Aśvodara 4; to Agni Kaumāratejas 5; to Agni...

One should worship on the petals with: "Salutation to Viśvamukha Agni, the face of the gods. One should worship in the cardinal directions with: "Salutation to Pṛthivyātman," "Salutation to Salilātman," "Salutation to Agnyātman," and "Salutation to Vāyvātman. One should worship in the corners with: "Salutation to Nivṛtti," "Salutation to Pratiṣṭhā," "Salutation to Vidyā," and "Salutation to Śānti. [There are] other powers as well.

They have not been mentioned out of respect [for brevity]. Having worshipped in this manner, one should dismiss [the deity]. The preparatory practice (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of forty-four thousand [recitations]. The fire-oblation (*homa*) should consist of milk-tree wood, sesame seeds, *rājī* (flax), and *havir* (clarified butter) in the proportions of one-eighth. The ritual applications (*prayoga*) are to be written in the section on the *astra* (weapon-mantra). The mantra of Tryambaka has already been written previously. Now...
