The Śatākṣī Mantra: Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ gāyatrī jātavedaḥ tryambakaṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaraṃ oṃ. This is the hundred-syllabled mantra (śatākṣarī). Its essence consists of the Sun, Fire, and Moon; its seers and other attributes are as previously stated. *Tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi* is the heart [mantra] (1); *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*.
Śiraḥ (Head): 2. *jātavedase sunavāma somam arātīyato ni dahāti vedaḥ*.
Veda-śikhā (Veda-Peak): 3. *sa naḥ parṣad ati durgāṇi*.

O Agni, you indeed know all the rivers from calamities; [this is] for the armor, *svāhā*. (4) We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes. (5) Just as a cucumber is released from its bond, so may I be released from death but not from immortality; *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ oṃ*, *phaṭ* to the weapon. (6)

Meditation is as previously described. Alternatively: May the Sun, whose body is perfected by the syllables of the Gāyatrī; the Fire, who is honored for his distinguished greatness through the Triṣṭubh meter; and the Moon, whose splendor is complete with the syllables of the Anuṣṭubh—may these three grant you your desired objects. Or rather, [may they grant] all that is to be remembered.

May that supreme, self-luminous, and radiant Greatness— which constantly pervades the world of moving and unmoving beings, which is free from phenomenal expansion, which grants liberation, which is the Praṇava containing the three divisions, and which is sung upon hearing— be for the fulfillment of your desires. Having meditated thus:

Having invoked the deity at the Śaurepīṭha, one should worship Him. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅgas*). The second, third, and fourth enclosures consist of three groups of eight [verses] joined with the *Gāyatrī* and the *Prahlāditā*.
The fifth enclosure consists of those [mantras] spoken by Jātavedas, beginning with the *Jāgatī*. [The sixth is] the *Tryambaka*...

One should worship four times with the mantras recited eight times each, and the tenth [deity] with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*). For one who worships and recites in this manner, the desired success (*siddhi*) is attained. Specifically, through recitation, liberation (*mukti*) is attained.

One hundred thousand (*lakṣa*) is the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), and the fire-oblation (*homa*) consists of sesame seeds (*tila*) in a tenth part of that amount. And it is said: [the syllable] *praṇava*.

The hundred-syllable mantra (*śatākṣarī*) should be recited daily with the three excellent mantras beginning with the *vyāhṛtis* and ending with the *tārā* (Oṃ), for the sake of attaining success in this world and the next; furthermore, one should recite the mantra for the sake of peace.

One of pure intellect, with self-restraint, should recite daily for a year the mantra beginning with *tat-pada*, followed by *āyuṣe* and *anubhādya*, and ending with *triṣṭubhādya*, even if devoid of ritual attendants (*gaṇa*).

This single hundred-syllable mantra has been proclaimed; the practitioner of mantra, for the sake of attaining desired fruits, for fame, for very long life, for pleasing all people, and for the perpetual attainment of prosperity (Indirā), should worship it daily in secret without sloth. Now, [the hymn] to Durgā from the Yajurveda: "Tām agnivarṇām... [and so forth].

I take refuge in Goddess Durgā, who blazes with ascetic power (*tapas*), who is radiant, and who is nourished by the fruits of action; salutations to her who is the supreme savior. There is no mention of the seer (*ṛṣi*) and other such details for this mantra. *Oṃ tām agnivarṇām*—salutation to the heart. 1. *Oṃ tapasājvalantīm*—salutation to the head. 2. *Oṃ vai rocanīm*. 3.
Namo to the one nourished by the fruits of karma—this is the *śikhā* (3). Oṃ, obeisance to Goddess Durgā—this is the *kavaca* (4).
Oṃ, I take refuge [in her]—this is the three *netras* (5). Oṃ, obeisance to the essence of the white nectar—this is the *astra* (6).
The Meditation (*dhyāna*): [Visualize her] as radiant as a thousand rising suns.

Having meditated upon the Goddess—who holds a conch, shield, bow, arrows, quiver, mace, severed head, and a garland, and who has three eyes—one should invoke her upon the Daurga-pīṭha and worship her. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (aṅgas) and [the goddesses] beginning with Prahlādinī. The preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) and so forth are as previously stated. This is the solar hymn (saura) declared in the Ṛgveda.

Rising, rising, O Sun of great splendor, ascending the highest heaven, O Sūrya, destroy my heart-disease and my jaundice. Praskaṇva is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandaḥ), and Sūrya is the deity (devatā) for this [hymn] used for the fulfillment of desired aims.

The worship and other rites are as before, like those for Ghṛṇi. In the Taittirīyaka, the five Bhr̥gus beginning with "He who is that Āditya" are well known; one should perform his worship and other rites as previously described. Now, the Vāruṇa mantra spoken in the Āgama of the Ṛgveda is:
"O Dhruva, being seated among the good dwellings, casting us away from sin, may Varuṇa release us from it. Thus they have spoken.

O Aditi, you who abide in forms, protect us with your blessings; may he, the giver, [protect us]. Vasiṣṭha is the seer (ṛṣi) of this verse addressed to Varuṇa; the metre (chandas) is Anuṣṭubh; Varuṇa is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of attaining great sovereignty and fulfillment.
"O Varuṇa, unloose from us our bonds: [the heart] from the firm, dark, and moist dwellings;

[the head] from the noose; [the tuft of hair] from the topknot; [the armor] from the speech of Aditi; [the two eyes] from the lap; protect us with blessings for the weapon, phaṭ! Now follows the placement of the syllables (akṣaranyāsa).

Ten [vowels] at the tips of the two joints of the feet; seven in the anus, the secret organ, the foundation (ādhāra), the belly, the back, and the heart; two in the breasts; one in the ear; ten at the tips of the joints of the arms; one in the chest;
eight in the cheeks, the nose, the eyes, and the pair of ears; one between the eyebrows; and one on the crown of the head.

"Single in all limbs"—this refers to the visualization (*dhyāna*). Having visualized [Varuṇa] as one who is adorned with garments, ornaments, garlands, and unguents; whose lotus-like hands are raised holding a noose, a goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons; and who dwells upon a clear lotus—may Varuṇa long bring about prosperity for you. Having thus meditated, [he should worship him] endowed with the qualities of Dharma and so forth.

Having invoked Varuṇa upon the pedestal, one should worship him. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*). [The second enclosure is as follows: Homage to Vāsuki (1), Takṣaka (2), Karkoṭaka (3), Dhanañjaya (4). (138b)
One should worship on the petals starting from the east with the mantra: "Salutation to Padma, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkha, and Kulika.

One should also worship Indra and the other [directional deities]. Having thus completed the worship and recited the mantra according to one's capacity, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations; the fire-oblation (*homa*) consists of ten thousand oblations of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
For the sake of liberation from debt, one should recite the mantra every day one hundred and eight times;
by this recitation, one obtains great and imperishable prosperity.
The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations of sugar-cane pieces soaked in ghee for four days, one thousand times each day; he will become very dear [to the deity] and be released from debt.
For three days, one who knows the mantras and has conquered the senses should offer oblations for the successful attainment of rain, using fresh reed-samidhs soaked in milk as prescribed.
By this method, the mantra-practitioner who has attained mastery, having reached the Śatabhiṣaj asterism,
should offer four hundred oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee.
For the destruction of debt, for prosperity, for subjugation, for health, and for spiritual accomplishment,
the practitioner, facing westward, should perform the libation with double the amount of water;
this is for the destruction of all calamities and for the total well-being of men.

Now follows the ritual procedure for the Five Brahmans (*pañcabrahmavidhāna*). Īśāna is the lord of all knowledge, the sovereign of all beings, the overlord of Brahman, the overlord of the Veda; may the auspicious Śiva, the eternal source of peace, be unto me. *Oṃ*. We meditate upon that Puruṣa, we contemplate Mahādeva; may Rudra impel us toward that goal. *2*. And from the non-terrible ones... *3*.
Salutations to you who are terrible, more terrible than the most terrible, and who exist everywhere in all forms as Rudras. || 3 ||
Salutation to Vāmadeva; salutation to Jyeṣṭha; salutation to Rudra; salutation to Kalavikaraṇa; salutation to Balapramathana; salutation to Sarvabhūtadamana; salutation to Manonmana. 4.

"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; salutations indeed to Sadyojāta! O Bhava, in every state of existence, be present for me; salutations to Bhavodbhava. Thus are the five mantras. For the Īśāna mantra, the seer is Īśāna, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Īśāna.

139a) For the *tatpuruṣa* [mantra], the *ṛṣi* is *tatpuruṣa*, the *chandas* is *gāyatrī*, the deity (*devatā*) is Bhaga; the consonants (*hal*) are the seeds (*bījas*), the vowels (*svara*) are the powers (*śaktis*).
Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the fourfold aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), preceded by the removal of all defects.

Having performed the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the *prāsāda* mantra: 1. *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ phreṃ hyauṃ sarvajñāta hṛdayāya namaḥ* 2. *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ sphreṃ hyauṃ amṛta-tejogālini tṛptāya brahma-śirase svāhā* 3. *Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ṣphreṃ hyauṃ jvalita-śikhi-śikhe*

Vaṣaṭ to the beginningless awakening, to the crest-lock (śikhā). Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ṣphreṃ hyauṃ, Huṃ to the wielder of the thunderbolt, the bearer of the thunderbolt, for the armor (kavaca). Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ṣphreṃ hyauṃ sauṃ roṃ hūṃ, Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes, whose power is never lost (alupta-śakti). Aiṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ ṣphreṃ hyauṃ, Śrīpaśu Huṃ.

*phaṭ* to the power at the end, *astra* to the weapon, *phaṭ* (six times). Then the mantras beginning with Īśāna are to be installed in five ways. As follows: having divided the Īśāna mantra into five parts, one should install them in order upon the eastern, southern, western, northern, and upper faces along with the [five] *kalās*. [The first part: *īśānaḥ*.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) five times with the *tatpuruṣa* mantra as follows: "Obeisance to Śaśinī, the knower of all sciences" (1); "Obeisance to Aṅgadā, the Lord of all beings" (2); "Obeisance to iṣṭā, the sovereign of Brahmā, the overlord of Brahmā, the Brahmā" (3); "May there be auspiciousness for me; obeisance to Marīci" (4); "Obeisance to Jvālinī, the eternal auspicious one" (5).

Having divided [the mantra], one should place [the parts] in order upon the eastern, southern, upper, and curved [sections]: 1. *Oṃ tatpuruṣāya vidmahe*, salutation to Nivṛtti; 2. *Oṃ mahādevāya dhīmahi*, salutation to Pratiṣṭhā; 3. *Tanno rudraḥ*, salutation to Vidyā; 4. *Pracodayāt*, salutation to Śānti. Then, having divided the Aghora [mantra] eightfold...
One should place [the mantras] upon the heart, the neck, the two eyes, the navel, the belly, and the chest: Oṃ aghorebhyaḥ taṃdryai namaḥ. 1. Atha ghorebhyaḥ mohinyai. 2. Ghorakṣamāyai. 3.
Ghoratarebhyaḥ mṛtyurūpiṇyai. 4. Sarvataḥ. 5.
139b) To Sarvamāyā, 5; to all Nidrās, 6; obeisance be to you, Bhayā, 7; obeisance to Jayā in the forms of Rudras. Then, having divided the Vāmadeva mantra into thirteen parts:
One should place [the mantras] upon the two seeds of Aghora, the two thighs, the two knees, the pair of shanks,

the buttocks, and the two sides: Oṃ Vāmadevāyai namaḥ (1), Oṃ Karālikāyai namaḥ (2), Jyeṣṭhāyai (3), Ratnāyai (4), Rudrāya (5), Ratyai (6), Kālāya (7), Kālinyai (8), Kalakāntāyai (9), Karaṇāya (10), Saṃyaminyai (11).
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with: "Salutation, salutation to Valā (12), to Īśānā (13), to Balavṛddhi (14), to Vikaraṇa (15), to Sthirā (16),

to Balapramathana (17), to Rātri (18), to Sarvabhūtadamana (19), to Grāmiṇī (20), salutation, salutation to Mohinī (21), to Unmanā (22), and salutation to Jarā (23)," one should again [place] Sadyojāta eightfold.
Having divided [the mantra], one should place it on the soles of the feet, the palms of the hands, the nose, the head, and the arms:
*Sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi namaḥ siddhyai* (1) *Bhave namo dyutaye* (2) *Abhaye namo lakṣmyai* (3) *Anādi-bhave namo medhāyai* (4) *Bhajasva māṃ namaḥ kāntyai* (5) *Bhava* (6)

Salutation to Svadhā; salutation to Udbhava. Salutation to Sthirā. O Mahādeva, for one who performs the ritual placement (vinyāsa) in this manner, the worship becomes distinguished. Just as it is said: "Ritual placement brings about the immediate presence in the creation of an image; likewise, it is declared to be the cause of power within the bodies of embodied beings. Wherever it resides—

Likewise, those who know the Śaiva Āgamas understand that when a man has placed his body upon a stone slab, the sacred field (kṣetra) extending one yojana around it belongs to Śiva. Having thus arranged [the ritual space] upon the Śaiva pedestal (pīṭha),
one should invoke the Lord, worship Him with the five-syllable mantra in sequence— namely in the center, and in the directions of the east, south, west, and northeast.
One should worship Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta in the intermediate directions, as well as the Kalās.
The second enclosure consists of the Aṅgas; the third consists of Ananta, Sūkṣma, and the others.
The fourth [consecration] is performed with Umā and the others; the fifth with the world-protectors (lokapālas); the sixth with their weapons. The remainder is as before.
Now follows the Saṃvādasūkta.

O bull, having drunk together with the two young maidens, the noble one has grasped all things. You are the eater of the sacrificial food; you shall be kindled. Bring hither riches for our protection.
Come together, speak together, and let your minds be united,
as the gods of old, being in agreement, partook of their portion.
The mantra is common, the assembly is common, the mind is common, and their thought is shared.
We two shall address the common mantra; with a common oblation, I offer in the common [fire]. 3.
United be your intention, united be your hearts; may your mind be one, so that you may dwell together in harmony. 4.

Thus ends the Saṃvāda Sūkta. Its seer is Saṃvanana, its meter is Anuṣṭubh, its deity is Agni Saṃvāda, and its application is for the fulfillment of desired aims. [The assignment of limbs: 1. To Brahmā, the heart; 2. To Viṣṇu, the head; 3. To Rudra, the tuft of hair (śikhā);
4. To Īśvara, the armor (kavaca); 5. To Sadāśiva, the eyes; 6. To the Self of All, the weapon (astra). [The Meditation (Dhyāna):]

One should invoke and worship the deity upon the fire-seat—him who is seated amidst the white and dark moon-kings, holding a bow shimmering in his hand along with a goad and the gesture of fearlessness; who is the embodiment of restraint (saṃvara), white as pure drops of milk, three-eyed, saluting the excellent wheel, and producing a sweet resonance. [One should worship] with the limbs (aṅgas).
The first enclosure [is formed] by the eight forms of Agni; the second by the world-protectors (lokapālas); the third likewise.
For one who possesses the practice of recitation (japa) and worship in this manner, the swift attainment of wealth occurs. Now, the mantra for the fire of prosperity:
*oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā*. Its seer (ṛṣi) is Bhṛgu, its meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī, and its deity (devatā) is Agni.
The application for the sake of obtaining abundant wealth is as follows: *sahasrārciṣe* is the heart (1); *svasti pūrṇāya* is the head (2);
*uttiṣṭhapuruṣāya* is the tuft (3); *dhūmavyāpine* is the armor (4); *saptajihvāya* is the eye (5);
and *dhanurdhara* is the weapon (6).

Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. With the syllables *bhūḥ*, *vaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, one performs the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual. Then, up to the power (*śakti*), the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is like that of the solar seat (*saurapīṭha*); there [one worships] Pītā (the Yellow One), Śvetā (the White One), and Aruṇā (the Red One).
Salutations to Kṛṣṇā (4), Dhūmrā (5), Tīvrā (6), Sphuliṅginī (7), Rucirā (8), and Jvālinī (9).

Salutations to the Lotus-Seated One who possesses all powers (10). The Meditation: May Pāvaka protect us for a long time—he who is three-faced, holding a spear, a svastika, a noose, a goad, and granting boons and fearlessness; adorned with various ornaments such as flower buds and the like.
[He is] serene. With his upper right and left hands, he holds a spear (*śakti*) and a *svastika*;

below those, a noose (*pāśa*) and a goad (*aṅkuśa*); and beneath those, the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*). Having thus meditated upon the God, one should worship him. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*s). The second [enclosure] consists of the powers (*śakti*s) of Jātavedas and the world-protectors (*lokapāla*s). [The mantra is recited] six hundred thousand times (*ṣallakṣam*).

The *puraścaraṇa* consists of a fire sacrifice (*homa*) performed with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), in which the oblation is offered ten times for every syllable of the mantra. Now follows another twenty-five-syllable mantra: *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ agne jātaveda iha āvaha sarvakarmāṇi sādhaya svāhā*. The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other details, as well as the visualization (*dhyāna*), are as before. Alternatively, [one may visualize] the Śakti-Svastika.

[The deity] is adorned with a garland of gold and is joined with the Kalpa tree; one should meditate on the [deities] beginning with Śakti, starting from the lower right hand, which holds a *darbha* grass ring, a rosary, a sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), and bestows the gestures of fearlessness and boons. *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, [this is] the heart; *oṃ agnir jātavedaḥ*, [this is] the head; *ihāvaha śikhā*, [this is] the crest-lock (*śikhā*).
All rites: *kavaca* (armor) 4, *sā*** (eyes) 5, *svāhā* (weapon) 6.
Now, the mantra for the horses: "Arise, O man! O tawny, reddish-brown, red-eyed one! Grant me [my desire], svāhā! 141a)

The seer (*ṛṣi*) and other [constituent parts] are as before. "Arise, O Puruṣa!"—this is the Heart (1). "O tawny-haired one!"—this is the Head (2). "O red-eyed one!"—this is the Topknot (3). "Grant me armor"—this is the Armor (4). "Bestow the eye"—this is the Eye (5). "Svāhā!"—this is the Weapon (6). *Oṃ* is the Seed-syllable; *svāhā* is the Power (*śakti*). The Meditation (*dhyāna*): [One should meditate on the Lord] emerging from the belly of the golden horse, which is like the interior of a celestial tree, wearing a deerskin...

I bow to the divine-formed Pavaka (Fire), who showers down heaps of wealth, grain, and jewels through his own apertures; whose pores and hair-follicles are perpetually sprouted with flames; who shatters the suffering of his devotees, and who bestows the fruits of dharma, pleasure, wealth, and liberation. [He who is] born from the limbs...

The enclosure is performed by the Vedas and the world-protectors (*lokapālas*). The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations. The fire-oblation (*homa*) is performed with ghee and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in ten parts (*daśāṃśa*). These [mantras] are to be recited by those seeking the power of the fire-mantra. Now, the Soma-mantra: *Soṃ somāya namaḥ*. Alternatively, [it is said that] Bhṛgu is the seer and Paṅkti is the meter. For this [mantra], Atri is the seer and Gāyatrī is the meter.

The deity is Soma; the seed-syllable is *SOM*; the power is *YAM*; the application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of Lakṣmī. The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) are: *SĀM*, *SĪM*, *SŪM*, *SAIM*, *SAUM*, *SAḤ*. Meditation (*dhyāna*): Seated upon a stainless lotus, with a most gracious countenance, holding a beautiful white water-lily in his hand, adorned with pure necklaces and other ornaments, possessing the hue of crystal and silver—[he is] the one who grants all desires.

"May your desired goal be attained, O Moon, the lord of luminaries! Having meditated thus, one should worship the pedestal beginning with Dharma and ending with the lunar maṇḍala; then, having invoked the Moon there, one should worship him.
[The deities] stationed on the filaments are: Tārāpati (Lord of Stars) 1, Rohiṇī 2, Kṛttikā 3, Revatī 4, Bharaṇī 5, and Rātri (Night) 6.

One should worship in the directions starting from the east with the mantras: "Salutation to Ārdrā," "7. Salutation to Jyotsnā," and "9. Salutation to Kalā. These [deities] should be meditated upon with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*).

One should worship Āditya (1), Maṅgala (2), Budha (3), Vṛhaspati (4), Rāhu (5), Śukra (6), and Ketu (8), as well as the guardians of the directions (dikpālas). The preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) consists of six hundred thousand recitations. The fire oblation (homa) should be performed with milk-rice (pāyasa) in the tenth part of that number. When the mantra is thus perfected, the practitioner becomes an abode of prosperity. [He should meditate on the deity] situated in the center of the heart-lotus, adorned with a necklace of *tāra* (Svāhā) beads.

Adorned [with these], the practitioner of the Tārāpati mantra should recite the mantra three thousand times. Even a pauper shall attain royal sovereignty within a year. One should recite it the previously stated number of times while meditating on the Moon upon one's head; thus, having overcome disease, death, and suffering, one shall live for a hundred years. Now, the mantras of Kuvera:

Svāhā to Vaiśravaṇa! 1. Svāhā to Pakvāśa! 2. Svāhā to Piṅgala! 3. Svāhā to Vividha! 4. Svāhā to Kubera! 5. Bhūḥ Svāhā! 6. Bhuvaḥ Svāhā! 7. Svaḥ Svāhā! 8. Bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ Svāhā! Hrīṃ! These mantras bestow wealth. [One should worship] the golden-colored [deity] upon a golden pedestal.

Having meditated upon Kuvera— whose two hands are adorned with golden caskets and baskets, whose belly is large, who is embellished with jewels, and who is illuminated by the *śaṅkha* and *padma* treasures— one should, at the conclusion of the *vaiśvadeva* rite,
offer eighteen *vaṭaka*-shaped fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter and held together by mutual contact into the fire itself, starting from the mouth.

One should offer oblations with these ten mantras; there will be the acquisition of abundant wealth. Or one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) mixed with ghee, or sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) of bilva wood smeared with ghee; there will be the acquisition of wealth. Now follows the mantra for the full vessel of food (annapūrṇā):
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, O Māheśvarī Annapūrṇā, svāhā! In the Śāradātilaka, this [mantra] originates from the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśvarī.
Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra]; the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chanda); Annapūrṇā is the deity (devatā); *hrīṃ* is the seed-syllable (bīja); *svāhā* is the power (śakti).

*Hrāṃ*, *hrīm*, and so forth constitute the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga). And the meditation (dhyāna) is as follows: Meditating upon that Mother, who is intent on the bestowing of food, who is the beloved of Bhava (Śiva), whose face and eyes are auspicious, and who is eager to behold the *tāṇḍava* dance of Rudra.
One should meditate upon her wearing variegated silk garments; having thus meditated and performed worship, one should recite the mantra sixteen thousand times.

A fire sacrifice (*homa*) with food mixed with ghee should be performed using one-tenth of that number. By reciting this mantra, there will be an abundance of food. Now follows the mantra of the Lord of Food (*annādhipati*): *annaṃ...*

"O Lord of Food, give me food; cause this food to be bestowed upon me, svāhā! For this mantra of the Lord of Food, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), the Avikṛti is the meter (chaṃdaḥ), and the Earth and Śrī are the deities (devate). For the attainment of abundant food, the seed-syllable of the Earth (bhū-bīja) and the seed-syllable of Śrī (śrī-bīja) are the seed and power (bīja-śaktī). With "agnau śrīm" and so forth, the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) is performed. [The mantra is: "Food for me..."
Heart: *annaṃ medehi* (Grant me food). Head: *annādhipataye* (To the Lord of Food). Crest-lock: *śikhā* (Crest-lock). Armor: *mamānnaṃ pradāpaya* (Cause food to be given to me).

Weapon: *svāhā* (Svāhā). Meditation (*dhyāna*): [Visualize the deity] clothed in garments of silver and gold, adorned with a golden island-enclosure, surrounded by celestial gardens and wish-fulfilling trees, and resplendent with a garland of jewels.

At the beginning of the day, for the sake of prosperity, let the minister, contemplating the mantra, recite this mantra for the attainment of food: "Seated upon the earth and the goddess Śrī, bestowing desired wealth upon the minister,
[I meditate on] the Kalpavṛkṣa tree situated on a golden island surrounded by a silver rampart in the milk-ocean, frequented by hosts of gods."
Beneath the forest, on that ground made of jewels, one should meditate upon the Earth and Śrī, who bestow all desired objects, in the presence of Kuvera, and worship them. (142b)

There shall be great abundance of wealth and grain. The *puraścaraṇa* consists of twenty-five thousand recitations. The *homa* should be performed with ghee and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) in a tenth part of that number. Now, the mantra of Bṛhaspati: *Vṛṃ vṛhaspataye namaḥ*. For this, Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Bṛhaspati is the deity (*devatā*).
*Vṛṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *maḥ* is the power (*śakti*). *Vrām*, etc., constitutes the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). As for the visualization (*dhyāna*):

one should meditate upon the Supreme Teacher of the Immortals, adorned with yellow garments and so forth, scattering jewels, gold, fine silks, and other riches from his right lotus-hand into a heap of clothing.

Meditating thus, one should sit for three days offering flowers smeared with ghee and gold—numbering one hundred on a long ground—to the deity; then, by sprinkling [the flowers] with water, one attains success in obtaining gold, clothing, and so forth.
By chanting the mantra of Bṛhaspati in this manner, the acquisition of wealth occurs. Now, the mantra of Śukra: "vastraṃ me dehi" (Give me clothing).

"Śukrāya svāhā! Having meditated upon Śukra—seated upon a pedestal, adorned with bright flowers and unguents, bestowing garments, jewels, and gold with his left hand upon the practitioner, and his right hand marked by the *vyākhyā* (explanation) mudrā—one should worship him. The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of ten thousand recitations; [one should offer] a thousand oblations of clarified butter.

The fire offering (*homa*): Having visualized Śukra in his true form within the fire, one should offer white flowers into his mouth sixty-three times, or one hundred and forty-seven times; then there will be the attainment of purifying jewels and an abundance [of wealth]. And it is said in the *Prapañca*: "Into the mouth of Śukra, with white flowers, offered into the fire in groups."
One should offer oblations twenty-one times for each of the seven [deities], using very white flowers and unguents with the left hand; likewise,
one should constantly offer garments, jewels, and other beautiful things, as well as wine.

Bestowing [the fruit] upon the practitioner while being meditated upon, he is endowed with the gesture of exposition (*vyākhyāna-mudrā*), possesses the supreme *kalā*, and is the junction of the *āpana* and *aliṅda* breaths. Now, the mantra of Vyāsa: *Oṃ vyāṃ vedavyāsāya namaḥ*. The meditation (*dhyāna*): [He is] surrounded by a multitude of sages, possessed of a joyful mind, as beautiful as a water-bearing cloud, and radiant with the light of exposition.

One should meditate upon Vyāsa, who possesses a radiant right hand adorned with a *mudrā*, who sits with one knee raised and his armpit firmly pressed against it, and who is devoted to the goddess of love and a mass of merit; this bestows pure Sarasvatī. And it is said in the *Prapañcasāra*: "The recitation of the *prakṛti* [mantra] one thousand times..."

There may be a procedure involving milk-rice and ghee performed ten times [the number of recitations]. This mantra bestows incomparable poetic skill, wisdom, explanatory power, and the wealth of fortune. Now, the Vedic mantras of the Goddess of the Day (Vāradevī):
"That which the speechless ones utter, the sweet voice of the gods has taken its seat as the sovereign ruler. *Catasra* *jha* *juṃ* *huṃ*.

duheṣayāṃsikasvidasyā paramaṃ jagāma | Asya Bhārgavanemi Ṛṣi, Triṣṭubh Chanda, Vāgdevī Devatā; the application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of speech. Vaṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Taṃ is the power (śakti), Draṃ is the pin (kīlaka). [The six limbs are performed] with ten, five, six, five, six, and ten [repetitions].

By the recitation of this [mantra], the accomplishment of Sarasvatī is attained. Now, the Gaurī-mantra: *Śrīgauri rudradayite yogeśvari huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. For this, Aja is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Trivṛt is the meter (*chandaḥ*), and Gaurī is the deity (*devatā*); its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of subjugation (*vaśya*) and other such powers. The visualization (*dhyāna*):
I bow to her whose head is adorned with the crescent moon, whose beautiful lotus-hands hold a noose and a goad,
whose limbs are as red as the bandhujīva flower, who is worshipped by hosts of gods, and who wears a crimson silken garment.

"May Pārvatī, accompanied by her flowers, grant you prosperity. Having meditated thus, one should invoke the Goddess upon the Śaktipīṭha and worship her with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings. One [round] is performed with the Mothers; the second with the World-Protectors (Lokapālas). The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of one hundred thousand recitations. An oblation (homa) of ten thousand [offerings] of milk-rice (pāyasa) should be performed. For the attainment of good fortune and other blessings, a woman should perform the recitation.

For the purpose of subjugation (*vaśya*) and for the sake of prosperity (*saṃpat*), a person should perform recitation (*japa*). At night, having written the name of the woman upon his own left thigh and covering it with his left hand, he should recite; she will become submissive and will come to him. Now follows another mantra of Gaurī consisting of sixty-one syllables: *hrīṃ namo brahma śrīrātiterājite*.

*Jaye vijaye gauri gandhāri, O Śaṅkarī of the three worlds, O you who bring all worlds under control, O you who bring all women and men under control! Su-su-du-du-ghere-ghere-vāvā-hnam! Svāhā!* The *ṛṣi* and other [limbs] are the same as for the Gaurī mantra. Then, with fourteen, ten, and eight [repetitions]...

The ritual for the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-vidhi) is stated in sequence by means of ten and eleven syllables of the mantra. The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) consists of ten thousand recitations. The fire-oblation (homa) is one-tenth of that, performed with milk-porridge (pāyasa) mixed with clarified butter. Having first recited the name of the person to be subdued (sādhya), one should then recite the mantra; this brings everything under control without exception. Now, [the mantra of] Gāndhārī:
The mantra: *kāñcita strīvaśaṅkari su su du du ghe ghe vā vā strīṃ svāhā*.
For this, everything is as before. One should recite the mantra after joining the name of either a woman or a man—either above the syllable *hoi* or below the syllable *vā*.
144a) She quickly brings [them] under control. Now follows the *Rājamukhī* mantra: *rājamukhi rājābhimukhi vaśyamukhi hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ devi devi mahādevi devādevi sarvajanasya mukhaṃ*.

*Mamavaśaṃ kuru kuru svāhā*. *Rājamukhi*, *rājābhimukhi*—the heart (1). *Vaśyamukhi*, *hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ*—the head (2). *Divi devi*—the crest-lock (3). *Mahādevi*—the armor (4). *Devādevi*—the three eyes (5). With the remainder [of the mantra], the weapon (6). All else is like the Gāndhārī mantra. For all people...

One should insert the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the appropriate place and recite it in an assembly or similar setting; one will certainly bring the king or anyone else under control. Now follows the mantra for conquering the earth: *bhage bhage kṣobhaye mohaye chedaye kledaya klinne svaśarīre hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This supreme and glorious mantra [is effective] throughout the three worlds.
Renowned by the name Bhūvijaya, as spoken by the Lord himself, a human being quickly attains all of this— freedom from misfortunes,
anger, poverty, impurity, lack of splendor, and the absence of knowledge and virtues—
merely through recitation (japa). Whatever one lacks, if one recites [this], one obtains it.

One obtains each of those things without a doubt. Now, the Ratnadhārā mantra: *ratna ratna mahāratnadhārāya svāhā*. For this mantra, Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), the deity is the one named Ratnadhārā, and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the acquisition of jewels and other such things. The limbs (*aṅga*) are formed by the divisions of the mantra. [It is visualized as] raining a stream of jewels upon the practitioner.

Meditating on [the deity] adorned with ornaments such as necklaces and crowns held in both hands, one should recite the mantra; great prosperity will arise. Now, the mantra of the Teacher (Śāstṛmantra).
Oṃ, homage to the Teacher, who, weary from hunting, has mounted his horse and is surrounded by his retinue; he comes from the forest for the sake of water—
homage to him who is other than a weapon.

The seer is Asyaraivataka, the metre is Paṅkti, the deity is Mahāśāstṛ, and the application is for the purpose of bringing all under control. One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantra-words. While meditating on the one who holds a staff, causing the target—who is bound by a noose—to fall at the feet of the practitioner, one should recite [the mantra]. The worship of his retinue is as follows: to the Protector (Goptṛ), 1.

One should worship with the mantra: "Obeisance to Piṅgalākṣa (2), Vīrasena (3), Śrībhava (4), Trinetra (5), Śūlin (6), Kṣa (7), and Bhīmarūpa (8). Having thus offered groats (*saktu*) to him at midday, one should offer water with cupped hands (*añjali*), as well as to his attendants (*gaṇas*).
One should offer one's own tasks to that [deity] who has rested;
with a pleased mind, having said "So be it," one should remember that he has indeed become manifest.
The mantra is: *Ṣaihaṃtāya śāstre goptre praśāstre | gāyatrī bhūtādhipāya vidmahe mahādevāya dhīmahi | tannaḥ śāstā pracodayāt*. Now, the mantras for desire (*kāma*): *klīṃ*.
The seer is Saṃmohana, the meter is Gāyatrī, and the deity is Kāma; [this is used] for the purpose of bringing all persons under one's control.

The application (*viniyoga*): *klāṃ klīṃ*, etc., for the six limbs. For the two eyes, however, there is meditation (*dhyāna*): [He is] ruddy, with ruddy garments, garlands, and body-unguents; holding in his own hands a noose, a goad, a trident, and a bow; radiant with a jeweled crown and various ornaments; seated upon a ruddy lotus.

One should contemplate the Self-born (Ātmayoni). Having meditated thus, one should invoke and worship the Deity upon the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, which is endowed with the nine powers: "Salutation to Mohinī, Krodhinī, Trāsinī, Staṃbhinī, Ākarṣiṇī, Drāvinī, Āhlādinī, Klinnā, and Kledinī. Drāṃ.

One should worship the arrows in a clockwise direction with the following: "To the arrow of drying, *drīṃ*; to the arrow of enchanting, *klīṃ*; to the arrow of inflaming, *saṃ*; to the arrow of intoxicating, *saṃ*.

Immediately thereafter, one should worship on the petals of the directions with the formula "Oṃ, obeisance" as follows: to Anaṅgarūpā (1), Anaṅgamadanā (2), Anaṅgamanmathā (3), Anaṅgakusumā (4), Anaṅgakusumāturā (5), Anaṅgaśeṣarā (6), Anaṅgamekhalā (7), and Anaṅgadīpikā (8).

And the world-protectors (*lokapāla*s). One hundred thousand recitations constitute the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). The fire-oblation (*homa*) consists of *kiṃśuka* flowers sprinkled with the three sweets (*trimadhura*), performed in a tenth part of the number of recitations. One should perform the recitation for the purpose of bringing all the world under one's control. Now, the Kāma-Gāyatrī: "We know Kāmadeva; we meditate upon the flower-bowed one; may that Bodiless One (*anaṅga*) inspire us. Oṃ klīṃ.

Homage to Kāmadeva, who is dear to all people, who deludes all people: blaze, blaze! flare up, flare up! bring all people under my control, svāhā! For this [mantra] as well, the seer (ṛṣi), meditation (dhyāna), and so forth are as before. Now, another method: to him born from nectar, whose banner is the makara, who is born of resolve, whose form is syllables, to the sugarcane-...
"Salutation to the wielder of the bow, the one whose arrows are flowers. Having performed the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with these words, one should meditate.

One should place the five seed-syllables, *drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, and so forth, on the forehead, mouth, throat, heart, and private parts. [He is] red in color, wearing a garland and ointment, adorned with ornaments, and holding a mendicant’s staff, a bow, and flower-arrows.

Having meditated and performed internal worship, one should perform the external worship. Having worshipped the deity with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*) is formed by the limbs (*aṅga*). Then [the second enclosure] is formed by the arrows (*vāṇa*): *hrīṃ* to Yuvati (1), *hrīṃ* to Vipralambhā (2), *hrīṃ* to Jyotsnā (3), *hrīṃ* to Subhru (4), *hrīṃ* to Madadravā (5), *hrīṃ* to Suratā (6), *hrīṃ* to Varuṇā.
7 Hrīṃ, to Lolā; 8 Hrīṃ, to Kānti; 9 Hrīṃ, to Saudāminī; 10 Hrīṃ, to Kāmacchatrā; 11 Hrīṃ, to Candrarekhā; 12 Hrīṃ, to Śukti; 13 Hrīṃ, to Madanā; 14. (145b)

One should worship in a clockwise direction with the mantra: *hrīṃ māyāvatyai namaḥ* (15 times). Then: *hrīṃ śokāya* (1), *hrīṃ mohāya* (2), *hrīṃ vilāsāya* (3), *hrīṃ vibhramāya* (4), *hrīṃ madanāturāya* (5), *hrīṃ patrapāya* (6), *hrīṃ yūne* (7), *hrīṃ kāmine* (8), *hrīṃ cūtapuṣpāya* (9), *hrīṃ ratipriyāya* (10), *hrīṃ grīṣmāya* (11).

*Hrīṃ* to Tāpa (12), *hrīṃ* to Uṣṇa (13), *hrīṃ* to Hemanta (14), *hrīṃ* to Śiśira (15), *hrīṃ* to Vasanta (16), *hrīṃ* to Madana (8), *namaḥ*. With these [mantras], one should worship the attendants of Kāma starting from the east. The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of one hundred thousand recitations. The fire-oblation (*homa*) with *palāśa* flowers should be one-tenth of that number. For one who recites thus...

And for one who worships [it], the attainment of Mahālakṣmī occurs. Now, the mantra for the subjugation of enemies consists of twenty syllables: Oṃ aṃ kaṃ caṃ ṭaṃ taṃ paṃ yaṃ saṃ haloṃ hrīṃ huṃsaḥ huṃ phaṭ svāhā. For this, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), and Mahāparvata and Mahāsamudra are the deities.

The deities are Mahāvahni (Great Fire), Mahāpavana (Great Wind), and the group of Pṛthivī (Earth). *Huṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the desired purpose.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantras beginning with *hṛllekhā*. We perceive no other meditation (*dhyāna*).
One should perform the worship and other rites with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). The preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of eleven thousand and six hundred recitations.
The homa is performed with sesame, mustard seeds, rice, *vrīhi* grain, clarified butter, and ghee, in ten parts according to their respective proportions.
For the purpose of subduing enemies, one should first visualize the syllable of the mantra as a mountain swallowing the enemy; then the second syllable as an ocean, in which the enemy is submerged.

One should visualize [the enemy] being burned by the third form, that of fire; being dried up by the fourth form, that of wind; obstructing the breath of the enemy with the two syllables *ha* and *loma*;
and obstructing the eyes, ears, and mouth of the enemy with the three syllables *hrīṃ*, *huṃ*, and *saḥ*.
One should contemplate [this]. One should meditate upon the enemy being consumed by the rising fire from the syllable *phaṭ* at the enemy's base.
Meditating thus and reciting the mantra, one kills the enemy even before reaching the mandala. Now...
The *lavaṇa-mantra* consists of five *ṛks*: 1. "O salt-water, you are sharp, you are fierce; your heart is [the essence].

The earth is the mother of salt, Varuṇa is the father of salt. 2. "Salt cooks and causes to cook; salt cuts and pierces. When salt is being consumed, where is sleep? Where is pleasure? 3. Of this [salt]...

It burns the limbs, it burns the flesh, it burns the skin; it burns the teeth, skin, bones, and hair, and from the bones it burns the marrow—such is the night for one pierced by the arrow and impaled upon the tip of the stake. That which is your night, O Great Night, that is your night, O Great Midnight. 4. Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ciṭi-ciṭi cāṇḍāli.

"O Great Caṇḍālī, bring [the person named] so-and-so under my control, svāhā! (5). In another mantra, they recite this additional portion: "In the city surrounded by an iron rampart, where black serpents are the gatekeepers, quickly bring Caṇḍī here by the salty splendor of fire. Others recite this as well. Its seer is Aṅgiras.
The seer is Anuṣṭubh, the meter is Anuṣṭubh, the deity is Agni Rātrī Bhadravālī; the application is for the sake of attaining subjugation (*vaśya*) and other such powers.

One should perform the five-limbed ritual (*pañcāṅga*) with the five verses in sequence. Alternatively: *Oṃ ciṭiciṭi* is the heart (1); *Cāṇḍāli* is the head (2); *Mahācāṇḍāli* is the crest-lock (3); *Amukaṃ me* is the armor (4).

"Bring [him] under control, O Netravedha! Svāhā! Astra! Meditation (Dhyāna): May the Fire-god protect us—he who rests upon a ruddy lotus, whose hands hold the sacrificial ladle (śruva), the spear (śakti), the bull (vṛṣabha), and the noose (abhaya); he whose radiance is immeasurable, whose movement reaches the end of the unborn (Brahman), and whose three eyes are wide open.
May she who wears garments and hair as dark as a blue tree, whose own voice is her necklace, who holds a goad, a skull, and a water-pot—

she who protects from worldly existence— protect you eternally. May the three-eyed Lord, upon whose lotus-like hand shine the discus, conch, sword, and trident, and whose crown has struck down many demons, protect you.
May Katyayani, whose limbs are graceful, protect us.
May she—fierce, with bared fangs, three eyes, and disheveled hair; holding a skull-cup, a trident, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a trident;
her heavy necklace of blood-dripping bells made from the skulls of the wicked—be for the attainment of your sovereign power.

"May Bhadrakālī be with you for a long time. Having meditated thus, one should worship her with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*). The preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) consists of ten thousand or three thousand recitations. The fire sacrifice (*homa*) should be performed with an offering of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) mixed with sacrificial food (*havis*), consisting of one-tenth of the total number.
Having thus performed the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), one becomes skilled in the practical application;
for the rites of subjugation and attraction, one should meditate on Agni Yāmavati.
One should remember Durgā Bhadrakālī during the rite of incantation for killing;
standing in water reaching up to the knees, one should mutter the mantra at night.
By this, the desired object to be accomplished becomes a servant in an instant;
the wise one should remain for a long time [submerged] up to the navel.
He for whom one thousand and eight recitations are intended is his sādhya;
the practitioner of mantra, standing in water reaching up to his neck, should recite the Ṛkya-cakra mantra.

Furthermore, having written [the mantra] on a leaf of the *tāpa* tree, interlaced with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), one should subjugate them again according to the ritual procedure for seven days.
Having placed [the substance] and boiled it overnight with water mixed with milk, the subject becomes submissive; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
If one cooks [the substance] in a fire of khadira wood for a month, that man shall become submissive.

Now, the Brahma-mantra: *Oṃ namo bhagavate brahmaṇe aṣṭau me putrā jāyantām akṣīṇatejase svāhā*. For this mantra, Saurabhi is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Brahmā is the deity (*devatā*), *Oṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*). [It bestows] eight sons, increased wealth, grain, and so forth.
The application for the sake of attainment:
147a) Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, homage to the heart; 1. To Brahmā, svāhā to the head; 2. To the Pervader...
*Vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (śikhā), three times; *Huṃ* to the armor (kavaca) for the birth of eight sons, four times;

*Vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes of undiminished splendor; *Svāhā* to the weapon (astra), *phaṭ*. Meditation (*dhyāna*): Viriñci, the source of the universe, seated upon a reddish lotus, red in color, adorned with various beautiful ornaments.

"May [the deity] grant you various enjoyments, sons, and so forth, with his own arms extended, holding the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the boon (*vara*), the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and the rosary (*akṣasūtra*). Having meditated thus and worshipped according to the rules with mental offerings (*mānasair upacāraiḥ*),
having duly presented the *argha* water, and having prepared the pedestal (*pīṭha*) beginning with the support (*ādhāra*), one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus upon it, starting from the east.

In due order, one should worship on the petals with: "Oṃ, salutation to Aṇimā," "to Mahimā," "to Laghimā," "to Garimā," "to Prāpti," "to Parakāmyā," "to Vaśitā," and "to Kāmāvasāyitā. In the center, [one should worship] with: "Salutation to Sarvaiśvarya. Then the pedestal [should be worshipped] with: "Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, who dwells in the lotus."

Having performed worship, one should invoke the deity into its pericarp and worship him with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings. The first enclosure consists of the limbs (*aṅga*). Beginning from the eastern petal, one should worship with: "Salutation to Ūrdhva (1), Pralamba (2), Ūrdhvakeśa (3), Vimohana (4), Gandhapati (5), Kāma (6), Kaliṅga (7), and Kapi (8). Thus it is said.

One should worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in their respective directions. Then, having recited [the mantra] according to one's capacity, one should dissolve the deity into one's own heart. One hundred thousand recitations constitute the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). The fire-oblation (*homa*) consists of ten parts performed with milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Bathing in the morning, with purified senses, wearing clean garments and unguents, one should perform this at the Ganges, or in a river, or at another sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).
In the auspicious Śaiva [temple], or in a great [shrine], one who has become sweet food through pure conduct [should enter].

Through merits, the wise man obtains all his desires day by day; thus he mutters this mantra daily. Whoever constantly recites this mantra—whether desiring wealth, seeking knowledge, longing for many sons, or desiring any other wish—shall surely obtain it.
He should transmit it to eight twice-born from four, and [recite it] daily at sunrise.

He who daily recites this one hundred or fifty times at the three junctions of the day, and drinks even water consecrated by this mantra, shall obtain wealth and his desired sons. For him who, seeking such prosperity, observes this mantra, there arises for his ancestral lineage the crossing over of hell. Now...

The Subrahmaṇya Mantra: *Vacarbhuve namaḥ*. This is the six-syllabled mantra of Sarasvatī. *Varadāya duḥsahinyai vāhuleyavacarbhuve skanda skanda su subrahmaṇya namaḥ*. O Lord, dweller in the cave (*guhāśaya*), *oṃ duṃ namaḥ parāyagoptre*. Thus is one [mantra]. The same applies to this as well. Now...
The mantra of the Teacher: *Bhāṃ*, obeisance to the Lord of Beings (*bhūtādhipati*). This should be recited at the beginning of the recitation of the *vali* offering.

Now, another: the five-syllable *revate namaḥ*. Having meditated upon the Teacher, the bestower of wealth, who is seated beneath the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times for the attainment of gold and the removal of impurities. Now, the mantra of Skanda: *svāmin vidhi svāhā*.
Mounted upon his shoulder was a celestial elephant, adorned with millions of tinkling bells;
it caused the wish-fulfilling tree to shake, making its fruits fall upon the earth.
One should meditate upon oneself as being filled with gold, jewels, and other riches while reciting the mantra;
by so doing, one's wealth, grain, and other prosperities will quickly increase.
One should worship the deity on the aforementioned seat as follows:
1. Devasenā, 2. Vidyā, 3. Medhā, 4. Prajñā, 5. Śakti, 6. Kukkuta, 7. Mayūra, 8. Dvipa.

One should worship [them]. In this way, Guha, Śrī, Sarasvatī, Jaya, Putra, and Vīrya bestow their powers. Now, as for the Teacher (Śāstṛ): one should meditate upon the Teacher, weary from hunting, mounted on a horse, surrounded by his attendants (gaṇas), appearing in the form of a deer, and having come from the forest for the sake of water.
At midday, having offered groats and water with the joined palms,
one should satisfy those [deities] and their attendants as well by drinking the water while reciting these mantras.
One should offer one's own tasks to that Lord who has rested;
we know the Lord of Beings, we meditate upon the Son of Bhava.

May he, our Teacher, inspire us. Homage to those who have reached the state of the Teacher. One should worship the Teacher. One should offer oblations at night. Homage to Mahāśāstra. Homage to Bhūtādhipati. To Rudrasūta. To Pañcakeśvara. To Sādhu. To Hari, and so forth. Now follows the mantra of Kṣetrapāla: *kṣaṃ*.

Homage to the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla). One should meditate upon him with upward-pointing tawny eyes, bearing a skull, holding a khaṭvāṅga staff in his hand, and adorned with all ornaments. The mantra for the offering (bali): Ehyehi guṣu 2 musu 2 hana 2 vighna 2 Mahābhairava Kṣetrapāla, accept the offering (bali) 2! Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ! To Anala, Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ!
To Agnikeśa; to Kāla; to Mahākrodha; to Piśitāśana; to Piṅgalākṣa; to Ūrdhvakeśa—Ṭhaḥ Ṭhaḥ! One should offer an oblation (*bali*) to these. Protection for children and all others is thereby secured.

Now follows the garland mantra (*mālāmantra*). Now follows the group of eight (*aṣṭakavarga*): *a ka ca ṭa ta pa ha lauṃ*. By the recitation of this group of eight, having placed [the mantra] above the collection of obstacles belonging to the eight mountain ranges, one draws [the space] upward with "haṃ" as the ether (*ākāśa*), and having placed that upon it, [one forms] the earthly mandala (*pārthivamaṇḍala*) with "laṃ".

Having placed it upon that [pedestal], having made it immovable by pressing down with a mace, and having meditated upon Vanadurgā standing atop a lion in her own yogic sleep-inducing state (yoganidrāmohanī), one should proceed while reciting her mantra.
All fears cease to exist. Now, the mantra for paralyzing speech:
"We worship the Four-Faced One; may we be delivered from the mouth of death, O Increaser!
Pour forth all that consists of Truth; bind, bind everything!"

Oṃ hrīṃ, O Valāmukhī, O you who paralyze the mouth at the place of assembly, paralyze the mouth! Paralyze the tongue! Ṭhāṃ ṭhāṃ svāhā! This mantra should be recited in the royal court or when engaging in debates and the like. Now, the mantras for the five nectars (pañcāmṛta): Oṃ, obeisance to Acyuta, the destroyer of disease, to Hari, the nectar! Oṃ.

Oṃ vaṃ, salutations to Ananta, the destroyer of disease, to Hari, the nectar; Oṃ aiṃ, salutations to Govinda, the destroyer of disease, to Hari, the nectar; Oṃ ṭhaṃ, salutations to Viṣṇu, the destroyer of disease, to Hari, the nectar; Oṃ.

One should worship in this manner: "Oṃ, obeisance to Acyuta; obeisance to Ananta; obeisance to Govinda; obeisance to Viṣṇu. For this mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) is Rojanāśana, the meter (chanda) is Anitagāyatrī, and the deities (devatās) are Acyuta, Ananta, Amṛta, Govinda, and Viṣṇu, for the purpose of destroying all diseases of our body.

The application (*viniyoga*). Now, the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*): Oṃ acyutāya hṛdayāya namaḥ 1 Oṃ saṃ anantāya śirase svāhā 2 Oṃ vaṃ amṛtāya śikhāyai vaṣaṭ 3 Oṃ aiṃ govindāya kavacāya huṃ 4 Oṃ ṭhaṃ viṣṇave astrāya phaṭ 5 Then, the meditation (*dhyāna*): In the region of the Ocean of Milk...
Seated upon a cluster of pearl garlands on this shore that shines with pure jewels,
he resembles a crystal gem, his limbs adorned with pearls.

May Mukunda—the one who holds in his hands the lotus, mace, and conch—purify you with joy, as he is surrounded above by abundant, bright clouds that rain down a shower of nectar. This mantra should be recited at the onset of fever and other ailments.
One should consume medicine and the like consecrated with this mantra; thus, diseases and other afflictions will be destroyed.
He goes. Now, the mantra of Dhanvantari: Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Dhanvantari, the thousandfold nectar, the destroyer of all diseases, the Lord of the three worlds, Viṣṇu; svāhā!
For this mantra, Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chaṃdas), and Dhanvantari is the deity (devatā); it is for the sake of health.

The application (*viniyoga*): One should meditate upon [the deity] bearing a medicinal casket the color of camphor, sprinkling nectar upon the sick person. Having touched the medicine or other such items while reciting this mantra, one should consecrate them;
by consuming them, the disease is pacified. Now, the Gārūḍa mantra: *kṣipa oṃ svāhā*.
Ananta is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra]; Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); Garuḍa is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is for the destruction of poison from serpents and other sources.

*Jvala jvala mahāgati svāhā*—obeisance to the heart (hṛdayāya namaḥ). 1. *Garuḍa cūḍāmaṇi svāhā*—svāhā to the head (śirase svāhā). 2. *Garuḍa śikhe svāhā*—ṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhāyai). 3. *Garuḍa prabhañjana prabhañjana*.

"By each distinction, terrify 2, crush 2, svāhā! To the armor, hūṃ 4! O you of irresistible power and irresistible command, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! To the weapon, phaṭ 5! O bearer of fierce form, terrifying to serpents, frighten 2, burn 2, reduce to ashes, svāhā! To the two eyes, vauṣaṭ 6! Then:
Meditation:
[He visualizes] a golden luster from the knees to the navel, a radiance from the navel to the ears, and from the ears to the ends of the ears, a color as red as saffron, which is other than white.
The wise man should meditate upon Garuḍa, who pervades the entire universe, whose limbs are empty, who is adorned with serpents,
who is clothed in blue garments, whose soul is equanimous, and who possesses great wings.
A person, remembering himself as Garuḍa, should mutter this mantra;
by merely looking at it, he will not be harmed by anything arising from the race of serpents.
Now follows the mantra of Citragupta.
Oṃ, homage to the wondrous Dharma-scribe, the official of the Yāma ledger!
Proclaim, proclaim the destruction of the birth, prosperity, and excellence of the enemy Jamalavara! Svāhā! [Meditation:
A crown blazing with a multitude of radiant jewels; a face with a radiant halo of light.
I perpetually worship Citragupta, who resembles the moon, who wears a beautiful necklace like a cluster of stars, who is intent on the work of reckoning merit and demerit, who wears anklets,
and whose feet are as radiant and variegated as a king’s. For one who recites this, Citragupta becomes pleased and [counts] only their merit.
If one does not [commit] evil... Now, the mantra of Karṇapiśācikā: Oṃ rūṃ hrūṃ!
O Goddess, for the sake of my command and ignorance, you whose body is adorned with gold, lapis lazuli, and pearls—come, come! Arrive, arrive! Having entered, having entered, enter my ear, O Bhūta!

O Śrī Vīracāmuṇḍī, who possesses the knowledge and vision of the future and the present, speak! Speak! Paralyze fire, paralyze water, and paralyze speech! You who create obstacles for the work of enemies and bring success to my own work; you who destroy the joy of my adversaries and bring fruit to my endeavors—Huṃ!
*phaṭ svāhā*. May my enemies be smeared at the tips of my feet!

One should always meditate upon the goddess who is red in color, holding a boon-granting gesture (*varada*), adorned with red garlands and red unguents, and fulfilling all the desires of the practitioner. Recite [the mantra] one thousand times with offerings anointed with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*).

The homa is performed with *palāśa* flowers in a tenth part [of the total]. For one who has thus completed the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), the Goddess comes again and again to his ear and reveals all supersensory knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*) and all the worlds.
It brings all enemies under one's control and accomplishes every success. Now follows the *apasarpinī* mantra:

"O *apasarpinī*, driving away the enemy, the great one given by Agni, the daughter of the Sun—may she direct that mind toward us; may the immortal goddess among the gods come to us, O *apasarpinī*, as one who is well-disposed."
Brahmā is her navel, Hari is situated in the region of her heart,
Śiva is her feet, the four Vedas are her feet, and both the Sun and the Moon are her eyes.
The limbs are the seats of the Vedas, the tail is the deities, and the hair is the sacred syllable Om; I bow to Nakulī, who is red in color, the all-pervading Sarasvatī.

Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Vāktarparī is the deity (*devatā*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of speech. For one who recites this mantra, speech becomes unimpeded in its flow. Now follows the Nakulī mantra: *Oṃ, O Nakulī, you whose lip is the cover; give the measured thunderbolt; with a tongue that does not falter, [bestow] speech.*

And [the mantras] beginning with *anumāveha*. For this [mantra], Viśvāmitra is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Nakulī Sarasvatī is the deity (*devatā*), and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining mastery over speech (*vāk-siddhi*). The rest is as before. Now follows the mantra of Mahārātri: *Oṃ, salutation to the hosts of Night (*rātrigaṇa*), who bring all under control; may they take hold [of me] for the sake of bringing all under control.*

"Oblation for him, for the sake of all peace, svāhā! Brahmā is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [verse], the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and Mahārātri is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of achieving subjugation and other such goals. This very mantra is to be used for the oblation at the commencement of the fire-sacrifice (homa) and other rites.
One should offer the oblation with the syllable *kṣrauṃ*. Now follows the mantra for Viśvāvasu, the Gandharva: *oṃ gandharvarāja viśvāvaso mama abhilaṣitāṃ kanyāṃ prayaccha svāhā*.
One who desires a specific maiden should recite this mantra while facing west; he shall obtain her.

Now another: Just as the Gandharva named Viśvāvasu, the lord of maidens, obtains a maiden along with her dowry, so [be it] to that Viśvāvasu; salutation to him. This [mantra] is also like the previous one. Now, the mantra of Rāvaṇa: Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, Rāvaṇa, the ten-necked one.

Salutations, salutations, salutations to the one whose neck was severed by Rāma, to the one whose hand was severed by Rāma, to the devotee of Śiva, to the knower of the four Vedas. This [mantra] is to be recited when terrified by Rākṣasas and others. Now follows the Pratyamgirā mantra: Oṃ, that cruel *kṛtyā* which the enemy prepares against us—may Brahmā overcome it for our victory.

May one desire the direct agent. For this [mantra], Brahmā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Pratyaṅgirā is the deity (*devatā*), *oṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of desired objects. Some say that it should be recited with the syllable *praṇava* (*oṃ*) and *hrīṃ* at the beginning, and *hrīṃ* and *oṃ* at the end; thus, it is to be recited enclosed by the *hṛllekhā*. Having performed the purification of the hands: *oṃ yāṃ kalpayati norayaḥ*.

*Hrāṃ*, salutation to the heart (1); *Krūrāṃ kṛtyāṃ hrīṃ*, to the head (2); *Vabhūvivahrūṃ*, to the crest-lock (śikhā) (3); *Tāṃ brahma hraiṃ*, armor (kavaca) (4); *Abhibhūtyai hrauṃ*, the three eyes (netratraya) (5);
*Pratyakkartāram icchatu hnaḥ*, the weapon (astra) (6). Meditation (*dhyāna*): [Visualize her] as black, bearing a sword and a shield.

One should meditate upon her with disheveled hair, adorned with jackals, her face terrifying with protruding fangs, possessing all ornaments, devouring the enemy, and impelled by the splendor of Śiva. The target is the mantra to be recited. The fire oblation (*homa*) should consist of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, performed in ten parts (*daśāṃśa*). Now follows another *Pratyaṅgirā* mantra: *Oṃ hrīṃ namaḥ*.

O you who are clothed in black garments, who ride upon a thousand lions, whose face possesses a thousand eyes, O you of great strength, unconquered, protector of your own forces, destroyer of the forces of others, and eradicator of the supreme mantras! 151a)

O Subduer of all beings! O Binder of all gods! Cut, cut all spells! Agitate, agitate! Shatter the enemy yantras! Break, break all chains! O Pratyaṅgirā, whose face is terrible with a tongue of blazing flames! Hrīṃ, obeisance! Because this is a mantra for attaining success (siddhi), [the following] seers and so forth [are prescribed].

There is no meditation [on her]. She is mounted upon a lion, clad in black garments, terrifying, with a dark-blue body, a flaming mouth, and holding a trident in her hand; she swiftly destroys the enemy.
Everything else is as before.

Now follows the Sahasrākṣarī Pratyaṅgirā: Oṃ! Homage to Cāmuṇḍā, who wears a garland marked with human skulls, whose retinue consists of vultures, owls, and ducks, who delights in the cremation ground, who utters the *huṃkāra* of the hell-wardens, who causes yawning, whose body is armed with swords, spears, javelins, and knives, who possesses a thousand arms, and who [grasps] the heart with her hands.

Within the body of Viṣṇu’s nature, consume all wicked ones with fire; hold [the fire] steady! Protect the human body! Render humans free from poison! Destroy the enemies! Scorch the wicked! Crush the trees like chaff!
Rend asunder weapon after weapon and the army of Kuru! [And likewise] the gonāsas, sārikās, and mosquitoes!
Bind the mouth! Bind the mouth! *drāṃ drīṃ drūṃ draiṃ drauṃ draḥ*. Through twenty-one recitations, [ward off] fire.

O you with hanging hair, O you with long-hanging hair, O you in blue garments, O you who are fond of white tigers, O you of great whirlpools, take away, take away these things in the form of Bhairava; take away, take away them in the form of Svaratara; go, go in the form of Rudra, at whatever time.
Raise up, raise up all that has been seen! Render the *kālakūṭa* poison poisonless, poisonless!
Destroy the fever—whether it be quotidian, tertian, quartan, visual fever, *sānnipātika*, continuous, or seasonal—with the eight-fold incense of *guggulu*.
151b) By this consecrated mantra, destroy, destroy the fever! Having consecrated white mustard seeds, I bind the ball of the *susārikā* bird;
draw her in, draw her in—the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Viṭ, Śūdra, the Raṅgiṇī, and the Mohinī!

Salutation to the eighteen Cāṇḍāla natures, who possess deformed fangs and are terrifying, who dwell on mountain slopes, who reside in Ujjayinī, and whose bodies are smeared with ashes: Oṃ Hrīṃ Hrūṃ Hrāṃ Yeṃ Kṣoṃ Kroṃ Namaḥ Svāhā. For this [mantra], there is no seer (ṛṣi) or other [constituent elements].
This supreme vidyā is accomplished with three thousand recitations;
one should offer oblations of sesame and black mustard seeds with a tenth part of that number.
Dhyāna:
She wears a tiger-skin garment and rides upon a black panther;
she has a terrifying face with sharp fangs, and is dark and exceedingly fearsome.
Holding a dagger, a thunderbolt, a trident, and a lance,
with her entire body smeared with ashes, she has dark, curly hair standing erect.
She who causes fear to the wicked and bestows fearlessness upon her devotees—
the Supreme Goddess should always be meditated upon with a mind focused on no other.
This mantra should be recited for the subjugation of ḍākinīs, bhūtas, and enemies, and so forth.
Now, the mantra for the destruction of fever:
O fierce one with the face of Kuvera, bring joy and bliss to Nandin;
O Fever, destroy the fever, death, and terrible fear—O Fever, destroy the fever!

Bind all directions! Bind the western direction! Bind the northern direction! Cut through, 2! Saturate, 2! Split, 2! Sever, 2! Strike with the pestle, 2! With the discus of Viṣṇu! [Destroy] the fever that recurs every day, every two days, or every three days; the fever by day, the fever by night, the fever at twilight, and the sudden fever—destroy them all!

*Chedaya 2 mahāsumukhi svāhā*. This mantra is to be recited for all fevers. Having written it on a palm leaf or similar material, wherever one binds it, the fever is immediately released. Now follows the Kārtavīrya fever mantra (152a).

King Kārtavīryārjuna, the bearer of a thousand arms—by his remembrance, that which has been stolen by gods or lost is recovered, svāhā! For this [mantra], Dattātreya is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ), Kārtavīryārjuna is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of destroying fear of thieves and so forth regarding lost property. Hrāṃ Hrīṃ.

*Hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ*, with *Kārtavīrya Hari* as the seer (*ṛṣi*), is the six-limbed mantra (*ṣaḍaṅga*). The visualization (*dhyāna*): I bow to the one of great power, the manifestation of Kārtavīrya, who possesses a thousand arms, holds a bow and arrows, wears red garments, a red crown, and earrings; he is the destroyer of the fear of thieves and other evils, and the bestower of desired boons.

Now, another mantra: Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Kārtavīryārjuna, who possesses a thousand arms; by means of your great strength and valor, paralyze all thieves, delude them, and slay them! Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is Dattātreya; the meter (chandaḥ) is Anuṣṭubh; the deity (devatā) is the Great Viṣṇu, Śrī Kārtavīryārjuna.

The application [of this mantra] is for the purpose of averting fear from thieves and the like; the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is as before. The visualization (*dhyāna*): His body is measured by a single thousand-fold staff-like arm; he shines with white garlands, bows, arrows, and fierce shafts, possessing the luster of the rising sun; [he is surrounded] by cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*).
May the wise Śrī Kārtavīrya be victorious—he who is adorned with radiant earrings swinging from his two cheeks, and who has completely fulfilled all those [desires]. Now, another mantra:
"May the son of Kṛtavīrya, the king with a circle of a thousand arms, an actual incarnation of Hari, protect my lineage. Of this [mantra]:
The seer (ṛṣi) is Dattātreya; the meter (chandaḥ) is Amṛtā Gāyatrī. 1. Homage to the heart, dear to Dattātreya. 2.
Svāhā to the head, the Lord of Māhiṣmatī. 3. Vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (śikhā), pleased by sporting in the waters of the Revā. 4. [To the armor] for the subduing of the lord of the Haihayas.
O mountain-shatterer, celibate youth, you of profound sound, destroyer of all conflicts, eradicator of all fevers, crusher of ḍākinīs! Hrīṃ hrīṃ hrāṃ hyaiṃ! Come! All poison!

*Hara-hara* 4 *ravalaṃ kṣobhaya oṃ huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. For this mantra of Hanūman, Hanūtanu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Hanūmān is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of pacifying all calamities.
*Añjanāsutāya* is the heart (*hṛdaya*). *Rudramūrtaye* is the head (*śiras*). *Vāyusutāya* is the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

The armor-mantra for Agnigarbha (4), the eye-mantra for Madūta (5), and the weapon-mantra for warding off the Brahmā-weapon (6). Because he is a solitary hero, there is no need for [the usual] surrounding protections (*pariṣad*). By means of all this, one accomplishes everything.
These and other applications and mantras arise; they are not written here due to the bulk of the text. Now...

The Prāṇapratiṣṭhā Mantra. Without the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra, all other mantras are fruitless. Thus it has been said: "I shall now proclaim the procedure for the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra for the sake of attaining all accomplishments; for without it, these aforementioned ritual applications would be as useless as those devoid of life. The mantra is: ĀṂ.

Hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa hauṃ haṃsaḥ! May my vital breaths (prāṇas) be here; may my life remain established here. May all my senses—speech, mind, sight, hearing, taste, smell, and breath—having come right here, abide happily for a long time. Svāhā Haṃsaḥ! *Prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (The Consecration of Vital Breath)
For this mantra, the sages (ṛṣis) are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; the meters (chaṃdas) are Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan;
the deity (devatā) is the Life-force Power (prāṇa-śakti) who effects the creation of the entire universe; the seed-syllable (bīja) is *Āṃ*; the power (śakti) is *Kroṃ*.

Its application (viniyoga) is for the purposes of subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), paralyzing (*stambhana*), eradication (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*). Oṃ.
Pṛthivyācāya huṃ 4, to the thousand-armed weapon, phaṭ 5.

153a) Now another [mantra]: Oṃ proṃ, homage to the Blessed One Kārta-vīryārjuna! O Hayakārta-vīryārjuna, you who possess a thousand arms, a thousand eyes, and are the destroyer of a thousand wicked ones; O ocean of the feet desired by all the virtuous, bestow passion!
O Kāmasmadvasuluṃpaka, ward off these bands of thieves with your thousand hands! Bind them with your nooses in hand! Bind them! Shatter them, shatter them with your thousand goads!
Crush them, crush them with thousands of arrows risen up by your own power! Svadhā! Svāhā!
Frighten with thousands of sounds emerging from your own conch! Cut down with thousands of vajras emerging from your own hand!

Terrify what is done by others! Roar, roar! Draw forth, draw forth! Cause to tremble, cause to tremble! Confound, confound! Intoxicate, intoxicate! Drive mad, drive mad! Heat, heat! Illuminate, illuminate! Dry up, dry up! Tear asunder, tear asunder! Paralyze, paralyze! Yawn, yawn!

Yawn! Yawn! Slay! Slay! Subjugate! Subjugate! Expel! Expel! Destroy! Destroy! O Dattātreya, O most beloved of the venerable feet [of Śiva], O Śrī Kārtavīryārjuna, completely uproot, uproot those plunderers, those thieves, and their entire hordes who have come from every direction to the ocean! Huṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! The seer and other components, as well as the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga), of this [mantra] are as follows:

And the meditation (*dhyāna*) is as before. There are many mantras such as: "Oṃ bhrāṃ! May he who revolves around me protect me; may he who possesses the brilliance of lightning protect me from all sides; may he who revolves around me protect me, like an archer with his arrows, possessing the radiance of the sun. Because of the bulk of the text, we do not write them down here. Now, the mantra of Hanuman: Oṃ namo bhagavate...
To Hanumān, whose prowess is manifest, who has traversed the circle of the quarters,
who has whitened the circle of the quarters with the play of his fame, whose body is like a diamond, the incarnation of Rudra,
the burner of the city of Laṅkā, the binder of the ocean, the death-dealer to the ten-necked Rāvaṇa, the consoler of Sītā, and the son of the Wind-god and Anjanā.
Obeisance to the one born from the womb, who brings joy to Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, whose army consists of monkeys, who is Sugrīva’s consort, whose nature is fire,
wind, and space, who is the sky, and whose essence is knowledge: Aṃ Kaṃ Khaṃ Gaṃ Ghaṃ Ṅaṃ Āṃ Jñānātmane.
To the heart, *namaḥ* 1. *Oṃ*, salutation to the essence of touch, taste, form, flavor, and smell;

*iṃ caṃ chaṃ jaṃ jhaṃ ñaṃ īṃ*, to Śakti, to the head, *svāhā* 2. *Oṃ*, salutation to the essence of hearing, skin, sight, and smell; *oṃ ṭaṃ ṭhaṃ ḍaṃ ḍhaṃ ṇaṃ huṃ*, to Valā, to the crest-lock (*śikhā*), *vaṣaṭ* 3. *Oṃ*.

To the self consisting of speech, anus, feet, and genitals, *namaḥ*. *Eṃ taṃ thaṃ daṃ dhaṃ naṃ aiṃ*, to sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), to the armor (*kavaca*), *huṃ* (four times). *Oṃ paṃ phaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ āṃ*, to the self consisting of speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and procreation, *namaḥ*. *Oṃ paṃ phaṃ vaṃ bhaṃ maṃ āṃ*, to splendor (*tejas*), to the three eyes (*netratraya*), *vauṣaṭ*. *Oṃ namaḥ*.
Salutation to the Self consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), mind (*citta*), and knowledge (*jñāna*). Aṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ haṃ laṃ kṣaṃ aḥ.

*Phaṭ* six times to the weapon of valor (*vīryāyāstrāya phaṭ*). One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the navel up to the heart. (1) One should perform the placement starting from the heart up to the navel with *hrīṃ*. (2) With *kroṃ*, [one should place it] on the head.
One should place [the mantra] starting from the head down to the heart (3); with the entire [mantra], perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) (4). The Meditation (Dhyāna):

I bow to the Goddess who is red, three-eyed, and seated upon a lotus that is as crimson as the rising sun; she holds in her lotus-like hands a noose, a goad, a bow, an arrow, a trident, and a skull-cup. Having meditated thus—

Having invoked the Goddess upon the Śaktipīṭha situated in the triangle, one should worship her. One should worship with "Salutation to Brahmā, 1 Viṣṇu, 2 and Īśvara, 3" at the three corners; and with "Salutation to Sarasvatī, 1 Lakṣmī, 2 and Umā, 3" at the three corners.
Then one should worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). Outside of that, on the eight petals, are Brāhmī and the others. Outside of that are the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Having recited [the mantra] according to one's capacity, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*).
One hundred thousand recitations constitute the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). The fire-oblation (*homa*) consists of four parts in the tenth portion, performed with clarified butter.
Thus accomplished, the mantra shall yield the fruits of the six rites;
by means of this mantra, the preceptor should establish the vital breaths everywhere.
At the end of the seed-syllable (bīja), one should employ the Dūtīs of those remaining at the beginning:
first Mṛtā, then Vasvatā, followed by Jīvahā and Prāṇahā.
This [series] has its tip drawn forth; it is a woman emitting sparks.
Having accepted these as fields, they are known as the nine messengers of life.
One should take away the life-breaths of the victim who is bound by the noose, whose mind is seized by Power (Śakti),
and who is drawn in by the goad.
Having fashioned an effigy of the person to be acted upon according to a measurement of twelve finger-breadths,
he should place that insect, together with the life-essence mantra, within its heart.
At the time of midnight, when the sādhya is asleep, [one should place the deities] in his heart-lotus:
first on the petals for Vāyu, Agni, Indra, and Varuṇa, and thereafter—
Within the pericarp of the lotuses of Īśa, Rākṣasa, Śītāṃśu,
and Yama, one should contemplate the vehicles joined with swans, which have the form of bees.

One should meditate with an intellect in the form of a bee upon that thread arising from the dot at the head, which has extended its body [downward] into the lotus of the heart of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
Having dispatched the bees residing in the heart-lotus of oneself through the path of the breath,
one should bring each individual bee into the heart-lotus of the person to be acted upon.
The practitioner should place [the deity] in an effigy or within his own heart according to the ritual procedure;
then, being self-controlled, he should perform the severing of the thread with the fire-seed syllable (RAṂ).
Having attracted the bees that carry the object of accomplishment, one should then immobilize them with the earth-mantra;
in this manner, one should perform the eleven-fold repetition in all ritual acts.
The meaning of this is as follows:
having dispatched the previously mentioned thread [of the *bindu*] along with the vessels for wine and so forth, in the form of a female bee (*bhṛṅgī*).
Having drawn forth the vital breaths (prāṇas) residing in the heart of the target, one should establish them within one's own heart or in an effigy using the seed-syllable *laṃ*;
this is what is meant by "after the act of establishing. Subsequently, with the fire-seed-syllable *repha* (*ra*), one should burn [the effigy].
In this manner, for each ritual application, one draws forth the vital breaths from the heart of the target eleven times.
One should cause [the deity] to abide within one's own heart, on a pedestal, or elsewhere; this is the secret.
The wise one should employ reddish-yellow [syllables] for subjugation and attraction;
smoky-colored ones for delusion and inciting hatred; and black ones for the rite of killing.
One should meditate on them as yellow for the rite of immobilization and for the practice of drawing in the vital breaths.
One should establish the life-forces (prāṇas) drawn from the heart of the victim within one's own heart;
in rites of cruelty, their establishment is said to be within a doll (puttalī).
In that regard, one who is skillful should always, during cruel rites, visualize the life-breaths of the victim as frogs and his own [life-breaths] as serpents.

Alternatively, one skilled in ritual application and knowing the mantra should, by means of this mantra, bring [the target] under control—using the syllables of the letters beginning with *ra* (Ra) written on the petals for Vahni, Śakra, Varuṇa, Īśvara, Rākṣasa, Indu, and Pretanātha; together with the *bindu*, *anta* (Visarga), and *kṣa*, combined with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), forming a *yantra* consisting of the essence of the vital breath (*prāṇātman*), supported by the earth and filled with syllables. Thus, the knower of mantras, proficient in the practice, shall subjugate [the target].
How much more so, then, all the gods and earthly beings? This is the method: O Devadatta, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are here!
Having said "the vital breaths," one should draw the vital breaths into the doll [with the mantra]: "Yaṃ, from the self of the elements (bhūtātman), I draw [the breath] forth" (1);
"Raṃ, from the self of Vaivasvata, I draw the blood forth" (2); "Laṃ, from the self of the life-seizer (jīvahātmātman)..."
