I draw forth the flesh, 3. Vaṃ; I draw forth this for the self that takes away life, 4. Śaṃ;
I draw forth the sinew for the self of the rainy season, 5.

Ṣaṃ! To the self of the dung-heap, I draw forth the bones. 6. Saṃ! To the self of great joy, I draw forth the body hairs. 7. Haṃ! To the self of sparks, I draw forth the fat. 8. Kṣaṃ kṣaṃ! To the self of the three strikes, I draw forth all the bodily constituents. 9. Thus it should be understood in rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*).

"I subjugate, I cause hatred, I delude, I kill"—thus one should infer [the appropriate mantras]. Now, the procedure for the worship of a single deity representing all the gods is described. The instruction of the Guru has been received: *Oṃ aiṃ īṃ aṃ ūṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya viṣṇur yoniṃ kalpayatu tvaṣṭā rūpāṇi piṃśatu*. May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms. May Śata... [etc. (as per the ritual).
May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you. Śrīṃ Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ. Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya. Oṃ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ. We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ;
may he impel our intellects. Hrīṃ Hlaiṃ Hlīṃ Hlauṃ. Oṃ, we worship the three-eyed one, the fragrant...

The nourisher of growth. Like a cucumber from its stalk, may I be released from death, not from immortality. *Klīṃ sahasakalaraiṃ hklāṃ hsrauḥ*. To Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda, to the beloved of the cowherd women, *svāhā*.
Viṣṇu is praised for his heroic power, like a terrifying beast dwelling in the mountains, whose three wide strides...
In their strides they encompass all worlds.
*Glauṃha sakalaraḍaiṃhasakalaraṃḍīhasakalaraṃḍau*. May the earth be gracious to us, a secure dwelling free from arrows; grant us wide-spreading shelter. *Oṃ namaḥ*.
To the Blessed One in the form of the Boar, *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*, the Striver: grant me sovereignty over the earth, cause it to be granted;

*svāhā*. The Swan dwelling in the pure [heaven], the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ-priest dwelling on the altar, dwelling in the house, dwelling among men, dwelling in the best [place], dwelling in Truth, dwelling in the sky, born of the waters, born of the cows, born of Truth, born of the mountains—this is the Great Truth.
155b) *gaṃ kapaṭala hrīṃ sahakala hrīṃ*. We invoke you, Gaṇapati, the lord of the hosts.
We praise you, the great poet among poets, the eldest king of the Brahmins, who are themselves seekers of the sacred word (*brahman*).

Ānaḥ śṛnbhūtibhiḥ sīdaspadanam. Oṃ bhūḥ, oṃ bhuvaḥ, oṃ svaḥ, oṃ mahaḥ, oṃ janaḥ, oṃ tapaḥ, oṃ satyam. *Tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi*. Oṃ jātavedase sunavāma somaṃ arātī yato nidahāṃ vedaroṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai namaḥ.
O you who possess the blazing trident, O you who consume the evil planets, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*! Arise, O Puruṣī! Why do you sleep?
A danger has come upon me; whether it be possible or impossible, *huṃ duṃ*, O Blessed Durgā, pacify it, *svāhā*! She crosses over all difficulties as if crossing the ocean.
May Agni burn away our misfortunes. Om, may He impel our intellects. Om, the Illusion, the Light, the Essence, the Immortal, Brahman, Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ, Om!
O Supreme One, O You who speak for the sake of the disciples, Om Vyom, Vyom, Vyom! Arise, O tawny and crimson-eyed one!
[Salutation] to Yakṣa, to Kuvera, to Vaiśravaṇa, the Lord of wealth and grain.

Grant me abundance of wealth and grain; give it, cause it to be given, svāhā! *Gagalaṃ rī grīṃ*, obeisance to the Great Gaṇapati, to Gaṇapati, the most excellent, the bestower of boons, the giver of fortune. *Oṃ namaḥ śivāya*, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa. We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May I be released from death as if from a gourd from its stalk; may you bring peace to all people for the sake of swift propitiation. Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, svāhā!

156a) This great mantra is common to all the gods; it consists of the Āgamas and the Vedas. It has no seer (*ṛṣi*) or other such [limbs]. Now follows the mantra whose essence is Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
May this one, whose self is the *haṃsa*, who blazes with the splendor of the fire of time (*yāma*), and who is our servant, protect us; salutations to Brahmā, the navel of the universe.
I bow to the fierce and noble Mahāviṣṇu, who blazes with faces on all sides,
who is the terrifying Man-lion, the auspicious one, and the death of Death itself.
We worship the Three-Eyed One, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity;
may He deliver us from death as a cucumber from its stalk, [delivering us] unto immortality.
For this mantra, the sages are Vasiṣṭha; the meters are Anuṣṭubh; the deities are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
and its application is for the fulfillment of desired aims. To the fierce, heroic, three-eyed one who is the essence of the *haṃsa*, salutation to the heart.
(1) We worship the Great Viṣṇu, the fire within the waters; *svāhā* to the head. (2) Blazing with splendor, the radiant one...
To the one facing all directions, the fragrant, the increaser of nourishment—*vaṣaṭ* to the *śikhā* (tuft of hair).

May the terrifying Nṛsiṃha protect us from death; may there be auspiciousness. Like a cucumber from its stalk—*huṃ* to the *kavaca* (armor). Salutation to Brahman; may I be released from death by death—*to the three eyes*.
"Vauṣaṭ! 5 Viśvanābhi, I bow to you; protect me from the immortal weapon! Phaṭ!

6"—having become purified, one should extract this mantra of the fire-god (Havirbhuj) in reverse order from this [verse], beginning with the letter *vi* (the sky), preceded by the nasal dot (*bindu*).
One who is thus established in oneself and free from attachment should speak words that are fragrant with glory;
and having spoken of the wind and the drop, one should indeed address them again with humility and compassion.
The vital breaths arise from the sky through the upward-moving *saṃjñā* (consciousness) that has died away;
one should know the moon, which pervades the universe, as being situated in the eastern syllable and again in the sky.
Then, having extracted the *pratiṣṭhā* [tattva], one who knows the mantras should speak with that [mantra] over the threshing floor (*khala*):
"Having extracted the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by means of this [mantra], [I shall proceed] as prescribed."
This is the weapon of the Kṛtyā; by means of it, one should take away the life-breaths of the enemy through mental concentration.
Furthermore, [the breaths] move within the Suṣumṇā, rising up from the base.
The Kuṇḍalinī, having ascended into the ether, blazing like a mustard seed,
entered within his mouth and turned back the enemy.

If an enemy should enter one's own house while one is engaged in the practice of the five fires (*pañcāgnisamavāyaka*), that enemy will die within seven days; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.

Having recited the mantra over mustard seeds and kuṭu flowers, and having stirred them with that oil, one should offer them as oblations into the funeral fire at midnight while reciting the aforementioned mantras; thus, the enemy is [subjugated].
Struck by the flaming weapon of the *kṛtyā*, he dies within a fortnight;
all eight types of funeral pyre fires, along with ointments for wounds and oils, [are employed].
On the fourteenth day at midnight, one should offer oblations seven times;
the enemy dies without a doubt, struck by the blazing weapon of the *kṛtyā*.
Having fashioned an image from chaff and bones, [one should worship] half of the enemy of Śikhin (Viṣṇu).
Having established the wind [element] and having repeatedly cut the blood with *vraṇataila*,
the enemy should offer oblations into the fires for seven days with the blood of a goat.
One struck by the flaming weapon of a *kṛtyā* dies hereof, there is no doubt;
the knower of mantras, having taken sand together with unbroken rice grains, should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Once it has been accomplished, one should scatter the atoms into water as desired;
that water, consecrated with the mantra of the Fire-weapon (Āgneyāstra), quickly burns [the enemy].
The best of mantra-knowers may burn the worlds up to the seventh heaven along with their inhabitants;
having meditated upon the enemy together with his body, he shall destroy that desired foe within three days.
Having fashioned a wooden effigy (nakṣatra-vṛkṣa-prakṛti) representing that wind-spirit,
one should anoint it with pungent oil, empower it with the Kṛtyā-weapon mantra, and have a carpenter fashion it at night.
Having cut [the effigy], one who has come [to the rite] should offer it into the fire of the funeral pyre; this applies to one who has died within seven days.
The "star-tree" (nakṣatravṛkṣa) is the tree corresponding to the asterism of that person to be subdued (sādhya).
The *kāraskara* is the *uśayadhātrī*, and the *uduṃbara* is a tree; furthermore, there are the *jaṃbu*, the *khadira*, the one called *kṛṣṇa*, and those known as *vaṃśa* and *pippala*.
There were stones named Nādārohitā and Upalaśaplakṣa,
as well as trees known as Aṃbaṣṭha, Vilva, Arjuna, and Vikaṅkata.
The *vakula*, *sāvara*, *sarja*, *vañjula*, *panasa*, and *arka*; the *śamī*, *kadamba*, *āmra*, *nimba*, *madhūka*, and *ṛkṣa* trees.
Then, on the fourteenth day under the influence of Mars, at midnight,
one should carefully collect ashes produced from a funeral pyre and saturate them with buffalo ghee.
One should have forty-four pills prepared there; they should be moistened with the blood of an unaging person and empowered by the wind-god.
If one offers oblations into a fire kindled with wood from a funeral pyre, the enemy shall die;
this ritual application was taught by the sages of old on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight.
Having placed the ashes arising from the heap of Raji wood into the five products of the buffalo,
one whose face resembles the fire of cosmic dissolution at the time of meditation should boil it.
One should recite the mantra for the protection of the gods; then, one should avoid that which has been dried out.
With wood from a funeral pyre, one should offer oblations into the fire of the pyre while chanting the Durgā-gāyatrī.
Taking lāṅgalī with its roots and stalks in a red vessel,
as well as ajagandhī, cakraka, and krośanikā according to the prescribed method.
One should also recite the Markaṭī mantra ten million times according to the rule;
then, on the fourteenth day under the planet Mars, at midnight within the interior of one's house.
If one buries [it], within seven nights it will bring about the destruction of the entire family;
each single [act] results in this.
The destruction of the family.

Having taken six sets of six drops and placed them in a jar in a clean place, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times while touching it; then, one should gradually bury it in a cremation ground.
If the name of an enemy is recited during the midnight of a dark night,
all those enemies, along with their families, shall die within six months.
Where each one is deposited...
[the wind] placed previously in the four [directions], forty-four-fold; smeared with the blood of a goat... on the fourteenth day...
In the Śārddhaka [chapter].
One should offer oblations for three days into a fire of *kāraskara* wood in the wilderness;
when the enemy is overwhelmed by the flames of the *kṛtyā* weapon, he shall go to the city of Yama.
There are applications for the feet.
Now, for three days, as follows:
There, Atripīṭha and Umareśa, accompanied by Mahāsena, [bestow their grace];
then, having [overcome] the fire of the Kṛtyā weapon, one should proceed against the enemy.
When joined with the fivefold nature and endowed with the three subtle elements, they take on the forms of fire due to the specific combination of the moon, fire, and sky.
One should indeed meditate with the intellect upon the enemy as having a face like that of a crow, separated from the sun.
Seized by the upward-rising Kuṇḍalinī,
[the breath] is cast into the root-center amidst the conjunction of the five fires.
If one carries [the enemy] by way of yoga, that enemy shall fall under the power of death;
where [he is], he is overcome by splendor, like a servant deprived of his light.
The practitioner should mentally burn [the enemy], situated within the solar disc, with its rays;
the enemy will undoubtedly go swiftly to the abode of Yama.
Having immersed himself in such a solar disc, the knower of speech, being self-restrained, should meditate upon the enemy situated therein while reciting the mantra according to his ability.
Whether it be for a hundred days or fifty, the enemy shall die within seven days,
wherever the practitioner may be, provided the mantra has been properly recited with purity.
Starting from sunrise until the sun has set,
a wise person should diligently recite the mantra for seven days during that time.
An enemy afflicted by a fever caused by the combination of all three humors (sannipāta) gives up his life;
one who has mastered the mantra in a temple of Durgā shall do so after three nights, provided he avoids food.
Meditating thus, one should recite [the mantra] incessantly, visualizing the enemy struck by the fire of the Day-Armament (dināstra);
then that enemy, deluded by fever, shall meet his death.
Having first fashioned an image of the enemy born under the natal asterism out of clay, one should cast it into water and recite the mantra while stirring it about.
And within three days of ten thousand [recitations], the deluded one meets his death.
Having prepared a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in front of Durgā, the practitioner of mantra—
Having recited that over the fire at its tip according to the prescribed rite with a concentrated mind,
one who is skilled in weapons should take buffalo dung smeared with red lac.
Having fashioned an image and consecrated it with the wind-mantra,
one should again meditate upon Caṇḍikā while reciting the weapon-mantra over the enemy.
And she stood upon the chest of a buffalo, her head crushed by a spear,
dancing upon the stage of his breast, endowed with eight arms.

With cries of "Hā! Hā! by the non-existent ones, and with the sound of "Hum" by those who had offered the asuras into the fire, she was seized—she who brings about the destruction of the three worlds and is resplendent with flames of fire.
With the corners of her two eyes rolling and her sprout-like lower lip bitten,
she was equipped with a sword and shield and surrounded by young maidens.
Having repeatedly cut [the victim] in the middle of the night, one should again offer an oblation with blood;
after three days, that son shall go to the other world.
Now, for Brahmā, the Anuṣṭubh [meter].

May he who is of the nature of the *haṃsa*, who restrains and controls, and who blazes with the splendor of fire—may he, the Brahman who is the navel of the universe, protect us from death; salutations to him!
Prajāpati is the seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra]; Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandaḥ); Brahmā is the deity (devatā); its application (viniyoga) is for the attainment of wealth, sons, and so forth.
"Haṃsātmaka" (of the nature of the Swan) is the heart; "apām agneḥ" (of the waters and fire) is the head; "tejasādīpyamānaḥ" (blazing with splendor) is the crest-lock (śikhā);
"san no mṛtyostrāyatām" (may he protect us from death) is the armor (kavaca); "namo brahmaṇe" (salutation to Brahman) is the eye; "viśvanābhiḥ" (the navel of the universe).
The sixth meditation is the Astra [mantra].
[He is] like ten thousand suns, wearing red garments, with a massive body,
and holding a sacrificial ladle (sruk), a large spoon (sruva), a rosary of beads, and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
Four-faced, with a magnificent body and long, tremulous eyes, wearing matted locks, the source of the universe, and resplendent with two earrings.
It was enveloped by waves of necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and golden waistbands,
and adorned with white flowers of all seasons and ornaments of every color.
It was being served equally from all sides by the foremost lions among the divine sages,
as it uttered forth the Vedas in the various branches and divisions throughout the quarters in their proper order.
Having meditated thus, one should again recite the mantra one hundred and eight times. Now, for the worship:
after the mental worship, one should perform the external worship.

Having worshipped the pedestal (pīṭha) beginning with the support (ādhāra), and having mentally fashioned an eight-petaled lotus upon it, one should worship in the directions starting from the east with the mantra:

"Obeisance to Nityā, Śraddhā, Dhārā, Pāvanī, Yogā, Śikhā, and Dhāyinī. Then, having invoked the Deity into its pericarp and displayed the ritual gestures (mudrās), [one should worship] with the Gāyatrī.
One should offer the *argha* with both hands (1); one should offer the *pādya* (2);
[one should offer] the water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the *hiraṇya* mantra (3); [one should offer] the *madhuparka* with the root mantra (4), [reciting] "dhruvās tvā... (5).
5. Bathing with [the mantra] "yuvastrāṇi"; 6. A garment with "haṃsa dṛṣat"; 7. A sacred thread (yajñopavīta) with the Vyāhṛtis;
8. Ornaments with [the mantra] "bhūṣaṇāni"; 9. Fragrance and flowers with "gandhadvāreṇa"; 10. One should perform the libation (sruti) with the Puruṣasūkta.
On the petals [one worships]: 1. Godāya, 2. Pramodāya, 3. Haṃsāya, 4. Sāmagāya, 5. Satyalakṣaṇāya.

One should worship with "Obeisance to Hiraṇyagarbha" (6) and "Obeisance to Viśvanābhi" (7). On those very petals, one should worship with "Obeisance to Śraddhā" (1), "Lakṣmī" (2), "Dhṛti" (3), "Tuṣṭi" (4), "Puṣṭi" (5), "Medhā" (6), "Sarasvatī" (7), and "Kriyā" (8). Again, on those same [petals]: "To Bhṛgu" (1), "Pulastya" (2), "Pulah" (3), and "Kratu" (4).

"Salutation to Aṅgiras (5), to Marīci (6), to Dakṣa (7), to Atri (8) — salutation. First, "Salutation to Vasiṣṭha. In this manner, [the deities] ending with the one holding a water-pot, an axe, a book, the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*), and the earth (*pṛthivī*) which is unbroken, continue until the end. Thus is the vow for householders who desire dharma, wealth, and pleasure. Some [say]:

The mantras herein have been made explicit. We know others besides these, but we do not write them down due to a lack of inclination. Hereafter, the true nature of the *praṇava* for one seeking liberation is described. It is as follows:
having risen from his bed and sipped water, he should, with a serene countenance in the morning, [place] his own guru upon his head.

One should contemplate with devotion the auspicious Śiva, who bestows knowledge and whose matted locks are adorned with the Jñānamudrā. Having established oneself in the Praṇava from the navel upward, one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra,
and Īśvara with offerings consisting of the twelve [syllables] dripping with nectar.
Having unified [the mind] for the purpose of uttering the *praṇava*, one should contemplate the supreme, consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*),
which is full of the bliss of self-existence (*svātantryānanda*) and beautiful with the bliss of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*).
Non-dual, supreme radiance, eternally stainless within this.

Having recited thus, and having performed the *nyāsa* of the limbs while contemplating the essential nature of all actions performed during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, under the authority of the bodily *dharma* prior to this moment— beginning with *oṃ*— one should conclude the day’s worship. Then, having gone outside and performed the necessary duties, one should bathe.

"O Gaṅgā, O beautiful one, I invoke you from the solar disc as the Vaiṣṇava-tīrtha for the purpose of bathing here. Come, O Gaṅgā; salutations to you who are endowed with all holy sites (tīrthas); salutations. While reciting this, having invoked her and worshipped her in the water—visualizing her as the form of consciousness (cid-rūpa), two-armed, adorned with pure garments and other ornaments—[one should proceed].

Having remembered the water as being completely full, one should immerse oneself while reciting "Destroy, destroy all my sins" (*saṃharasaṃhara*), and having repeated the root mantra as many times as possible, one should rise, perform the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, and sprinkle oneself with the water. Then, having come to the bank, put on a garment, sipped water (*ācamana*), performed six rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) with the syllable *praṇava* (Om), and [performed] the purification of speech and so forth...

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), sprinkled oneself with water consecrated by the *praṇava*, offered the *argha* with the *praṇava*, and offered libations (*tarpaṇa*), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Having drunk that consecrated water three times and dismissed the sacred site (*tīrtha*), one should go to the place of recitation. Having performed the washing of the feet, one should enter within.

Having performed the rites of drying and so forth by means of the three syllables beginning with *a*, one should visualize a lotus upon a pure spot accompanied by the *praṇava*-yantra; likewise, having contemplated one's own seat for both [deities] as being similarly endowed with the *praṇava*-yantra, and having visualized the syllables and the lotus, one should take water with the right hand and cover it with the left while reciting the *praṇava*.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times and sprinkled [water] over oneself, one should sit while uttering "So'ham" and pay homage to the Guru and others; for it is thus:
from the lineage succession beginning with Paramaśiva down to the lotus feet of one's own Guru.

Saying "I bow," one should bow with the head and recite: *Oṃ gurubhyo namaḥ*, *Oṃ gaṇapataye*, *Oṃ durgāyai*, *Oṃ kṣaṃ kṣetrapālāya*, *Oṃ sarasvatyai*, *Oṃ paramātmane namaḥ*. Having thus consecrated the left and right shoulders, as well as the left and right sides, and the front and the heart, one becomes the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) of the *praṇava*.
The Seer (ṛṣi) is either the Supreme Self (paramātman) or the deity; the syllable Ā is the seed (bīja); the syllable OṂ is the power (śakti); the syllable Ma is the field (kṣetra);
the Praṇava is the designator (vācaka); Brahman is the designated (vācya); and its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of liberation (mokṣa).
The Praṇava is the son of Brahmā, belonging to the lineage of Laugākṣi. The inner controller (antaryāmī) of the letter A is the Seer Brahmā, or else the Seer is Gāyatrī.
The meter is Gāyatrī (2); the deity is Brahmā (3); the element is Earth (4); the nature is the Ṛgveda (5);

the world is Bhūrloka (6); the sacred field is the Gārhapatya fire (7); the accent is Udātta (8); the location is the navel (9); the quality is Rajas (10); the ritual extraction is the morning libation (Prātaḥsavana) (11);
the Vyahṛti is Bhūḥ (12); the function is Prāṇa (13); the channel is the Iḍā (14); and the state is the waking state (Jāgrat) (15).
The Universal Puruṣa (16), yellow in color (17), the act of creation (18); its application is for the purpose of creation.
Of the syllable *Oṃ*: 1. the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Brahmā, Atri, Vāyu, or Viṣṇu; 2. the meter (*chaṃdaḥ*) is Triṣṭubh; 3. the deity (*devatā*) is Viṣṇu; 4.

the presiding divinity (*adhidaivata*) is Rudra; 5. the principle (*tatva*) is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), whose nature is the Yajurveda; 6. the world is Bhūḥ; 7. the field (*kṣetra*) is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; 8. the accent is the Anudātta (low tone); 9. the location is the heart; [and its quality is] Sattva.

10. Guṇa; 11. Mādhyandina-savana; 12. Bhūva-vyāhṛti; 13. Aṣāṃvṛtti; 14. Piṅgalā-nāḍī; 15. Svapna-avasthā (dream state); 16. Taijasa-puruṣa (the luminous person); 17. Vidvid-varṇa (the letter 'vi'); 18. Sthiti-kriyā (the act of maintenance); 19.
Viniyoga for the purpose of maintenance. For the syllable *Makāra*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Vāmadeva, Rudra, or Sūrya.
The Jagatī meter (2), Īśvara as the deity (3), Rudra as the presiding divinity (4), the element of space (5),
the nature of the Sāmaveda (6), the heavenly world (7), the Āhavanīya sacrificial fire as the field (8), the circumflex accent (svarita) as the tone (9),
the space between the eyebrows as the location (10), the quality of darkness (tamas) (11), the third pressing of the soma (12), and the Kharvī Vyāhṛti (13).
The function of Vyāna (14), the Suṣumnā channel (15), the state of deep sleep (16),
the Prājña Puruṣa (17), the white color (18), the act of withdrawal (19), and its application for the purpose of dissolution (20).

For the half-mātrā: the Saṃvartaka fire is the seer (ṛṣi), Virāṭ is the metre (chandas), Puruṣa is the presiding deity (adhidevatā), the Maruts are the secondary deity (adhidaivata), the world of Soma is the principle (tattva), the nature of the Atharvaveda is its form, the color is white, the state is the fourth (turīya), and its application (viniyoga) is for the sake of the Lord of Prāṇa within the individual soul (jīva). Having thus recollected this, one then [proceeds] with the mantra for the purification of the fingers.

Having placed [the seed-syllables] upon the fingers of both hands simultaneously according to the sequence of instruction—starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger—and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) by extending [the hands] from the elbows to the tips of the fingers, one should establish the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in the cardinal directions and the threefold enclosure (*prākāratraya*) that rests upon them. Thus: *Oṃ Aṃ Oṃ Namaḥ* (1) *Uṃ*.

"Ūṃ Ūṃ Namaḥ" (twice); "Oṃ Maṃ Oṃ Namaḥ" (thrice). Having thus pervaded [the body] from the feet to the head—visualizing the Virāṭ, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Jñānātmaka, which consist of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as dissolved into the fire—one should recite the Praṇava for the withdrawal into the Self that identifies with that [fire], which is of the nature of consciousness. By this very recitation...
The attainment of knowledge occurs. If one wishes to perform external worship, then one should do so in this manner.

For the *praṇava*: Prajāpati is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the divine *gāyatrī* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the deity (*devatā*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of knowledge. Aṃ Oṃ Āṃ, salutation to the heart (1). Iṃ Ṛṃ Iṃ, [salutation] to the head (2).
Uṃ Ūṃ Ṛṃ, *vaṣaṭ* to the tuft of hair (*śikhā*) (3). Eṃ Oṃ Aiṃ, *huṃ* to the armor (*kavaca*) (4). Uṃ Ūṃ Aṃ, [salutation to the eyes]. (5)

*Vauṣaṭ* to the two eyes; *A-uṃ-aḥ* to the weapon, *phaṭ*. Or [one may use] the six *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *oṃ bhūḥ*. Meditation (*dhyāna*): [One should meditate upon] Viṣṇu, adorned with a radiant crown, armlets, bracelets, a mace, a sacred thread, and a series of necklaces reaching to his waist; possessing a jewel upon his chest and great crocodile-shaped earrings.

I bow to Him who is adorned with the foremost ornaments, whose hands hold a discus, a conch, and a lotus, who shines with the luster of yellow silk, whose radiance is like the rising sun, and who is seated upon a lotus.

Having meditated thus, one should invoke the deity as oneself upon a seat (pīṭha) endowed with powers such as Vimalā and the rest, and worship it with the realization of the identity of the self and the seed-syllable.
One should dissolve the qualities beginning with smell, which consist of earth and the other elements, into that [deity] by means of the consciousness of reabsorption.

The first enclosure consists of the limbs: "Salutation to Vāsudeva," "to Saṃkarṣaṇa," "to Pradyumna," and "to Aniruddha"—thus in the cardinal directions. [The deities are] like crystal, gold, and the full moon.

They should be meditated upon as having blue luster, four arms, and holding a conch, discus, mace, and lotus; they wear crowns and armlets, and are clad in yellow garments. [The mantras] "Oṃ, obeisance to Śānti," "Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī," "Oṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī," and "Oṃ, obeisance to Rati" are to be placed in the corners. Then the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be worshipped. All of these have arisen from that very source and reside therein.

One should remember that [the deities] have entered; having remembered this, one should dissolve them into oneself. Thus, the act of worship should be performed with a single-pointed mind. One hundred thousand recitations constitute the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite). An oblation (*homa*) consisting of ten parts of milk-rice mixed with ghee should be performed. Having thus meditated upon Viṣṇu as being of the nature of one's own self, one should worship Him. This [teaching] imparts knowledge by which the attainment of supreme bliss occurs.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of Various Mantras," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhī.
Now we shall write the Āgneya weapon (mantra):
*ragnistyatāridudhuṃ siṃdhavenāsvāvinirgāduniṣadaripaṇaḥ sadaverihādanito yadatī rāmamaṃsomavāsusedavetajāraṃ*. The seer of this Āgneya weapon is Mārīca; its metre is Triṣṭubh.
The meter is *chaṃdas*, the deity is Agni Jātavedas, and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of crushing enemies. The six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) is as follows: 1.

*Ragnistanādiridhuṃ sidhane jñānātmane hṛdayāya namaḥ* (To the Knower of the Self, whose heart is the source of the flames of fire, obeisance to the Heart). 2. *Nāśvāvinirgādu śaktyai śirase svāhā* (To the Power that issues forth from the non-horse [the wind], svāhā to the Head). 3. *Niṣadaripanaḥ valāyai śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (To the strength of the one who destroys the enemy, vaṣaṭ to the Crest-lock). 4. *Sadavetihādani...* (To the one who consumes through the eternal truth... [The fourth limb, the Armor, is implied].

Vauṣaṭ to the three eyes for splendor (tejasa). Huṃ to the armor (kavaca) for sovereignty (aiśvarya), [the mantra] *toyatī rāmamasoma*. Phaṭ to the weapon (astra) for valor (vīrya), [the mantra] *navāvasusedavetajāraṃ*. [The assignment of mantras] is to the thumbs, fingers, shins, beautiful knees, and the pair of thighs.
161b) Now,
[the channels] are in the head, the navel, the heart, the two breasts,
the two sides, the back, between the shoulders, at the base of the arms, and in the arms.
It is provoked in the forearms, at the wrists and hands,
in the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears, and in the temples, the crown of the head, and the skull.
The wise one should gradually arrange the syllables arising from the *astra* mantra.
Likewise, [one should place them] on the crest-lock, forehead, eyes, ears, lips, and tongue;
as well as on the throat, arms, heart, flanks, waist, private parts, thighs, and knees.
The wise practitioner should assign the words of this mantra to the shanks and the feet;
the visualization for its application will become clear through the actual practice.
As before, there should be the recitation and the satiation; one should offer oblations according to the previous number.
For its accomplishment, one should offer cooked *caru* made from the five products of the cow.
The number of recitations is one thousand, and the fire-oblation (homa) is one-tenth of that;
one should perform the worship as before, [worshipping] the Śaktis in reverse order.
In all cases, the instructor should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī twice its usual number;
however, for a rite of a cruel nature, he should perform it according to the procedure of reverse order.
The rites of pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika) should be performed in the forward order;
at the time of the ritual application, one should recite the eight bases in the reverse order.
This mantra becomes perfected subsequently through this procedure:
the five-syllabled foot beginning with "gna" is to be known as consisting of the organs of knowledge.
The first [seed-syllable] beginning with *dhva* is remembered as having five phonemes and consisting of the nature of the organs of action (*karmendriya*).
The third, beginning with *svā*, has five phonemes and consists of the nature of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*).
The first [pāda] consists of seven syllables, followed by a second of eight syllables;
the fifth pāda, beginning with 'da', is proclaimed to have the form of a wave (urmi).
The six-syllable [mantra] beginning with *varṇa* is said to have six hairs;
its first syllable is the fifth letter, which is said to consist of the sixth and so forth.
The eighth syllable, beginning with the letter *sa* (suvarṇa) and consisting of five phonemes (*pañcārṇa*), is of the nature of speech;
thus, through union with the principles (*tattva-samāyoga*), the attainment of the quarters (*pāda-labdhi*) is proclaimed.
From each respective syllable of the mantra, so many fire-deities arise;
they are the primary forms and images, radiant with the splendor of their own respective colors.
With blazing faces like those of Keśava, possessing terrifying fangs and fearsome forms,
these deities born from the senses were impelled toward the upward gaze.
The deities are said to have animal faces and to belong to the faction of spirits;
born from the feet and the soles of the Creator, they do not adorn either [the two].
Those born from waves have upward faces, while those born from hair have faces turned sideways;
all these women born from the waters are recorded as being of neuter gender.
The color-deities (varṇadevatās) are considered to face downward, sideways, or upward;
they face toward [the practitioner] in auspicious rites, while facing away in other rituals.
Deities with blazing faces arose, facing him;
by them, through the mantra, he would consume the kingdom along with its mountains and forests.
A wise person should employ a missile under a human asterism;
one should discharge it under the Asura asterisms and withdraw it under the divine asterisms.
The three [asterisms] beginning with Pūrva-phalgunī, followed by Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, and Rohiṇī—
these the wise call the asterisms belonging to human beings.
Jyeṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Mūla, Dhaniṣṭhā, Āśleṣā, Kṛttikā, Citrā, and Viśākhā are the deities of the syllables of the stars.
Aśvinī, Revatī, Puṣya, Svātī, Hasta, Punarvasu,
Anurādhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Śravaṇa are the asterisms presided over by deities.

One should initiate an attack on the Nandā days; one should discharge weapons on the Sūriktā days; one should perform the seizing of cattle on the Bhadrā days; and on the Jayā days, it is most excellent for the conquest of enemies.
O Lord of the day of Mars, one should ward off the commencement [of a rite] on that day;
or the withdrawal [of the rite] should take place on the day of Jupiter or Venus.
The wise one should discharge the torrential stream of weapons against those who are steadfast, and withdraw the weapons when both sides are in danger.
One should discharge the weapon during the dark fortnight with the moon [waxing],
and during the bright fortnight, one should gradually withdraw the weapon back into oneself.
The wise one should perform the emanation and reabsorption of the sun during both fortnights.
Facing the west, one should perform all rites everywhere;
[one should place] all the syllables of the target, together with the ritual action, upon the tree of the lunar mansion.

In that case, the mantra practitioner, using a fire kindled [for the rite], should offer oblations into the blazing fire with the syllables of the mantra, numbering as many times as there are letters in the mantra; thus he shall cause the death of his own life-force.
Beginning from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
[one should avoid] the scent of thorn-apple, poisonous trees, and the wind blowing from the vicinity of the akṣa tree.
Having become self-restrained, one should offer into the fire a thousand individual leaves smeared with mustard oil; thus one shall go from an enemy's city to one's own city.
The *viṣavṛkṣa* is the *kāraskara*; the *akṣavṛkṣa* is the *vibhītaka*. Regarding the term *rājīrāī*:
one should offer oblations for seven nights with white mustard seeds (*siddhārtha*), oil, and red substances, using black pepper (*marīca*) at the time of the *viṣṭikāla*, while reciting this mantra.
The enemy is subdued by fever due to the destruction of his own sin;
the white mustard seeds are successful during the rainy season and at the time of the Bhadrā constellation.
Having written the name of the enemy on a palm leaf according to the prescribed rite,
and having encircled it with the Fire-weapon mantra (Āgneyāstra), one should place it within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
If one performs the oblation with black pepper while enraged, the [target] becomes afflicted by fever.

Having written the name of the enemy surrounded by the *āgneyāstra* mantra on a palm leaf, one should bury it in the middle of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), place [the fire] upon it, and perform the oblation; this is the meaning. Then, taking that [leaf], if one throws it into cool water, he will become submissive.
Having ground the seeds of *yāmārgava* together with black pepper and honey,
one should then throw them into water containing an excessive amount of salt and boil them.
With images of bears and wolves mixed with salt,
one should place a small amount upon the heart, the mouth, and the nose.

With a ladle shaped like a blue lotus, one should take the salt-water boiled from the tree corresponding to the victim's name and birth-star (nakṣatra). While reciting the fire-weapon mantra (*āgneyāstra*), he becomes afflicted with fever within a short time.
Reciting the fire mantra, one should pour a little water at a time onto the effigy at its heart and other parts.

Having thrown *aṃbhasila* into boiling water, one shall slay the enemy without effort. [The term] *aṃbhasila* refers to salt-water. At night, having heated an image of the enemy with hot, pungent oil and consecrated it with mantras, one should heat it in a kindled fire while reciting the mantra in reverse order (*pratiloma*).
One is afflicted by fever immediately; death will occur for him within three days.
With sharp oil and mustard oil,
and with sea salt mixed with asafoetida, poison, and cumin,
a doll fashioned from the body of the victim's birth-star is boiled.
Having poured water face-downward with a stick,
desiring to strike the head of the poison-tree, one should recite the Astra mantra in reverse order while striking that head.
Within seven days, the enemy, deluded by fever,
shall meet his death when sea salt is mixed into water from the ocean.
The fire was swallowed by the king of serpents from the chariot of the Sun;
that poison was neutralized by the oil for wounds, and it was scorched by the rays of the sun.
Having visualized one's own enemy with his face turned downward, one should offer libations with the water previously mentioned while gazing at the sun; thus the enemy will become dear to death.
Having meditated upon the terrifying Durgā, who bears a pestle and a trident,
[one should offer] a buffalo [image] with sprouts from poisonous trees heated in ghee.
Having offered oblations, the knower of mantras instantly causes the enemy's army to vanish.
Having meditated upon the goddess previously described with four *kāraskara* fruits and four black peppers, [he should perform the rite].
One should offer oblations for three days with the blood of a goat;
this will effect the eradication of the enemy's army—of this there is no doubt.
Having meditated upon the goddess Agniśūlakikā, blazing like the fire of universal destruction,
one should [perform the rite] with seeds of thorn-apple (dhattūra) soaked in mustard oil.
Having offered oblations, he should delude his enemies with red pepper or mustard seeds;
he should meditate upon Durgā, who resembles black collyrium and holds a trident and a sword.
Having offered oblations with seeds produced from the *nakṣatra* tree or those derived from the *dhattūra*,
or with black pepper or mustard seeds, one shall burn up one's enemies.
One should meditate upon Durgā, who resembles black collyrium and holds a trident and a sword,
[and who is smeared] with wounds produced from the Nakṣatra tree and with oil derived from the Vraṇakṛt tree.

One should offer oblations with *samidh* twigs of the *dhanyā* tree for one month to cause wounds to enemies; [using] oil of *bhallātaka* and oil of *siṃha*. [One sees] a woman mounted upon a lion, running, chasing after the enemy.
Arrows released from the bow, their tips aglow with flames of fire.
While remembering Durgā as she releases [the poison], one should visualize her holding a trident and a sword;
one should offer libations with water mixed with *ullava* and contemplate her as having a mace in her hand that destroys even the most formidable diseases.

One should daily offer oblations of parched grain soaked in buffalo ghee, along with excellent fuel-sticks of *vibhītaka*; or else, by using *kodrava* grains, the army of the enemy shall be eradicated.
One who knows the mantras should, for seven nights, perform oblations at night into a fire kindled with the wood of the *sādhya* tree while afflicted; thus he shall subjugate kings.
One should meditate upon Durgā as she holds a noose and a goad, red in color, and all-pervading.
If a practitioner of mantra offers oblations at night with blossoming *phalinī* flowers sprinkled with sandalwood water, the entire world shall come under his control.
Phalinī is priyaṅgu.
Having visualized Goddess Sindhudurgā— who resembles the autumnal moon, from whom supreme nectar flows, and who holds a noose and a goad— one should [worship] her with the best of sacrificial fuel.
One should offer oblations with *tasara* grass sprinkled with honey for the attainment of rain [to the goddess] who holds a skull,
a trident, a noose, and a goad in her hands.
One should meditate upon Durgā as being like a hibiscus flower;
having offered oblations of salt and *puṇḍarīka* flowers mixed with the three sweets.
One who knows the mantras will undoubtedly attract those who are drawn [to him] and those who remain on the ground.

The "three sweets" (*madhuratraya*) consist of ghee, sugar, and honey. This [mantra] is extremely difficult to master; it should be recited [with care]. The six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) end with *vīriṇāṃ* in three [sections], and the limbs beginning with *durvāṇāṃ tāpya* are proclaimed as belonging to Durgā.
She who begins with "viśva" and ends with the letter "a" is proclaimed as Viśvadurgā;
she who begins with "siṃdhvī" and ends with the letter "ta" is proclaimed as Sindhudurgā.
She who desires fire and other such things is proclaimed as Agni-Durgā;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the courtyard, one should worship her with fragrant flowers and other offerings.
One should worship the Goddess daily by the very path previously described;
"Atiṣat" is the name of Durgā’s weapon, consisting of syllables.
"O Agni!"—this is the Agnidurgā weapon.
One should offer a bali-oblation to the three [deities] at night; it bestows all accomplishments upon the four.
Having performed this, one wards off the assault of diseases and malevolent spirits, and causes those who are terrified to flee.
Having worshipped the fire as prescribed with fragrant and captivating flowers,
the practitioner, standing before it with a focused mind, should recite the mantra.
This recitation shall bring about all accomplishments; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
One facing west should offer oblations with salt sprinkled with sweet substances.
By means of the number of syllables in the mantra, the practitioner of mantras shall bring his enemies under his own control.
Having washed the śāli rice and purified it, he should prepare the clean grains.
Having recited the mantra over the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
the wise practitioner should again cook the sacrificial oblation (caru) in the consecrated fire while continuing to recite the mantra.
Having worshipped the Goddess as before, one of clear intellect should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee with the *ruṇāna* mantra into the fire.
Having performed the pouring of the remnants into the vessel, he should have the person to be treated consume it;
he should bury the remaining food at the door and the poured-out residue within the courtyard.
Malevolent spells, diseases, and disturbances caused by spirits and other such calamities are pacified;
furthermore, one should consume the life-force of spells produced by others through this ritual bath.
With rice, oblation, milk, the best fuel-sticks of milky trees,
and clarified butter mixed with the three sweets— one should perform these separately one thousand times each.

One should perform oblations; he will certainly become a ground for accomplishments and a successful practitioner, when the sun is situated in the sign of Aries on a day appropriate for the mantra-knowledge.
In a river flowing toward the ocean, constantly in the water of lotuses,
having lifted his feet and cleared away the sand, he should dry them thoroughly.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) over the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should fry [the materials] with a ladle made from the wood of the Brahma-tree (palāśa) over the consecrated sacrificial fire, while reciting the mantra for the sake of accomplishment.
When the sun is situated in Leo, Aries, or Sagittarius, during the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) of the dark fortnight,
and when the asterisms are Viśākhā, Kṛttikā, Mūla, Hasta, Uttarā-phalgunī, or Maghā;
A wise person should perform the laying of the sand on the Rohiṇī or Śravaṇa nakṣatras, or on a Saturday or Tuesday; avoiding other days, he should carry out the rite.
For the protection of houses, villages, and kingdoms, auspicious sands—
measured by a *prastha*, an *āḍhaka*, or a *ghaṭa*— should be placed in pits located in the center and other parts of these areas.
Having recited the mantra, the preceptor should cast nine [offerings] into them and worship them in sequence:
beginning with the central deity, the goddesses, and the weapons, ending with the skull-cups.
Having worshipped the discus, conch, sword, shield, arrow, bow, and trident with the Astra-mantra, one should offer the bali-oblation at the conclusion of the worship.
One should offer oblations to the constellations, planets, zodiac signs, and the world-protectors;
wherever one protects by performing these rites, there prosperity increases.
Minor planets, great diseases, thieves, spirits, and reptiles—
all these go to destruction by this rite; there is no doubt about this.
Thus, there are many such varieties. Now follows the *dināstra* (the weapon of the day).
Agni crosses over all difficulties like a ship across the ocean; he burns away the enemies who offer no Soma to Jātavedas.
May the Giver of Wealth carry us safely across. The Ṛṣi and other details are as previously stated.
"Agni, the destroyer of the enemy"—to the heart, *namaḥ*. 1.
*Vicenaśvānirgādurīṃ*, svāhā to the head (2); *tiṣaripaṇaḥ sarūṃ*, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock (3);
*daveti hādaniraiṃ*, huṃ to the armor (4); *toyatī rāmamasorauṃ*, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes (5);
*mamā āsunase vṛvetajāraḥ*, phaṭ to the weapon (6). The meditation (*dhyāna*) shall be stated hereafter at the time of practical application.
It comes to be.
The wise man should contemplate the enemy situated within the orb of the sun as having a face like honey and removing poison, held from its base to its tip by the Kundalini.
When one casts [the breath] into the mūlādhāra, where the fire of Time (Kālāgnirudra) instantly blazes forth, the enemy, seized by the flames of that day, gives up his life-breaths.
The enemy, who has risen from the *mūlādhāra* like the fire of time (*kālapāvaka*) and reached the *svādhiṣṭhāna* with limbs increased by the rays of the sun,
has his body consumed by the fire of the five vital winds (*pañcavāyu*) perfected through the *ādhāra*.
Meditating thus, one should mutter the mantra; immediately he shall become the beloved of Fever.

The self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the region above the *mūlādhāra*. The five winds are *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth. By means of the fire—the fire rising from the *mūlādhāra*—the enemy residing in the *maṇipūra* has his body burnt by that fire.
Meditating thus, he should recite the *dināstra* mantra; he shall fall under the power of death.
Located in Maṇipūra, in the upper portion above Svādhiṣṭhāna,
the enemy situated in Anāhata is utterly consumed by the fire previously described— that is, by the mantra-enemy.
Bound swiftly with a noose, one is led away by the servants of Yama.
Anāhata is the location of the wind above the navel.
One who has reached the station of purification and is tormented by the river of enmity and other passions is said to be head-downward; such a person will quickly become lifeless within three days.
The station of purification is the region above the previously mentioned station of wind.
Standing in water reaching up to the navel and meditating on the orb of the Sun,
one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times while visualizing the enemy with all his limbs consumed by fire.
If one recites [the mantra] for less than seven days, he goes to the realm of Yama;
beginning from the first day (Āravāra) up to the seventh day (Saptāra), one should recite the mantra.
From sunrise until sunset,
the enemy afflicted by *sannipāta* fever shall fall under the grasp of Yama.
On Saturday,
one should burn the enemy placed within the command by means of the fire of the weapon-mantra through meditative concentration;
abandoning son, friend, wife, and others, he should seek death.
Regarding the word "ājñāyām" (in the command), it refers to the division from the station of purity.
Having stayed for three nights in the abode of Durgā, the practitioner of mantra should abstain from food.
Contemplating the enemy whose body is pierced by the day of the week, one should recite this mantra; the enemy, afflicted by fever, shall go to his death.
Having touched the image of Durgā, reciting the mantra while keeping it in mind for three days,
one [sees] one's own enemy impaled on a trident and consumed by the fire of the "Day-Armament" (dināstra).
Afflicted by a great fever, he becomes a guest of Yama;
his enemy, having entered the solar orb, is bitten there by serpents.
Meditating on him whose entire body is scorched by the fire of poison, one should satisfy him with warm water;
then the goddess Yamavallabhā will appear.
Having visualized the enemy as one whose body is seized by a flame issuing from the solar disc,
one should recite the mantra; thus, that person plays in the presence of Yama.

Having perceived one's own enemy situated within the solar orb conjoined with a planet and pierced by arrows consisting of mantras, the knower of weapons should recite [the mantra] ten thousand times.
The messenger of Yama does not go swiftly to the abode of Yama with an enemy who is seized by Rahu while under the influence of the planets.
Resembling the fire of universal dissolution, like another Night of Time (Kālarātri),
the Goddess sits upon the shoulders of a lion, bearing a trident and a noose.
He saw her standing beneath the solar disc, burning her enemies with disheveled bodies by means of sparks issuing from her three red eyes.
With prominent fangs and lower lip, her face terrifying with dancing eyebrows,
she threatens her own enemy with a finger in her fearsome form.
Illuminating the quarters of the sky with a mass of light from her fangs,
she was terrifying as she tore open the chest of her enemy with her trident.
One should recite the mantra for three days and destroy one's own enemy;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), [one should visualize the goddess] possessing a radiance equal to the fire of universal destruction.
Wearing red garments, wrathful, and endowed with three red eyes,
she is mounted upon a lion, charging and pursuing her enemies.

Having severed that head with a sword, the practitioner of mantras, abstaining from food for three days, should meditate upon Durgā and recite her mantra as it instantly ascends to the expanse of the sky.
By this very procedure, even an enemy shall become dear as death;
one should perform these rites during both the days and the nights.
Having constructed a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), he should bury a buffalo— the seed-mantra of the west-facing liṅga— before it, upon its head.
When that fire has been properly kindled, the supreme instructor,
known as the practitioner, [should offer oblations] accompanied by the name of the mantra and the name of the one to be accomplished.
Having visualized the Goddess within the solar orb, one should offer a thousand oblations of excellent *kāraskara* fuel-sticks sprinkled with goat’s blood.
Terrible as the fire of universal dissolution, adorned with thirty-two arms,
and equipped with uplifted weapons, she dances upon the head of a lion.
She had large fangs and was most terrifying, with blazing hair directed upward;
her mouth was filled with red flesh and food, and the tips of her rolling eyes were agitated.
By this rite, the enemy, tormented by a great fever,
abandons his own body along with his sons, friends, and wife.
Having suspended the serpent above the water with mantras,
the practitioner [should visualize] Durgā, who resembles a thousand suns, situated within the solar disc.
She who has a thousand hands and feet, a thousand eyes, heads, and faces;
whose limbs are bound by a thousand serpents; and who terrifies the three worlds.
Meditating with this [mantra], one should satisfy the serpents with water mixed with milk;
thus, even an enemy bound by the noose of Time shall be released from life.
Resembling ten thousand midday suns, she was not an elephant but like Narasimha;
she sat upon a terrible lion, her appearance being most fearsome.
Meditating on Hitā as impaled upon a trident, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
for three days, one should offer libations of water mixed with milk into the mouth of a serpent.
One shall go to the realm of Yama; there is no doubt in this regarding the gift [of an image] made of wood or stone, once it has been installed and consecrated with the wind-mantra.
Then, having cast her into the water according to the ritual procedure during a period of despondency,
she appeared like the sun and moon, bearing a sword and a shield.
Seated upon a lion, she is filled with hundreds of sparks issuing from the meeting of her three eyes; richly adorned with serpents as ornaments, she strikes terror into the three worlds.
Meditating on the reality of the sword as being bestowed [upon him], one should recite the mantra ten million times;
by this procedure, the enemy becomes seized by death.
Having prepared an excellent triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the temple of Durgā,
he offered the consecrated Mahiṣī into the blazing fire there.
Having repeatedly cut up a doll smeared with the blood of a goat and empowered by the wind-mantra, one should offer it as an oblation at night while it is still possessed of that goat's blood.
Having meditated upon Durgā, dancing in the midst of Mahiṣa’s chest,
of terrible appearance as she pierces Mahiṣa’s body with her trident;
She who terrifies the gods served by her with her loud, boisterous laughter;
she who resembles the fire of universal destruction; and she who is endowed with three wandering eyes.
With her lower lip bitten, possessing fangs and a terrifying lotus-face,
she is equipped with a sword and shield, and is surrounded by a multitude of maidens.
By this method, the enemy goes to the presence of Yama;
this "weapon of the day" has been described as the cause for the subjugation of enemies.
Now, the Kṛtyā-weapon:
*raṃ daṣada ripanaḥ sada vetihādaniyataḥ yato yatī rāmam asedhavāna su davedravetajāgni stanāri dudhuṃ sindavenākhā vinirgādu araṃ*. This is the sequence.
The six limbs. Now, the ritual application:
the best of mantra-knowers should perform the applications as enjoined by the *Astramantra*.
One should [visualize] the Goddess Kuṇḍalinī, who has the form of a serpent, risen from the *ādhāra* (the foundational center).
Then, through the path of the aperture of the *suṣumṇā*, she reached the region of space;
having seized her enemy with her mouth, she returned toward her own home.
Having visualized [the enemy] as blazing, ignited by tongues of fire, one should recite the mantra;
within seven days, the deluded enemy meets with death.

On a Tuesday, one should offer a *kuḍava* measure of red mustard oil and white mustard seeds, consecrated with mantras, into the funeral fire; within merely half a month, [the result] will be achieved.
Burnt by the flame of the *kṛtyā* weapon, the enemy shall go to the city of Yama.
On the fourteenth day at midnight, the practitioner [should take] eight bones from a funeral pyre.
One should smear [the offerings] with wound-oil and offer them into the funeral fire;
by this rite, the cowardly enemy meets his death.
The performer of the rite should establish an effigy made from the bones of chaff, drenched in oil from a wound of an enemy, and offer it as a sacrifice at night while it is still possessed of life.
Having repeatedly cut [the enemy] with a saw, the foe dies within seven days;
having touched the ashes from a cremation ground, one should recite the mantra while facing the enemy at night.
One should scatter water boiled with the Kṛtyā-weapon mantra into a pond or similar body of water;
then, when this [water] is drunk, it swiftly destroys all people.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take the ashes of a deceased person,
mix them with buffalo ghee, and consecrate them by reciting the mantra as many times as there are syllables in it.
These consecrated pills, having been properly empowered by the recitation of mantras and the breath,
one of firm mind should offer as oblations into a fire kindled with wood.
If, fourteen days prior to the [full] moon, an enemy should become dear to death,
one should cast cemetery ashes and white mustard seeds into the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
168a) While recollecting the Goddess, whose splendor is like the fire of cosmic destruction,
one should roast [the victim] on a fire kindled with funeral pyre wood while muttering the mantra.
One who is skilled in mantras should offer ten thousand oblations of ghee in the temple of Durgā;
then, taking that ash, he should scatter it over the enemy's army.
That army, split in many ways and deluded by the disease of fever,
abandoned its weapons and fled at the time of battle.
Poisonous wood, charcoal, and gravel-wood.
By casting [the mantra] into the house, one may effect the expulsion of a son-in-law and others in an instant.
A pill made from seven recitations, along with sugar, [is effective] in the dwellings of Durgā.
Having recited the mantra and taken up a vajra from the eastern direction consecrated by the Mahendra-mantra,
one should, while reciting the mantra, bury it in the enemy's house on the fourteenth lunar day.
Success is achieved through sons, wife, and so forth.
One should roast that buffalo in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as before;
having recited the mantra further, one should scatter these [remnants] throughout the house, village, and city.
That region quickly perishes, consumed by the fire of the mantra;
[the three poisons are] Brahmadaṇḍī, Markaṭikā, and Krayakrāśanikā.
Having seized [the object] on Saturdays when it is under the influence of Kulika while reciting the mantra,
one should bury it in the house of an enemy on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight while reciting the mantra.
Insanity shall arise for the enemy along with his sons, wife, and others.
One should recite the mantra of either *brahmadaṇḍī*, *markaṭī*, or *kākavacchū* individually; through this, the maṇḍala becomes fruitful.
One should bury six "six-dot" [charms], accompanied by cooked rice, within a doll.
Having touched it, one should mutter the Astra-mantra starting from midnight on the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
then, joined with the name of the enemy, one should bury this in a cremation ground.
That enemy, along with his family and kinsmen, shall quickly perish.
(168b) *Ṣaḍvindu* means "six dots" (*ṣaṭka*), which refers to a specific type of insect (*kīṭaka-viśeṣa*).

The mantra-practitioner, having touched the skull-cup with as many repetitions of the *sakala* mantras as there are syllables, should recite the *astra-mantra* preceded by the rite of establishing the vital breath (*prāṇasthāpana*).
On a Thursday, on the fourteenth day, in a cremation ground at the foot of a poisonous tree,
one who is struck by the flame of the *kṛtyā* weapon should offer oblations soaked in blood.
The enemy, utterly deluded by a great fever, shall go to the city of Yama;
one should place all the skulls— the severed heads of living beings—
into a jar filled with the blood of the aged.
Having covered him with a skull, one should conceal him with a red cloth.
One should worship with red flowers and other offerings, and having touched [the object],
one should recite the mantra while joined with darkness on a Tuesday at midnight, accompanied by a *kāraskara* tree.
One should offer oblations into the fire at a cremation ground, and the enemy shall go to the city of Yama;
having fashioned a jar from the wood of the tree belonging to the victim’s birth-star, one should fill it [with the enemy's name].
One should place that cat there with the five products of the buffalo;
then one should perform all rites, such as recitation and worship, exactly as before.
When the fire has been kindled with *kāraskara* wood and augmented by the *kṛtyā* mantra,
one should offer ten thousand oblations of wound-oil (*vraṇataila*) and then [pour] this jar [of water] back again.
Having uprooted [the plant] up to its head, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind;
by offering it into the fire, the enemy shall die within three days.
A *viḍāla* is a cat.
*Vraṇataila* is *bhallātaka* oil.
A beautiful buffalo calf that has fasted for one night [should be used].
The knower of mantras should cause a prastha of buffalo ghee to be drunk with the mantra.
With all his limbs bound with kuśa grass and his life-force firmly established,
the knower of mantras [should place him] in a fire kindled with kāraskara wood, using wound-oil.

Having performed the fire sacrifice, O child, one should offer ten thousand oblations with a concentrated mind; by this, on that very day, the enemy shall go to the city of Yama, while [the practitioner] remains happy.
When the fire has been placed in a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and kindled with mantras,
and has been worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) for ten thousand times in the prescribed sequence.
Then, for seven days, one should apply a paste of *rājī*, *bhallātaka*, and sesame seeds;
thereafter, the buffalo cow who has reached the time of delivery is placed [near it] once again.
Having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, he should touch her while reciting the mantra with a *kūrca* [grass-bundle],
proceeding from the head down to the private parts according to the ritual procedure, while meditating upon Vatsa.
Having drawn [the victim] forth, one should offer into the kindled fire that which has fallen into the hand;
when this is done, a Kṛtyā arises from the blazing fire.
She shall devour the enemy before long, even if he is protected by the Lord;
she enters the fire again and seeks out even the doer.
The best of mantra-knowers should perform such rites;
for the sake of self-protection, he should recite mantras such as the Mṛtyuñjaya.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Mantras for the Astras and Others," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the venerable Āśāditya Tripāṭhin.
Now, while the yantra is yet to be described, the preliminary technical definitions regarding the substances for the fire-oblation (homīya-dravya) are written down.
Now, however, the general rule for the substances used in the fire-oblation is prescribed:
one karṣa of clarified butter is prescribed for the oblation, and one śukti of milk is likewise recorded.
The five products of the cow (pañcagavya) have been described by the wise as being equal [in merit];
honey, milk, and cooked rice in the measure of a single eye are declared to be equal to them.
There should be a handful of curd, parched rice equal to a fist,
flattened rice of that same measure, and likewise, roasted barley flour as prescribed.

The jaggery should be half a *pala* in measure; the sugarcane is prescribed to be measured by the number of its joints; and one should likewise prepare the leaves, flowers, and fruits, each as a single unit.
They know that plantains and oranges should each be offered individually;
a citron is prescribed in four pieces, and a jackfruit is traditionally divided into ten.
The wise know that coconuts are to be split into eight pieces;
a bilva fruit is divided into three, and a kapittha fruit is split into four.
Indeed, these urvāruka fruits are cut and prepared in three ways;
other fruits are cut into pieces, and the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) should be ten finger-breadths long.
Three stalks of *dūrvā* grass are prescribed, along with *guḍūcī*, *caturaṅgulā*,
and a handful (*muṣṭi*) of rice, or even mung beans.
The rice grains should be half that amount; the kodrava should be measured by a handful;
the sesame seeds should be the size of a palmful, and the mustard seeds should be of that same measure.
Twenty *marīca*s make one *śukti* in measure; twenty *śuktis* make one *pura*; a *vadara* is the measure for a *rāmaṭha*, which is recorded as being equal to that.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron,
along with tittilī and bījāmāna, have been specified by the masters.
Thus end the substances for the oblation.
Now, the specific forms of the fire:
one should always meditate upon Vaiśvānara as standing during the oblations of fuel-sticks;
as lying down during the oblations of clarified butter; and as seated during all other matters.
In all ritual acts, the wise one should offer oblations into the fire within the mouth;
for it is declared that an offering into the ears results in disease, while an offering into the eyes results in blindness.
There is mental distress in the nose and loss of wealth in the head;
[the complexion] resembles gold, vermilion, the rising sun, and powdered saffron.
The color of fire is proclaimed as beautiful, having the luster of gold;
its sound, like that of a kettledrum, a cloud, or a lordly elephant, brings auspiciousness.
Resembling the *nāga*, *caṃpaka*, *punnāga*, *pāṭala*, and *yūthikā* flowers; resembling the *padma*, *indīvara*, *kahlāra*, *sārī*, and *arguggula*.
The experts in the Tantras have stated that the smoke of barley husks possesses an auspicious fragrance; the flames of the fire, free from flickering, move clockwise and resemble parasols.

Smoke as white as a kunda flower or the moon, which arises from the fire while one is performing recitation, bestows auspiciousness not only upon the practitioner but especially upon the entire kingdom; such smoke is declared to be bringer of good fortune.
A black mark on a dark-colored [body] destroys the recitation for one who is muttering;
however, one resembling a crow quickly destroys one's own kingdom.
A sound from fire resembling a harsh voice brings about total destruction;
a foul odor from the fire will bring suffering to the sacrificer.
A crest that is severed or distorted causes death and the destruction of wealth;
smoke-colored like a parrot's wing or possessing a luster similar to yellow garments [is likewise inauspicious].
It causes the destruction of the Raghu lineage and of cattle before long;
when such faults exist, the preceptor [should prescribe] an expiation.
The preceptor should offer oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra as an expiation.
Thus is the fire-oblation (agnihoma) to be understood. Now, regarding the yantras: therein is the Mātṛkā-yantra.

The third [mantra] is declared to be the supreme destroyer of all ailments; it is a yantra shining with the syllable *tārttīya* as its pericarp, with filaments appearing through pairs of vowels, possessing beautiful petals blooming at the beginning of creation, and encircled by the earth (*vasumatī*) as its abode; it is resplendent with the four corners and possesses the color of the lord of stars (the moon), being the very seat of the mantra of syllables.
The seed-mantra of Tripurā is *sauḥ*; this is the third seed-mantra. The rest is easy to understand: the Lord of Stars is the Moon, and its seed-mantra is *ṭaṃ*.
The water-seed syllable *vaṃ* is in the corner. As for the three-metal seal (*trilohinī-mudrā*), it is as follows:
The three metals—silver, gold, and copper—are considered to have the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire respectively;
silver is remembered as the Moon, gold as the Sun, and copper as the Fire.
The portions of metal are specified by the number of the vowels and other syllables;
with those metals, one should fashion a mudrā that is joined together without being [previously] calculated.
Having recited [the mantra] more than a thousand times, a person should touch it and offer oblations;
the practitioner should pour clarified butter upon it with the previously mentioned number.
Having placed that seal (mudrā) into the pitcher according to the procedure prescribed for consecration,
one should, with a concentrated mind, invoke and worship the Goddess with the ritual offerings.
Having consecrated him, the Guru should give that ring to the disciplined disciple, saying:
"This red [ring] is the destroyer of minor diseases, poisons, and fevers."
One should provide special protection against beasts of prey, thieves, wild animals, and the like;
by wearing this, a lord of men attains victory in battle.

In the reduction of the vowels and other syllables, there are sixteen parts of copper, which is of the nature of fire (Agni), ten parts of silver, which is of the nature of the moon (Soma), and sixteen parts according to the count. This Vāritamudrā bestows the aforementioned fruit. Now, the Mahālakṣmī Yantra.

The yantra consists of the name of the person for whom the rite is intended, preceded by *Oṃ* and followed by the word "Sādhya," repeated twice, joined with the *Śrī-śakti-māra* mantra, located in the filaments;

on the petals of the sun-lotus are the radiant syllables of the mantra; outside that is a lotus with consonants as its filaments, surrounded by two sets of eight beautiful lotuses, and the earth-disk (*bhū-vimba*) with the *Astra-mantra* (*Vaṣaṭ*) at the end, together with the *Tvaritā-mantra*.
One should draw it surrounded [by the enclosure].
This is the Mahālakṣmī yantra, which bestows the fruit of all sovereignty.
It pacifies all suffering and wards off all calamities; what need is there to say more here? There exists nothing superior to this.
The meaning of this is as follows:

having drawn a lotus with twelve petals, one should write "Oṃ" in its pericarp; in the center of that, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) conjoined with the three seed-syllables—namely, the Śrī-bīja, the Hrīṃ-bīja, and the Klīṃ-bīja.

One should surround the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) in the filaments with the *guṇa-mantra*. On the twelve petals, one should place the twelve syllables of the mantra; outside of that is a sixteen-petaled [lotus]. In its filaments, the consonants are placed in pairs, and on the petals, the sixteen vowels. Outside of that is a pair of earth-mandalas (*bhū-vimba*) with the *tvaritā-mantra* ending in *vaṣaṭ*.

One should encircle it. In its corners, one should write *ha*, *kṣa*, and *auṃ*. This is the Mahālakṣmī Yantra. Now, the triple-layered Yantra of Bhuvaneśvarī: surrounded by the seat of the Power (*śakti*), containing the goal and the ritual action, encircled by fire, and further enveloped by powers—this is the Yantra that bestows all desired objects.
The triple-layered square situated in the center brings about good fortune and prosperity. Its meaning is as follows:
having drawn a hexagon, one should write the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* in its center, and within that, together with the name of the person for whom the rite is intended (*sādhya*).

"Protect, protect Devadatta from the discourse of karma," and so forth. One should write the syllable *īṃ* in the three corners. Outside of that, one should write *hrīṃ*. How [should this be done]? Each one of these seed-syllables (*bīja*) should be encircled clockwise by the letter *ra* and the vowel *ī*, and they should be bound to one another. Then...

The letters *hari*—namely the vowels *i* and *r*—are indicated. By this, [one writes] *hrīṃ hraṃ*. This is the traditional method of writing (*makṣa*). Then one should write *hari īṃ hara īṃ*, or alternatively, one may write *hrīṃ īṃ hraṃ īṃ*.
Outside of that, one should encircle it with fifteen syllables. Furthermore, one should encircle it with a "house of earth" (*bhūgṛha*).
One should likewise draw this triple-folded yantra, which bestows liberation. Thus ends the triple-folded yantra.

Now follows the six-fold yantra of Bhuvaneśvarī: the name of the practitioner situated within the seed-syllable, accompanied by the syllables *sa-ra-sa-ma-mau-ma-ṭa-yā*, surrounded by *ramā* (the goddess Lakṣmī) and *manmatha* (the god of love), and encircled by fire... [and so forth].
Within the petals are the three seed-syllables beginning with "Oṃ"; the center contains the Self and the Non-Self, topped by the syllable "Ī" and flanked by Hari and Hara;
outside, it is encircled by six well-bound "Siṃcilipis," surrounded by two squares of the earth, and adorned with the Cintāmaṇi and Nṛsiṃha mantras at its auspicious corners.

The meaning of this is as follows: One should write the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within a hexagon. How so? The name of the person to be accomplished is placed in the portion of the letter *ra* of the seed-syllable, and the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is placed in the portion of the vowel *ī*. Between these two, one of the two [names] is placed in the middle of both.

One should encircle the five syllables of the *śara-sauvāra* mantra with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*, the seed-syllable *klīṃ*, and the fire-seed-syllable (*raṃ*). Outside of that, one should write the [mantra] together with the self (the name) and accompanied by the *anusvāra* in the center of a hexagon.

In the three southern corners, one should write those same [syllables] as the objects of attainment (*sādhya*) along with the *anusvāra*; and in the northeast corner of the hexagon, [one should write] the center.

The letter *ī* with an anusvāra on the two cheeks [is written] as "hari-hara. Outside the hexagon, as before, the seed-syllables of the hexagon are joined with the letters of the alphabet. With two earth-triangles (bhū-koṇa), starting from the east, the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha is placed in the corners as "cintāmaṇi. This is the sixfold yantra. Now, the Tvaritā yantra: in the center of the lotus...

One should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) within the center, containing the desired object of accomplishment (*sādhya*), upon a ten-petaled lotus. The letters beginning with *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) are situated on the ten petals, and the seed-syllable of the six-cornered [figure] is located in the city of the earth (the square). This is clear from the context below. This *Tvaritā* yantra, when worn, pacifies acts of sorcery and malice, and removes the fear of wild beasts and thieves.
Especially bestowing victory—thus ends the Yantra of Tvaritā. Now follows another Yantra for Tvaritā herself.

One should write "Tāre Huṃ" within the hollow of the lotus, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya); one should write the eight syllables of the mantra upon the eight petals, and outside of that—

The *Tvaritā* yantra, which is encircled by the goddess Śakti, surrounded by a jar, situated upon a lotus, and bearing the face of a lotus—this is the subjugating (*vaśyakara*) yantra that removes fear from planets and the like, bestows prosperity (*lakṣmī*), and grants fame. Thus ends another *Tvaritā* yantra.

One should draw a lotus endowed with petals; then, in its pericarp, one should write the *tāra* (the syllable Om) together with the name of the practitioner (*sādhya*) situated within the *śakti*. Then, in sequence upon its filaments, one should write the syllables of the *mardinī* mantra, followed by pairs of golden-colored syllables. Furthermore, having arranged the mantra-syllables according to the three qualities (*guṇa*), one should write them upon the petals. At the end, one should write [the remaining syllables].
On those petals,
the Yantra of the Dwellress of the Vindhyas— encircled by the letters of the Mātṛkā and situated between two Bhūpuras— is declared to bestow all prosperity.
It is especially a provider of protection, a destroyer of minor malevolent rites and the like;
it bestows sovereignty upon those who have lost their kingdom, and grants subjugation to those desiring to bring others under their control.
It bestows sons upon those seeking sons and brings the pacification of disease to the sick; what more need be said here? This yantra is a wish-fulfilling gem.
The meaning of this is as follows:

one should write the syllables of the mantra of Mahiṣārdinī on the eight petals in pairs; above that, on the sixteen petals, one should write three syllables each of the mantra of Vanavāsinī. This is the Yantra of Vanavāsinī.
Now, the Tripurabhairavī Yantra: One should inscribe the syllables of the *Vīṇā* mantra three times within the nine triangles starting from the center;
having written the syllables of the *Gāyatrī* on the openings of the eight petals of the lotus, it is surrounded by the alphabet.

The Yantra known as Tripura, which agitates the three worlds and bestows prosperity, is formed by the letter *bhū* (the earth) surrounded in its corners by two *vi* (fire) joined with *manmatha* (the god of love).
Having invoked [the deity] into this Yantra, one should then worship it properly.
It should have been consecrated by the performance of recitation (japa) and encased in three layers of lac and iron.
If one holds in one's arm a mechanical device that brings victory in battles,
it shall bring victory even over the gods, and one's poetic skill shall become abundant.
"It shall increase longevity, health, friends, sons, and grandsons.
The meaning of this is as follows:
having constructed a nine-yoni wheel, one should place the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the mantra within the *yonis*, beginning from the upper northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*).

Furthermore, one should write [the syllables] again in their respective order. Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus above that, one should place the syllables of the Gāyatrī three times on each petal. Above that, having fashioned a circle, one should place the Mātṛkā syllables in its center.
Above that, one should draw two anklets (*nūpura*) and write the seed-syllable of Manmatha (*manmathabīja*) in its corners. This is the yantra.

This bestows the fruits as described. Thus ends the *Tripurabhairavī* Yantra.
