Now, the *Mahāgaṇapati* Yantra: One should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in the center of a hexagon; within it, the city of fire (the triangle) surrounded by the quarters, then Lakṣmī, Māyā, Kaṃdarpa, and Bhūmi; thereafter, in the six compartments, one should write the six seed-syllables.

173b) The wise man should write the syllables of the root mantra upon the eight-petalled lotus surrounding that [central figure], and the remaining syllables according to their qualities on the petals, ending with the final syllable on the palāśa leaf;
it should be encircled by the letters.

This is the Yantra of the Lord of the Gaṇas, described according to the sequence [of the ritual], consisting of the nooses (pāśa) and goads (aṅkuśa), and encircled by two earths (the square boundary lines) and two houses (the inner squares). Having written it on a superior birch-bark with lac, saffron, yellow pigment (rocanā), and musk—or on gold—with all these substances, one who wears it shall obtain prosperity that is to be prayed for by all. The meaning of this is as follows: [The diagram consists of] the nooses and goads as stated in the sequence, surrounded by two earths (forming the outer square) and two houses (forming the inner grid). Having inscribed this upon excellent birch-bark with lac, saffron, yellow pigment, and musk, or upon gold, he who wears it shall attain a fortune sought after by everyone. Having inscribed this upon excellent birch-bark with lac, saffron, yellow pigment, and musk, or upon gold, he who wears
Having drawn a triangle, one should write within it the *praṇava* (oṃ) together with the name of the practitioner (*sādhya*) and the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa.
Outside that, a hexagon; and outside the triangle, in the four directions, one should write "hrīṃ klīṃ glauṃ.

In the six corners, one should write the six seed-syllables beginning with the *praṇava*. In the junctions of the corners, one should write the limb-mantras (*aṅgamantra*). Above that, an eight-petaled lotus.

One should place three mantra-syllables on each of the petals of the lotus, the remaining syllables on the final petal, and surround the exterior with the letters of the alphabet in both direct and reverse order; this is the Mahāgaṇapati Yantra.

174a) Now, the Rāma Yantra: one should write the *tāra* (OM) in the corners and on the petals; thereafter, the group of vowels (*svaragaṇa*) in the filaments (*kiñjalka*), and then the *mālā* (the mantra string) in the centers of the petals.
The mantra syllables, white and facing the qualities (guṇas), should be placed in the eighth [square];
having encircled the mantra syllables with the ten-syllable [mantra], one should place the letters beginning with 'ka' in the outer enclosure (bhūpura).
One should draw the seed-syllables of Nṛsiṃha and Varāha in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
this yantra, consecrated through japa and other rites, should be fashioned from materials such as gold leaf.
One should bestow the splendor of victory and valor supported by one's own arm;
thus has been declared the ritual procedure for the Rāma-mantra, which is honored by the sages.

In the corners, write the syllables of the mantra. There, at the junctions, write the syllables of the *sandhy-aṅga* mantras; then, in each [corner], write the *hṛllekhā* seed-syllable and the *kāma* seed-syllable. Above that, draw an eight-petaled lotus; on its filaments, write six syllables of the *mālā-mantra* on each petal, and five syllables on the eighth petal. Above that—

Having encircled [the central deity] with the ten-syllable mantra, one should subsequently encircle it with the letters from *ka* onwards, and then enclose it within a *bhūpura* (fortress diagram). One should place the seed-mantra (*bīja*) of Varāha in the cardinal directions and the seed-mantra of Narasiṃha in the corners. This is the Rāma-yantra.
Now, the Varāha-yantra: in the center is the seed-mantra preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ); in a pair of fire-fortresses (triangles), one should place the letters of the discus.
The six limbs, known as the best, are situated at the joints; the vowels are located upon the filaments in the petals that form the support.
One should place the mantra-syllables, numbering fourteen (vedasaṃkhyā).
Then, having written the letters beginning with *ka* on the filaments of the petals in the outer circle,
and having correctly inscribed the mantra-syllables in pairs upon the sixteen-spoked lotus situated at the heart of the god of love (*madanagata*) with the syllables joined together,

one should subsequently surround it with the seed-syllables of the corners of the earth (*kṣmākoṇa-bījas*), interspersed in the middle with the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya-nāmārṇa*), using ladles (*darvibhiḥ*).
It is surrounded on the outside by the letters of the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the letters of the mantra;
within its corners, one should write the seed-syllable of the earth (bhū-bīja) conjoined with the object to be accomplished;
and upon the eight spikes, one should inscribe the form of Vārāha together with the seed-syllable of the earth.
The sky of the lunar orb of all the lords is impelled by the stream of seed-syllables;
[it is prepared] with yellow orpiment, guggulu, camphor, lac, saffron, and sandalwood.
On an auspicious day, for the sake of accomplishing one's desires, the practitioner should draw the yantra with a pen made of cow-dung and water, ground together,
or even with my own [hair].
One should write this yantra on a golden plate for the attainment of royal fortune;
on birch bark for the acquisition of one's own desires; and on linen cloth for the attainment of land.
One should construct the yantra desired by oneself, perfected through recitation, worship, and other rites;
this very yantra has been successfully accomplished within the kingdoms of Rāmapattana.
One who desires to bury [the image] should worship it with its limbs in the various directions;
[thereby one is protected] from minor ailments, death, disease, and the great terrors of spirits, serpents, and other beings.
The deity cannot be seen by force in that place;
this is the meaning.
Outside the six-cornered [figure] of the sādhya, there is a four-petaled [lotus].
The syllables of the wheel are in the corners, and the six limbs are at the joints.

On the four petals, one should place two instances of the eight-syllabled mantra of Nārāyaṇa; on the [remaining] petals, four repetitions each of the Vārāha mantra. Outside of that is a sixteen-petaled lotus; in its filaments, the pairs of vowels from *ka* to *śa*.

On the petals, one should write two mantra-syllables; above that, the syllable *śravaṇa* (the letter *śa*) with the seed-syllables of the Earth and Varāha containing the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) within them;

then, with the mantra-syllables. One should draw an eight-pronged [wheel] encircled by the Earth-mandala together with the *sādhya*, the Earth-seed syllable, and the corners. This is the Vārāha Yantra. Now, the Cakra Yantra: the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*).

One should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within the [central] circle, and the remaining six syllables of the mantra upon those very [circles]. Then, one should place the limbs (*aṅga*) at the joints;

thereafter, one should draw a sixteen-spoked wheel with sixteen syllables situated within a city of eight [squares], and write the *sādhya* together with the *tāra* (Oṃ) in the center of the hexagon, and the remaining syllables on the six corners. Furthermore, one should place the limbs at its joints.
One should duly place the syllable *hauṃ kṣāṃ* in the center, having recited it according to the prescribed method;
this recitation, accompanied by the ritual scattering of offerings (*saṃpāta*), bestows welfare upon pregnant women.
This yantra destroys malevolent spells, planetary afflictions, and insanity.

This is the meaning of the word *tāram*: having written the *praṇava* (Oṃ) together with the *sādhya* (the name of the person for whom the rite is intended) in the center of a hexagon, one should place the letter *ṭha* in its interior, the six syllables of the mantra in the corners, and the *aṅga-mantras* at the joints;
above this, there is a sixteen-petaled lotus surrounded by two square enclosures (*bhūpura*).
175b) "The sixteen syllables upon the sixteen petals. Now he describes the consecration:
"The bark of trees with milky sap such as the *palāśa*, along with *malayaja* (sandalwood) and *pura* (gum)."
Saffron, jasmine buds, bilva, apāmārga, and mustard seeds.
Sesame, dūrvā grass, and barley; the goddess Tulasī, a pair of goads (aṅkuśas), Lakṣmī, gorocanā, a lotus, and cow dung combined.
Reciting the mantra, one should cast Viṣṇukrāntā combined with Marka into a vessel filled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and into the consecrated fire.
Having established it [in the vessel], one should boil it properly until it becomes ash;
then, taking that, one should again recite [the mantra] one million times while focusing the mind on the deity.
One should smear all the limbs with this and apply a small amount to the head;
it wards off the effects of sorcery, malice, planetary possession, insanity, disease, and suffering.
It pacifies all enemies, removes all sins, is supreme,
bestows auspiciousness and subjugation upon men, and wards off every affliction.
It is especially recommended for those who are pregnant or afflicted by loss of strength;
indeed, no protection greater than this is proclaimed to exist in the worlds.

*Malayaja* is sandalwood; *puru* is *guggulu*; *yāminī* is turmeric; *devī* is *sahadevī*; *lakṣmī* is the *bilva* fruit. All of these should be placed in a full pitcher containing the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). [Recite the mantra] ten million times, one hundred thousand times, or twenty thousand times. He now describes the method for preparing the *pañcagavya* with ghee: *mustā*, *maṭī*, and *niśā*.
Citraka, elā, yaṣṭimadhu, vacā, vṛṣa,
pāṭhā, viḍaṅga, mañjiṣṭhā, drākṣā, dārvī, rohiṇī,
and the three fruits (triphalā)— with these as a paste, [one should prepare] ghee in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should drink a *prastha* measure of this, duly prepared with the following mantra;
it bestows peace, grants sons to women, and removes the fear of *bhūtas* and *pretas*.
There is nothing purer than this for protecting the fetus:
mustā, āmōpya, niśā, haridrā, vahnī, and the root of citraka.

176a) Yaṣṭi is liquorice (madhuyaṣṭi). Rohiṇī is kaṭukī. Phalatraya consists of the three fruits beginning with harītakī. One should properly cook one prastha measure of ghee [with these]. Consecrated by mantra, it bestows the fruit of liberation. Now, O Puruṣottama...

This yantra consists of a hexagon shining with the limbs of the target (sādhya) aroused by desire; outside of this is an eight-petaled lotus whose petals are bound by the qualities of the Gāyatrī and the syllables of the Mālā-mantra numbering six; it is further surrounded by a square enclosure (kṣoṇīpura), and the corners are occupied by the god born of the mind (Manobhava). This is the yantra.
The meaning of *jaganmohana* is as follows: Having drawn a hexagon, one should place the *kāmabīja* (the seed-syllable of desire) in its center.

Above the hexagon, there is an eight-petaled lotus; for each mantra, three syllables of the *kāmagāyatrī* are assigned to each petal. Again, above that is another eight-petaled lotus; on each of its petals, six syllables of the *mālāmantra* are assigned.
Then, for the purpose of subjugation, she should hold the Bhūpura along with the Kāmabīja; thus ends the Puruṣottama Yantra.

One should write the mantra of Dhūmāvatī in sequence upon a pair of fire-palaces (triangles) marked with tridents. In the center and the corners, one should place the yantra consisting of the wind-palace (hexagon), along with the seed-syllables of fire, wind, and fire (Ra, Ya, Ra).
With the seed-syllables Daṃ, To, Śā, Rvī, Śa, Viṃ, and Taṃ, the mantra of Dhūmāvatī is proclaimed for the destruction of enemies.

The one who effects suppression should bury in a cremation ground an object fashioned from a *preta*-rag with poison and golden water; this will certainly destroy the enemy. The meaning of this is: a hexagon...

One should write the Dhūmāvatī mantra one by one. One should surround it on the outside with the enclosure of the letter *va* (the wind element), and then with the letter *ra*. Outside of that, one should surround it with the letter *ya*. Having written this on a cloth from a corpse (*pretavastra*) using the juice of the *dhattūra* plant and a pen made of a crow's feather, one should bury it in a cremation ground. The eradication of enemies will occur. [Furthermore,] having written "Mā," it should be placed within a pair of squares of the letter *a*.

The knower of mantras should write the syllables *oṃ ṅa ṇa na āñ ja kā ra* together with Dhūmāvatī upon the petals in its corners. Enclosed by a circle, this yantra, further surrounded by three houses of Vāyu (*yaṃ*), when placed on ground frequented by spirits at the edge [of a village], shall cause enmity between enemies. The meaning of this is: having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus—
In the center of that, place the syllable *māṃ*; in its two compartments, the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*);
with four *ma* syllables; and the letters *ṅa*, *ṇa*, and *na* on the petals. One should encircle it externally with the *ghumuṭikā* and other [protective diagrams].
This should be written upon a cloth from a corpse using the juice of *dhattūra* and a pen made of a crow’s wing. It is to be deposited in a cremation ground.
The cause of hatred:
177a) In the midst of the eighty-one squares, within the fire-triangle, one should write the target, and then *kṣtrūṃ* and *śrūṃ*.

Having first inscribed the seed-syllables *vrūṃ* located in the directions within the rows, one should then write the remaining [syllables] starting from the northeast (*īśa*) and the night-stalkers (*niśācara*). Outside that, one should draw the diagram (*yantra*) encircled by the mantra of Kālī, surrounded by the enclosure of Yama and the enclosure of Agni-Yavana.
One should write it with the charcoal of the eight poisons, resin, and lamp-soot.
This wheel, which is incapable of being suppressed, [should be placed] upon a ragscreen with a crow-feather [inscribed],
or at a Vibhīta tree, an anthill, a cremation ground, or a crossroads.
The mantra-practitioner, standing on the right side, should bury this at the half-moon [of the lunar fortnight];
by this means, the enemy—the adversary—will die within seven days under all circumstances.
If he should fall, overcome by great diseases,
that is proclaimed as the *śilācakram*.
If one draws a female monkey with poison-tipped arrows facing downwards where there is a howling at night, misfortune shall prevail there.

Having first inscribed the name of the one to be subjugated within the center of the city [of the yantra], one should then draw the goddess Jambha upon the petals situated in the cardinal directions and the god Smara upon the petals in the intermediate directions. Furthermore, one should place the syllable *samānaka* (the letter *ya*) in the corners, surrounded by the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*). This yantra brings about subjugation and removes the fear of planetary afflictions and other such evils.
It removes minor malevolent spells.
177b) The meaning of this is as follows: in the center of an eight-petaled lotus is the seed-syllable *tuṃ*, and in its center is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*). Then...

That [syllable] is in the petals of the directions. *Jaṃbhe jaṃbhini, mohe mohini, andhe andhini, rundhe rundhi svāhā*—this is everywhere. Now, the Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra: having formed a pair of earth-fortresses (bhūmipura), one should write the Māyā-bīja, the Manmatha-bīja, the name of the target (sādhya), and the letter Ca at the corners.

One should write the name of the practitioner's own target situated within the syllable *KṢĀṂ*, surrounded by the "City of the Earth" (*mahīpura*)—which is encircled by the syllable *SAṂ* and elevated above—which has the syllable *UCCAIḤ* in its center, interlaced with the vowels (*sārṇa*), and enclosed by the three-syllabled *Mṛtyuñjaya* mantra.

Then, one should place the deities upon the filaments; on the eight petals, the names [of the targets] should be written, encased within the mantras of their respective classes (*vargeṣu*). This is the Yantra.

The supreme [mantra] called Mṛtyuñjaya is declared to be formed by joining the palms like a lotus bud; it destroys poison, fever, and diseases of the head, bestows glory and victory, grants luster and nourishment, is subjugating, and accomplishes all rites and goals. Its meaning is as follows: having drawn an eight-petaled lotus, on the petals...

Having made the filaments golden, one should place the syllable *kṣa* in the pericarp of the lotus; in its center, one should write the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*), interwoven with the syllable *māṃ* and enclosed within the three-syllabled mantra *mṛtyuñjaya*. On the eight petals, one should write the name enclosed by the three-syllabled mantra. On the edges of the petals, one should write the eight groups of consonants (*aṣṭavarga*). Above [the lotus], there should be two lotuses.

A folded yantra bestows the fruit of liberation. Thus ends the Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra. Having written the syllable *oṃ*, the *māyā* (hrīṃ), and so forth, [the mantra] with the girdle (*mekhalā*), the bride (*vadhū*), and the mantra within the pair of fire-houses (*vahnigṛha*), one should draw this on birch bark (*bhūrja*) in the center and the corners; it effects the destruction of enemies and serpents. The meaning of this is: having drawn the pair of fire-houses...
One should write the syllable Oṃ in the center, Hrīṃ in the corners, and Svāhā on the girdle.
Having set aside the seed-syllable *nṛ* (na) and the syllable *gl*, one should inscribe there [the letter] *kṣa*;
it should not be surrounded on the outside by the noose (*pāśa*) and the goad (*aṅkuśa*).
It is further enveloped by the syllable *ṭa* situated in the center of the mandala of the earth,
and it is surrounded on the outside, in due order, by the letter *la*s joined with the nasal bindu.
The entire activity of the seed-syllables of the Mātṛkās at the end of creation is performed in verse;
and the two desired [syllables] are fashioned on the cloth of the belly, situated in the center.
If one buries it at the front of an army, it certainly effects its immobilization.

In the center, one should write the seed-syllable (bīja) of Śrī Narasiṃha; then, outside of that, on the filaments (kesara), one should write the vowels, and on the two lotuses, the moon, and the central hub (indraka), one should write the Gāruḍa mantra. Having written the semi-vowels (antastha) in the directions of Vāyu, Agni, Nairṛti, and Śiva, the Garuḍa yantra—surrounded by the consonant groups (varga) and encircled by eight spokes—is completed. It is further encompassed by the Saṃvartaka mantras.

The meaning of this is as follows: In the center of an eight-petaled lotus is the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha; the vowels are on the filaments; the Gāruḍa mantra is in the middle of the western, northern, and southern petals; the letters *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va* are on the petals of the northwest, southeast, southwest, and northeast; it should be surrounded externally by the Boar-mantra (*Varāha*), and further outside by the eight *kṣa*-syllables. This is the yantra.
For one who retains it in memory and beholds it, all poison is destroyed.

178b) Now, the Kāmayantra: One should write the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) surrounded by *smara* (the seed-syllables of love), with the word "kāma" written in the center; thereafter, one should write the syllables *tāra*, *pika*, *pakṣa*, *para*, *nāśā*, *pi*, *jhaṃṭīśa*, and *pā*.

One should draw this yantra on eight betel leaves within the eight petals of a lotus; having performed the recitation (*japa*), one should place it inside a betel leaf and consume it, and the person [to whom it is given] will be brought under control. The meaning of this is: having drawn an eight-petaled lotus inside a betel leaf, one should write the seed-syllable of Kāma (*kāmabīja*) in its center, encircled by the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

One should encircle that with the seed-syllables of desire (*kāmabīja*). Afterwards, one should write the seed-syllables to be described below on each of the eight petals. How so? *Tāra* is the syllable *oṃ*. One should write *oṃ*, *khaṃ*, *ṛṃ*, *uṃ*, *eṃ*, and *yaṃ* on the eight petals, and tridents at the tips of the petals. This yantra brings about subjugation (*vaśyakara*). Now, the Govinda-yantra. First...

One should draw four groups of eight lines extending east, south, and north, joined by tridents at the corners and provided with two side-walls; then, having written the letters of the verse one after another in the eight petals of the lotus within the central square, one should write the eight syllables in the spaces between them, and outside of that—

This Yantra of the Son of Devakī, surrounded by twelve syllables, when written on birch bark or similar material and worn constantly on the arm according to the prescribed rite, bestows the fruits of all desires.
When written on a board made from the wood of the Palāśa tree and properly consecrated, it should be buried in a cow-pen; that [Yantra] [brings prosperity] to the cows.
Growth arises.
179a) Now, the materials for writing.
The preceptor should draw these yantras with a golden stylus, using saffron from Kashmir, lac, musk, elephant ichor, and sandalwood.
A practitioner of mantra should never wear a yantra that has been cast upon the ground, touched by a dog, burnt, mixed with discarded flower offerings (nirmālya), spread out, or stepped over.
Now, the forms of the yantras—namely the Sarvatobhadra, Navanābha, and Pañcābja mandalas—which are useful for initiation and other rites, are being described. The Sarvatobhadra is as follows:
One should make it four-cornered with four compartments provided with diagonal threads,
and one should apply four threads at all four corners as well.
Then, there shall be fish in the squares; one should drop [the cord] upon those threads.
One should draw thirty-six of them in length and breadth, and in the center, a lotus with all its characteristics.
The outer area should be yellow with one row [of squares], and the pathways (vīthikā) with two rows;
one should arrange the door-ornaments (dvāraśobhā) and sub-ornaments (upaśobhā) with the remaining two rows.
Then, following the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, the wise practitioner should draw a lotus,
having set aside one-twelfth part of the area of the lotus field on the outside.
One should divide that middle portion into three equal parts using clay:
the first shall be the place for the pericarp (karṇikā), and the second for the filaments (keśara).

Therein, the tip of each petal is stated to be one-third of the [petal] portion; the wise [practitioner], according to the rule, should determine the measurement of the space between the outer [edge] and the stalk.
Having placed the crescent moons around the tips of the filaments and having drawn them at the junctions,
one should then cast the seed-syllables (mūtras).
The wise one should draw the stalk with the same measurement as that of the tips of the petals;
in the space between them, in their center, on both sides of the thread.
Then, one should draw the tips of the petals evenly with the outer hand; from the base of each petal, one should fashion the filaments in pairs.
This lotus is declared by those who know the tantras to be common [to all].
One should wipe away three squares for the sake of the foot [of the deity] at the corners of the pedestal.
With the remaining squares, the learned one should fashion the limbs of the pedestal;
he should sweep the squares situated along the pathways according to the sequence of rows.
Then, one should worship the doors in the cardinal directions using two and four squares;
furthermore, there shall be divisions on the sides of the doors consisting of three and one square-padas respectively.
The secondary ornaments (upaśobhās) should be formed with one [square] and then with three squares;
the four corners should be formed with the remaining six squares.
One should color that captivating maṇḍala with five colors:
yellow should be made from turmeric powder, and white from rice flour.
Safflower powder is red; that produced from burnt husks is black;
and the Vilva and others are said to be the five colors, with the Vilva being dark.
The auspicious white lines, one finger in height and width, are beautiful;
the pericarp is yellow in color, and the filaments are reddish.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra over the petals with white-colored powder and their joints with black powder; alternatively, yellow pigment alone may be used.
The filaments should be yellowish-red, and the petals should also be reddish;
the joints should be yellow in color, or alternatively, yellow or black.
One should color the interiors of the pedestals; the feet should be auspiciously reddish, its limbs white, and likewise the four walkways.
One should draw wish-fulfilling creepers endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruits,
variegated with various colors and enchanting to the sight of all.
The doors are white in color; the ornaments (śobhā) are said to be red;
the secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) are yellow in color; and the corners (koṇa) have a black luster.
Three lines should be drawn on the outside, black, red, and white in sequence;
that is known as the Sarvatobhadra mandala, which is common to all.
The meaning of this is as follows:

In the manner described, seventeen equal lines should be drawn extending east-west and north-south to form the grid squares. One should draw a lotus with six central squares. Within the lotus, the filaments are yellow, the petals are reddish, the junctions of the petals are white, and the outlines are black.

A pedestal (*pīṭha*) should be made with one row of lotuses. With three by three squares, yellow and other colors [should be applied]. Red [squares] should be made in four squares. On the two rows above the pedestal, walkways (*vīthīkā*) of various colors should be made on all sides. Two rows remain at the top; in their corners—
On the four sides, a green area should be made with six squares; and with three squares adjacent to that, half of that size, yellow secondary ornaments (upaśobhā) should be made.

The doors consist of four squares, and two [squares] are white in color; thus they are to be understood in the cardinal directions. Then, outside the maṇḍala, three lines of white, red, and black color should be drawn.
In this way, the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala becomes beautiful on all sides. Now...
The nine-petaled mandala is now described.
The wise one should arrange sixty-four squares within a square;
with four of those squares, there shall be a lotus in the center, and again around it.
One should fashion four pathways ending at the edge of the mandala, and one should draw lotuses in the squares situated at the cardinal directions.
The wise one, having divided the four corners situated at the sides into sixteen parts,
should erase [the lines] to form the shape of a svastika using white, yellow, red, and black [pigments].
One should fill those svastikas with powders, beginning from the east, according to the very path previously described; one should complete the remainder in the same manner.
This mandala, which bestows all accomplishments, is declared to have nine centers.
The meaning of this is as follows:
nine equal lines should be drawn extending from east to west, and likewise nine lines should be drawn extending from north to south.
In this way, a perfect square consisting of sixty-four squares is produced. Of that—
Having divided each corner into four corners, they should be made into sixteen parts.

181a) Within the sixteen squares, by means of three squares and one, the form of a *liṅga* is produced; likewise for each of the other three. In this manner, a *svastika* should be made in each of the four corners, with four squares in each of the cardinal directions.

A set of four lotuses should be made; one lotus is placed in each of the four corners situated in the center. The remaining rows of corners should be made extending to the boundary of the four walkways (*vīthī*). Thus, the mandala with nine centers (*navanābha*) is formed. Now, regarding the five-lotus mandala: this mandala of five lotuses is said to be devoid of the *svastika* symbols.

For the purpose of worshipping the deity during initiation (dīkṣā), three auspicious mandalas should be prepared. In the place of the svastika, within the four corners, a square should be filled with colored powders (varṇikā). As before, five lotuses should be made in the four directions and in the center. Four pathways (vīthī) should also be made. Thus it is said.
The nineteenth chapter, titled "Description of Yantras," in the *Mantrakoṣa* compiled by the illustrious Āsāditya Tripāṭhī.
Now, the mudrās employed at the beginning of the worship of the deities and other rites are written down;
the mudrās for invocation and so forth are demonstrated in their proper order.
With those [flowers] which have been arranged, the mantra-deities rejoice;
with hands joined in añjali, they are offered flowers that have been perfectly prepared.

The mudrā called Āvāhana (Invocation) has been described by the teachers as the seventh; that same mudrā, when turned face downwards, is said to be used for the rite of Sthāpana (Installation). || 1-2 ||
With the two fists joined together and the pair of thumbs raised up, this mudrā is prescribed by the teachers and others for the purpose of invoking the presence [of the deity]. (3)
That very [power], pregnant with the Śrī-guṣṭha, is proclaimed as Sannirodhā. || 4 ||
The placement of the six limbs upon the body of the deity constitutes the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the act of making [the deity] complete).
The left hand forms a fist with the index finger extended long and pointing downwards;
this is declared by the best of preceptors to be the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā.
Furthermore, with the little fingers and ring fingers mutually facing and interlocked,
and likewise the index and middle fingers joined, this is proclaimed as the Dhenu-mudrā.
The best of teachers should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) according to the prescribed method.
With the thumbs interlocked and the fingers of the hands extended,
this is declared by the wise to be the Mahāmudrā for the purpose of supreme transformation.
One should employ these mudrās in the ritual of the deity sacrifice.
Now, regarding the *akṣamālā*:
because it is joined with the [senses] prior to initiation (*ādīkṣā*), it is celebrated as the *akṣamālā*.
One should fashion a rosary for recitation (*japamālā*) from beads numbering according to those [senses].
One should recite [the mantra] over Rudrabhūmālikāsūra according to one's heart's desire;
a rosary fashioned from lotus seeds is considered a destroyer of enemies.
A garland made of knots of kusha grass destroys all sins;
it is said that one made with jīva fruits bestows the wealth of sons, O son.
A rosary fashioned from silver jewels, established for the present,
bestows the fulfillment of desires when it is crafted from golden ones.
A garland fashioned from coral bestows abundant wealth;
a crystal garland grants good fortune, and one made of pearls confers prosperity.
A garland fashioned from conch shells and gems brings about imperishable fame;
a garland composed of all these materials together results in liberation for men.
Now, the six rites (ṣatkarma) employed for subjugation (vaśya) and other purposes are being written down.
For in this tantra, I shall correctly explain the characteristics of the six rites (ṣaṭkarma), which,
in accordance with all tantras, bestow the accomplishment of the fruits of their application.
The wise proclaim the six rites (ṣatkarma) to be pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), immobilization (staṃbhana), causing enmity (dveṣaṇa), expulsion (uccāṭana), and finally, killing (māraṇa).

The pacification (*śānti*) is declared to be the removal of diseases, malevolent rites (*kṛtyā*), planetary influences (*graha*), and so forth. (1) The subjugation (*vaśya*) of all people is declared to be their state of being obedient. (2) The obstruction of the activity of all beings is illustrated as "stambhana" (paralysis).
4. Causing hatred among those who are affectionate is considered *vidveṣaṇa* (inciting enmity). 5.
Driving away from one's own country and so forth is proclaimed as *uccāṭana* (expulsion). 6. The taking of the life-force of living beings is declared to be *māraṇa* (killing).
Having understood one's own deity and the [proper] times and so forth, one should accomplish the ritual acts;
[the deities are] Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Durgā, and Kālī, in their respective order.
The deities of the six rites have been declared; one should employ them at the beginning of the ritual actions.
The directions of Īśa, Candra, Indra, Nirṛti, Vāyu,
and Agni are assigned in sequence for ten ghaṭikās, beginning from sunrise.
The seasons, beginning with spring, occur day by day throughout the day and night;
they are known as spring, summer, the rainy season, autumn, winter, and the cool season.
Winter is prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika), spring for rites of subjugation (vaśya);
the cool season (śiśira) is to be known for rites of immobilization (staṃbhanā), and the Veda is said to be for rites of inciting hatred (vidveṣa).
The rainy season is to be known for the rite of expulsion (uccāṭana), and autumn for the rite of killing (māraṇa);
furthermore, [the mudrās] are named Padma, Svastika, Vikaṭa, and Kukkuṭa.
The wise call these seats "Vajra-prahva";
the six mudrās should be known in sequence as the lotus, the noose, and the two maces.

The [yantras] known as the pestle (muśala), the arrow (asallikha), and the sword (khaḍga) are used in rites such as pacification (śāntika). For the rite of pacification, water is recommended; for subjugation (vaśya), fire is declared to be the element.
For the purpose of immobilization (staṃbhana), the Earth element is praised; for inciting enmity (vidveṣa), the Ether is proclaimed;
for expulsion (uccāṭana), the Wind is remembered; and for killing (māraṇa), Fire is considered best.
In the respective waters of each element, properly combined with their respective maṇḍalas,
one whose mind is sharpened should perform the various rites using blades of grass.
Water, the end [of the alphabet], water, earth, space, wind, and fire—
these are the seed-syllables of the mantras for the six rites, respectively.
Ganthana, Vidarbha, Sampuṭa, Ropaṇa, Yoga, and Pallava— these are the six types of arrangement for the six rites.
One should interpose the letters of the name with the syllables of the mantra according to the prescribed rule;
this is known as "tying" (granthana), which is highly recommended for rites of pacification (śāntika). || 1 ||
One should write the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished situated between pairs of mantra-syllables;
this is to be known as *vidarbha* by practitioners for the rite of subjugation.
When a mantra is placed at both the beginning and the end [of another], it is known as *saṃpuṭa*;
this is declared by those who know mantras to be excellent for the purpose of paralyzing (*saṃstambhana*).
A mantra that has the name at its beginning, middle, and end is considered to be "causing enmity" (vidveṣaṇa). This excellent method for causing enmity is highly praised. || 4 ||
At the end of the mantra, the name [of the target] should be placed; this is considered the application (yoga) for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana).
At the end of the name, the mantra should have the syllable *pa* as its "sprout" (*pallava*) when used for the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*).
White, red, yellow, mixed, black, and smoke-colored are proclaimed;
by color and by mantra, these deities are declared for the six types of ritual actions.
The materials for drawing the yantras are sandalwood, gorocanā, turmeric,
soot from a house, charcoal, and poisons for rites of killing.
Hawk-feathers, fire, lumps of salt, the juice of thorn-apple,
house-soot, and the three pungents (trikaṭuka)— these are declared to be the eight poisons.
Having correctly understood the mudrās of Time and the other deities, the wise practitioner should employ the six rites for the sake of attaining the results as described.

The hawk [is successful] when the breath is in the hawk-position; the house-lizard and the lizard [are successful] when it is in the lizard-position; the fire-caterpillar [is successful] when it is in the fire-position; and salt-clods and salt-impurities [are successful] when it is in the salt-position. Thus, for a person who knows all this, each respective action succeeds, and not otherwise. This is how the rising of the breath occurs in water and the other elements.

183a) Fire is above, water below, the comet (Rāhu) is across, and the wind is in between; these are to be known as filling all directions within the cavity of the earth. Thus, in rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and others, the *Svarodaya* must be consulted at the commencement [of the rite]. In pacification (*śānti*), [the following applies]:

For subjugation (*vaśya*), the gentle lunar days (*tithis*) are auspicious; for other rites, the cruel ones are used. For pacification (*śānti*) and subjugation, the soft (*mṛdu*) and fixed (*dhruva*) asterisms (*nakṣatras*) are used. For immobilization (*staṃbhanā*), the fixed asterisms are used. For killing (*māraṇa*) and so forth, the previously mentioned [cruel] asterisms are used. For pacification and subjugation, the gentle days of the week (*vāra*) are used; for others, the cruel ones. [This applies to] pacification, subjugation, and immobilization.

Fixed signs are [auspicious] for other [types of rites], while cruel signs are [suitable] for cruel rites; gentle places are for gentle rites, and similar places are for cruel rites. Many such varieties should be understood regarding the recitation (*japa*) of the respective mantras and so forth. This is the summary of the mantras. Apart from these, the specific details of the mantras and so forth—
We do not write [more] here for fear of excessive length. O virtuous people, our constant devotion is directed toward you;
indeed, that which is beneficial to all people must never be kept secret from you. If the most closely guarded mantras have been revealed here, it is for the sake of ease... [and so forth].

That jewel of the collection of mantras which was concealed by those learned in all the scriptures within various Āgamas has now been made manifest in my *Mantrakośa*; taking it up, may you become happy. (2)
The learned Bhaṭṭasamāpa, a treasure-house of virtues, who was established by Nakti,
the son born of the one named Premakara, and who was pleased with Śivāditya—
the lord of Āśāditya— composed this *Śrīratnamaṃtrāvalīkoṣa* for the sake of the virtuous who possess [this] treasury.
What fear of poverty can there be on earth?
Thus ends the description of the mudrās and so forth in the *Maṃtrakośa* compiled by the illustrious Āśāditya Tripāṭhī.
(Folio 184a)

Whatever has been written here that is of impure syllables—due to defects in the mirror, confusion of the intellect, a particular haste in reading, or the speed of writing—for that, O virtuous ones, the scribe is indeed to be forgiven. (1)
With his back, hips, and neck bent, and his gaze fixed downward,
he should protect the manuscript he has laboriously written as if it were his own son.
No one other than a learned person knows the labor involved in writing a book;
only Hanumān truly knows the exhaustion of leaping across the ocean.
May those who, having observed all this effort, steal our book, suffer the destruction of their eyesight, eternal grief, and leprosy of the entire body. || 4 ||

Written on Wednesday, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa in the illustrious Śaka year 1565, under the asterism Anurādhā, by the son of Manohara, the venerable Madanantarāma. May there be auspiciousness! O Lord of all that is moving and unmoving, this world has attained its foundation through You; everything has been made virtuous, yet the pair [of opposites] has been fashioned devoid of cleverness.

Is the mango tree, fashioned from a large seed with its excellent nectar-like juice, not superior? If you consider it inferior because it was produced from the breasts of a powerless woman, then you surely do not understand.
